hook: Claude or ChatGPT?
text:
Claude or ChatGPT?

Both can research, write, code, and make spreadsheets.

Here are the differences to pay attention to:

1. ChatGPT-6-Astra: websites and images.

You need to compare five suppliers, put their prices in a spreadsheet, and make a presentation.

I’d start with Astra.

ChatGPT Work has its own cloud computer and browser. It can open websites and do the work without your laptop staying on.

It also has an image-generation tool. Ask it to make the illustrations for your slides in the same chat.

One detail: its browser isn’t your browser. It won’t automatically have your saved logins or the files on your desktop. You choose what to share.

—

2. Claude Fable 5.1: a lot to read, then something to write.

You have six reports, tables buried in huge PDFs, and a presentation tomorrow.

Try Fable 5.1 for comparing the reports, finding conflicting numbers, and turning the findings into a brief.

Then ask for the slides.

Claude’s new Docs and Slides tools let you edit the work inside the conversation. Change a sentence yourself, ask Claude to rewrite a section, and download the presentation as PowerPoint.

If you spend your day reading and revising documents, try this on your next report. These tools are still in beta and rolling out.

—

3. Yes, Claude can use a computer too.

But its built-in browser needs the Claude desktop app open and online.

You can close your laptop while Claude does cloud work. If the task needs your local files, browser, or desktop apps, leave the computer awake and the app open.

And Fable itself doesn’t generate photos. For that, ChatGPT has a built-in image tool.

—

So here’s where we’d start:

• Web tasks & generated images: ChatGPT Astra.
• Heavy document work: Claude Fable 5.1.
• Coding: give both a task from your own project.

Both can do much of the same work. These are starting points, not rules.

Bonus prompting tip: tell either one what you want back.

“Read these reports” doesn’t say what you need.

Try:

“Read these reports, explain where they disagree, and give me five slides with page references.”

Now it knows what to deliver.

Ruben Hassid wrote a guide on how to prompt both models:
chatgpt.rubenhassid.ai

Pro tip:

For my day-to-day work, I care less about which model I’m using and more about what it knows about my business.

If I want help with sponsorship pricing, I need to give it my audience data, current packages, and past campaign results. If I want a newsletter that sounds like me, I need to share my own writing, the interview transcript, and who I’m writing for.

• “Help me grow my business” gives AI very little to work with. 
• “Here’s what we sell, here’s what’s working, and here’s where I’m stuck” gives it something useful.

Before switching models, ask yourself: have I actually given this one the information it needs?

Impressions.

text:
I'm guesting on Lenny's newsletter today! I'm diving into a set of tricky positioning roadblocks and how to get around them. 

In my mind, there is a set of obvious positioning roadblocks (the team doesn't agree on the positioning, the sales team won't adopt it, the positioning is overly broad), then there are the more challenging positioning roadblocks:

⛔ Disagreement about what to position AGAINST - a specific misalignment across the team around what a prospect compares us to in a deal, becoming overly focused on hypothetical competitors, and becoming distracted by noisy competitors that do not show up on short lists.

⛔ PESSIMISTIC product thinking - attempting to differentiate against an overly long list of theoretical competitors, defining best-fit customers too broadly, dismissing sales team insight about why customers buy, and becoming overly focused on fixing problems rather than fortifying differentiation.

⛔ The DIFFERENTIATED VALUE is POORLY DEFINED - overly focused on features prospects don't understand, overly vague or undifferentiated value propositions, too many themes, confusing value with objection handling

⛔ The company isn't in agreement on WHAT they are positioning - are we positioning a product, the company, or a set of products? Do we sell a lead product and then position the others as cross-sell or up-sell opportunities?

Do any of those sound familiar? Get the solutions over on Lenny's newsletter here - https://lnkd.in/gabnxcRK

text:
Today, an exec says to me, "Must be easy to have a newsletter that's all guest posts." I hope Lenny Rachitsky doesn't mind, but I told him this story:

Early last December, Lenny reached out to me about something, and I pitched him on an idea for a guest post. We went back and forth on ideas and settled on something. 

I spent a week over the holiday break writing a big, messy 8,000-word essay on positioning stuff and lobbed it back at him.

Lenny does a first deep pass on it, and we go back and forth for a week or so. 

Next, he loops in one of his editors, who did a structural edit (publishers do this with books - this edit makes sure the structure works and it flows for readers). Her feedback was great, and I spent another couple of weeks rewriting it to incorporate it. The editor, Lenny, and I then go back and forth for about a month or so - adding and removing sections, messing with titles, and rewriting the confusing bits (aside - there are many confusing bits 😂).

Lenny thought a graphic might help, so a graphics person was pulled in, and we messed around with that for a couple of weeks. 

We are now in late February and ready for a proper copy edit. A copy editor was added to our group, and we had a few iterations on the wording before we reached a final version. 

We spent another week or so messing around with titles and subtitles, and then it's ready to go. 

Three months start to finish - that's how you make it look "easy."

Lenny's got a great podcast out today talking about how he grew the newsletter to 1.2 million subscribers - it's worth a listen.

Lenny's podcast on how he grew the newsletter here - https://lnkd.in/gRSiKW_k

95% of Americans are paying more for home insurance. 

Insurance is becoming a real problem — and a changing climate is driving it:

When claims rise, premiums rise.
When premiums rise, homeownership gets harder.

That pressure doesn’t stop with homeowners.

It hits buyers.
It hits sellers.
It hits real estate agents.
It hits lenders.

And if it keeps spreading, it can hit the wider economy too.

This isn’t random — more frequent and severe weather, fueled by a changing climate, is pushing the system to its limits.

The numbers already show the shift. 

In the highest-risk ZIP codes, homeowners paid 82% more on average, and nonrenewal rates were about 80% higher. 

Across the country, premiums rose in 95% of ZIP codes from 2021 to 2024.

This isn’t just a trend — it’s being driven by more frequent and severe weather tied to a changing climate.

This is already happening, and it’s time to name it: the Climate Insurance Collapse.

I had the opportunity to join Mark S. Babbitt and S. Chris Edmonds on Mastering Workplace Culture, and one thread we kept returning to was this: Just because we can do something with AI doesn’t mean we should.

We’re living in a time where the pace of technological capability is outpacing our collective reflection on its impact. And in that gap, leadership matters more than ever.

In our conversation, we explored what it looks like to lead at the intersection of AI, data, and human behavior—and the responsibility that comes with it.

The real question isn’t “How do we use this tool?”
It’s “What kind of impact does this create at scale?”

Are we building trust—or eroding it?
Are we creating connection—or simulating it?
Are we amplifying clarity—or noise?

Ethics can’t be an afterthought. It has to be operational. It has to show up in decisions, in boundaries, and in what we choose not to do.

Because in the end, culture and technology are not separate conversations. The systems we build will always reflect the values we hold.

And the organizations that get this right won’t just move faster—they’ll move with intention.

text:
The Metropolitan Opera tagged Timothée Chalamet in a clapback video after he said nobody cares about opera. That same Met Opera has pulled $120 million from its endowment since the pandemic and just signed a deal to send its company to Saudi Arabia every winter to stay solvent.

Chalamet's grandmother danced with the New York City Ballet. His mother danced with NYCB and on Broadway. His sister trained at the School of American Ballet for nine years until a biking accident ended her career.

He grew up backstage at the Koch Theater at Lincoln Center.

A kid who grew up inside this art form described what the numbers already show.

Ballet attendance has dropped 52% since 1982 (a decline that predates the internet). Half of America's 150 ballet companies ran deficits in 2023. Only 1% of American adults attended an opera.

Even Gia Kourlas, the New York Times' dance critic, defended his point.

Millions of people who have never bought a ticket decided he was attacking their values.

Because ballet and opera work like Patagonia jackets or Moleskine notebooks; you don't have to use them for them to be load-bearing in your identity. Saying "nobody cares about opera" doesn't threaten opera. It threatens the self-image of someone who believes they're the kind of person who cares about opera.

The clip sat online for two weeks without incident. Then it resurfaced right as Oscar voting closed. Marty Supreme had nine nominations. It won zero.

Doja Cat was one of the loudest voices. Then she posted a follow-up admitting she'd never seen a ballet or an opera in her life. She called it what it was: "a modern way to garner clicks, likes, approval."

Then she said: "I think I just wanted a hug."

The ballet companies, meanwhile, still need to sell tickets.

text:
On Xiaohongshu, China's most popular lifestyle app, over 40,000 posts use the hashtag "full-time sons and daughters." These are college graduates whose parents pay them a monthly salary to do chores. Not as a joke. As a career.

A 22-year-old named Cheng in Jiangsu province cleans, walks his sister to school, and runs errands. His parents pay him 4,000 yuan a month (about $550).

This is what elite overproduction looks like when it collides with the one-child policy.

China produced 1 million college graduates in 1997. By 2025, it will produce 12.22 million. That increase over the past decade alone (4.6 million people) is larger than the entire annual graduating class of the United States.

Now add the one-child policy's "4-2-1" structure: four grandparents, two parents, one child. Every yuan, every sacrifice, every dream compressed into a single person. When that person graduates and can't find work, the failure lands on every adult who funded every tutor, every exam prep course, every semester.

The 2025 civil service exam saw 3.4 million applicants compete for 39,721 positions. One slot at the China Vocational Education Association drew 16,702 applicants. PhD holders from Tsinghua are teaching high school math.

So graduates invented their own vocabulary. Tang ping (lying flat). Bailan (let it rot). Neijuan (involution). And now, "full-time children."

Peter Turchin started as a beetle ecologist, became a complexity scientist, and coined the term "elite overproduction" to describe what happens when a society produces more credentialed, ambitious people than there are positions for them to fill. He argues you can predict a forest fire without knowing which cigarette starts it. China spent two decades stacking timber. The one-child policy concentrated it. The credential pipeline kept it growing. And the labor market dried it out.

When millions of young people independently develop shared language for opting out of an economy, they're doing something beyond venting. They're arriving at the same diagnosis from different directions.

hook: In March 2024, a 23-year-old K-pop idol publicly apologized for having a boyfriend. And within the system she works in,
text:
In March 2024, a 23-year-old K-pop idol publicly apologized for having a boyfriend. And within the system she works in, it made perfect sense.

Karina, the leader of aespa, was reported to be dating actor Lee Jae-wook. They'd been together about a month. Fans responded by dispatching LED trucks to SM Entertainment's headquarters. One message read: “Do you not get enough love from your fans? Why did you choose to betray your fans?”

One week later, Karina posted a handwritten apology on Instagram. She wrote: “I know very well how disappointed the MYs (aespa’s name for fans) who have supported me up until now must be.”

On Weibo, one user wrote: “If she really cherished her fans, she wouldn't have fallen in love in the first place.”

This looks irrational until you understand the product. The idol industry, in Korea and in Japan, sells emotional exclusivity. Agencies enforce dating bans. In 2015, a Tokyo court upheld a no-dating clause, ruling it was “necessary for idols to win the support of male fans.”

A judge describing the business model in plain language. At YG Entertainment, male and female trainees reportedly eat at different times to reduce even accidental eye contact.

The average investment in a single trainee runs between $21,000 and $26,000 before they ever debut. Some train for a decade. The dating ban protects that investment by protecting the customer's belief that the relationship is real.

AKB48 built their entire model on this: handshake events where fans pay for ten seconds of eye contact. One fan spent roughly $330,000 on CDs to influence a popularity vote.

So when fans demand an apology for dating, they're not being irrational. They're responding to an incentive structure that was built for them. The question isn't why fans act this way. It's who designed the system that taught them to.

hook: China's high-speed rail network carries $839 billion in debt. Most lines lose money. Stations sit empty on weekdays. It
text:
China's high-speed rail network carries $839 billion in debt. Most lines lose money. Stations sit empty on weekdays. It is also the most consequential infrastructure project of the 21st century. Western analysis struggles with this because it can only hold one of those facts at a time.

The Lanzhou-Xinjiang line was designed for 320 trains a day. In its early years, it ran eight. Revenue couldn't cover electricity costs. Western analysts had their word: boondoggle.

By end of 2024, the network carried 3.3 billion passengers across 48,000 km. The Beijing-Shanghai line posted a 38% profit margin. Airlines lost entire route categories. Domestic flights under 800 km dropped from 26.4% to 15.9% of total aviation.

In 2008, California voters approved high-speed rail. That same year, China opened its first HSR line. By 2025, California hadn't laid a single piece of track. In that window, China built 48,000 km.

Frame Chinese rail as "current cost vs. current ridership" and it looks like waste. Frame it as "infrastructure on a 20-year timeline against projected urbanization" and it looks like one of history's largest successful bets.

Same data. Different lens.

A Western analyst evaluating Chinese rail doesn't consciously choose to apply a four-year planning horizon. That horizon comes embedded in the political system they think inside, so deeply internalized it feels like objectivity.

The demand showed up. Just on a schedule invisible to anyone whose sense of time was borrowed from a system that plans in four-year cycles.

Those eight trains were a real measurement. So were the 3.3 billion passengers that came after. The only thing that changed was how much time you gave the data before deciding what it meant.

hook: In some Korean organizations, skipping after-work drinks is treated as a worse offense than missing a day of work. It's
text: In some Korean organizations, skipping after-work drinks is treated as a worse offense than missing a day of work. It's called hoesik. A 2020 survey of 659 Korean workers found only 45 percent said they were free to choose whether to attend. Thirteen percent said attendance was flatly mandatory. The rest went because they were afraid of how it would look if they didn't. The drinking follows military-grade protocol. The most senior person takes the first sip. Everyone waits. You pour with both hands. You turn away from your superior when you drink. You accept whatever is poured for you. Then you cycle through multiple bars in a single night: dinner with beer, second round with soju, third round at a whiskey bar, fourth round at karaoke. Eighty percent of employees in one study reported binge drinking at least once in the prior year. Twenty-three percent did it weekly. Almost 60 percent reported drinking during the daytime, and 55 percent said they were obligated to do so because of work. Sixty-five percent went back to the office afterward. In 2018, a new employee at a workshop couldn't drink well. His boss was present. He was pressured through multiple rounds. He lost consciousness and passed away. A court ruled it an occupational accident, reasoning that a new employee at a workshop attended by his superior had almost certainly been coerced. Seoul's traffic patterns track the whole cycle. Monday nights are light because workers leave their cars at the office to go drinking. Friday has the worst rush hour because everyone is finally driving home to their families. This isn't team bonding; it's an obedience test with deep roots in the Korean military culture every fighting-age male internalizes. And the system doesn't need you to enjoy it. It only requires that when someone above you tells you to drink, you drink.

hook: Chappell Roan went from one million to twenty million monthly Spotify listeners, then posted TikToks begging fans to sto
text: Chappell Roan went from one million to twenty million monthly Spotify listeners, then posted TikToks begging fans to stop stalking her family. That escalation is not a bug in modern fame. It is the direct, predictable consequence of a frame installed a decade ago. March 2014. Ellen DeGeneres wanders into the front rows of the Oscars with a Samsung phone. Bradley Cooper holds it. Meryl Streep grins like a fan. Fifteen seconds. The tweet crashes Twitter for 24 minutes. What made it electric was what it performed: the most famous people alive doing the same thing 200 million others did on their phones every day. For most of the twentieth century, celebrity ran on engineered distance. Studios fabricated romances, suppressed scandals, controlled every image. When Loretta Young got pregnant by Clark Gable, MGM's fixers staged a fake illness, announced a fake adoption, and forbade the daughter from being photographed without a hat - her ears looked like Gable's. That distance was not decoration. It was load-bearing. It determined which questions audiences could even think to ask. The Oscar selfie collapsed it on live TV and on Twitter, just as social media was maturing, in front of 43 million people. The message: they are just like us. Social media finished the job. Thousands of daily micro-inputs; stories, comments, bedroom livestreams. Each one training the audience's brain to process a one-sided connection as mutual. So when Chappell Roan exploded, her fans didn't feel like strangers approaching a celebrity. They felt like friends being ignored by a friend. The frame said "no distance." The audience believed it. And the consequences arrived on schedule; not because fans are broken, but because they trusted a frame that was never built to survive proximity.

hook: In Seoul, they call Louis Vuitton bags "the 3-second bag" because you spot one every three seconds on the street. South
text: In Seoul, they call Louis Vuitton bags "the 3-second bag" because you spot one every three seconds on the street. South Korea spends more per capita on luxury goods than any country on Earth. The average salary there is $1,400 a month. Kim Jin-sook, an office worker in her early 30s, spends half her salary saving for a designer bag. She opted out of all other leisure. The bag, she said, was "the only joy in my life." After 1945, Japan, Korea, and China each ran compressed economic miracles where personal consumption became proof the national project was working. Your purchase was the receipt for the recovery. That became the frame for what a successful life looks like, and it got installed in a single generation. The economies moved on. Apartments in Seoul now average over $1 million. Youth unemployment in China hit 21.3% before the government stopped publishing the number. The markers of adulthood the frame was built to certify (house, marriage, family) became unreachable. But the frame doesn't update when conditions change. It reroutes. The consumption energy that was supposed to flow toward a home gets concentrated into the one purchase that still delivers a visible status signal. Korean culture coined a word for the result: pyeonbaekjok. Someone frugal in daily life but extravagant in specific symbolic purchases. Skipping meals to save for a bag. Taking the bus to afford a watch. Christine Lee, 30, earning $24,000 a year, bought a $1,200 handbag. Her reasoning: "We can't buy a house, it's too expensive, so why should we save money for the future?" The frame was installed by someone else, for an economy that no longer exists. Every three seconds on a Seoul street, you can watch it run.

hook: The same week my daughter started confiding in ChatGPT, I was reading a book Zack Kass wrote for his daughter.
text:
The same week my daughter started confiding in ChatGPT, I was reading a book Zack Kass wrote for his daughter.

One evening, driving back from my daughter's horse-riding lesson, I asked her how class went. She was quiet, focused on her phone. When I asked what she was doing, she said she was logging her riding experience to ChatGPT. 

I asked her why. Her answer paused me.

She said when she tells us about her day, sometimes my wife and I are still coming out of work mentally and may not fully focus. But ChatGPT, she said, listens carefully, encourages her progress, and gives her ideas on what to improve next.

That was a moment of realization. AI is not only changing our roles at work. It is quietly changing our roles as parents, leaders, teachers, and friends.

That same week, I was reading Zack Kass's new book, The Next RenAIssance: AI and the Expansion of Human Potential.

What made it personal was not just Zack's view of AI. It was the way he wrote it — almost as a note to himself and his newborn daughter.

That hit close to home.

I first met Zack at Deluxe Exchange in 2024, later invited him to speak with our Board, and spent time with him on a flight last year, just before his daughter was born. Many of my views on AI were shaped by those early conversations.

Reading this book, I could hear the same person I had come to know — optimistic, thoughtful, and deeply human.

What I appreciated most is that Zack does not reduce AI to tools, prompts, or hype cycles. He argues that today's tools will disappear quickly as systems become more intelligent.

What will endure? Agency. Judgment. Character. Adaptability. Humanistic qualities.

The book frames AI not as an endpoint, but as the beginning of a new renaissance — where intelligence becomes abundant, and the real question becomes what humans do with that abundance.

Two ideas stood out:
→ The most valuable organizations will use AI to help humans become more human — better at judgment, creativity, care, and connection.
→ AI will make things cheap, and people more precious.

The book is optimistic without being naive.
The guidance for his daughter is the guidance for us all:
- Go outside.
- Learn how to learn.
- Optimize for humanistic qualities.
- Lead with optimism.

I've read this book three times — once as a leader, once for my own career, and once as a parent. This book uses simple language to bring everyone into the conversation on this otherwise complex subject.

The right response to AI is not fear. It is awareness, agency, and responsible optimism.

Congratulations, Zack. This book is authentic, accessible, and deeply relevant — exactly like the man who wrote it.

If someone in your life keeps asking, "What should I do about AI?" — send it to them. The answer is not a tool. It is a way of thinking.

Where are you on this — still running your career and parenting on the old playbook? Or have you started rewriting both?

hook: One-third of all GoFundMe money goes to healthcare costs, and 88% of those campaigns fail to reach their goal. The count
text: One-third of all GoFundMe money goes to healthcare costs, and 88% of those campaigns fail to reach their goal. The country that invented prepaid hospital care for fifty cents a month now crowdfunds children's gene therapy. The fifty cents is literal. In 1929, a former school superintendent named Justin Ford Kimball got hired to fix Baylor University Hospital's books in Dallas. Teachers owed the most and could pay the least. He ran the math: fifty cents a month per teacher covers 21 days of inpatient care. Operating room, anesthesia, lab work, all included. 1,300 teachers signed up at the onset of the Great Depression. The model spread city by city through the 1930s as Blue Cross; local, voluntary, nonprofit, and completely disconnected from employment. Then in 1942, Congress froze wages for inflation control. Factories desperate for labor couldn't raise pay, but the law excluded insurance benefits from the freeze. So employers offered health coverage instead. The IRS made contributions tax-free in 1943. By 1953, employer coverage jumped from 9% to 63% of Americans. The Revenue Act of 1954 codified the tax deduction into federal law, making the whole arrangement permanent. The wage freeze expired. The system didn't. A wartime loophole, a tax ruling, and a revenue act; three decisions, none about healthcare, built the room 158 million Americans stand in. One in six workers stays in a job they want to leave because losing coverage isn't survivable. 530,000 families file medical bankruptcy each year. The ACA didn't meaningfully reduce that bankruptcy rate. Nobody designed this system. Nobody voted on it. A workaround from 1942 never got replaced. After long enough, it stopped looking like one.

hook: I accepted a counteroffer early in my career. It was one of my biggest mistakes.
text:
I accepted a counteroffer early in my career. It was one of my biggest mistakes.

I had been at my job for 2 years and I had an offer from another company. It came with a better title, more money, and remote work.

When I resigned, my boss asked for 24 hours. They came back with a salary match & a verbal promise. They said a promotion was coming next quarter.

My gut told me to leave. My friends told me to leave. But I stayed because I wanted to believe them.

Next quarter arrived. There was no promotion. They told me the budget was frozen until the end of the year.

When the end of the year came, a reorg hit. My boss was let go. My role got dumped into a larger team. The promised promotion track vanished.

The other company filled the role I interviewed for, a month later.

Companies “promise” counteroffers because buying themselves more time is cheaper than finding your replacement. 

Always get everything in writing. Or just walk away.

text:
In today's newsletter, I'm talking about Positioning in the Age of AI and some considerations for both native AI and SaaS businesses right now. 

1️⃣ A point of view is no longer optional - where the market is changing quickly, customers will look to vendors to give them advice on what sort of a future they should be planning for. Five years ago you might have been able to get away without a point of view on how your part of the market is going to change, today this is critical. 

2️⃣ Position against your true competition (but plan for the future fight) - many of the companies I am working with today understand that the competitive landscape will be different in a couple of years. The key is to ensure you are positioning for the fight you are in right now, while product is planning for ways to win the fight of tomorrow. Letting your positioning get ahead of where your customers are right now is risky.

3️⃣ Hype the heck out of the future (where you can), but connect it with where customers are today - buyers are worried about investing in technology that might become outdated or "legacy" as AI improves. They are also worried about their current investments as the landscape changes. Not only do you need a vision for the future, but you also need to demonstrate to customers the steps you will take with them from where they are today to where they want to be. 

4️⃣ It's never been more important to understand how customers ACTUALLY think - in times of great technology changes, it's easy for us to get lost in the hype. It is very important to find ways to keep your finger on how customers are thinking and behaving. If you don't have programmatic ways of doing that (a customer advisory board, executive customer sponsorships, win/loss analysis), there is no better time to start.

creator: Zack Kass
hook: On AI’s poor public perception, here’s what I have to say:
text:
On AI’s poor public perception, here’s what I have to say:

Most technologies have gone through a period of distrust and/or disdain early in their adoption curves. AI is not unique in this regard.

What is unique is the context into which AI is arriving.

In places enriched by the last wave of technology — namely San Francisco, New York City, and London — AI is largely viewed as the next engine of growth.

In places that have experienced stagnation, hollowed-out industries, declining social mobility, or institutional decay, AI is viewed far more skeptically. 

China is one of the most revealing examples. Public optimism around AI is dramatically higher there basically the rest of most of the world (even SF).

Having been to China almost 9 times in the last 5 years, I can tell you why: The CCP has gone to extreme lengths to ensure that electricity and the internet (in particular) diffused to the benefit of the average Chinese citizen: for nearly 30 years the Chinese middle class has expanded and so have their reasonable expectations — a brand new BYD costs $6k USD, healthcare is better, faster, and cheaper year over year, and a 21-year old can purchase a home on an entry-level salary.

And that brings us to why AI polls so poorly with US college graduates right now.

I maintain that the kids don’t actually hate AI. They hate what the last wave of technology did to them.

They hate that we sacrificed their souls and spirits at the altar of a digital display. They hate feeling perpetually distracted, manipulated, and anxious.

And they especially hate that the modern economy somehow delivered same-day shipping, gas station sushi, free global communication, and an infinite scroll of outrage, gambling, pornography, and comparison... while housing, healthcare, and education became prohibitively unattainable.

People think they distrust technology. If that were true then young people would move to Cuba or North Korea. No, what they really distrust is a society that has produced remarkable innovation while failing to make a beautiful life easier to obtain.

If AI only produces more cheap content, more spiritual dereliction, and more wealth concentration, public disdain will become public unrest.

If AI materially lowers the cost of living and produces a wave of novel science breakthroughs, it will quickly be viewed like electricity.

If you’re a policy-maker, please repeat after me:
- Healthcare should mostly be provided outside of the hospital, at a fraction of the current cost.
- Education needs rejuvenation, not merely digitization. And college should not burden students financially for decades.
- Housing cannot function as a speculative asset class. We should build dramatically more of it and pass non-resident taxes in a lot of cities.

If you’re a concerned citizen:
- Go outside more with your friends and family.
- Keep your screens away from your bedrooms and dining room tables.
- Put pressure on policy-makers to repeat after me above.

hook: Slop as a derivative of the decreased cost of production is nothing new.
text:
Slop as a derivative of the decreased cost of production is nothing new. 

The printing press gave us Shakespeare and conspiracy pamphlets. The telephone gave us on-demand emergency services and telemarketers. The internet gave us an anxious generation that is testing lower on average than the one before, but also has a higher occurrence of savants.

The slop problem is pronounced right now because the cost of producing slop on the internet is basically zero, and (critically) a lot of algorithms actually reward it.

Phrases like "humans must always remain in the loop" and "we must remove bias from the machines" are essentially nonsensical, but they are repeated ad infinitum because they appear morally and intellectually defensible. 

Sadly, they are indefensible ideas that are actually shaping policy discussions, and there's no effective way to hold their authors accountable on social media. 

The Beautiful Future will not be built repeating socially approved abstractions about AI ethics (or anything else, for that matter); it will be built by bravely committing to bold visions, exploring unpopular ideas of achieving incredible outcomes, and cultivating moral, high-agency humans who know how to use unmetered intelligence to create a better world.

On this note, I'm going to write a lot more on Substack. I prefer medium-form writing and, at least for now, it is the most rewarding place to think out loud.

Here's my latest (found in the comments because that's what the LinkedIn algorithm prefers, apparently).

hook: NitroGen just won CVPR Best Paper Honorable Mention! Feels like a full-circle moment: 4 years ago, MineDojo, our first M
text:
NitroGen just won CVPR Best Paper Honorable Mention! Feels like a full-circle moment: 4 years ago, MineDojo, our first Minecraft AI agent, took Outstanding Paper at NeurIPS.

NitroGen is an open-source Foundation Agent that learns to act across 1000+ 2D and 3D virtual worlds. Each world is a physics simulation with its own rules, dynamics, and motor commands. We're on a quest for general-purpose embodied AI that masters not only real-world physics, but every possible physics across a multiverse of simulations.

A surprising discovery: our GR00T N1.5 architecture, originally designed for robots, adapts almost effortlessly to worlds with wildly different mechanics. The recipe is simple and bitter-lesson-pilled: (1) a 40K+ hour, high-quality dataset of public in-the-wild play; (2) a highly capable foundation model for continuous motor control; (3) a Gym API that wraps any simulated environment to run rollouts. GR00T N1.5 learns to compress and map 40K hours of pixels to diverse actions. 

Humans are extraordinarily good at adapting to vastly different physics and rules - something that continues to elude our most advanced, trillion-scale LLMs. The more virtual worlds an agent can adapt to, the better it develops embodied reasoning, perception, and motor coordination. All critical pieces in the grand puzzle for robotics.

During my PhD, a tiny neural net that played 50 Atari titles with 84×84 grayscale window was considered mind-blowing. OpenAI Five and AlphaStar then went superhuman, yet stayed brittle, overfit to one environment at a time. NitroGen is our shot at the next rung: a dataset, a benchmark, and a competent base model checkpoint for embodied *generalization*. 

NitroGen is only the beginning, and there's a long way to hill-climb on capabilities. We open-source *everything* for you to tinker: code, pretrained weights, the full action dataset, and a whitepaper with real details.

Today, robotics is a superset of hard AI problems. 
Tomorrow, it might become a subset, a dot in the much larger latent space of embodied AGI. 
Then you just prompt and "ask for" a robot brain.

Congrats to the co-first authors, Loic, Anas, and Guanzhi, and thanks to all the colleagues across multiple institutes for making NitroGen happen!

hook: When we have big changes in a market, (like now with AI) it's important to communicate a clear point of view about the f
text: When we have big changes in a market, (like now with AI) it's important to communicate a clear point of view about the future of the market. This is different from your vision for the product or even the business. Your point of view on the market is what you believe the world will look like. It's the reason you are building what you're building and why. We need to remember that buyers don't eat sleep and breathe tech the way we do. They do their homework in a purchase process, but they also want to hear what we think. When Sam Altman says he imagines AI will be sold "like electricity" and "people will buy it from us on a meter" - you are seeing a very consumer-oriented point of view about the market from a company that thinks about the future of the market that way. Contrast that with Anthropic's Dario Amodei saying "AI will write 90% of code" - you are hearing a point of view that is more B2B oriented from a company that thinks differently about the future of the market. Contrast those points of view with Microsoft's Satya Nadella - "Models are becoming a commodity...the performance of your AI application will depend on how well your data is brought into context." "The intelligence layer is only as good as the context you give it." That's a very different point of view. Here the big models are on the side and the center is "business context" meaning the docs and PowerPoint and email that lives in Microsoft systems. So when you talk to your customers, do you have a point of view on your market? What about your competition? I'm going deeper into this in the newsletter - link in the comments.

I’ve thrown multiple 7-figure in person events now that all follow one core thesis. 

The room you’re coming to is the product. 

In order to do that, there are a few decisions that are non-negotiable when I throw an event for 8-9 fig founders:

1. We book the entire property. Whether it’s Coworth Park in London, a wine farm in South Africa, Al Maha in Dubai. Every person on site for three days is either staff or a member of the event, there are no outsiders walking through the lobby.

2. We cap the room at 60-70 hand-selected operators. The vibe of the room matters more than the headcount, so we'd rather turn the right people away than let the wrong one in.

3. We bring in speakers from outside the info space, we brought in a founder who exited at a $1B valuation, another 9-figure operator who talked about bootstrapping, and my own personal M&A advisor on how to invest in companies. The most useful sessions are almost always the ones that don't directly apply to what the room does day-to-day.

4. The unstructured time matters as much as the sessions. The dinners, the nights out, the 5am conversations on a balcony. The friendships people leave with are worth more than any session takeaway.

Every choice traces back to the same thesis, the room you're in is the product. 

Every year we improve on what we did the last time, can't wait to show everyone what we have in store for 2026.

Since I joined OpenAI in 2021 I’ve been obsessed with the adoption gap: the space between what technology can do and what companies (or societies) actually do with it.

I wrote about it throughout my book, and I spend most of my time working on it today.

The future has always been built by people willing to do the hard, unsung, and often invisible work of helping organizations change.

That’s especially true in the SMB and mid-market economy.

These companies are the backbone of prosperous communities. They provide competition in the market, create nearly 50% of the jobs, sponsor local teams, support local causes, and contribute to communities in countless other non-economic ways.

The firms helping them adopt new technologies don’t receive the same attention as the frontier labs, but their work matters enormously (and at some point even more).

Which is why I was particularly excited to write the foreword for HubSpot's latest State of Ecosystems Report.

It’s a thoughtful look at the people and partnerships helping new technologies make their way into the real economy.

They’re doing important work, and I’m glad to see it recognized.

1. Safety harness

Letting 8 robots run unattended overnight means safety has to be more than a hint in the system prompt. ENPIRE hardwires it in 2 layers: (1) hard kinematic limit that trips an immediate task failure and auto-resets as soon as a robot leaves its safety envelope, and (2) a torque-limited compliant gripper so a bad contact or misaligned insertion ends in a safe stall, instead of crushing the robot or the object at hand. 

We make safety more conservative than usual so humans can sleep tight. In reality, we still need a few human operators to watch over the "robots of loving grace". 

2. Definition of /done

An agent that can edit its own reward will game it for sure. ENPIRE fixes the goalposts before the fleet can move them. Here's the recipe:

Collect a few minutes of success & failure demos
-> Ask agent to write code using computer vision tools to classify success and measure against groundtruth
-> Agent hill-climbs on classifier until reliably good
-> This classifier becomes the real-time reward function that directly computes on sensor streams 
-> *Freeze* the reward function before AutoResearch. It's sacred, enshrined in a Gym env that no one can touch.

3. System telemetry design

Robot-seconds is by far the scarcest resource, followed by GPU-seconds, and finally tokens. We instrument all three and surface them to ENPIRE for live resource awareness rather than letting it hill-climb in a vacuum. 

We define:
- Mean Robot Utilization ("MRU"): the fraction of wall-clock time when the robot is actively executing an experiment. Otherwise the hardware is sitting idle and waiting for the next code commit.
- Mean Token Utilization ("MTU"): tokens consumed per minute, our proxy for how hard the agent is actually thinking. A low MTU means the agent is stalled, waiting on a robot rollout to finish instead of doing research.
- GPU utilization: fraction of wall-clock time when GPU is active. 

... and evaluate on two budget-to-outcome metrics:

1. Tokens-to-Success: token budget the fleet burns to complete /goal.
2. Time-to-Success: wall-clock time to /goal

hook: Most people buying private tech are not investing.
text:
Most people buying private tech are not investing.

They are collecting logos.

SpaceX. Anthropic. Stripe. Databricks. ByteDance. Anduril.

The name feels good. It sounds good at dinner. It makes you feel like you are close to the future.

But a logo is not an investment thesis.

That was one of the sharpest parts of my conversation with Peter Singlehurst on BILLIONS.

Peter built the private companies team at Baillie Gifford from scratch. They have invested billions into some of the most important private companies in the world.

When we talked about the evolution of private markets he separated two markets that people often confuse.

Primary markets have become much more professional.
The best companies raise from investors they choose. They share information. They select partners. They can say no to hot money and bring in long-term institutional capital instead.

But secondaries are different.

That is where the weird behavior starts.

People hear about a company in the press, see the valuation moving, see other investors trying to get in, and suddenly they want exposure.

But they often have no financials.

No management access.

No real information rights.

Sometimes they have not even seen a proper set of accounts.

They just want the name.

That is not investing. That is status with a subscription agreement.
And I get it.

Owning a famous private company is emotionally powerful. It feels different from owning a fund. When someone asks what you invest in, it is much more exciting to say “SpaceX” than to explain a diversified private growth vehicle.

But this is exactly where people get into trouble.

Because in private markets, the asset is only one part of the deal.

The route to the asset matters just as much.
Who is the seller?
Why are they selling?
Is the GP aware?
Do you have information rights?
Are you buying from someone who knows more than you?
Is the valuation based on fundamentals or on a temporary supply/demand imbalance?

The irony is that the best private companies may genuinely be some of the best investments of the next decade.

But that does not mean every way of accessing them is good.

A great company can still be a bad investment at the wrong price, through the wrong structure, with the wrong information.

Private markets reward access.

But they punish lazy access.

Hope you'll enjoy our conversation as much as I did 👇

Clara Shih and I hosted our first (in-person/virtual) offsite for New Work Foundation (NWF) yesterday in San Francisco (thanks to Bessemer Venture Partners for hosting!)

Our mission for the non-profit is to "equip young workers in America with the AI tools, skills, and community to navigate an AI-reshaped economy."

1. Everyone Wants to Help: When you state a universally important and shared goal like "helping young people to get started in their lives," the outpouring of support is limitless. We had ~25 all-volunteer humans join the meeting across all walks of life, from Gen Z folks looking for work to experienced executives searching for meaning. text:
Today, we give robots a /skills library that self-evolves and compounds indefinitely! Introducing ASPIRE: a robot solving its 100th task is no longer as clueless as solving its first. Coding agents observe multimodal sensory traces from simulation and real robots, launch an evolutionary search over control programs, and distill the best know-how into an ever-expanding library. 

ASPIRE is a new type of continual learning: "training" is skill refinement instead of gradient descent. 
"Trained model" is a repo of sensorimotor skills instead of floating weights. 
“Distributed training” is a panel of agents each practicing a different skill instead of sharded minibatches.

Here's the beauty: ASPIRE gives the tired terms "sim2real transfer" and "cross-embodiment transfer" a whole new meaning. Bridging the sim-to-real gap is notoriously brutal. An end-to-end policy has to swallow both the visual shift (sim looks toyish next to a real camera) and the subtle contact physics it never quite gets right. ASPIRE sidesteps the mess, because it doesn't ship pixels or weights across the gap, but ships the know-how. The robot still has to practice in the real world, not zero-shot, but it gets there way faster because it isn't rediscovering the strategy from scratch. Same for going single-arm to bimanual hardware, which usually requires new data and retraining from zero. ASPIRE achieves up to ~10x cut in "transfer learning” tokens (yes, tokens are the new unit of *training* compute ;)

Check out our gallery of 150+ tasks and 90+ skills the robots taught themselves, all on the website! Kind of wild that we can ship the "learned weights" as an HTML page rather than a GGUF. We'll open-source the full stack so your own robot library starts compounding from ours!

hook: I recently filmed 2 videos. Here are some quick reflections on both experiences to help you choose which one to use.
text:
I recently filmed 2 videos. Here are some quick reflections on both experiences to help you choose which one to use.

Video 1: Word-for-word; 2-3 hours spent scripting.

 Video 2: Bullet point; 30 minutes spent scripting; converted from a newsletter, and mostly riffed based on the original copy.

Word-for-word scripting:

Without a teleprompter, word-for-word scripts are semi-useless. Glancing back and forth at a word-for-word script and trying to remember each line feels almost no different to using bullet points. If you don't have a teleprompter, it's probably not worth writing word-for-word.

Pressure felt way higher. Because I'd honed the script to try and make it awesome, I felt pressure to deliver every line perfectly. Unlike bullet point scripting (where my delivery could elevate the script), delivering word-for-word lines felt like I had more to lose.

But... I felt in control. All that being said, I turned the camera off feeling confident about how the final product would turn out. 

I didn't have the same level of certainty with my bullet point video - even though I had more fun making it.

Bullet point scripting:

Prevents perfectionism. You know how it goes... an almost-finished script takes you another three days to edit because you can't avoid the desire for "perfect". 

But a bullet point script sidesteps this completely. You're basically planning the structure and trusting your future self to deliver the material confidently.

I had way more fun. Eeeek. Business model imploding. But I can't deny... the freedom of bullet-point scripting made it much less of a drag.

But... I forgot what I'd said a lot (which was stressful). I had several moments where I was 30 seconds into a riff, messed it up, then couldn't remember where to restart. 

This is the reality of riffing. It loads more mental pressure onto filming day. And as the session gets longer, it gets harder to remember if you're still on track.

So... what to choose?

The reality is, it's entirely personal. If you want filming day to be stress-free, and to retain complete control over the output, write word-for-word. 

If you want writing to feel less stressful, and to have the freedom to express yourself naturally on filming day, write bullet points.

Word-for-word or bullet points? Comment below 👇

hook: We scaled a robot model natively to 8,000 timesteps of context, 5 minutes worth of muscle memory, with constant inferenc
text:
We scaled a robot model natively to 8,000 timesteps of context, 5 minutes worth of muscle memory, with constant inference cost. Robot policies used to live their lives a few frames at a time (< 0.1 sec), instantly forgetting what just happened. We pushed to 3 orders of magnitude beyond SOTA. 

Introducing RoboTTT. Test-Time Training (“TTT”) carries a tiny model *inside* the model. Every incoming sensor reading triggers one gradient step on that tiny core, so the history keeps getting compressed into its weights. The hidden state has a fixed size (literally a small neural net), so the robot can “grok” arbitrarily long experience with little overhead. Learning continues indefinitely after deployment.

We can then put an entire video in context as prompt! RoboTTT enables one-shot in-context learning from human video: in circuit board assembly, a human demonstrates a never-seen configuration once, and the robot imitates it faithfully. 

Humans drop things all the time, but we pick them up so fast that we don’t even notice. That reflex to fix is half of our physical competence. RoboTTT shows self-improvement on the fly: the robot is skilled at recovering from its own errors mid-episode, and each fix enters its context to inform the next move. The TTT core distills a general-purpose, failure-to-correction mapping from the training data.

One more thing. What excites me the most is a new Context Scaling Curve: from 128 to 8K timesteps, closed-loop performance hill-climbs steadily with no sign of saturation. 8K-context pretraining beats 1K by 62%. What LLM enjoys, robotics should too. Soon, even 1M context is not a fantasy.

Congrats to all our collaborators at NVIDIA and Stanford!

An engaging YouTube video doesn't have a single "payoff" at the end. It has payoffs every 90-120 seconds.

#1 - Listicle: e.g. "17 cheap purchases that save me time"

Framework:

Setup: "Next, let's talk about [{thing that matters} in relation to {overall video goal}]."

Tension: [Provide context on why it matters, and how getting it wrong would impact the viewer.]

Payoff: "That's why item number three is [reveal item, briefly conclude how this solves {thing that matters}]."

#2 - Tutorial: e.g. "How to build a website using Figma"

Framework:

Setup: "Step 1 is [X]. This is gonna allow us to [do thing audience wants / thing that relates to goal of tutorial]."

Tension: [Show the step-by-step process.]

Payoff: "So, now we've [achieved X], that's gonna [help achieve thing audience wants / avoid negative consequences]."

#3 - Vlog: e.g. "We visited Kyoto's most expensive restaurant"

Framework:

Setup: [Hint at X exciting/interesting thing in the location you're arriving at.]

Tension: [Show events building up to X using plenty of voiceover and carefully selected footage.]

Payoff: [Reveal X.]

#4 - Video Essay: e.g. "How much protein do you ACTUALLY need to build muscle?"

Framework:

Setup: "But [something intriguing] has [changed/happened] which could [impact the topic in an unexpected way]."

Tension: [Explore the topic to drive tension.]

text:
Most DTC brands are still playing the old ecommerce game.

Get people onto the website. Give them enough products. Let them browse until they find something to buy.

That worked when the website was the centre of the buying journey.

It isn’t anymore.

Today, the journey starts in the feed.

Which means the advantage is shifting from product range to distribution range.

More creators.
More hooks.
More stories.
More content.

This Toplux magnesium supplement is a perfect example.

According to my scraper, one product has generated an estimated $46.1 million in TikTok Shop GMV.

It has been promoted by 15,600 affiliates through nearly 50,000 shoppable videos.

The brand pays a 25% commission, but only when those creators produce a sale.

Then I pulled the creator-level data.

The top 100 creators generated almost two-thirds of the entire $46.1 million.

That is the point.

They didn’t build a network of 15,600 affiliates because every creator would win.

They built a system capable of taking nearly 50,000 shots because nobody knew which creators, hooks and videos would break out.

Now look at the halo effect.

The exact same product had 40,000+ purchases on Amazon in the past month.

At its current $26.97 price, that represents more than $1 million in monthly Amazon demand. It is Amazon’s Choice and has nearly 7,000 ratings.

Can we prove every Amazon sale came from TikTok? No. You would need the brand’s Amazon analytics to measure that properly.

But this is what demand creation looks like.

Someone discovers the product from a creator on TikTok, then buys wherever they already trust the checkout. TikTok creates the demand. Amazon can capture the sale.

So if you’re only measuring direct TikTok Shop GMV, you’re probably undervaluing the content.

You need to watch branded search, Amazon organic sales and direct traffic alongside platform-attributed revenue.

The brands that win the next era of DTC won’t necessarily have the widest product range.

They’ll put their best products into more feeds, through more creators, with more angles than anyone else.

The new shelf space is content.

creator: George Blackman
hook: There's something sneaky you should probably cut out of your next hook.
text:
There's something sneaky you should probably cut out of your next hook.

At the end of most educational hooks, you have a value proposition. That's the part where you explain exactly what your video covers. Something like:

✅ "So in this video we're going to rank the top 10 value-for-money Pokémon cards, and exactly where to buy them."

This is a great value proposition.

On the other hand, here's a value proposition that's too long:

❌ "In this video I'll show you how you can achieve [X]. To do that, I'm going to tell you a story - a story that will reveal the three main mistakes you're probably making, how to avoid making those mistakes, and the simple strategy I used to [overcome them]."

After reviewing a couple of videos I worked on, plus some of my students' graphs, I saw that value proposition sentences like this negatively impacted retention.

The problems:

1/ Repetition - We explain, twice, that "I'm going to show you how to achieve X". Cut one.

2/ The "How" - we explain the meta of how the information will be delivered ("I'm going to tell you a story"), rather than simply... telling the story.

So, here's that same value prop, re-written with repetition removed, and the "How" reframed:

✅ "In this video, I'll reveal the three main mistakes you're probably making, and the simple strategy I used to [overcome them]. To explain the first mistake, I have to tell you about a make-or-break moment in my career, when I almost [caused disaster]…"

Rather than explaining that we're going to tell a story soon, we deliver the value prop and then just tell the story.

DO outline your video's structure:

 ✅ "...using my 3-step system..."
 ✅ "...with these 5 tips..."
 ✅ "...by ranking the top 10..."

DON'T explain the "how":

 ❌ "...I'm going to tell you a story..." (just start telling the story!)
 ❌ "...I'm going to give you some background, and then we'll get into it..." (just give the background... you don't have to justify yourself!)
 ❌ "...we're gonna break this down over the course of this video..." (just break it down then, no need to warn us first!)

Save for your next hook 🔖 ...and watch your retention improve!

Pals, there's a hillside in Montana where your phone turns into a paperweight and the sky puts on late-night shows with lightning and actual stars, the kind you forget exist when you live under streetlights. 

I spent last week at my third Arcadia Leadership Experience and I'm still a little foggy from it in the best possible way.

I've been running full-throttle at work for longer than I want to admit. I didn't know just how tired I actually was until I finally sat still in the creek long enough to feel it (and y’all know sitting still has never really been my thing!).

Incredible sessions from Christina Brown, Barrett Brooks, MK Getler-Porizkova, Adam Jay, Jake Reni, Dale Zwizinski, Steven and Merritt Grace Davis, Tyler Calder, Heather Cooper, Esq. and Blakely Graham, Lindsay Tjepkema, and Sam Yarborough and Jason Yarborough 🐻 provided the fuel for reflection and the stage for transformation.  

A camp full of talented go-to-market humans cracked open the way people do once the LinkedIn performance drops away and it's just humans under tents comparing scars. 

The first crack showed up for me during breathwork, led by Shannon Hawley Mariani, of all the places I expected to get undone. I went in planning to lie there and mentally draft emails. Somewhere in the middle of it I just stopped fighting whatever I'd been fighting. Thanks, Cory Snyder. It turns out saying yes to everyone who needs something from me carries a cost, and I've spent years handing my people the leftovers and calling it love. So I’m now reimagining #opentohelp (again) so both can coexist in harmony. 

Table Nine said something that stuck with me hardest all week: there is loneliness when there is tension between our ambition and our values. Half the room had lived it and the other half went quiet doing the math on their own life.

Later, after a values exercise that boiled me down to four words—family, friends, service, and integrity—I was standing by the fire belting show tunes and Disney songs with my dear pals, Lindsay Tjepkema and Katie Lambert like it was middle school again. Ruth Madigan showed up this year with her uncle Tim, easily my favorite new addition! 🤣 I got hugged and hugged back more times than I can count, for more reasons than I can count. 💛

Better people make better leaders. I’m sure I’ve read that on a poster somewhere. This week I watched strangers become something like family over four days with zero bars of service, and it stopped being a hollow poster line.

Sam and Jason Yarborough 🐻, thank you for building this again and again! I don't have better words yet. Ask me next year. And to those many Arcadians who made this week unforgettable: THANK YOU!!! 💛

Tomorrow: I’m headed back to my second Highline, in Jackson, Wyoming! My body has notes about doing this again so soon…and…I can’t wait for more hugs and human-to-human connection! 

Your pal, 
Pete 💛


H/t to my good pal David Gray for capturing some absolutely stunning moments on film! ⚡️

hook: A scientist in Japan demonstrated that the air inside a forest strengthens your immune system for a full month! The stud
text:
A scientist in Japan demonstrated that the air inside a forest strengthens your immune system for a full month! The study is fascinating: 

Qing Li, an immunologist at Nippon Medical School in Tokyo, took 12 men on a 3-day forest trip. These were slow walks with no breathing exercises and no set route.

Then he tested their blood and found a surge in natural killer cells -- the immune cells your body uses to fight cancer and virus-infected cells.

Remarkably, the effect didn't fade when they went home, it was still measurable 30 days later.

A control group that walked the same distance through a city showed no change at all.

Pine, cedar, and cypress trees release compounds called phytoncides to defend themselves from insects and bacteria. You breathe them in, and Li believes they switch your immune cells into high gear.

hook: One of the biggest traps in business is thinking every bottleneck needs another person.
text:
One of the biggest traps in business is thinking every bottleneck needs another person.

“I need to hire someone to solve this.”

Sometimes you do.

But a lot of the time, you’re trying to outsource 20 minutes of work that you are still the best person in the world to do.

When Tahnee and I were building Culture Kings, I was still doing all the buying at $50 million in revenue.

At more than $200 million, I still signed off on every PO.

I was also inside the ad account every day.

Every morning, I ran a stand-up where we broke down the daily P&L and contribution margin:

What’s working?

What’s not?

What do I think is about to happen?

What should we be excited about?

What risks are coming?

I did it because I had years of specific knowledge in my head. Transferring that judgement to someone else would have taken far longer than doing the work myself.

Founders are constantly sold the dream of delegation.

Hire the person.
Get out of the weeds.
Make the income passive.

Of course that sells. It sounds like freedom.

It also isn’t always true.

I’m watching people in their 20s build businesses to $10 million with almost no staff.

Ask them why they haven’t hired a full-time person and they look confused.

“What would they do for 40 hours a week?”

That question tells you where business is going.

The new leverage isn’t always headcount.

It’s AI, skills, systems and context that let one switched-on founder do the work of an old-school department.

And this isn’t all doom and gloom for employees.

In fact, I think it creates a massive opportunity for the best ones.

We’re moving from a world where people are paid for hours to one where they’re paid for results.

An employee with real skill, specific knowledge and AI leverage can create an outsized result. That gives them a chance to earn based on the value they create, rather than the number of hours they sit at a desk.

The best people won’t need to hide inside a 40-hour job description. Their knowledge will compound, their output will multiply and they’ll be paid accordingly.

This is the golden age for entrepreneurs and high-agency employees.

But dinosaur corporate bureaucracies built around headcount, hours and layers of approval?

They’re cooked.

Before you hire someone, ask yourself:

Is this genuinely a 40-hour-a-week role?

Or is it 20 minutes a day of high-value judgement that I’m uniquely qualified to make?

If you have no intention of selling your business, stop pretending the goal must be passive income.

Your active involvement, in the right state, making the right decisions, may still be the highest-return asset in the entire company.

Sometimes, as the founder, you’ve just got to do it.

hook: Have you considered that maybe the world doesn’t need your book on AI? In this line of work, you come across lots of boo
text: Have you considered that maybe the world doesn’t need your book on AI? In this line of work, you come across lots of book proposals, and the strongest trend is people who are not very experienced in technology writing about artificial intelligence. As if a large part of the authors, especially those in leadership, felt an urgency to publish just something in this area. Now, it can also become a great book. But the chances of success are… well, pretty much the same as with an electrical engineer really feeling the urge to cover psychological safety. Not good, no matter how strongly he feels about is. I have two recent experiences that lead me to say this. The first is attending SXSW London this past spring. It’s a wonderful festival. As a business seminar organiser, I truly envy them. I decided to attend some twelve talks on AI because I felt that I wasn’t up to date. I would say that 10/12 of those talks were a huge miss: people responsible for AI in large organisations or consulting houses, using their stage time to say the exact same things that everybody else was saying. I'm sure they themselves got a great kick out of it. The two exceptions were people from smaller companies who had actually changed their whole operating model with the help of technology, or people from the technology companies that actually develop these models. Listening to everyone else was pretty much a waste of time, even for someone like me, who I myself consider technologically illiterate. And the other experience: in a project with a publisher, I had to go through a few titles from the past few years on AI written by leadership experts. In light of what is the standard for publishing a book on AI today, they hadn’t aged well. Some appeared outright foolish, even though their authors are great minds. Of course, I have also come across some great titles on the topic. Lot's of them actually. I'll name a couple. For example, I attended the Association for Talent Development (ATD) conference in LA, listened to Zack Kass speak, and bought his book The Next RenAIssance. Even though I don’t share his techno-optimistic worldview (I personally don’t trust that capital has a conscience, and I think the winner of this rat race will cash out to the max), his book is a masterpiece of insight and argumentation. Also, his presentation was a riot. He used to work for OpenAI. The other example is Mohan Nair ’s Unreachable – How Not to Lose Your Mind in an AI-Obsessed World. Unlike many authors in this field, Mohan is a true technologist. I would still urge you to write on AI, just like I did here, from your own angle. So, write that book, but write it from a POV where you’re more qualified than most authors – because you want to write something that rings true also after a few years. And maybe include a chapter or two on AI, because it sure is a topic to cover. Just don't produce anything foolish.

hook: One of my students shared a hook he was working on for a new script. Alongside it, he shared an AI rewrite of the same h
text:
One of my students shared a hook he was working on for a new script. Alongside it, he shared an AI rewrite of the same hook.

His question was simple: "Which do you prefer?" A few of us debated this in the comments underneath, and something unexpected happened.

None of us agreed.

I thought his version was significantly better. He thought AI's version was better than his own. Another student preferred elements of the AI's version, and elements of his.

This lack of consensus intrigued me, so I decided to discuss the topic on my podcast, Making It. 

My co-hosts, Jamie and Gwilym, are two YouTube strategy people, and I wanted to know whether they'd be able to reach a consensus.

So I created a little game for them!

I broke down each version of the hook - the human version, and the AI version - into 7 key "moments". 

My co-hosts had two tasks:
- Guess which version was written by AI.
- Decide which they preferred.

Their responses were incredibly revealing 👀

Firstly, they correctly identified the AI sentences in 7/7 scenarios. Secondly, they preferred the "human" sentences in 6/7 scenarios.

This was what I expected. AI outputs have plenty of little "tells" that reveal a human didn't write it, so I wasn't surprised they'd correctly identified them. 

But then something happened that I really didn't expect.

To finish the episode, we read both hooks in full. And despite having overwhelmingly preferred the human writing in the individual sentences...

...when taken as a whole, they actually preferred the AI version. 

Even though its individual sentences felt clunky, the flow / structure of the AI made it feel like a more complete package.

Takeaways:

Don't... 👎 let AI write your scripts line-by-line. It constantly slipped into annoying jargon and buzzwords.

Do... 👍 use AI to help create structure, to turn a brainstorm into something that flows. Then rewrite using human intuition. This will be a lot faster with the underlying structure locked in.

Take a look at the final slide - can you tell which is AI? Let me know 👇

text:
The BEST prompt for AI agents I've heard over the last 12 months is ONLY 3 words, and it comes from someone who managed multi-billion dollar P&Ls in AI, led a 100 person org at AWS, and now runs a brilliant AI workforce of 34 agents:

1. Her best prompt is just "do smart things"

She gives the agents all her context first, her calendar, email, Stripe, goals, and transcripts, then lets them decide what's worth doing. She realized every task still started as a thought in her own head, which meant the company could only ever be as good as what she remembered to ask for.

2. Her human team talks to her agents in Slack. She has a channel where a teammate can ask "did that financial services client reply to Ali's email," and the agents answer directly, so people stop waiting hours for her to get back to them. 

3. Since an AI agent costs almost nothing, she hired the person she'd never put on payroll. 

One does nothing but ask how to make everything ten times better. Another just watches the other agents work and flags where they get stuck.

4. She avoids old job titles, because the second you call one your CMO, you've rebuilt a 2015 company with robots. Most of her sub-agents run on cheaper, smaller models and do the job fine.

5. Run an AI watchdog instead of a dashboard. Point one at your Slack to catch two people doing the same work, at your calendar to flag conflicts, at your analytics to tell you what to post tomorrow. Almost nobody does this yet.

6. She keeps a daily "brain dump" that feeds the agents.

At the end of each day she dictates what's in her head that isn't written down anywhere, the stuff that only lived in a meeting or a Slack thread, and it goes into a wiki the agents read. That's how they get the context that email and calendar miss.

7. She uses a "last 30 days" research skill to spin up on anything fast. Before running a workshop for 200 execs in an industry she doesn't know, she fans out agents to scan and synthesize the last month of news, then walks in sounding like she's followed it for years.

That's my convo with Allie K. Miller on The Startup Ideas Podcast . Pretty much her biggest tips for using AI agents.

Credit first: the new xAI x Cursor agent is the easiest on-ramp yet to an always-on, cloud-hosted AI teammate. It's a real fit for:
* Anyone who posts about AI for a living - we have to stay current 😊
* People who kept meaning to try OpenClaw but found the setup daunting. This is that idea with the plumbing hidden.

Where it lost me:
1. Context. Default retrieval is internal knowledge plus web search. Instead of asking which folder holds my real content, it invented a format from public docs.
2. Review. There's no file editor in the chat. Long artifacts had to be read and fixed in another tool.
3. Control. No model choice, no effort dial, and an approval system that makes you pick between being nagged all night or writing permanent allow-rules.
4. Memory. No viewer, entries truncated mid-sentence, and facts I corrected still sitting there.
5. Flow. Message it while it's working and it silently discards the turn in progress.

The most telling moment: I did do real work in it. Then the work became reviewing and editing many files in context, and I ran back to Claude Code and Cursor to finish the job.

I'm bullish on Cursor, which is exactly why I'm watching this one. The open question: will the super-user answer be these capabilities arriving in the tools we already use, or Grok Bot growing the visibility and control it deliberately left out?

hook: The question I get most right now is "what should I turn into an AI agent?". Here is the 5 part test I use (works for Cl
text:
The question I get most right now is "what should I turn into an AI agent?". Here is the 5 part test I use (works for Claude/Codex/Grokbot etc):  

1. It has a repeated trigger, so the same kind of task keeps happening over and over. 
2. The inputs are stable, so the information comes in a predictable shape every time. 
3. The tools are clear, so there is a defined set of things it can actually go do. 
4. There is a measurable finish line, so you can tell when it is done and whether it worked. 
5. There is judgment in the middle, so each run is a little different and needs a real decision made in the moment.  

The first 4 are really just asking "can this be automated at all?" The 5th is the one that matters, because judgment in the middle is what makes it an agent instead of a simple automation.  

Once you see it this way, you start spotting agent work pretty much everywhere.

hook: Losing your audience's trust rarely happens overnight. So let's take a look the scriptwriting mistake you were told woul
text: Losing your audience's trust rarely happens overnight. So let's take a look the scriptwriting mistake you were told would grow your channel faster... ...but which gradually burns the trust you built up with your viewers. And it comes down to this: We all know negativity sells. Negative headlines. Scary tweets. Comment section ragebait. As human beings, we're drawn to negative things more than positive things. It's called loss aversion - we're more scared to lose something than we are excited to gain something so we instinctively pay more attention to the things that could impact us negatively to help us avoid them. And this is exactly why most YouTube videos are framed through a negative lens. There's nothing wrong with negative framing. Until it becomes disingenuous. Or "fake". The truth is: most YouTubers don't do this deliberately. But they're so used to framing the stakes of their video through a negative lens that they start to prioritise this fear-based approach over all else. So on your next video, when you're figuring out how to write the hook, or working on a segment setup, start by thinking of the negative frame you could use. And if it feels authentic... stick with it. Because we know it's effective. But if it doesn't... consider what the positive frame might look like. [Swipe for some examples of negative vs. positive framing.] If you're telling your viewers to PANIC in every single video... ...you'll eventually sound like the boy who cried wolf. And if you're not being authentic, your viewers will start to lose trust. A genuine positive frame always beats an inauthentic negative frame! Found this useful? Save this for when you're framing your next video 📌

hook: What jobs will AI replace? That is the wrong question.
text:
What jobs will AI replace? That is the wrong question. 

History tells us automation is rarely one-size-fits-all. Some roles will disappear like the elevator operators of yesterday. For most jobs, it’s more nuanced. The impact on a specific occupation depends on which specific tasks within that job get automated. 

When automation causes the work remaining to require more expertise, wages rise because it’s harder to qualify for the job. When automation results in less expertise being needed, wages fall because many more people can enter the job, competing down wages. Already, these various cases are playing out.

Simple AI exposure scores miss the important nuance of whether AI automates the expert skill or the inexpert one. Debates about whether AI creates or replaces jobs miss the point about job quality. 

The question for society then isn’t whether AI will replace jobs, but what happens to the quality, security, and social contract of the work left behind and what we will do to help people caught in the transition.

creator: Jim Fan
hook: Seeing a hype wave around GEN-1.5, and rightfully so. Lots of respect to Pete & Andy for executing so well. The secret i
text:
Seeing a hype wave around GEN-1.5, and rightfully so. Lots of respect to Pete & Andy for executing so well. The secret is in the naturally repetitive motions in human-collected data. There're 2 main sources for such repetitions: 

(1) Symmetric patterns. Sorting, tidying, and assembling almost never finish in one motion. Open any assembly manual from IKEA, and you find most objects symmetrical. You drive one bolt, then its twin, then the next pair. Every {bolt A, bolt B} pair is a natural continuation in context, and the second instance is a free training signal that imitates the first ("prompt").

(2) Recovery. Humans drop things all the time, but we pick them up so fast, we don’t even notice. That reflex to fix is half of our physical competence. The key insight is to keep the failed first half instead of trimming it away. If the model consumes the full arc, fumble, catch, continue, then recovery shows up organically at test time. It's funny that in-context improvement results from *NOT* over-sanitizing your data.

The other critical ingredient is UMI. I've been saying for a while that teleop will not last, and GEN-1.5 is driving the final nail in the coffin. UMI is essentially a human wearing the robot gripper to collect data directly (human → data). Teleop inserts a layer of separation: human → VR/skeletal device → robot → data, which bleeds out all the human "physical intuition". The subtle sleight of hand we perform constantly with objects, the micro-adjustments, the feel of a part snapping into place, is nearly impossible to capture when you can't feel the environment directly.

Once you have enough data, many behaviors can actually be zero-shot. For example, you don't even need finetuning to pick up a novel object. The model "just knows" what to do given a similar scene in the training distribution. Whether in-context learning truly works or not also depends on how far away the test is from training. Currently, the demos are still a bit too simple to conclude.

I'm cautiously optimistic. Still, it's a great day in robotics.
