creator: Jim Fan
hook: The sense of touch is the most criminally under-explored modality in robotics. Imagine doing sleight of hand wearing thi
text:
The sense of touch is the most criminally under-explored modality in robotics. Imagine doing sleight of hand wearing thick oven mitts. That's exactly how a robot feels today if it were alive. A magnetic piece snapping into place, a paper cup peeling out of a stack, a USB negotiating its way into the port - all invisible to the camera.

Learning how to feel must be a full-stack co-designed effort. We are open-sourcing a principled methodology called "T-Rex":

1. Tactile as first-class citizen of the model. Our mixture-of-transformer runs two clocks asynchronously: a slow visuomotor expert plans the motion, and a fast tactile expert refines it in real time with high-frequency corrections at 4 "touch ticks" per vision tick. Forces change faster than frames arrive, so the architecture had to as well.

2. Open data. The largest tactile dataset ever released to our knowledge: a 50-hour (~5,500 episodes) high-quality, carefully synchronized robot play corpus, collected on SOTA tactile hand hardware with 22 degrees of freedom. Available today on HuggingFace!

3. Training recipe: T-Rex extends our prior work, EgoScale. Human egocentric videos for pretraining, a diverse dose of tactile robot play for mid-training. Our experiments show this bridges contact-free pretraining to contact-rich manipulation remarkably well.

Pixels are cheap and everywhere, but they run out of steam at the moment of contact. Tactile will carry the last mile. The next scaling curve will be measured in hours of touch.

T-Rex: Tactile-Reactive Dexterous Manipulation
Website: https://lnkd.in/gZsDt_kz
Open dataset: https://lnkd.in/gRVm9xWi
It is a great collaboration between NVIDIA and Berkeley, led by Dantong Niu and co-advised by Trevor Darrell.

text:
An employee came back from maternity leave and skipped the worst part: starting over.

Maria Colacurcio, CEO of Syndio (and one of the strongest AI-advocate leaders I know), wrote about putting two dozen of her people through an AI bootcamp (mine, full disclosure). One team member, Jackie, missed it while on maternity leave. When she returned, her colleagues handed her the AI skills they had built during the program. In Maria's words: "She started where they finished."

This is the part of AI upskilling I want more leaders to notice. Agent skills are becoming the unit of knowledge transfer inside teams. Onboarding, standardization, ramp-up after leave, cross-team handoffs: all of these change when expertise is an artifact you can hand someone.

HOWEVER, one thing to add: reused skills come with a catch I call the "hand-me-down problem": they mostly fit, and "mostly" can quietly hurt you. Three rules for inheriting a skill someone else built:
1. Read it before you run it. A skill encodes its author's context, preferences, and shortcuts. Know what you are adopting.
2. Tailor it to your work. Trim the parts that encode their style. A skill overfit to its creator will confidently produce work that isn't yours.

text:
Lots of people are afraid AI is going to take their job. And in the process, they fall into 5 predictable traps. 

The people inside the trap are often the most diligent, informed, and self-aware professionals in the knowledge economy. 

They read the headlines. They see the shift coming. And they're still stuck.

Stress, burnout, and job-related anxiety are at all-time highs and keep climbing every year - a predictable result of an entire professional class grinding harder in a game that's becoming unwinnable. 

From inside the trap, the response feels rational, responsible, and even forward-thinking. 

In response to AI commoditizing knowledge work, most people are trying to become a better, smarter, faster knowledge worker. 

This is equivalent to the factory worker grinding harder on the factory floor, competing with the robots that would inevitably take their job a few years later. 

Most universities, media channels, and corporate cultures are all pointing people directly into the trap: the way to survive the AI wave is to work harder, learn more, and be the best at using AI. 

Nobody is telling you this, but here's the secret:

The exit from the trap requires one thing: Reorienting to the question the scale of AI is actually posing. 

The trap is built around becoming a better knowledge worker. How do I become a better, smarter, faster player in a game that's ending? 

The situation is posing a different question: What can a human do that the AI automation of information processing and execution can't replicate? If information is infinite, what is the new scarce resource in the emerging economy and how do I develop it? 

The trap is grinding harder with AI. 

The exit from the trap is using the efficiency gains created from AI augmentation to develop new skills that AI can't replicate.

hook: I sat with a marketer recently who told me, “It’s a great time to be a marketer; because of AI, distribution is the only
text:
I sat with a marketer recently who told me, “It’s a great time to be a marketer; because of AI, distribution is the only moat left.” Unfortunately, I had to set them right. Distribution is no moat. We argued.

First, they tell me Microsoft crushed Slack because of distribution. Teams went from 20M users to 270M in three years. Slack went from 12M to 26M. Point made. Argument won?

The problem is, Teams isn’t a distribution story. It’s an expansion story. Microsoft could bundle Teams to existing customers cheaply, since they were already locked into enterprise contracts.

If distribution were a real moat, then Google would be crushing AI. They have, by far, the largest distribution engine on earth: Search, Chrome, Android, Gmail. But Gemini is still trailing ChatGPT and Claude by a long way.

Then I ask the marketer what their current distribution playbook is. It’s data enrichment, AI prospecting, paid advertising, and AEO.

Good playbook, no moats. Very few of us have Microsoft’s or Google’s ecosystem.

I explain it like this. You have new customers (distribution) and existing customers (expansion).

New customers + attention: Paid reach, SEO, virality, creators. The playing field is won or lost by product quality (not marketing), marketing execution, and the ability to scale channels. The other thing I’m seeing for AI-native companies is being the first to catch fire for a use case and capturing all that attention really matters to their growth.

New customers + network effects. Slack tried this with Slack Connect. Network effects are undefeated. They are a real moat. But they are a function of your product, not marketing. And incredibly hard to do and scale. 

Existing customers + attention. This is what Microsoft did with Teams; they have a large customer base and could easily market to it. This is leverage, not a moat.

Existing customers + Switching costs / Pricing. This is a real moat. The product is entrenched in the core functions of the business, and the company has real pricing leverage vs. its competitors.

Network effects, switching costs, and bundling (pricing) are real moats; everything else is execution and ability to scale.

Marketers create leverage, but not moats. 

Who wins the argument?

Agentic loops and graph engineering matter a lot to knowledge workers. However, getting them to deliver the desired results cost-effectively is not trivial. Ask the 1,600+ people who showed up live yesterday to learn one skill: making AI work until the job is done.

Nathaniel Whittemore and I ran our first Frontier Lab of Superintelligent and The AI Daily Brief. The recording was sent to registrants. 

Here is the core, in five ideas:
1. All agentic tools run in loops under the hood. The core difference is configuring a command to run autonomously longer, and the skill is setting the finish line properly. 
2. Loops were created for coding where verification is straightforward. Knowledge work succeeds on a loop exactly when you invent a boring, checkable finish line: counts, citations, format rules. "Make it insightful" is not checkable. "200 unique data points, each with a source URL" is. Flaky "done" criteria will get your loop to yield mediocre results. 
3. Selecting which use cases to automate on a loop is a skill you need to master: Recurring reports, research sweeps, experiments with clear success criteria, audits against a checklist: loop them. Executive comms, hiring, strategy: there, your judgment is the actual work product - don't loop.
4. KISS and know when to expand: Regular agent usage as the default, then one loop when required, progress to a team of agents when the signals say so: Fan out when self-review starts rubber-stamping, parallel work runs serially, or when quality plateaus. The first specialist to split out is a reviewer with fresh context.
5. The knowledge worker's proficiency map for August 2026: understand agents, define agentic workloads, configure loops, configure teams, know when to reach out to which technology.

Yet we've both been glued to Netflix's recent documentary, Mourinho, which follows the career of one of the world's greatest football managers. Sure, I probably gain a little extra something from it because I did grow up watching players from this era. But my partner is still completely drawn in by... well, by what? Well, the truth is: this documentary is not really about football. If it were, she wouldn't be interested. Actually, it's about tension. Drama. Story. Now, I know many of you reading this are educators, not entertainers. And I understand that having (sorry José) an absolute maniac as your protagonist certainly keeps people watching. But as YouTubers, we can lean into the exact same principles: ▪️ Hooks set up the drama. They show the viewer why they should care. They make the video's consequences feel personal. ▪️ Segments build tension. They remind the viewer what's at stake throughout. They explore smaller stories within the overarching narrative that help reveal the final payoff. ▪️ End-screen CTAs preview what happens next... if the viewer watches just one more video. If storytelling can make somebody with almost zero interest in football watch a 3-hour football documentary... ...then we should have no problem convincing an already interested audience to watch our videos for 15 minutes, right? (Ok, fine, it's maybe not that easy.) But you get the point. Storytelling is art, yes. But it's also maths. Watch enough of these football documentaries, and you start to notice the same structures appear over and over again. Storytelling on YouTube is no different. Yes, you should add your own personal flair... but don't overcomplicate it. Focus on core scriptwriting frameworks for YouTube. Double down on the principles that keep your audience watching; abandon those that don't. What do you think? Comment below with your thoughts (and if you watched the doc too)! 👇

hook: Veritasium just explained how to PERFECTLY pair a title and thumbnail.
text:
Veritasium just explained how to PERFECTLY pair a title and thumbnail. 

And I think they’re making some of the best packaging on YouTube. 

Whenever I make a video, 40% of the process goes on generating the idea and honing the title and thumbnail. So hearing Derek Muller, the creator behind Veritasium, talk to Jon Youshaei about why his packaging works so well immediately interested me. 

He breaks down what he calls the 'double barrel' method. 

Derek tells you to think of the title and thumbnail as two barrels firing at the same time. Instead of repeating yourself with a title that says the same thing as the thumbnail, you should be creating tension between them. The mistake is having both barrels say the same thing. 

The title and thumbnail should also complete each other. The ideal combination creates meaning that neither element can communicate as powerfully on its own.

Finally, a double barrel thumbnail should be scannable - the viewer should have read it before they’ve even decided to. It should also make sense immediately, without too much work from the viewer. 

Derek points to his video ‘How One Company Secretly Poisoned The Planet’ as an example.

First of all, I’ve always thought Veritasium are *incredibly* good at communicating how one small factor can have a massive impact in their titles. The fact it’s ‘One Company’ that poisons the ‘Entire Planet’ is what makes the title so gripping. The same goes for their video ‘The Man Who Accidentally Killed The Most People In History’. 

But here’s what the double barrel adds. 

There’s the gripping title and the thumbnail that sparks curiosity. But over the image is the question ‘How was this allowed?’ The tension exists between the text on the thumbnail and the text in the title. 

So you read the thumbnail text and your brain asks ‘how is what allowed?’ And then you read the title ‘How One Company Secretly Poisoned The Planet’. Those things combined are powerful. 

Ultimately, the title and thumbnail are responsible for whether a viewer will watch your video. 

Really interesting to hear the genius thought process behind the most viewed science videos on the internet.

text:
I’ve talked to a bunch of marketing leaders about AI. Nearly all are stuck on: Should all my marketers be part engineers now, or should I hire actual marketing engineers? These are the notes I’m sending back.

What is a marketing engineer? A marketer who builds your AI systems (not code). They’ll build context, skills, feedback loops, quality gates, MCP connections. Listings for this job are live at companies like OpenAI & Ramp,  between $140K and $268K. I see this as similar to the evolution of data engineering and GTM engineering.

Do you need to hire a marketing engineer? 

I’d approach it like this:

- For startup / growing teams. Every marketer will need to understand how to build AI systems & workflows. This is a core skill now, like understanding data became a decade ago. In some cases, AI can assist with the work; in others, it can help marketers spend more time elevating their work. This means AI competency needs to be a core part of the hiring process.

- Large enterprise teams. I’d centralize. I do believe large teams would benefit from a dedicated marketing engineer who can architect the system the whole team runs on. At this scale, building context, workflow volume, integrations, quality gates, and governance is a full-time job.

The wrong answers are the inverse.

A large team where the AI system is totally decentralized is chaos. A small team where it’s centralized means one person will be a huge bottleneck, and it’s not forcing you to hire the right kind of profile, e.g., someone with the craft of marketing + AI system thinking.

Ultimately, the modern marketing leader needs to own the AI strategy for their own team. That shouldn't be outsourced to someone else.

hook: I just worked out I've spent over 4000 hours learning about GenAI in since 2022 🤯. Here's my list of 12 things AI is BRI
text:
I just worked out I've spent over 4000 hours learning about GenAI in since 2022 🤯. Here's my list of 12 things AI is BRILLIANT at:

I've split into Doing, Thinking & Systems: 

DOING 

- Getting you off a blank page. 
You know what needs writing and the document stays empty. Ask for a rough version and the hour goes on editing instead.

- Reshaping what you've already got. 
Turning some big and complex into short bullets or a social post. It's an excellent content repurposer.

- Repetition with a judgement call in it*. 
40 replies that each differ slightly. A hundred survey comments to group by theme. 

- Capability JUST outside of your reach.
It doesn't replace skills you don't have, but if you can describe what good looks like (and recognise it the other side) it can really expand out your skill set.

*If it repeats with no judgement call at all, that's automation.

THINKING 

- Reading more than you ever could. 
It can read and digest huge reports and docs in seconds, and pull out the bits you need (if your prompt is good enough)

- Being a translator. 
Translating the complex stuff into simple stuff. Or into bullets. Or riddles, or whatever floats your boat. 

- Being someone to think with. 
Ask AI to pressure test your decisions, show you results from different angels, play devil's advocate. Get further on your own.

- Practice and build confidence
The difficult conversation, the interview, selling to a dodgy ICP. It plays the other person, stays in character, and lets you practice how you'll deal with it.

SYSTEMS

- Holding a standard steady. 
We've now got Skills - active SOPs that work way better than documents to get the same standard, every time, across your organisation.

- Getting knowledge out of one head. 
One person knows how the report gets built, what the client hates, where everything lives. Now we can pick their AI brains even if they're off on holiday.

- Finding the answer in the pile. 
Old proposals, policies, emails, it's in there somewhere. AI reads the pile and hands over what you need, in seconds.

- Making "never worth the time" worth it. 
Tidying the CRM. Writing the internal FAQ. Personalising all 50 instead of just the top five. Stuff you've never been able to justify the time for is now possible. 

So, which of these do you use? 
Fellow AI geeks, is there anything you think I've missed? 

💾  Save this for next time you need AI use case inspiration (isn't it mad the sign for save is still a floppy disk...)

text:
You don’t need another SEO vs GEO debate.

You need a strategy that makes you visible.

In AI search, visibility largely comes down to 3 things:

1. Whether AI can find you
2. Whether it trusts you
3. Whether it can understand and cite your content

This 6-pillar checklist combines the SEO fundamentals that still matter with what you need to do differently for AI search 👇

1. Brand Presence & Mentions
→ If AI can't find you, it can't recommend you.
☐ Search your brand across every major AI model and log the gaps
☐ Get into "Top [X]" and "Best [X]" roundups - that's what AI pulls from
☐ Show up on Reddit, Quora, forums, and review sites consistently

2. Entity & Authority Signals
→ AI recommends what it trusts. Make sure that's you.
☐ Lock down your Wikipedia, Wikidata, and Knowledge Panel
☐ Attach real credentials and author bios to everything you publish
☐ Earn backlinks from credible sources, AI uses citation networks to judge trust

3. Content Optimisation
→ Be easy to extract, easy to quote, easy to surface.
☐ Answer the question first and expand second because AI rewards directness
☐ Structure with Q&A blocks, subheadings, and schema markup
☐ Refresh your top pages regularly - outdated content gets ignored

4. Conversation & Community
→ The best AI visibility starts in human conversations.
☐ Find what your customers are actually asking - support tickets, sales calls, forums
☐ Create comparison and "versus" content, AI synthesises these constantly
☐ Contribute to discussions authentically

5. Technical & Crawlability
→ None of this works if AI crawlers can't reach your site.
☐ Unblock GPTBot, ClaudeBot, and PerplexityBot in robots.txt
☐ Keep your site fast, mobile-friendly, and structurally clean
☐ Monitor server logs monthly for AI crawler activity

6. Monitoring & Adaptation
→ You can't grow what you're not measuring.
☐ Track mentions and citations across AI models
☐ Study what competitors are doing that's getting them recommended
☐ Use Searchable to monitor AI visibility and ad displacement in real time

creator: Anthony Pierri
hook: Most homepages are written for an audience that doesn’t exist.
text:
Most homepages are written for an audience that doesn’t exist. 

If you sell into the enterprise, you (or someone on your team) has likely uttered these two phrases: 

1) our buyers don't care about the product
2) our buyers only care about business outcomes

And so you go and write the page filled with business outcomes (and zero product info) to convince the executive in your head who 1) doesn't care about products and 2) only cares about business outcomes.

It may be true that executives don't care about products and only care about outcomes...

...but those people don't read homepages. 

There's a reason that high-level executives have people who report to them. 

They task THOSE people with finding and vetting vendors, reading homepages, etc., in order to create shortlists.

Then they expect those same employees to go through the buying process (mostly without them) and then only loop them in at the very final moment. 

At THAT time... they will likely want to make sure that there will be a positive ROI of the purchase, especially if it's a high ACV purchase. 

But this ROI-focused information will be presented to them likely by their own employees, who have been prepped by your AEs a co-created business case. 

The place they WON'T look to make sure you'll drive business outcomes? 
Your freaking homepage. 

On the flip side...
There are some executives who DO care about the product. 
And THOSE executives might actually read the homepage. 

In either case, make sure the audience you're writing for ACTUALLY exists, and tailor your message accordingly.

creator: Amanda Natividad
hook: Nuance in your marketing metrics is more important than ever.
text:
Nuance in your marketing metrics is more important than ever.

YouTube recently updated how it counts views. Now, Views include any time a video autoplays, even if the user scrolls past. The legacy view metric, Engaged View, filters out those who immediately scrolled or swiped away.

Who else is counting Views as soon as playback starts? Instagram and TikTok. 

But not Facebook, which counts the view after about 1 millisecond. Not LinkedIn either, which requires at least 2 continuous seconds... which is kind of like Pinterest but not really, because Pinterest also requires that at least 50% of the video be visible on the screen too.

Sorry, I would have written this less confusingly — if it were actually less confusing.

This is the reality marketers live in. The word "views" has several asterisks attached to it. It means something different everywhere, and it's up to us to manage the implications up, down, and laterally with our teams.

This means every dashboard needs footnotes. And the more automated they get, the more important human interpretation — and metric literacy — becomes.

hook: 4 years ago, I was anticipating the launch of my first book, Financial Feminist.
text:
4 years ago, I was anticipating the launch of my first book, Financial Feminist.

And since then, I've sold nearly 350,000 copies (a New York Times bestseller). 

But did you know that the average sales of a published book are 3,000 copies? For the ENTIRE LIFETIME of the book.

Here's what I learned about marketing and selling a book.

1) Publishers are there to distribute, not to help market. 

Expect to do 95% of the marketing yourself, even if you're with one of the big guys.

2) Pre-sales are CRUCIAL. 

If you can announce the book 3-6 months before it goes on sale, you've just given yourself way more time to build trust and to do ramp-up campaign. 

All pre-sale orders count 12:01 am on release day (I had sold over 17,000 copies before the book officially went on sale -- which means before I appeared on Good Morning America at 7 am on book release day, I had already sold thousands of books.)

3) Do lives on social media -- the best is a "free workshop" that is a section of the book. 

You provide value, and at the end, you can organically plug the book (have a copy in hand that you can literally just show in front of the camera when you say "I talk about this more in my book Financial Feminist...")

4) One of the biggest parts of getting on bestseller lists isn't just the number of copies sold, but WHERE they're sold. 

10,000 Amazon copies probably won't get you there. Instead, focus on indie bookstores -- better for you the author, AND a great way to support local businesses. 

Supply 4-5 bookstores (that can ship nationally) with signed copies (we did signed inserts), and link these bookstores on your book sales page ("order from these bookstores to support local AND get a signed copy!") We had thousands of sales this way. And the coolest part? 

These bookstores told me that they saw a HUGE difference in their revenue, and that this was one of the most successful sales campaigns they had EVER done for a book. Example: financialfeministbook.com)

5) Your book should be full of value. 

And when you promote your book, serve before you sell. Talk about the value proposition, about how much this book will impact the reader. And the moment you have good reviews, share the hell out of them.

Sometimes, I look at my to do list for the day and I get a big lump in my throat.  It all feels too much. 
 
If you’ve met me, you’ll know, I’m a super energetic and driven person but right now, my workload is ridiculous. 

We’re dreaming big, growing fast, which means we’re hiring fast, changing fast, thinking fast.  It’s go-go-go all the time, every day, no let-up. 
 
I'd say most days I’m all pumped up and whizzy and smash through it with a big grin on my face. On those days, there’s nothing like that feeling, I bloody love it. 
 
But on others, I feel anxious, daunted and overwhelmed. I worry about my mental health and wonder why the heck I'm doing this to myself. 
 
I’m getting better at managing those days though. One big thing that helps is to break it into small pieces.  
 
I saw a brilliant TEDX Talk live once called “I’ve Got 99 Problems But Parkinsons Ain’t One” by Emma Lawton. She spoke about how she handles the challenges of her life with Parkinsons by breaking (and gamifying) everything she has to do in a day into tiny tasks.  
 
Her idea (and dazzling attitude) has stuck with me ever since, and it really helps on those daunting days.  
 
I write every single thing I’ve got to do that day – including walking the dog, brekky, gym, proposals to write, meetings, delivery, etc. And I put them on individual sticky notes, and stick them to the wall by my desk. (Or my face, for a photo for LinkedIn, which is harder than you might think). 
 
As I go through the day, I tear them off as I do them, and everything feels so much more doable. I end the day feeling really accomplished too. 
 
I’d love to learn more about strategies to deal with huge volumes of work. How do you deal with those overwhelming days? Any tips/tricks much appreciated.

hook: “AI capabilities are changing so quickly that any positioning we develop will be out of date in two weeks. How do we han
text: “AI capabilities are changing so quickly that any positioning we develop will be out of date in two weeks. How do we handle that?” I heard this from a CEO at an AI founder roundtable last week. Here's how I think about the problem and how to handle it. One of the benefits of using a structured positioning process is that we can revisit the steps and determine whether anything needs to change. So let’s say your big foundation model provider of choice releases something new, and then your offering, in turn, gains new capabilities. Has your positioning changed? Maybe. Maybe not. If we look at how we developed the current positioning, we can work through the same steps to see if it needs to change. 1️⃣ Step 1 - Competitive Alternatives - Does this change in capabilities mean your prospects would now compare you to new competitors? Have you seen proof of that in conversations you have had with prospects? 2️⃣ Step 2 - Distinct Capabilities - Looking at the list of alternatives, has your list of distinct capabilities changed? Obviously, you have new capabilities, but maybe your competitors do too (since they are using the same models). Focus on the truly differentiated stuff here. 3️⃣ Step 3 - Differentiated Value - Here is where we get to the important part. The competitors may or may not be new, the capabilities may or may not be new, the big question is this - does any of that shift our value themes? Frequently the answer is no because often the new capabilities strengthen a theme we are already positioning around. If that is the case, we add the capabilities under an existing theme as part of the explanation of how we deliver that value. The positioning itself does not need to change. However, if we now have new value we can deliver to customers that we couldn’t before, we'll have to go back to the drawing board and redo the positioning. ⭐ Doing positioning in a structured way makes knowing when to shift it much easier ⭐ Notice that this would be much harder if we weren’t following a process to do positioning. If we are simply vibing our way through it, we will always be trying to assess how big the change is, and your positioning is left flapping in the wind every time Anthropic or OpenAI drops something new. I'm walking through a specific example of this in the newsletter this week - link in the comments to read it.

hook: Does a newsletter teaching you how to set up multiplayer AI for marketing need to be 8,000 words?
text:
Does a newsletter teaching you how to set up multiplayer AI for marketing need to be 8,000 words?
Well, in my personal experience just writing one, it does.

Here's why: Everyone is stumbling through this and no one is doing it the same way.

So I decided to talk to 3 teams, all ahead of the game with a lot to teach other teams: Simon Heaton at Buffer, Daniel Lambert at LangChain, and Lauren Volpi at Mintlify

6 things I learned from their approaches to mutliplayer AI:

1. Focus on the context layer before you build a pile of skills.
Most teams I talk to have this backward, then wonder why their skills aren't adopted or produce bad outputs. Your skills are only as good as the context they run on. (Mintlify)

2. Keep your context outside of Claude and GitHub.
Put it somewhere your team already updates, like Notion, Asana, or Airtable, and let Claude read it from there. (Buffer)

3. Let everyone build, but have a clear DRI for the whole system.
Anyone on the team at Buffer can build, but one person reviews what ships to everyone.  (Buffer)

4. Have a standard for what you ship to the team.
LangChain builds production agents, and makes sure each one checks these boxes: ease of use, model-agnostic, traceable, and self-improving. 
With this level of quality control, the team can trust the shared agents.  (LangChain)

5. Find what people are already solving on their own.
When a use case gets big enough, turn it into a shared skill or agent. Don't bother standardizing the one-offs. (LangChain)

6. Think agentically to go multiplayer.
Your context has to be readable by agents, not just by people. This is true for internal knowledge bases and external content. (Mintlify)

This newsletter is a roadmap to help you figure out multiplayer AI: 
Multiplayer AI = Your whole team uses and improves the same AI system, instead of everyone being stuck in single-player mode building their own thing.

Would love to hear how more teams are doing this.

Bonus: This newsletter is also accessible in MKT1 MCP, and our newsletter skill is free.

text:
I've had so many marketers DM me this year: "Inbound marketing isn't working anymore; what should we do?" I'm sharing a new set of marketing principles with them.

1. Taste > Keywords: A lot of inbound was built on being visible when prospects had questions via search. That's collapsing. HubSpot's own data showed an 80% drop in search traffic last year, the largest we've ever recorded. Today, you need content consumed across a diverse set of channels (e.g., YouTube, newsletter, podcast, social, etc.). The art of marketing has never been so important. Be what your customers choose to consume.

2. 1:1 > Segmentation: We've lied forever in B2B that we did personalisation. We aggregated large swaths of companies together based on limited criteria like company size, geo, role. AI promises that you can truly provide 1:1 marketing via email and chat. The biggest gains HubSpot saw in the past 12 months were from email. Crazy, but AI is a huge unlock.

3. Creative Testing > Audience Testing: There's a new way to do paid advertising. For years, so much of paid advertising was spent optimising audience targeting and budget. The platforms can now do that targeting better than you. The best teams are scaling creative and letting the platforms choose the best audience for them.

4. Creator Channels > Brand Channels: I've long believed that over time, a large % of B2B attention goes to creators vs. brands. We've seen that happen for years in B2C; it's now unquestionably happening in B2B. Whether you hire creators, partner with creators, or pay for creators to promote on your behalf. They are now an essential part of any marketing program. And in B2B, it's not just for glossy brands. I've seen examples of it work for small companies in niche industries.

5. Answer Engine Optimisation > Search Engine Optimisation: More and more buyers are going to an AI assistant before they ever type a query into Google. G2 found 51% of B2B software buyers now start their research in an AI chatbot more often than a search engine. They don't scan page 1. They ask, and the model answers. The job is no longer to rank for the question. It's to be the source the model cites when it answers it.

6. Sprints + Outcomes > Quarterly + Activity: Marketing teams can no longer work in quarterly cycles, long planning processes, and measure success on activity. Product/engineering/growth teams have worked in sprint cycles with clear outcomes for a long time. The best marketing teams I see now run the same way. Weekly sprints, one outcome per sprint, ship, measure, adjust. Outcomes are the results

It’s why we encoded these into a new book launching this month called Loop: Outlearn, Outmarket, Outgrow. You can pre-order now :)

text:
This excerpt from Carl Sagan's 1949 high school yearbook reveals a young man already seen by his peers as a once-in-a-generation intellect. He is lavishly compared to a dictionary (Noah Webster), a genius (Einstein), and a walking encyclopedia, while also possessing the charismatic flair of an actor like John Barrymore. Most telling, however, is his stated ambition to become a research astronomer, a goal the author declares an absolute certainty. This was not mere teenage bravado; it was a recognition of a prodigious talent already hard at work.

The true glimpse into his visionary nature comes from his response to a question about leisure. When asked what he did in his spare time, the 15-year-old Sagan flatly stated, "I have none!" This was not a complaint but a declaration of purpose. His every moment was already consumed by a singular drive to learn and discover. He intuitively understood that the monumental task he had set for himself to unravel the secrets of the cosmos and then explain them to the world—would require every ounce of his focus, leaving no room for idle time.

This early commitment was a direct prophecy of the man he would become. That relentless drive fueled the creation of the iconic Cosmos series and a library of profound books, all while he actively contributed to NASA's planetary exploration programs. Carl didn't just become the research astronomer he envisioned; he became its most powerful communicator. His lack of "free time" in youth was the investment that later paid the incredible dividend of opening the eyes of millions to the wonders of the universe.

Before buying another AI tool, enterprises should ask one question:

Where does the data actually live?

Because most AI pilots look simple in a demo.

Then reality hits.

The data is in regulated databases.
The documents are in internal systems.
The apps run close to operations.

Security teams do not want sensitive data moving everywhere.
IT does not want another stack to patch, monitor, and explain.

That is why enterprise AI is not just about the model.
It is about the data architecture the model runs on.

A practical checklist:
1- Can the AI access business-critical data without unnecessary movement?
2- Can it respect data access, residency, and security requirements?
3- Can apps, databases, and agents run close enough to reduce latency?
4- Can IT automate patching, scaling, backup, and lifecycle management?
5- Can the system reduce complexity instead of adding another isolated AI stack?

This is why Oracle’s Base Database Cloud@Customer is interesting.
It brings the same public cloud control plane and database automation directly to customer distributed locations, with support for databases, applications, and private AI agents closer to the data.

Its about more control over where AI runs, where data stays, and how much operational burden IT has to carry.

text:
Agentic loops and graph engineering started with coding agents. Engineers used loop commands to let an agent keep working on a codebase until the tests passed, and organized several agents into a graph when one could not carry the job. Those same practices apply remarkably well to knowledge work, and that is what my session with Nathaniel Whittemore was about. It is now an The AI Daily Brief podcast episode.

What you'll hear:
1. The core skill is identifying which of your tasks can run on a loop, and then writing a proper finish line for them: criteria a machine can check on its own, such as counts, citations and format rules. Anything that depends on taste and judgment, like executive communication or hiring decisions, does not belong on a loop unless a human checkpoint is designed into it, and even then it is a stretch.
2. Loops are a powerful modality worth knowing well, and they earn their place only when the task calls for them. When a strong model does the job well in one shot, that is the right tool. We fired a live loop chasing 200 source-verified data points, a task no single pass can finish, to show exactly where the line sits.
3. When one agent stops being enough: how to describe a piece of work as a graph, decide which parts can run in parallel, and assign several specialized agents to it rather than one, including where the human sits in that flow.

hook: Stop adding context to your AI projects! It's making the responses worse. Despite the insane (and slightly worrying) wee
text: Stop adding context to your AI projects! It's making the responses worse. Despite the insane (and slightly worrying) weekly advances of AI, the most common complaint I still hear is: “ChatGPT doesn’t sound like me.” If that's you, you've probably tried the most obvious thing: Just add more context. I remember being at dinner with a friend who showed me one of his AI projects in Claude. He must have had 20+ documents inside it. And one of my community students does something similar - collecting advice from the best YouTube strategists he can find… …and putting all of it into one project. It seems logical. More knowledge = better responses, right? Not necessarily, for a simple reason: Eventually, your context starts fighting itself. For staters, even your own style guide can contain contradictions. Now imagine adding a newsletter swipe file from two YouTube strategists to your context pile. One writes their hooks using "Target, transformation, stakes". The other uses "Proof, promise, plan". Who's right? Whose formula should ChatGPT or Claude use to write your hook? And this is just the start of your troubles. Imagine how these contradictions will build up once you start adding 15, 20, 30 documents to your projects. The problem is, the AI doesn’t have a little judge inside it to decide which rule is correct. Sometimes it favours one. Sometimes it compromises. Sometimes the answer changes depending on your prompt. And it only gets worse. Because AI models become less reliable at finding and using the right information as the amount of context grows. Large AI projects may pull in information they think is relevant, rather than actually reading every document in full. That means the absolute gold dust you heard in a podcast and added to your scriptwriting project yesterday... might never get read by the AI. Think of it like this: Continually adding more context documents to an AI project is like adding endless ingredients to a recipe. Each ingredient might be tasty. And some will work really well together. But pretty soon, you'll end up with a big bowl of brown slop. So... what's the solution? Well, Anthropic (who makes Claude) explained this very helpfully: Use the “smallest possible set of high-signal tokens.” In other words: Keep your context minimal. Keep it relevant. And every so often, clean it up. So, if you've got a project in ChatGPT or Claude that's getting a bit out of hand, start a new chat and paste the prompt in the comments below. More context can help. But only when it’s the right context.

AI told three novice climbers Mount Shasta was only an 8-hour ascent.

It was really a 2-day hike, and they needed to be rescued after 30 hours.

They used Google's Gemini to plan the trip in California.

It told them the summit was an 8-hour ascent and to pack simple carbohydrates rather than fats, because fats "take too long to digest". 

So they set off at 3am with food and water for a short day out.

→ By 1pm they were only at 11,000ft, past the turnaround, they kept going anyway
→ They summited at 7pm and called 911 for directions in the dark
→ Then their phone died, taking with it the AllTrails app that had been their only map
→ They spent the night out before rangers reached them on Monday morning and walked them down

Nick Meyers, the lead climbing ranger, said this is "the first year where we've started to have some AI fallout".

The climbers said "We relied too much on AI rather than our own critical thinking."

That's why we must recognise the same habit, whether you're planning a climb or signing off a report at work. 

Ask the model where the fact, figure, or assumption came from and how sure it is. 

Then put the same question to someone who has actually done it. 

Triangulating ideas with real humans will never go out of style.

hook: A founder told me last week that his attention was fried and "needed to do a dopamine detox".
text:
A founder told me last week that his attention was fried and "needed to do a dopamine detox".

I hear a version of this every month… It's BS.

Dopamine detoxes don't work. They can't work. Dopamine is a neurochemical your brain secretes. You cannot fast from it any more than you can fast from your own blood.

The entire premise is broken.

And I get why it's easy to buy: the diagnosis feels right. You ARE spending ten hours on enticing, easy work: the inbox, the tabs, the Slack messages, the "research."

It does feel like an addiction. So abstinence sounds like the cure.

Except the real cure to being permanently distracted is changing what makes the brain secrete it in the first place.

When the first thing you do every morning is email, you train your brain to anticipate easy, shallow work.

By the time you sit down for the hard task at 2 pm, you're negotiating against a brain that already got paid a hundred times for the easy stuff.

Of course it refuses.

You trained it to refuse, one easy task at a time.

That's why the average founder wastes up to 70% of his day in distractions (ten hours at the desk, three that move the needle).

And this compounds for years. Run those wasted hours at your own rate, and you know exactly what it's been costing you.

The solution is to flip it: the hardest, high-leverage task goes first, in a protected block, before anything else. Nothing matters until that's done.

Then a short rest-and-recovery protocol, and back at it.

Another block on the 2nd-highest-leverage work.

Do that daily, and the payoff starts attaching to the hard thing itself.

Starting gets easier.

The task that would have rolled forward all week ships before lunch.

The day compresses on its own: done by mid-afternoon, evening actually yours.

And at a 6-figure revenue level, where every hour that counts is founder labor, the hours are the revenue input. More of them, and the number follows.

I call it dopamine sequencing.

Not detoxing, not monk mode, not deleting apps for a weekend just to redownload them by Monday.

Sequencing.

Hard things first, until they're automatic and lower-level work becomes repulsive.

Nothing is wrong with your brain. It learned the wrong order, and order is trainable. Every elite founder you admire runs some version of this, whether he named it or not.

What goes in your first block tomorrow?

hook: The CMO role is in decline. Some founders I know aren't hiring for it anymore. They're building marketing differently.
text:
The CMO role is in decline. Some founders I know aren't hiring for it anymore. They're building marketing differently. 

CMO roles in B2B are down 10 percentage points in 12 months.

I’ve talked to some founder friends. They see marketing as growth and brand. They’ve repeatedly hired a leader who fails at one end. Or, more commonly, they can’t find anyone who can spike at both ends. They end up putting brand into product and demand/growth into sales, and just not hiring a CMO.

Why is this happening? 

Founders have changed. The most common question I used to get from my founder network was “Is my marketing leader any good?” I still get asked that, but a new generation of founders has real takes on marketing; they’re in the weeds and have a very high bar for what they think marketing should be.

The work changed. AI pushed both halves of marketing to the extremes. Growth/demand is more technical than ever. Brand/product marketing has to be better at narrative and positioning than ever. It’s so hard to spike at both ends. 

Marketing has never mattered more, and that’s why the role is shrinking. Expectations are rising faster than the talent to meet them.  

Splitting marketing isn't the long-term solution.

A great marketing leader excels at hiring talent and retaining talent. It’s how they build a team that spikes at both halves. But to do that, the marketing leader needs to know what good looks like. They themselves need to be incredibly strong at both ends. That talent pool is small.

But the talent pool of a sales leader who can hire an exceptional demand leader and retain them, and a CPO who can hire an exceptional brand/product marketing leader and retain them, is even smaller. You’ve just doubled the problem. And now you’re building a marketing team with no shared quality bar. You’re also deciding that growth/demand and brand/product marketing are very separate things. That’s not true.

Take, for example, a company scaling via paid advertising. Paid at scale has to align with positioning, or you're forgettable the moment you stop spending.

The CMO role isn't dying, but it’s currently in decline. Expectations went up, and the talent pipeline didn't.

My advice:

If you're a marketer who can do both halves, this is the best moment there's been to be one — cash in. You’ve earned it.

If you're a founder: not hiring a CMO beats hiring the wrong CMO. Hold the bar, build a keep-warm list of your dream hires, take them on as advisors, angel investors, etc, and wait for the person who meets what you need.

P.S - did a full episode on Marketing Against the Grain, out today.

Some personal thoughts I shared on episode 237 that dropped today:

I’m not sure if it's just a momentary thing, but GPT-6 Astra is the first model release where I feel more dread than excitement.

For the last couple years, as I have pleaded with people on the podcast to take AI’s impending impact on jobs and society seriously—and have a sense of urgency to prepare—I’ve described it more as a gradual slope than a cliff.

I am increasingly starting to feel like the slope is nearing the cliff.

While the technology is racing ahead in its capabilities, we have school systems banning it, politicians calling for bans on data centers and more powerful models, and we have citizens protesting against AI and vilifying the people building it.

Meanwhile, some government officials seem to only be able to view it through the single lens of, “If we don’t build it someone else (i.e. China) will.”

Something has to give here.

I’m honestly not sure what to feel right now. 

It’s like I’ve been watching this train coming at us for the last 15 years (I started researching AI in 2011), and now, all of sudden, everyone is in panic mode because we, as a society, didn’t do enough to prepare.

I feel like I haven’t personally done enough. Maybe I could have done more to convey a sense of urgency, but I didn’t want to create fear. So I tempered my words. 

I feel like the lab leaders failed to understand the significance of what they were building, and be proactive about presenting solutions to the impact it would have. 

I feel like business leaders and educational leaders waited too long. 

Now we are stuck in a very challenging period of time in which the labs are going to keep racing ahead building more capable models. The economics of their business models—and the competitive environment between labs and nations—require it (in their minds).

The public will increasingly push back. 

Rightfully so.

hook: B2B isn't B2C. People don't shop for "concepts." They shop for capabilities.
text:
B2B isn't B2C. People don't shop for "concepts." They shop for capabilities.

I'm in a WhatsApp group with Kyle Poyar and a bunch of founders, entrepreneurs, consultants, freelancers, etc. 

People will commonly ask others for recommendations both for service providers and for software products. 

And the WAY they phrase these questions is extremely consistent:

"Do you know anyone (or anything) that does ________?"

That blank is always filled in with specific activities, functions, capabilities, etc. 

It is NEVER filled in with business outcomes.

I scanned for weeks and weeks to see if anyone had been "shopping for an outcome." 

It simply does not happen. 

Nobody is asking, "do you have any tool recommendations that will increase my revenue?" 

If you're in any communities or groups yourself, go look at how people ask for recommendations.

Likely, you'll see the exact same thing:

"Do you know anyone who does SEO?"

"Does anyone have a tool they'd recommend for recording sales calls?"

"Is anyone using a platform for automating LinkedIn outreach?"

These "dark social" conversations are happening at the level of capabilities, not outcomes.

This is extremely important in how you position your product.

Go look at your homepage: do you clearly spell out the CAPABILITIES that your product or service offers?

Do you explain the specific use cases your product supports?

Or do you mainly lead with OUTCOMES that you drive? 

If you haven't done the former, they won't care about the latter.

Peep Laja runs Wynter, arguably the biggest qualitative market research platform in B2B, and he has seen this represented over and over in their qualitative survey data. 

People don't care about the "why" until they first understand "the what" (sorry Simon Sinek). 

The reason B2C is different is that when you're selling shoes, you don't first need to explain what a shoe is. You can assume a baseline level of understanding and then sell "athleticism" or "adventure" or whatever.

But in B2B software, it's completely flipped. 

To put it as simply as humanly possible...

WORKERS do WORK.

WORKERS want to know if your software will support the actual WORK they are doing.

And they actually care about THAT more than whether or not you stand for "adventure" or "the future of work" or whatever.

→ Optimises for rankings on search results pages

AEO (Answer Engine Optimisation):

That overlap is where teams go wrong.

__

Companies say they value creativity, performance, judgement, adaptability, well-being, and leadership.

hook: Boy, people are really missing the point of this headline. The AI jobs apocalypse is POSTPONED, not eliminated - for two
text:
Boy, people are really missing the point of this headline. The AI jobs apocalypse is POSTPONED, not eliminated - for two huge reasons, and the data in The Economist illustrates both:


The Economist says AI has created about 1 million American jobs against about 200,000 layoffs. Which leads to a lot of "See? AI creates jobs!"

But we gotta look deeper at the data:

REASON 1: The jobs boom is from BUILDING AI, not using it.

That's where the word 'postpone' comes in.

About 320,000 of those jobs are building data centers - electricians, HVAC specialists, grid engineers. About 640,000 are building the AI itself - engineers who make the models, data annotators, "heads of AI," stuff like that.

The boom comes from constructing the thing. But the impact of companies actually putting AI to work has barely registered.


REASON 2: Most people are not really using AI yet.

I hate to sound like a broken record. But there is a vast chasm between AI being ABLE to do a job and AI actually DOING a job. (We're in a ton of companies, we see this.)

A treadmill can absolutely get you into shape. Whether you get on it every day is a completely different story.

Most people type a question into a chat box a few times a week. And that qualifies as "an AI user."

But a power user runs agents that do the research, the analysis, the planning - work you used to bring in consultants for - in an afternoon. 

That's not me saying you're behind if you're not running agents - agents are simplier than people imagine. Working with agents is really just a *way* of working, not some brainy robot built by a genius. Anyone can do it. It's not so different than working with chatbots.

Now, in the rare corners where people ARE really using it, the article has its most interesting data. 

The jobs that were supposed to disappear first are growing. Paralegal employment rose about 11% from 2023 to 2025. Market-research analysts rose 6%. The national average was about 2.5%. AI made those people faster, which made their services cheaper, which created more demand for them. 

But even The Economist hedges here - it's "possible" demand rises - because the using-AI economy is still too small to measure.

Now compare that to the jobs actually falling: customer service, down 10%. Admin assistants, down about 15%. Those are roles where AI is being used ON people - deployed from above to absorb routine tasks. The paralegals are using it themselves.

When AI gets used on you, your job shrinks. When you use AI, your job grows.

Don't read this headline as "we're safe" as much as "we're early."

I'm not being pessimistic, just reminding us that we gotta move on this.

hook: After training 400+ founders, I can tell you the one signal every single one of them reads backward. It shows up the sec
text: After training 400+ founders, I can tell you the one signal every single one of them reads backward. It shows up the second you sit down to do the thing with the biggest impact on the business right now: outreach, hiring, firing. As you get close to the hard thing, your chest tightens, and your mind goes looking for an easier task. And you don't do it. Every founder I've worked with read that tightness the same way. As a stop sign. As evidence that today isn't the day, or worse, that something in them is off. Nothing is off with them. They just haven't learned how the brain works yet. Your brain is a prediction machine. It runs a model of the world, uses it to guess what happens next, and builds that model from everything you've done so far. That model is the map that subconsciously drives your behavior. And the map is never the territory. Tasks that are easy, sometimes downright simple, get labeled hard and complex by a brain that has never done them, and that label is what creates the tightness. Every prediction it makes carries some error, and the map uses that error to update. Your brain treats the task as a threat and, under stress, reverts to its defaults. Which means the moment you most want to leave the desk is the only moment the map is open for editing. Nothing else opens it, not the podcast or the book about focus or the retreat or whatever. Direct, live exposure to the thing does. You can know exactly why you avoid outreach and keep avoiding it for another year: the map moves on evidence, and the evidence it accepts is the completed rep. Your brain rewires on completed reps, not on knowing better. You can rewire those defaults, and that's all performance training is. You didn't choose that map. Nobody did. It shipped with defaults built for a world where the thing that made your chest tighten could kill you, and it has been doing what it was designed to do. Save energy, avoid the unknown, keep you where you were last week. That wasn't your fault. It is now, because it's trainable. You already know this. You do it three times a week in the gym. The last two reps are the ones that hurt, and you have never once read that as a sign to quit. You read it as the part that counts. Your brain reads the same signal. Apply the same logic to the tasks you're tempted to avoid. The founders who scale don't face less resistance than you do. I've tracked this for six years. They stopped treating the signal as information about themselves and started treating it as information about a default that needs updating. That's the whole use of performance skills: find the highest leverage task, go straight at it, finish it, update the map, and move up a level.

text:
I spent months trying to hand the AI side of my business to my team.

It made sense at the time. I don't have spare hours lying around, and getting someone else to figure it out felt like the sensible way to get it off my plate.

Then I spent two days at a business summit last month and realised I had completely skipped a step.

A few different speakers came back to the same idea in different ways: before you hand something over, you need to understand it properly yourself.

So, naturally, I spent the flight home doing exactly that.
I built my own AI Bot. Her name is QUEEN. We're already besties.

It's funny how quickly something shifts once you actually get stuck into the work yourself. I'm still learning, but I now understand what I'm asking my team to do, what good looks like, and where AI can genuinely make things easier.
And that got me thinking about Property Assist.

We have spent years helping property managers take work off their plates. Inspections are a good example. You don't need to personally walk through every property to know what's happening in your portfolio. You need the right people, the right systems and enough visibility to stay in control.

I've always believed in that kind of delegation.

What I hadn't applied as well to myself was the bit that comes before it: understanding the work well enough to know what should actually be handed over.

I had skipped that step with AI.

Joshua Scutts described every task as essentially being either human judgement or plumbing. I really liked that distinction.

Simon Beard's point about decision-making being the apex skill in business tied into that for me too.

And before you automate anything, his process was simple: question it, delete what shouldn't exist, simplify what's left, then speed it up and automate it.

Alex van Staden reinforced that idea from another angle. The human designs the system, the agents run it. And his advice was to start with one agent solving one real problem rather than building some elaborate army of bots before you've figured out what you actually need.

I'm thinking less about "How can I automate this?" and more about "Do I understand AI well enough myself to decide what should happen next?"

There was another idea from Emil Juresic that I've been thinking about too: don't just score the business, score yourself. Because a bigger business isn't much of a win if the person running it is slowly getting crushed by it.

That one hit a little differently.

The summit meant two days away from my kids, which I felt more than I expected. At some point, I'd quite like to bring a nanny to these things so I can squeeze in some kid time between the businessy stuff.

I'm only half joking.

I came home with plenty of notes, but that's the one thread I keep coming back to.

Build the business. Use the technology. Delegate the work.
But understand what you're building before you hand it over.

Still thinking about that one.

hook: Why does AI's business advice sound smart but feel generic?
text:
Why does AI's business advice sound smart but feel generic?

Researchers are calling it “trendslop”…

It describes what happens when AI defaults to buzzy, fashionable ideas over well-reasoned ones. 

Ask an LLM a strategic question, and you’ll often get back in return something that sounds smart but reads a bit like a highly sanitised, jargon-filled LinkedIn post.

A recent HBR article tested this by having researchers run seven leading LLMs, including Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, and Grok, across core strategic tensions. 

Across thousands of simulations, the models clustered tightly around the same “trendy” answers regardless of context.

LLMs are trained on the internet, which produces far more content about “finding your unique value proposition” than case studies on supply chain efficiency. 

So the models absorb what sounds good in modern business discourse over what actually works in competitive markets. Hiring, positioning, product decisions, anything that requires a real trade-off gets shaped by this exact invisible hand.

“Workslop” is AI-generated content that looks good but lacks the meaty substance to move the task forward.

“Trendslop” is workslop showing up in strategic advice. Answers that look like finished thinking but actually carry none of it whatsoever.

If anyone with the same prompt would get your answer, the model knows nothing about your situation, so it reaches for what’s common. Your context is the missing piece of the puzzle.

Give the LLM your position first, robustly, then ask it to do the task. I recommend asking the following:

1. Make the strongest case for the unfashionable option 
2. Surface companies that succeeded by doing the opposite of what’s trendy
3. Steelman the case for and against my idea before you provide your recommendation

You might just surprise yourself.

After all, these questions rely on your judgement, and that’s the part no prompt can replace.

I wrote about Workslop here: https://lnkd.in/e97ae9PD

And follow me Alex Banks for daily AI highlights and insights.

text:
A robot in a Dutch onion field is making 28 irreversible decisions every second, and not one of them involves a human.

Herbicide rules are tightening across Europe. Agricultural labor gets harder to find every season. Most responses to that squeeze have been incremental.

cropr, a Dutch startup, went the other way. Their autonomous Weedr scans every plant with onboard cameras. AI classifies it as crop or weed in real time. Only then do the lasers fire, burning the weed's chlorophyll with millimeter precision while the crop beside it stays untouched.

No blanket spraying. No chemicals. Far less impact on the soil. The machine navigates itself with GPS RTK, runs 24 hours a day, and fires 28 shots every second across onions, carrots, chicory, and lilies.

I went deep on this one because it clarifies something I think leaders are underweighting. We have spent three years discussing AI that drafts, summarizes, and recommends. This is AI that acts, physically, with no undo button. A misclassification does not produce a weak paragraph. It destroys a crop.

That raises the bar on model accuracy, edge latency, failure modes, and liability. It also raises the ceiling. Once perception gets cheap and reliable enough, entire categories of chemical and manual input become optional.

Agriculture is simply where it surfaced first.

creator: Clara Shih
hook: My life was completely changed by 9/11.
text:
My life was completely changed by 9/11.
Not right away. On that bright, blue Tuesday morning, I was moving into a new apartment in Hudson Heights, way up near the George Washington Bridge, far from Ground Zero. My TV wasn't yet working, and social media didn't exist, so I didn't see the footage until that evening, sitting in a neighborhood restaurant, watching the towers fall over and over. I didn't know anyone who died.
But two and a half years later, freshly divorced and dating again, I met a sweet man at a mutual friend's birthday party. When he asked me out, I asked my friend if there was anything I should know.
“He’s so nice,” she said. “But his fiancee died on 9/11. That’s how I know him. Through her.”
My heart sank. Newly divorced woman and 9/11 widower? The odds of romantic success seemed low.
On our first date, walking through Central Park, he told me he had met his fiancee on September 11, 1999. He'd made an anniversary dinner reservation for that night, only to fall to his knees in his office after hearing the news.
I could barely hold it together as we walked past Strawberry Fields. I bent down to pet a passing beagle puppy. “Amy loved dogs,” he said sadly.
Amy Hope Lamonsoff was 29. A professional event planner, she had arrived early that morning at Windows on the World, at the top of the North Tower, to set up for a company breakfast.
After a few dates, he invited me over for dinner. As I sat on the couch, he knelt down and put a small, incredibly heavy slab of rock in my hand. “They gave all the victims' families a piece,” he said. It was a piece of the Twin Towers, inscribed with the 9/11 date.
For a long time, I was overwhelmed by Amy's presence in our relationship, and by the images and memories of 9/11 that seemed to hang over the city even years later.
A couple of years after that, he took me to the Family Room at One Liberty Plaza, a private place for victims' families set up in 2002, overlooking the World Trade Center site. It was filled with photographs, missing-person posters, handwritten notes, poems, cards, artwork, flowers and stuffed animals.
It was suffocating.
Twenty-five years later, 9/11 rarely comes up between us anymore. My husband and I have been happily married for 18 years, and 9/11 is also connected to something beautiful: my niece was born that day in 2008.
But it will always remain hard to wrap my mind around the fact that the end for Amy Hope Lamonsoff was a new beginning for me.
I hope you Google her. She is still missed fiercely by those who knew and loved her.

hook: (Warning: rant incoming) Okay, I hate this "AGI era" talk. It means nothing outside IPO pricing. Is GPT6 amazing? Yes. B
text:
(Warning: rant incoming) Okay, I hate this "AGI era" talk. It means nothing outside IPO pricing. Is GPT6 amazing? Yes. But AGI-ra talk isn't about work, it's about a tool. It's like saying "With this new treadmill technology, everyone will finally be healthy!" Work doesn't change because of a tool. It changes when people work differently.

Let me vent a little more here.

We keep confusing technical breakthroughs with behavior shift, and we've done it monthly since 2023. 

Each phase - internet access, voice, images, computer use, better voice, connectors, agents - figured to be THE MOMENT. None were. Everyone's still using it like a search engine. Why? 

Because this is not about tech. It's about behavior.


How is it possible that we are letting the tech get SO FAR AHEAD of the people using it? 

People don't need the latest in treadmill technology. They need somebody helping them change small habits so they put on their running shoes and get out the door every day. 

If you're a leader in a company: focus on your people and getting them great with chatbots. Nobody wants to hear that, I get it. 

But that's where the first level of value lives - not in leaping ahead to agents your enterprise can't use and your people (the ones who actually deliver the value!) have no concept of.

The delta between companies that use AI well and companies that don't has nothing to do with tech. 

It has to do with whether their people have shifted their behavior. And that doesn't live up in the GPT6 stratosphere. It lives down with people using Copilot better, every day.

What about disruption and job loss? 

Will AI get so good it can replace people? 

Probably, yeah. 

But the AGI crowd talks tech in one breath and "over the next few years" in the next. If the tech is already here, the only thing those few years are waiting on is people.

Think about what would actually have to happen for this tech to change work at scale:

Either everyone suddenly starts using AI well - and if people were using even a basic chatbot with real proficiency, you'd already see disruption in the labor market.

Or the tech gets so revolutionary that enterprises can simply buy it and replace people. That's not how tech works, and it's not how corporations work.

We are not weeks away from AI taking over jobs. AI still can't run a vending machine by itself. Does that sound like AGI to you? No, of course not. 

But the AGI goalposts moved. Before it was "run a company." Now it's "does brilliant things." Those are VERY different.

AI needs people. Left alone, sure, it can do amazing things 4 out of 5 times - and that fifth time, it loses a client. 

Nobody takes that bet. 

Here's the reality:

Most people are still using a basic chatbot. That's not the end of the world. Because the gap that matters is at the lowest levels of AI, not the highest.

And we are spending all our time on the highest.

hook: At the core of AI, you really just need:
text:
At the core of AI, you really just need:
 
1) a thing that does
2) connections into tools
3) a place to hold stuff
4) a spot to share and update
 
In slot 1, we're talking AI agents like Codex or Claude Code or GrokBot. Whether you have a daily driver or a mix and match, doesn't matter. Just an LLM-based system that can spin up hundreds or thousands of agents across multiple tasks at once.
 
In slot 2, we're talking toggling them toggles and connecting Codex to places like Gmail, Stripe, Magnific, Remotion, web browser, computer use, etc. Your risk tolerance will determine how many toggles you toggle. I now feel comfortable with both Codex and Claude Code having access to my GDrive, Fireflies, etc. and did not feel comfortable when the tool connections first came out.
 
In slot 3, when AI creates a document or a dashboard, where is it? This could be Google Drive, Dropbox, GitHub, your local storage, Obisidian. But it needs to be a place for your agents to build up their artifacts, task managers, and brain. Their memory. The more multiplayer your system is, the more IAM and cloud matter (aka local storage won't cut it).
 
In slot 4, you need a hub. When AI completes tasks for you or wants to ask you something, where is it doing that? I use Slack as my team's hub and we have enabled Claude Tag and built our own Claude Code apps as well.
 
Am I missing anything? Let me know.

text:
I read around 300 posts last week. I could tell which ones were written by someone who actually cared.
 
Five hard truths about AI on LinkedIn, plus what to do instead, and what the data says about your reach.
 
For our November update we are analysing over 400,000 new posts, as AI content leaves fingerprints, and the numbers show them.
 
Five things I keep coming back to.

 
1. "Everyone has access to the same AI. That's exactly why your own opinion just became the scarcest asset on LinkedIn."
 
Sameness is not your best path to impact.
 
→ Before you prompt anything, write one personal sentence nobody else could have written. Build the post around defending that.

 
2. "AI writes your post in 6 seconds. Your audience decides in 3 whether you actually meant any of it."
 
These first 3 seconds decide whether the next 30 happen.
 
→ Alway write your hook yourself. Don't tell me you don't have 20 words in you.

 
3. "Your competitors are posting more than ever. They're also saying less than ever."
 
Volume went up across almost every industry (+18%). Average engagement per post did not follow (-16%).
 
→ Consider cutting your posting frequency by a third and put those hours into commenting.

 
4. "If a prompt can produce your thought leadership, it was never leadership. It was formatting."
 
Frameworks, lists, and tidy takeaways are easy to generate, however judgement is not.
 
→ Add the thing AI cannot know. A number from your own work. A client conversation. A decision you got wrong.

 
5. "We asked AI to save us time on LinkedIn. Now we spend that time reading everyone else's AI."
 
Feeds full of competent, forgettable content train people to scroll faster.
 
→ Read your draft out loud. Every line you would never say to a colleague gets deleted.

 
None of this makes AI the enemy. 
I use it daily. 
But I use it to sharpen what I already think, never to decide what I think (!)
 
That distinction shows up in the performance data more clearly than I expected.
 AI didn't lower the bar for content. It raised the bar for having something worth saying.
 
The November update of the Algorithm Insights Report 2026 goes deep on this: how AI-assisted posts actually perform, where reach drops off, and what it does to conversion.

hook: It's everywhere, but what does "AI Literacy" actually mean?
text:
It's everywhere, but what does "AI Literacy" actually mean? 
I asked Hugh Milward, VP of External Affairs at Microsoft

My own definition of AI literacy is simple and has 4 dimensions:

1. Understanding what (generative) AI is (that it's not Google) 
2. How to speak to it so it understands 
3. What it's good and bad at 
4. How to stay safe using it 

It's the very basics, a 'get started here' button.

And it's essential for EVERYONE. 
Not just white-collar workers. 
Not just those of working age, either. 

I feel AI, if taught properly and accessibly, could actually start to solve some of the big issues we have with digital exclusion in the UK. 

For example, I'm watching my mom use her voice to search using Gemini AI now instead of fiddling around with Google. Because she's using her voice, she's naturally giving it the context it needs to give her a good result. I'm teaching her to think carefully about the results she gets. 

For me, the next step after AI Literacy then is proper skill-building: the frameworks, the features, the workflows, and I call that "AI Fluency".

I'm really keen to hear your thoughts on: 

(a) What AI literacy actually is to you
(b) How can we build literacy for everyone, not just digital natives at work?

PS It's been a long time coming, and I know I've promised it for ages, but our free AI Literacy for All course is finally on the way (blame it on my perfectionism)

Meta Ads verandert hard. Gisteren kregen we bij Meta een kijkje in wat eraan komt. 🚀

Op uitnodiging van Meta was ik, samen met Sebastiaan en Luuk, bij Soho House Amsterdam voor een aantal sessies over de nieuwste ontwikkelingen binnen Meta Ads.

Voor mij vooral waardevol omdat veel van wat besproken werd direct aansluit op hoe we bij CRE8 naar groei kijken.

Niet alleen advertenties draaien en optimaliseren, maar continu kijken waar we voor onze klanten meer groei kunnen realiseren.

Een paar dingen die ik meeneem:

→ Creators & Partnership Ads worden een steeds belangrijker onderdeel van performance. Niet alleen creators inzetten om content te maken, maar hun bereik en geloofwaardigheid direct koppelen aan advertising.

→ Video wordt nóg belangrijker. Meer dan 60% van de tijd op Instagram en Facebook wordt besteed aan video. Dat betekent voor ons: nog slimmer nadenken over hoe we content produceren én hoe we bestaande assets met AI sneller doorvertalen naar nieuwe formats.

→ Creative diversity is key. Niet eindeloos variaties maken op dezelfde advertentie, maar verschillende concepten, hooks, formats en boodschappen ontwikkelen. Van één losse asset naar een compleet creative systeem.

→ AI gaat daarin enorm versnellen. Creatives genereren, statische beelden naar video vertalen en campagnes steeds verder automatisch laten optimaliseren.

Al met al super waardevolle learnings!

Veel van wat we gisteren hebben gezien, kunnen we meenemen in de manier waarop we bij CRE8 campagnes bouwen en klanten laten groeien. Sterkere creatives, meer relevante content, slimmer gebruik van creators en AI en uiteindelijk meer resultaat uit hetzelfde advertentiebudget. 

Niet wachten tot ontwikkelingen de standaard zijn, maar ze vroeg begrijpen en direct onderdeel maken van onze aanpak. 🚀

Thanks Meta, Leo Pinto, Rebecca Hindle, Ciara Harrison & Enrique Avila Asapche voor de uitnodiging en interessante sessies!

text:
Harvard studied why strategy execution fails.

Only 50% of middle managers could name ANY of their company's top priorities.

These are the people you're counting on to deliver the plan.

Yet most companies have so many priorities, their teams can't tell which ones to work on.

Critical Success Factors fix that. They're the 3 to 5 things your business MUST do well to win.

D. Ronald Daniel at McKinsey wrote about them in 1961. John Rockart at MIT Sloan gave them the name in a 1979 Harvard Business Review paper.

They've been around for 65 years, but most leaders still don't use them.
