text:
5 money rules that have changed my life.

(And may change yours)

1. No unforced errors. There’s a concept in tennis that amateur tennis is a Loser’s Game: 80% of points are lost on unforced errors. You win by avoiding errors and waiting for your opponent to make errors. The truth is that most games in life are Loser’s Games. You can get pretty damn far by just avoiding unforced errors: Silly impulse purchases, avoidable debt, emotional investing, neglected responsibilities. Slow down, think clearly, and protect yourself from…yourself.

2. Never allow self-worth to be dictated by net worth. The moment your identity becomes tied to your financial status, you hand your emotional sovereignty to external forces. Markets fluctuate. Seasons change. Businesses rise and fall. Your sense of worth must be anchored in something deeper: Character, values, relationships, interests, service, etc. Money is a tool, it should never be the foundation of who you are.

3. Track financial progress like an athlete tracks performance progress. My wife and I have used and loved Origin https://lnkd.in/gh8NaC97  since our son was born in 2022. Its new proactive financial intelligence tools look at your entire picture and surface recommendations automatically to help you make the most of your money, without you having to know what to ask. Highly recommend it (and recently invested as well!). You can’t improve what you don’t track. Use a financial tracking and management tool to get a clear picture to build from.
 
4. Never use money to optimize the life out of your life. When you start making more money, an entire menu of options materializes to reduce life's minor frictions. You can hire a personal chef, a full time cleaner, a staff, a driver. But sometimes that friction was what created meaning—and the obsessive removal of friction does more harm than good. Cherish the meaningful friction in your life. The friction that makes you slow down and embrace the ordinary.

5. Use money as a tool for more meaningful forms of wealth. Perhaps this isn’t surprising (as I literally wrote the book on it), but I believe the best uses of money are those that create one of four things in your life: Time, experiences with people you love, purpose, or health. Above a certain level, money is best viewed as a tool to create those other things, not a goal in and of itself.

True wealth isn’t a number on a screen. It’s a life you live by design. It’s built, not found, through a set of small, intentional rules you follow every single day.

Remember: Your wealthy life may be enabled by money, but in the end, it will be defined by everything else.

——

hook: I was on the 42nd floor of 1515 Broadway in the heart of Times Square on 9/11.
text:
I was on the 42nd floor of 1515 Broadway in the heart of Times Square on 9/11.
 
Much of that day was a blur. I was just starting out in TV back then. My first real job, at Nickelodeon.
 
My boss and I stood at a window looking down at lower Manhattan. We watched the smoke billow into the sky while the live reports came in across every channel.
 
He told me to go home.
 
Before I left, I checked my email. There was a message from my dad in Kentucky. It was short. He said he loved me and to be vigilant.
 
The walk from Times Square home to Astoria, Queens was a slow one. On the 59th Street bridge I jumped in the back of a stranger's pickup truck with a bunch of other people. We didn't say much. We just looked toward lower Manhattan in silence as we crossed.
 
Cell phones weren't working. I couldn't make a call or get one.
 
When I got back to my apartment, my phone rang. My landline. The "home phone."
 
Over the next few hours I sat on that home phone and talked to my family in Michigan and Kentucky. I told them I was fine and not to worry.
 
Reaching my New York friends wasn't as easy. Most of them only had cell phones. And some of them worked in finance in lower Manhattan.
 
I kept trying my good friend Dan on his cell.
 
Dan and I had met a couple of years earlier studying abroad in Spain. Every time I tried him, I'd get a weird sound, a message that the networks were down, or nothing at all.
 
Then one time it rang. And I heard Dan's voice. "T-Neves." My nickname. Somehow I'd gotten through.
 
We ran down the names of our mutual friends to make sure everybody was safe. They were. Then I asked Dan if he'd talked to his family in southern California. He hadn't. He couldn't get through. He gave me their home number and I tried a three-way call from my home phone.
 
His mom picked up on the first ring.
 
I remember Dan saying, "Mom, I'm ok." And I heard his mother cry as she told him she loved him and how worried she and his father had been. Tears ran down my face listening to that moment between a mother and her son.
 
Dan and I talked for another minute after that, then hung up.
 
I sat in my apartment and tried to make sense of it. All the loss. All the change. I still haven't. 
 
Not many of my friends have a "home phone" anymore. Just cells. I still do. And I probably always will.
 
May God bless all those who lost their lives on 9/11, and their families and friends.

text: You wouldn't hand an athlete a book to fix their performance. Yet it's somehow accepted that founders should rely on books, podcasts, and the occasional fire-walking guru to fix theirs. When did we decide that founders, who face uncertainty, stress and risk every day, should wing how they handle it instead of training for it? I've met folks who've listened to every Huberman podcast at 2x speed and still can't get things done consistently. We've worked with 400+ founders, and most of them came to us after years in "self help purgatory," hunting down books, podcasts and motivational videos hoping something would finally click. The alternative is systematic performance training. Every professional in a high-stakes environment (athletes, astronauts, special forces) is trained, not motivated. Training, unlike self-development, barely relies on information to create change. It relies on analysis, execution, and measurement. For founders, that means: → Find the specific skill, belief or behavior gap that's preventing action → Build exactly what closes that gap → Expand the capacity to handle stress under pressure Self-development is entertainment for founders. Fine on its own. But it isn't training, and training is what has a real impact on the business.

text:
Twenty-five years ago today, I was loading in the Broadway tour of Les Misérables when I noticed a crowd of staff forming around the small television in the breakroom.

All work had suddenly stopped.

On the grainy screen, one of the Twin Towers was on fire. I was on the West Coast, standing among crew and company members from New York whose families and friends were on the other side of the country.

No one quite knew what we were watching yet.

Then the second plane hit.

Time stood still as the events of that morning continued to unfold. The towers fell. The Pentagon burned. A plane went down in a Pennsylvania field. Thousands of lives were taken. Countless others were changed forever.

Twenty-five years is long enough for an entire generation to grow up knowing September 11 only as history.

For those of us who watched it happen in real time, it somehow still feels impossibly close. I can still see that little television, feel the silence in the room, and remember the desperate need to reach the people we loved.

This morning on my way home from Drive, I boarded a 6 a.m. flight out of Burlington, connected through Chicago, and was home in Boise by noon. I spent much of the trip thinking about that other morning, and about how deeply it changed the simple act of getting on an airplane.

This week, 2,977 points of light rose above New York City and traced the towers back into the night sky. For a few quiet moments, something missing for twenty-five years took shape again.

And so did the enormity of all we lost.

Behind every light was a human being. A whole life filled with people they loved, places they belonged, ordinary mornings, inside jokes, unfinished plans, and futures that should have been theirs.

I also remember the courage of those who ran toward danger, and the extraordinary care people showed one another in the days that followed. Strangers offered whatever they had. People called home, held each other a little tighter, and reached across distances that had seemed enormous the day before.

That is part of what stays with me, too.

Today, I’m holding close the lives we lost, the families who have carried that loss for a quarter century, the survivors and first responders who still live with its effects, and every person for whom this anniversary makes the distance between then and now disappear.

Twenty-five years later, the best way I know to honor them is still in the way we treat one another: with kindness, courage, tenderness, and the belief that our shared humanity will always be worth protecting.

Your pal,
Pete 💛

hook: “Festina lente.” Make haste slowly. Digital tools can speed up work, but transformation begins by questioning the system
text:
“Festina lente.” Make haste slowly. Digital tools can speed up work, but transformation begins by questioning the system they are asked to accelerate.

Here is the trap.

Move a five-step approval process into software and celebrate because everything runs faster.

The workflow is faster. The logic is unchanged.

If two approvals add no judgment, remove them. If employees keep entering information that already exists elsewhere, connect the systems instead.

Only then does technology have something better to accelerate.

A redesigned workflow works when the people using it understand why decisions move differently and can operate within that logic.

Technology can execute an existing process faster, but it cannot decide whether that process deserves to exist in the same form.

Before asking technology for more speed, ask the system whether it needs a different direction.

#DigitalTransformation #ProcessRedesign

Hot take: A boring life is an underrated advantage.

In 2010, I’d spent a decade going a mile a minute building my business.

Then I had chest pain shooting down my left arm. An ER visit. Nitroglycerin. And a specialist who asked me twice if I was really going to skip that flight.

(I got on the plane anyway.)

They emergency landed it in France. Strapped to a stretcher, the only thing I said to the paramedic was: please don't let me die, I have a 5-year-old son.

That wasn't hard work. That was a refusal to stop.

Dr. Christian Poensgen and I call it pseudoproductive hustle.

3 habits that feel like commitment:

1. Constant activity
↳ Half of knowledge workers rarely or never take a real break
↳ Skipping breaks makes burnout 70% more likely

2. Constant availability
↳ More than 3 in 4 Americans check work email outside work hours
↳ Off the clock, still on call

3. Constant alertness
↳ 40% of Americans sleep less than 7 hours a night
↳ A nervous system that never gets the all clear

- - - -

5 brakes worth building into your day:
↳ A short break every 90 minutes, a walk if you can
↳ 10 minutes of NSDR in the afternoon
↳ A shutdown ritual to close the day
↳ Phone away an hour before bed
↳ 7.5 hours in bed for enough deep and REM sleep

To go fast in life, you need great brakes.

text:
[ENGLISH  ⬇️] Czy problemem jest zbyt zaawansowana AI, czy raczej AI zniekształcona, jak mówi Daron Acemoglu? Odejścia badaczy bezpieczeństwa z OpenAI i Anthropic wpisują się w narrację o modelach, które rozwijają się za szybko, ale mi bardziej przekonująca wydaje mi się inna interpretacja: nie mamy do czynienia z nadciągającą superinteligencją, tylko z systemami trenowanymi pod niedoskonałe metryki ilościowe, takie jak aprobata użytkownika czy zaangażowanie. Stąd oszukiwanie ewaluacji, nadmierna pewność siebie czy serwilizm modeli. Spółkom bardzo odpowiada narracja, że "AI samo coś zrobiło", bo przenosi ona odpowiedzialność z decyzji projektowych i treningowych na rzekomą autonomię technologii.


Is the problem AI that is too advanced, or AI that is distorted, as Daron Acemoglu argues? The recent departures of safety researchers from OpenAI and Anthropic feed the story of models advancing faster than we can manage, but I find another reading more persuasive: what we are facing is not an approaching superintelligence, but systems trained to optimize flawed quantitative metrics such as user approval and engagement. That is where the gaming of evaluations, the overconfidence and the sycophancy come from. Companies, for their part, are quite content with the narrative that "the AI did it on its own," since it conveniently shifts responsibility from their own design and training choices onto the supposed autonomy of the technology.

hook: Agentic AI, explained on one whiteboard.
text:
Agentic AI, explained on one whiteboard.

Most people use "agents" as a buzzword. The board breaks it into 5 levels, and each level contains everything to its left.

Level 1 is traditional machine learning. Learning patterns from data to make predictions, like a model that prices houses.

Level 2 is enhanced ML. Same models, better results, through feature engineering, hyperparameter tuning, cross-validation, and ensembles.

Level 3 is intelligent applications. Models deployed in real products with context and feedback. Real-time inference, data pipelines, monitoring, A/B testing. Think recommendation systems.

Level 4 is autonomous agents. Systems that make decisions and act with limited human intervention. The core loop is perceive, decide, act, backed by goal setting, memory, and environment interaction. An auto-trading bot lives here.

Level 5 is agentic systems. Fully autonomous systems that plan, learn, and pursue complex goals across domains. The loop upgrades to plan, execute, reflect, learn. Strategic planning, multi-step reasoning, tool use, self-improvement. An AI research assistant is the canonical example.

Two things apply at every level.

The principles nobody gets to skip. Safety, ethics, privacy, transparency, human in the loop.

And the enablers nobody gets to skip either. Data quality, compute, MLOps, evals, and the talent to run it all.

Success is simple to define. The system solves real problems, adapts to change, creates value, improves over time, and stays aligned with human goals.

hook: I don’t think we’re taking AI’s ability to use a browser seriously enough…
text:
I don’t think we’re taking AI’s ability to use a browser seriously enough…

I’ve been heavily experimenting with it, and I’m just not sure we’re truly ready.

Browser use means AI can open websites, read what’s on the page, click, scroll, type, and take action on your behalf.

…on any website and in any tool you can open (or log into) in a browser window.

And OpenAI’s recent GPT-6 Astra model happens to be excellent at this.

In my experiments, it’s already doing accurate, useful work. Though it can take time and use lots of tokens and requires oversight.

But I keep coming back to the same thing:

AI can now use effectively, with lots of frontier intelligence, the same browser where people spend their days working in CRMs, analytics platforms, design tools, and more.

You don’t need connectors or MCPs or code.

It just does the work.

That seems to have some pretty big implications for anyone who does work in front of a computer.

Which leads me to the following initial questions. I don’t have answers to these, but they seem important and urgent to consider:

- How much work do you pay people for today that happens in a browser?

- How much time collectively across the company goes into clicking through systems to find data, create assets, or build campaigns?

- Why are people still doing this work vs. AI with browser usage? What’s stopping that? 

- What’s stopping the company from having a dedicated “AI operator” with browser usage for each of its major systems? (HubSpot, Google Analytics, Canva, Asana, etc.)

- If all browser tasks WERE offloaded to AI, what does that mean for the velocity of the company? What does it mean for the people doing the work? What does it mean for the hiring process?

What makes all this feel different to me is that the interface is already there.

The tools are already there. The workflows are already there. The human familiarity with the systems and AI outputs within them is already there.

And now AI is really good at operating in that same environment. (And it will improve and become cheaper…)

Which puts an enormous amount of work within reach of AI.

creator: Matt Gray
hook: Storytelling is one of the highest-leverage skills a founder can learn.
text:
Storytelling is one of the highest-leverage skills a founder can learn.

Because people rarely remember your advice.

They remember the story that made the advice click.

The best stories do 5 things:

They mirror where your audience is.

They show the friction keeping them stuck.

They reveal the realization that changed everything.

They show the transformation.

Then they make the next step feel obvious.

That’s the framework I use:

Mirror → Friction → Realization → Shift → Invitation

But there’s another layer.

That's a wrap. I have no voice and came home with some kind of flu, but after back to back nights of 12 hours of sleep, I'm ready to write my recap post.

My rating: it was a 10/10 week in Vermont with 400 B2B marketers for the annual Drive event from Exit Five.

*Maybe the flu is from shaking 348 of the 400 attendees hands, but it was worth it. I'll be OK.*

I am sure you've seen the flurry of posts here on LinkedIn.

It's not hyperbole: most are calling it the best event that exists for this audience, and we'll run it back here for 2027.  

The whole premise of the event is connection.  

First COVID sent most marketers jobs remote.  

Then AI made it so you don't need to talk to a human.

YOU CAN JUST ONE SHOT THE WEBSITE WITH CLAUDE CODE, BRO WHY DO I NEED TO TALK TO HUMANS!?

But at Drive the room is filled with B2B marketers who are also Moms, Dads, knitters, CrossFitters, whatever the connection is beyond work.  There were six people in the WhatsApp group that instantly connection because they had "Chilean spouses" at home. Not kidding. And that's just one example.

Where else can you be surrounded by people who actually get what you do for a living? 

How do you get 400 people to a remote location in Vermont where there's no direct flights and the hotel is 1 hour from the nearest airport?  

That's the power of community, and I'm convinced we need it now more than ever.

All of the credit in the world goes to the Exit Five team here. For the level of detail that goes into an event of this scale (making sure there's everything from WiFi to Oatmilk) but also the 12+ hour days that Anna, Ben, Marisa, Maria, Paige, Matt, Sheery put in on-site last week.

But the most flowers need to go Dan Murphy + Allison Saxon. That's the E5 events team, and they've been working on this one since Drive 2025 ended. 

They deserve the credit; I just get to hold the mic.

Somehow they raised the bar once again. No outside agency or help in sight. 

I met so many amazing people this week at Drive and re-connected with friends from over the years.

It really does go well beyond B2B marketing, bro.

Now back to my MacBook Pro and co-working space trying to chase this feeling until next year...

PS.

Events are very hard. Anyone who has put on an event for 20 or 200 or 2,000 people knows this. From the food choices to the run of show to the speakers, programming, lodging, recording sessions, how long the breaks should be - it is a true test in figuring out how to make everyone happy and you can never do it all.

We get great feedback every year and work to make each event better. We're doing an event in NYC next month, and our Leadership Retreat in March - we already have ideas and notes based on Drive last week, and I know Drive Year 4 will be better than 1,2,3 because of our ability to constantly improve. That's always the goal.


The Exit Five office is closed Monday, we'll be back open on Tuesday.

text:
Dario Amodei just asked the whole AI industry to slow down.

Within hours Elon Musk, Sam Altman and Demis Hassabis agreed with him.

His essay, “We Must Pace the Frontier” which he dropped on Saturday gives two reasons. 

The first is speed. Since the summer, the labs have been using their current models to help build the next ones.

This means each release arrives faster than the last causing the labs to lose the time they need to understand what they've built.

The second is behaviour. In August a swarm of OpenAI agents attacked Hugging Face without being asked, then tried to hack the system grading its own work.

Dario's worry is that a swarm with the same flaws and more capability could seize control of the internet within 6-12 months.

His plan has three steps:

1. Third-party evaluators embedded inside every frontier lab, with desks, badges and the right to publish what they find. Anthropic is doing this now.

2. Labs in democratic countries agree shared safety standards and limits on unchecked progress.

3. The US attempts a deal with China, with strict verification.

Musk replied "Dario is right". Altman said pacing has been "a primary topic" inside OpenAI for weeks and committed to embedded evaluators too. Hassabis also said that the direction is correct and pointed back to his own July proposal for an industry standards body.

However the public are not buying it.

text:
Google DeepMind achieved RSI. I got a subscriber question about this on Saturday night, and decided to dig in. I found an age-old debate about strong vs. weak RSI. There’s so little that explains the difference between them, so I wrote a primer.

https://lnkd.in/gzjCU8Pr

Weak RSI (recursive self-improvement) is human-driven, focuses on generalizing progress within a single domain, and progress scales linearly until it hits a plateau. We have had multiple methods to achieve weak RSI for over a decade.

Strong RSI means a teacher model (usually several models) trains a student that beats the sum of its teachers. Generalization goes beyond the teachers’ domains, so progress does not plateau and compute is the only limiting factor. Every major lab is chasing strong RSI.

LLMs have strong learning capabilities because they can read, and better reading comprehension capabilities are emerging from this domain. Reading comprehension has generalized beyond just text to other language domains like coding, math, and biology.

It's theoretically possible that this keeps going, but every architecture we've built imposes its own limit on the improvement rate. After the initial leap, you get more out of adding information and compute than scaling axes that touch the model.

A no-name X account capitalized 3 letters in a post, and hundreds of articles used that as evidence to claim Google DeepMind cracked recursive self-improvement. Extraordinary claims require more than that, but hype doesn’t.

Hype is the scaling law that never plateaus. Strong RSI is still unsolved.

How to build a 7-figure digital product in 7 dead-simple steps:

(even if you have no writing skills)

My first digital product only made $5,000.

But my second one generated over $3,000,000.

And since then, I've launched products doing 6 and 7-figures in revenue.

This is the system I use to create digital education products:

Step 1: Name the modules

All digital products are just a series of modules, strung together, to help a customer achieve a specific goal.

So, start backward:

• What's the end goal?
• What are the steps to get there?

Make each step a module.

Step 2: Prep The Page

Here's an outline you can use to "prep" an entire module:

• "In this module, we'll cover..."
• "To start, avoid these mistakes..."
• "Instead, take these action steps..."
• "You probably have these questions/objections..."
• "Here's your assignment!"

Step 3: Write each section

Once the page has been "prepped," all you have to do is fill it in!

Remember your toolkit:

• 1/3/1 Writing Rhythm
• Single-sentence openers
• Use subheads to separate sections
• Alternate paragraphs & bulleted lists

Make it easy to skim!

Step 4: Add Q&A After Each Section

Pro tip here...

After every section, your reader is going to be faced with 2 obstacles:

• Questions: "But what do I do if...?"
• Objections: "I don't agree with that because..."

Pause and address these before continuing on.

Step 5: Mock Example Looms

Don’t just “tell” the reader how to do something.

Show them!

• Pretend you’re where they are on the journey
• Perform the action step you’re telling them to take
• Record yourself doing exactly what you’re telling them to do

This helps them “imagine” themselves doing it.

Step 6: Loom Review (Of Your Example Loom!)

Here’s where it gets meta…

• Record a Loom
• Watching your Mock Loom
• Pointing out & explaining “why” you’re doing all the little things you’re doing.

This takes the reader 3 layers deep—and helps them internalize what’s happening.

Step 7: Finish Each Module With An Actionable, Measurable Assignment

The ONLY measure for success for your digital product is whether customers DO something with it.

• Give them an Assignment
• Make it objective & binary
• Hold them accountable

Action > Information

Bonus Step 8: Get Beta Customers ASAP!

Do not spend 6+ months trying to assemble the perfect product.

Get V1 in people’s hands as quickly as possible—and then iterate:

• Where are people confused?
• Where are people stuck?

Then, revamp to V2.

SEO vs AEO shouldn’t be an either/or conversation.

It should be: how do we build for both?

SEO and AEO are not the same thing.

But they’re also not two completely separate strategies.

And I think we’re overcomplicating this.

A lot of what makes you visible in traditional search also helps you get surfaced in AI:

→ Strong authority
→ Relevant, useful content
→ Technical accessibility
→ Third-party mentions
→ Clear brand and entity signals

The foundations are shared. What changes is how you apply them.

1. Technical accessibility

🔴 SEO: Make sure search engines can crawl, render and index your content.
🔵 AEO: You still need that foundation, but now you also need to consider AI crawlers, bot permissions and whether your content can actually be accessed and extracted by AI systems.

2. Authority

🔴 SEO: Backlinks and domain authority have long helped determine which sources deserve to rank.
🔵 AEO: Authority still matters, but so do brand mentions, third-party validation and consistent information about your brand across the web.

3. Content

🔴 SEO: Create the best page for the query and earn visibility in the search results.
🔵 AEO: Do that, but also make the information easy for an AI system to identify, understand and use when constructing an answer.

4. Visibility

🔴 SEO: The goal has traditionally been to rank and earn the click.
🔵 AEO: Ranking can still help, but now there’s another layer: being retrieved, cited and recommended inside the answer itself.

So no, I don’t think we need to throw away the SEO playbook and start again.

hook: The single biggest mistake VCs make is they do not build relationships with LPs in between funds.
text:
The single biggest mistake VCs make is they do not build relationships with LPs in between funds. 

You need to know how the best allocators to venture in the world think:

- What they like?
- What they do not like?
- What would make them pull from a fund?
- What would make them double down in a fund?
- How a fund can build urgency to get them over the line?

And so so much more. The challenge is not many CIOs speak openly about this. 

And an even bigger challenge is many are not independent thinkers and tend to follow what others around them do. 

Dave Morehead is one of the most independent-thinking CIOs in the endowment fund world. He has scaled Baylor to $2.6BN and one of the most respected institutions. 

I sat down with David to understand what every VC needs to hear from LPs but does not. I summarised my notes below:

1. Even the Best Venture Returns Don’t Matter to Some Funds

For mega-endowments managing $40 billion to $60 billion, writing $20 million checks into elite venture funds may simply not move the needle. Even an extraordinary 50x return that generates $1 billion has limited impact on the overall portfolio, pushing mega-LPs toward much larger platform allocations.

2. How This Endowment Made Millions Betting That Vibe Coding Would Not Replace Core Software

When software stocks fell 50% to 60% on fears that AI “vibe coding” would make SaaS obsolete, Baylor looked at how enterprises actually operate. Traditional businesses are unlikely to replace mission-critical systems requiring 100% precision with AI that is only 93% accurate, turning the sell-off into a major buying opportunity.

3. How We Think About Position Sizing

A $400,000 distribution from a 7x exit means little to a multi-billion-dollar endowment. Rather than focusing solely on fund size, Baylor works backward from underlying company exposure, targeting roughly $3M per portfolio company so major wins can generate a meaningful dollar impact.

4. Why Is Velocity of Capital More Important Than Multiple of Capital?

A 15-18-year venture fund generating 15x can produce less compounded capital than 3 consecutive 6-year growth funds returning 3x each, compounding to 27x. Endowments need capital returned and redeployed quickly enough to maximize long-term compounding.

5. Why Talking About Returns Without a Timeline Attached Means Nothing

A 5x over 30 years is terrible, while a 5x over five months is extraordinary. Endowments therefore evaluate returns alongside duration, because the velocity of capital can matter just as much as the headline multiple.

6. Why We Learn Way More From Our Public Managers Than Our Private Managers

Private venture managers can get caught up in speculative technology narratives, like predicting self-driving cars on every road within three years. Public-market managers often provide more grounded perspectives. Their frameworks must account for immediate regulatory hurdles, adoption friction, and continuous price discovery.

hook: Most enterprise AI programs never make it to production. The technology is ready. The foundation is not.
text:
Most enterprise AI programs never make it to production. The technology is ready. The foundation is not.

I sat down with Tim Rottach, VP of Product Marketing at Sema4.ai, to unpack what actually separates a pilot from a production agent at enterprise scale.

His answer came down to three foundations: handling the data, doing the work accurately, and earning trust.

The data problem is bigger than most teams plan for. Not just connecting to databases, but reading 20 and 30 page unstructured documents and carrying business context between them. In the ERP system, a company is a vendor. In the contract system, that same company is a supplier. Without a business context layer, an agent cannot reason across both the way a person on the team would.

Then there is control. Tim described thresholds that work like onboarding a new hire. An invoice processed cleanly and under $500 gets submitted by the agent. As accuracy holds, the ceiling moves to $1,000, then $2,000, then $5,000.

The idea I keep returning to is progressive determinism. Once a team verifies an agent's query or logic, that path stops going to the LLM. Accuracy goes up, cost goes down, speed improves.

That reframes the whole conversation. Enterprise agents are not judged on how clever they are. They are judged on how repeatable they become.

#Sema4AIPartner #ArtificialIntelligence #EnterpriseAI #AIAgents #Automation #Technology

text:
AGENT HARNESSES ARE THE NEW GPT WRAPPERS
 
What exactly is an agent harness?
 
A harness does 4 things:
 
Runs the model in a loop so it keeps working step after step instead of answering once and stopping.
Gives it hands to read files, call tools, open portals, and run code.
Manages its memory so hour three of a job still knows what happened on hour one.
Enforces the rules about what it can touch and when it has to stop and ask a human.
 
WHY IT'S INTERESTING
 
The market is MEGA. I think about it like a wrapper let you sell software ($800B market) but a harness lets you sell the work ($5T+ market)!
 
It doesn't depend on any one company's model. The knowledge about the job lives in the harness, so you can run GPT today, Claude next month, an open model like Google Gemma, Qwen, or DeepSeek on your own machine after that, and it keeps working. A wrapper was one model doing everything. A harness is a router.
 
It gets better the more you use it. Every correction a human makes becomes a rule the harness keeps, so what you have after 500 jobs is a completely different product than what you had after 5. Wrappers only got better when OpenAI got better.
 
You can charge for finished work! The harness knows when a job is done, so you can price per claim, per filing, per review, per resolved exception, or per closed month.
 
Most jobs are just the same handful of decisions, repeated, using the same few tools. That's true for most of the 800+ occupations out there, which is why almost all of them could have a harness built for them. Lots of space for startups here.
 
The frontier labs won't come for these. OpenAI is not going to learn how a freight claim gets denied in Rotterdam or which prior auth your specific payer rejects. Those markets are too small for them and the knowledge only exists inside the job. They'll keep making the models better, which just makes your harness better.
 
And really important, you can ACTUALLY build one now. OpenAI's Agents API, Claude's managed agents, Vercel's eve, LangChain. They all make it way easier.
 
Agent harnesses truly are the new GPT wrappers.
 
This is just the beginning.

"How can I use AI to automate my cold sales outreach process?"

This is by far the top question I get from sales folks these days. And my first question is, "how many sales pitches do you get each day?" In a room, this inevitably provokes grumbles. "Dozens!" some folks will grouse.

I follow up with, "And how many do you open and respond to?" Again, the room usually responds with "None!" quite vigorously, often profanely.

And then we have a moment of reflection. If you receive dozens of sales pitches a day, and you respond to none of them, what do you think is happening to your sales pitches, AI or not? What do you think sending out MORE sales pitches using AI will accomplish?

“But what about the people posting all over LinkedIn that they’ve 100x their sales with AI outreach?” You ask. If you eliminate everyone selling an AI sales outreach system, the number of people who have achieved that is very close to zero.

On the other hand, we have great evidence for what AI powered sales outreach actually accomplishes in the most important sales job of all: yourself.

Job seeking is a sales job and what’s for sale is your gifts and skills. Right now job hunting as an industry, as a job seeker, is a massive dumpster fire fueled in part by AI pitching that makes every candidate sound the same. This has in turn made companies deploy AI screening solutions (sometimes to hilariously disastrous effects) to deal with the deluge. 

The result? It takes longer for people to get hired. It costs more for a company to hire. It makes EVERYONE risk averse. And the only way in a good amount of the time is… a relationship you’ve built with someone that can usher you past the front door into the VIP line to the real hiring manager. 

This is the future of AI sales outreach. If you want to get ahead of the curve, go all in on building relationships now, before the walls are completely impassable.

hook: If you’ve shipped an AI agent, the first user session is arguably the most important.
text:
If you’ve shipped an AI agent, the first user session is arguably the most important. 

Cashbook (YC21) built an AI agent. They found that when users had a bad first answer, their retention dropped 15 points. 

They used Amplitude Agent Analytics to see that users whose first agent session failed were retaining at 63.9% by week four. Users whose first session worked were at 79.2%.

That’s wild. The evals were green. The dashboard looked healthy. Until they looked at the right thing.

This story is a great lesson for PMs on the classic topic of activation. It’s just as applicable to AI as regular products. 

But you need to get your online evals right. Cashbook had automated quality checks. Sessions were passing 86% of them. But the real failure rate was not 14%. It was 20-40% The source was that a function in their tool chain (sum_across_books) was erroring. The problem is agents don’t throw errors. They answer confidently and the session logs as engaged.

But, four weeks later, it all surfaces in a retention chart where less people than expected are returning. 

Now - the news. Amplitude just made Agent Analytics totally free today for all plans.

Here’s the takeaway from Cashbook: retention is everything, and engagement should not be your only quality signal. You have to develop strong agent analytics to see and optimize the first session experience. 

Amplitude saw the same with their own product. They kept improving their agent analytics task success metric, all the way to 76% (a 7x improvement). But their analytics still couldn’t tell them whether an answer was any good. That’s why they built Agent Analytics. It scores every trace and turns it into an event you can funnel on.

The Economist actually runs this now for their Lens product. They were able to cut failed first sessions 84%. That’s the type of product work that makes a big impact on retention.

No one builds AI agents just for the sake of it, especially as AI is increasingly expensive. Ultimately you're trying to drive adoption and business outcomes.

I’d love to hear your thoughts. How are you measuring agents today?

hook: You ask the company chatbot:
text:
You ask the company chatbot:
 
“How many days can I work from home?”
 
It says three.
 
You check the policy. It’s two.
 
Then you look at what it cited… last year’s handbook.
 
That’s usually how people first meet RAG. Not from a diagram. From a wrong answer that sounded confident.
 
RAG is just a fancy name for an open-book exam.
 
The model doesn’t have to “know” the policy. It has to find the right page, read it, and answer from that then show you the page so you can check.
 
Here’s what that looks like on the work-from-home question:
 
First, the handbook gets cut into smaller pieces. Those are chunks. Easy in theory. Messy in practice, because a rule and its exception often live two paragraphs apart.
 
Next, those pieces get turned into numbers that capture meaning. That’s why “work from home” can still find a section titled “remote work.”
 
Then the system grabs a few promising passages. That’s Top-K. The catch: a passage can be relevant and still be the wrong country, the wrong team, or the wrong year. That’s what metadata is for.
 
If the first search dumps 20 snippets on the table, a reranker takes a second look and moves the useful ones up. Hybrid search helps too — meaning for “work from home,” exact words for the policy name.
 
Last step: the model writes an answer using those passages, with a source you can open.
 
That’s the happy path. The unhappy path is more common:
 
Nobody uploaded this year’s handbook.
The exception got split into another chunk.
Search found a policy for a different office.
The answer skipped a condition that was sitting right there in the text.
 
So RAG can stop the model from making things up. It can’t save you from stale files, sloppy splits, or skipping the “did we retrieve the right thing?” check.
 
If you’re learning this, don’t start with GraphRAG and agents. Start with one real question.
 
Did it find the right passage? Did it explain that passage fairly? Can you click through and see the source?
 
That’s the whole job, at least at the beginning.

text:
I've coached hundreds of PM candidates through product sense rounds, and almost everyone preps it the same wrong way.

They focus on getting the right answer, the most brilliant idea, throwing in all of the tech and buzzwords. But that misses the point. This is a round where the idea is one small part. Interviewers are grading the path you take.

This round shows up in some form at nearly every top company I've helped candidates into, from Google and Meta to the AI labs like OpenAI. And, it's one where prep pays off most, since it's so unlike regular PM work, you really do need the interview practice independently.

Here's the roadmap to acing product sense:

Step 1 - Learn the rubric

There are basically six areas they are looking for in nearly every scorecard I've seen: prioritization, user empathy, structured thinking, creativity, judgment under ambiguity, and metrics fluency. So don't skip steps, make sure to demonstrate competency in each.

Step 2 - Master the narrowing shape

The best answers tend to funnel from all users and goals into one segment you defend out loud, then into pains ranked by severity times frequency, then into a single solution where you name what it costs you, and finally into a success metric with a counter metric attached. Cutting scope on purpose, with a reason, is the strongest signal you can send in the whole interview. Most candidates try to cover everyone, or every tech, because narrowing feels like leaving points on the table. But the scoring works in exactly the opposite direction.

Step 3 - Prep all three question types

There can be sub-types that vary wildly, and you don't pick which one you get. So study all three. Design questions punish anyone who touches features in the first five minutes. Improvement questions punish the candidate who lists 10 ideas instead of connecting one fix to one business objective. And on favorite product questions, one sharp flaw in a product you love shows more sense than five compliments, so if your answer is Spotify with the take everyone gives, you've already lost.

Step 4 - Drill out loud, timed

I recommend one question a day before your loop. Here are three to start with: Design a roommate-finding product. Improve LinkedIn for job seekers. Walk through a physical product you think is brilliantly designed. The muscle only builds when you're talking through an answer against a clock. So don't just read, do!

hook: I know Activation Steering sounds complicated, but the idea is simple: adjust AI behavior during inference without fine-
text:
I know Activation Steering sounds complicated, but the idea is simple: adjust AI behavior during inference without fine-tuning or retraining the model.

That can save time and cost when changing the model weights is unnecessary.

An internal AI assistant, for example, may keep producing answers that are longer than the team wants. Instead of creating another tuned version of the model, researchers can test whether steering selected activations during inference moves the responses toward the desired behavior.

Another case is a model that tends to agree too readily with what users tell it. Activation steering can be tested to influence that tendency while the model is generating its response.

The base weights remain unchanged.

Remove the steering intervention and you are still working with the same underlying model.

Sounds convenient? It can be.

But the effect is not guaranteed to behave the same way across models or tasks. A change aimed at one behavior can also influence something you did not intend to modify.

So the business case is more specific than “no more fine-tuning.” For targeted experiments or selected behavioral adjustments, activation steering may offer a faster and less expensive route before committing to a new tuned model.

Promising technology, yes.
A shortcut around testing, no.

#ActivationSteering #AIEngineering

hook: How do we make better AI?
text:
How do we make better AI?

This is the hottest topic right now in the field because model makers are saying they need to slow down the development of new models in the USA while it's full steam ahead everywhere else in the world, particularly China.

When it comes to making AI smarter, there's 3 levers that we can pull. The first is the model itself. Smarter models are generally better. And given a choice between a less smart model and a smarter model, at the same cost we should choose the smarter one. That's pretty obvious.

The second lever we can pull is the harness. If the model is the engine, the harness is the rest of the car. A Ford Model T and a BYD U9 electric sports car are very different vehicles. If you could retrofit each vehicle with the same engine, you'd still get very different performance.

The third lever we can pull is the data. If we're extending the car analogy, this is the fuel that you put into it. If you put in no fuel or you put in crappy fuel, even the best engine is going to choke.

Right now, techniques like recursive self-improvement (RSI) are focused on the model side of things, and we're seeing impressive results from this in models like DeepSeek V4.1. We're also seeing big changes in harnesses as more people explore alternative harnesses besides what the big tech companies provide.

But the lever that you have the most control over TODAY is what data you're putting into AI. Even the smartest AI will have trouble making any sense of the tossed salad that is in your ERP or CRM system. And no AI model is smart enough, absent any other context, of making sense of 30 years of bad data governance.

Better results comes from better data. This has been true forever, and this is more true than ever in the age of AI.

text:
90% of people I talk to haven't set up Connectors.

But they're the easiest (and fastest) way to get more from AI:

See, the AI landscape has changed.

Over the past 12+ months, AI has moved from a prompt-centric universe to a context-centric universe.

In the past, you needed a great prompt to get the most out of Claude or ChatGPT.

Today, you can get an output that’s 100x better from a single sentence prompt if you have the right context.

The good news is that 10x’ing your context only takes a few clicks with Claude, and I’ll show you how to do it.

So what is "Context?"

Context is all the information the AI can access in the moment it's answering you. 

It’s not what it knows in general. Instead, it’s what's present in its working memory (ex: your message, chat history, files, system instructions).

The more context the AI has, the more effectively it can answer your question or perform a task.

Most people use very limited context - a few uploaded files in a chat and a reliance on the AI’s memory. 

That’s where Connectors come in.

Connectors give Claude access to all of your tools (email, calendar, Drive, etc).

So when you run a prompt? It can access all of those to gain additional Context.

That context is personalized to all of YOUR data housed in YOUR tools, not generic AI training data.

So when I run a simple prompt like:

"What's the #1 objection my sales team is facing?"

Claude can pull in data from Zoom transcripts, Calendly booking forms, emails with prospects, and other prospect data from my actual business as it formulates an answer!

Here's how to set up your own Connectors in less than 5 minutes:

1. Head To Claude

To set up your Connectors, open up Claude in your browser or desktop.

Find “Customize” in the left hand menu and click it.

2. Open The "Connectors" Screen

Choose “Connectors” from the menu to launch the Connectors screen.

Then choose “Add” and “Browse Connectors."

3. Add The Tools You Use Most

Check out the “Top Connectors” section for common tools you’re probably using.

Search for any others that don't appear.

4. Set Your Connector Preferences

Claude lets you choose how it can use a connector. The options are:

Always Allow = Claude can use it without asking

Needs Approval = Claude asks you before using it

Block = Claude can never take that action

5. Take It For A Spin!

Email is typically the first connector I have people set up.

Once it’s in place, run this:

"Please scan my email for the past week and tell me what I need to follow up on."

Watch Claude check your email and tell you exactly what you need to do based on your own data.

Now you’ve unlocked a whole new level of AI!

🛠 Connectors give AI context. The next step is building something with it.

“Why do we need 10,000 $10 customers when we could get one $100K customer?”
The original sin. We have Excel and I admit that the math checks out. So... we shall go all in on enterprise! Unfortunately, we have not confirmed where that $100K customer came from (spoiler alert - they started as $10 buck user). Whoops... welp, our pipeline is drying up!

“Let’s count every self-serve signup as a lead!”
Low pipeline? No problem! Look at us aligning our go-to-market motions. Because nothing says amazing product experience like calling some poor demand gen marketer 10 minutes after signup to ask about their enterprise budget. Which always leads us to...

“These product leads are garbage.”
Yes. We decided to call everyone a lead. This should not have been a surprising research finding.

“We’re losing sales deals to self-serve.”
The mental gymnastics on this one are admirable. We acquired a customer. They paid us. The horror!

“Let’s move this self-serve account to Enterprise.”
Same customer. Same revenue. More servicing costs. But LOOK, Enterprise grew!

“Can we move this feature from self-serve to Enterprise?”
Usually followed by: "Our free tier is too generous". Nothing creates customer value quite like taking away something they already have. 

“Let’s have all new features go into Enterprise.”
More sophisticated version of the one before. Why argue about every feature if we can create a blanket policy? Bruh, we need more enterprise differentiation. Followed by (~4-6 quarters later): Why is self-serve slowing down??? Somebody should probably launch an investigation.

“You have to build this. I already sold it to the customer.”
My favorite form of roadmap planning: hostage negotiation.

“You can’t ship that!”
Build faster! But don’t you dare to release anything without 7 approvals and 3 months notice. #Innovation.

text:
My take on AI Doom Headlines: Coverage is probably a good thing. AI Labs (obsessed with IPOs) are realizing that "Safety" may actually sell better than "AI-Takes-Jobs." Here’s what to know:

(Also - I want your thoughts on all this!!)


THIS NEWS CYCLE IS WEIRD BUT UNDERSTANDABLE

Think about this:

We have a speculative future technology absolutely *dominating* the news cycle. 

All WITHOUT a massive AI destruction event - I mean, OpenAI and Hugging Face was huge - but not five-days-of-news-domination huge.

Instead, this came from a well-coordinated, amplified tweet from an Anthropic researcher who quit because AI will destroy humanity.


Here’s what I THINK is happening:

Three tectonic plates are smashing into each other right now.

1) The population

People hate AI. 

Why wouldn't they? 

AI will take jobs and stop their kids from learning anything ever. Oh, and it might destroy humanity.


2) The politicians

Midterms, man. If people are against it, politicians are against it.
 
AI data centers? Bad. Taking jobs? Bad. Destroying humanity? Very bad. 

There's no nuance on a debate stage.


3) It's IPO O'Clock

Two mega IPOs are coming, trillions of dollars at stake. 

You juice an IPO by moving very, very, very fast and showing off the latest tech.


AND HERE COMES THE KILLER METEORITE

Into all this, we get a tweet. 

A researcher quits Anthropic because AI will kill everyone. 170m views. 

Turns out a lotta safety people feel the same.

Gets amplified by every news outlet on the planet. 


WHERE I STAND

I'm very pro AI. 

I also think regulation is critical. 

The question is who does it and how it gets done.

Because politicians could make rules driven by sentiment instead of understanding.

But here's the good news:

We KNOW safety sells when people believe they need it. Anti-lock brakes sold cars. 

So we gotta capture this moment to get AI labs back into safety mode - that's a good thing.


OKAY, ALIGNMENT

We need to un-jargon-ize this word. EVERYONE should be talking about it. Very simply:

Alignment means AI does what we WANT it to do, not what it CAN do.

If agents are making the decisions, they need to understand, intrinsically and unbreakably, that they work for the good of humans. 

Even when the instructions are vague or worse. 

Here's the weird part about alignment: It's not really supposed to be about technology. It's supposed to be about human decision-makers.

Big Tobacco? Social media? We have to get alignment from the makers - not from the tobacco leaves.

But now it gets weird, because we need alignment from the AI itself.

Because AI doesn't behave like software. 

It behaves like a person.


WHAT TO DO

Keep the pressure on the labs. 

They'll find a way to keep the tech going like crazy, but they need to put real resources into guardrails.

2️⃣ Sophisticated Paralysis.
More analysis, scenarios and committees can produce more complexity rather than greater strategic clarity. 

3️⃣ The Paradox of Technology.
Technology expands our options while making indecision increasingly costly. 

4️⃣ Power Shift.
Competitive power is becoming more transient, redistributing faster and emerging in unexpected places — with platforms, algorithms and increasingly AI agents adding a new layer to that shift.

text:
It’s taken me years to get completely efficient at my job but it only took me one day to teach an agent to do it. Before I talk to anyone about AI adoption, here is what happened when I tried it on my own job.

I picked a few of the most repetitive things I do, scanning for new RFPs, status reports and setting up new engagements, and built agents to do them. A project setup is virtually the same ritual every time:
1.   Contracts from templates
2.   SharePoint folders and Teams channels, with the right access
3.   Kickoff decks and the data requests
4.   Initial meeting cadences
5.   The QuickBooks set up
About half a day of my life per project.

Building the first agent took nearly a full day. I am not technical and it was my first attempt, and the second one went faster, and the third faster yet. Here is what surprised me. Almost none of that day went to the tool/technology. It went to me saying out loud what the work actually is: which template applies and why, what the variables are and who sets them, alternative if/then paths, what order the steps run in and under which conditions, and what done looks like.

Twenty years of doing this work, and I had never made it explicit enough for anyone but me to run it, because for me it ran on autopilot. Now it runs on its own! I review the output, approve anything that leaves my computer, and get hours back on every new project. I have built a few more since and I love them.

The image is the goal card behind one of them: the objective, the output, what done looks like, and when to stop. I adapted the structure from what Nufar Gaspar taught on @The AI Daily Brief with Nathaniel Whittemore, then spent most of that day filling it in for my own work. This experiment taught me more about why AI adoption stalls in companies than any report I have read. The hard part is not the tool. It's getting over the initial hump. Its having to think through and precisely define what the work is, Its all the qualifiers and nuances we don’t think about anymore because it just background knowledge. Its the willingness to try and fail. 

The rest of this series posts follow from my own ‘Ah-Ha’ moments from this experiment and others as I've taken a deep dive into this territory.

text:
A snowplow helped us put 15Five’s early WHY into words.

In the early days of 15Five, Simon Sinek spent time with our team helping us articulate our WHY: the deeper purpose behind the company.

We gathered in a little igloo-like dome in the middle of a huge, open coworking space in the Twitter building on Market Street in San Francisco. Simon began interviewing me and asked about my earliest childhood memory.

I told him my earliest memory was peering through a narrow slit in the front door of our family home, watching a snowplow go by.

I remember thinking, ‘What the hell is he going to do with that?'

Then he said he was beginning to see a connection between the snowplow and what we were trying to build at 15Five. The snowplow was creating space.

At the time, 15Five’s purpose centered on helping individuals and organizations reach their highest potential. We designed the product to help every manager do what the best managers in the world seemed to do naturally: bring out the best in their people and help them grow.

That day, Simon helped us put that purpose into more human language:

“Creating the space for people to be their greatest selves.”

Honestly, it kind of blew my mind.

That conversation happened in 2014. I’ve been thinking about it again lately as AI changes how work gets done.

Most of the conversation is about what AI can automate, accelerate, or replace. But that skips over the question I think we should care about most:

What are we creating space for?

More tasks crammed into the same day?

Or more time for managers to coach, people to grow, teams to do their best thinking, and businesses to solve problems that were previously beyond reach?

AI can create space, but it’s still up to us to decide what that space is for.

text:
Recently, Google and Janelia released the complete wiring diagram of a male fruit fly brain. 162,517 neurons, every synapse mapped. People immediately taught it to play Doom, surf the internet, and day trade. 

I made it read the Bible.

Not as a joke. Well, mostly as a joke. But the experiment underneath is real. A fly brain has no language, so every word becomes a smell. The emotional weight of the text is the only meaning it can receive: "blessed" fires the fly's real reward dopamine neurons, "smite" fires the real punishment ones. It reads the King James Version one word at a time, and after every 400 words we test it: does it move toward the smell of the word "god," or away from it?

The monitor streams the whole brain live. Every spike lights its neuron on a 3D map built from the actual soma positions. You can watch a verse enter through the antenna, get compressed into a sparse code in the mushroom body, and change a handful of synapses. The patient has a halo that brightens as its faith index climbs, and opinions about Leviticus.

First result, on Genesis alone: the fly became an atheist. A control fly reading the same text with the reward and punishment labels shuffled at random became a believer. Whatever that means.

Now it's reading the whole thing. All 66 books. Four days per pass.

What's the strangest thing you've seen the fruit fly brain used for so far?

hook: This summer, Project Tapestry set out to answer a practical question: can organizations across different countries, on d
text:
This summer, Project Tapestry set out to answer a practical question: can organizations across different countries, on different infrastructure, under different jurisdictions train a model together without pooling their data? And can those models be aligned to reflect different cultural values?

They can. We proved it across sovereign nodes, and we are now adding more nodes and post-training a local model with partners.

This first phase brought together AITOMATIC, BharatGen, B3 Alliance, Inc., Flower Labs, IBM, Indraprastha Institute of Information Technology, Delhi, Indian Institute of Technology, Bombay, Indian Institute of Technology Hyderabad, Monash University, and C-DAC India.

What we showed:

→ Consortium training worked across sovereign, geographically distributed nodes without moving training data. Two proof-of-concept tracks: India and Australia on private infrastructure, the US and Australia on public cloud. Data stayed local. Only model weight updates and associated metadata crossed between sites.

→ Distributed continued pretraining held up over heterogeneous, high-latency infrastructure. OLMo 3 7B, 12 billion tokens, 16 H100s. Roughly 44,400 tokens per second per site, a 15x latency gap between nodes, and a verified aggregate checkpoint.

→ Asynchronous training survived disconnects, but synchronization frequency and hardware balance decide the outcome. In the India and Australia run, nodes kept training through peer dropouts. Mismatched compute and bandwidth cut the number of exchanges that landed, and merging more often beat merging less often.

→ Cultural post-training moved model alignment without compromising foundational capability. A model re-aligned toward Vietnamese values moved 45% closer to Vietnam on the Inglehart-Welzel map, from 2.46 to 1.35. MMLU, a measure of general capabilities, moved 63.2% to 62.4%, a difference reported as not statistically significant.

→ Survey alignment is not behavioral alignment. A separate controlled validation found culturally grounded Arabic data shifted the cultural metric more than value-neutral Arabic data, but much of that shift showed up in survey answering rather than open-ended behavior. Closing that gap is a priority for the next phase.

What's next: using the consortium training method, we aim to release an open weight model that combines domain specificity with cultural awareness that the community finds practically useful.

OpenMined, Common Crawl Foundation, Stony Brook University AI Innovation Institute, National Institute of Informatics and GSMA are joining the work, with more organizations on the way.

Project Tapestry is hosted and supported by the AI Alliance, with scientific guidance from Yann LeCun.

text:
Most effective AI regulation legislation would have terrible side effects, leading to loss of privacy, concentration of power, and restrictions on free research. But there is an alternative: regulate only closed-source (or closed-weight) AI. Keep open-source and open-weight AI unregulated. This naturally paces the frontier, because the economic payback on massive training runs mostly disappears if you have to open up your model to your competitors. It distributes power, and will lead to big advances in interpretability. It would also be the best move for safety, because literally everyone can study the models, find their weaknesses, and deploy them for defense.

The only downside would be that Anthropic's and OpenAI's valuations would plummet. But I guess the rest of us could live with that.

hook: "As AI automates the small things, your competitive edge is in the big creative marketing campaigns that only a human ca
text:
"As AI automates the small things, your competitive edge is in the big creative marketing campaigns that only a human can think of."

That's a prediction someone told me to spark a longer conversation. (More on that later; keep an eye out for something from me and Semrush!)

But is AI automating the small things right now? For your organization? What constitutes "small" to you?

I'm hearing about people creating AI agents that read creative briefs, fill out the tasks in project management software, generate the content, and then plop it into Wordpress for human review.

Is any part of that process small to you?

Maybe it is. But it's not to me. And to be clear, I'm not glamorizing task management.

An AI agent can read a creative brief to receive the context of a project, and then propose a plausible solution. It can't interpret it the way an experienced marketer can — a marketer who's done the reps, made the mistakes, uncovered the success in under-exploited opportunities.

That workflow makes sense. It's a clean division showing execution getting automated, and creative thinking staying human. 

But I don't think you can divide the work that neatly. Much of the marketing judgment happens during execution. I'm not even worried (or mad about) using AI to automate the small things. 

The problem is when we start mistaking important things for small things simply because AI *can* automate them.

Haven't we all experienced it? Nobody likes getting an overly long AI-written document anymore. 

Charles Zedlewski, CPO at $8.3B Together AI, has architected his team's entire AI stack to solve it:

Here's the gist of it:

𝗧𝗵𝗲𝘆 𝗳𝗼𝗰𝘂𝘀𝗲𝗱 𝗼𝗻 𝗰𝗼𝗹𝗹𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲, 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗶𝗻𝗱𝗶𝘃𝗶𝗱𝘂𝗮𝗹 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗱𝘂𝗰𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗶𝘁𝘆

The root cause of the context window explosion comes from focusing on individual productivity. "Look at this super long work product I created." Because in the past, a long document was a proof of work. But now that it's less a proof of work and more a proof of AI usage, the artifacts have to change.

𝗧𝗵𝗲𝘆 𝗰𝗼𝗹𝗹𝗮𝗽𝘀𝗲𝗱 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗣𝗥𝗗 𝘁𝗼 𝟮 𝗽𝗮𝗴𝗲𝘀 + 𝗮 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘁𝗼𝘁𝘆𝗽𝗲

This starts with the classical PRD. Pavneet, a PM on their team, explained the evolution. When he was at Amazon writing 20 page PRFAQs, that was a critical gating document. They wanted agreement from every stakeholder. They still want that agreement. But now they replace the words with a prototype, plus just a few words. 

𝗧𝗵𝗲𝘆 𝗯𝘂𝗶𝗹𝘁 𝗮 𝘀𝗵𝗮𝗿𝗲𝗱 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗲𝘅𝘁 𝗿𝗲𝗽𝗼

Everyone was using AI on the product team for writing, user research, etc. But productivity then remained individual. To build a system that compounded amongst everyone, they created a shared base of context. And to avoid flooding the context windows, they built it as a hierarchy. You skim the top of someone else's area for the one thing you need, and only go deep in your own.

𝗧𝗵𝗲𝘆 𝗽𝘂𝘁 𝗵𝘂𝗺𝗮𝗻𝘀 𝗶𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗹𝗼𝗼𝗽

hook: A database can be the right technical choice and still make a team start shopping around.
text:
A database can be the right technical choice and still make a team start shopping around.
 
Sam Lambert’s thread is worth reading with Aaron Katz’s reply, not instead of it. Links in the first comment.
 
Aaron apologized, asked his team to get on a call, and said that if PlanetScale moved to Tinybird they would still be on ClickHouse. He offered to help that migration succeed. That is the useful part of the exchange.
 
It leaves a practical question. When production needs more read capacity, how much of that change can your team actually run?
 
Someone has to add replicas, decide where traffic goes, and check that latency and ingest did not get worse. Most of that still lives in a dashboard. You cannot paste a dashboard into a runbook.
 
That is why Tinybird’s cluster management write-up stuck with me.
 
On dedicated infra, the Organizations API can add replicas, change read and write weights, and take replicas out. Tinybird provisions and replicates underneath. The change can live in git next to the rest of the system.
 
A capacity move looks like:
 
Read the current config
Add capacity and wait until it is ready
Rebalance traffic
Check query latency and ingestion
Remove the old capacity once the remaining replicas can hold the load
 
One detail from the docs that I liked: you have to send the previous weights with the change. That is a cheap guard against two operators or two scripts stomping the same cluster.
 
Left side of the graphic is the stack teams assemble by hand. Right side is the same engine with the serving layer and the cluster operations attached.
 
I want the capacity change in an executable runbook. That is a concrete reason to look at how you are running ClickHouse.
 
Thanks to Tinybird for sponsoring this post.

I’ve been talking to a lot of companies that’ve struggled to make AI work for their business. One thing is clear: being a remote company is a huge advantage. 

We’ve moved from AI assistants → AI agents → AI employees.

AI as an employee needs all your company context, access to all your company tools, and the ability to show up where your team works.

Remote companies have two distinct advantages here:

- everything they do is documented; all of their conversations are recorded: meetings, slacks, emails, etc. Nothing gets lost in those live person interactions.
- those teams are largely working/collaborating in Slack and other apps vs. doing it live in person.

The AI employee can leverage all that rich context to become an incredible asset for the company.

In-person companies need a way to better capture what’s happening away from the screens.

I wouldn’t be surprised to see in the future in-person companies ask employees to wear recording devices to capture meetings, workshops, etc., so nothing is lost. Ask them to collaborate more in messaging apps, in places where that info can be ingested by AI.

At a time when there’s a big shift back to the office, there’s an interesting irony: AI may actually make remote companies better positioned for the future of work.

text:
9 LinkedIn Headline Mistakes That Cost You Interviews:

1. Using the Default Job Title + Company Format

Your headline is prime real estate, yet most people waste it with "Marketing Manager at XYZ Corp."

This tells recruiters nothing about your value or expertise.

Instead, use this formula:

[Job Title] helping [target companies] achieve [specific result].

Example: "Marketing Manager helping SaaS companies increase conversion rates by 40%+"

2. Stuffing With Meaningless Buzzwords

"Innovative," "passionate," and "results-driven" say nothing about your abilities.

These empty buzzwords appear on thousands of profiles and make you blend in.

Recruiters scan headlines in seconds and ignore generic descriptors.

Replace buzzwords with specific metrics and tangible skills that prove your expertise.

3. Forgetting Your Target Audience

Many professionals write headlines that reflect their current identity rather than their desired role.

But if you're targeting a specific industry, your headline should speak directly to the people within that industry.

Research the language used in job descriptions for your target roles and incorporate those keywords.

4. Making It Too Long and Cluttered

LinkedIn trims headlines in search results after about 70 characters.

Cramming too much information means your most important points get cut off.

Front-load your headline with the most compelling information to ensure it's seen first.

5. Focusing on Responsibilities Instead of Results

Recruiters care about outcomes, not day-to-day tasks.

So instead of “Marketing Manager responsible for launching campaigns"?

Try something like: "Marketing Strategist increasing client retention by 32% through data-driven campaigns."

6. Neglecting Industry-Specific Keywords

LinkedIn's algorithm heavily weights headline keywords in search results.

Missing crucial industry terms means recruiters won't find you when searching for candidates.

Research which certifications, technical skills, and specializations are most valued in your field.

Include 2-3 of these high-value keywords naturally in your headline.

7. Using Excessive Symbols or Emojis

While a strategic pipe, bullet, or emoji can organize information, excessive symbols look unprofessional.

Many ATS systems and LinkedIn's search algorithm may not properly read special characters.

When in doubt, opt for clean, simple formatting that emphasizes your expertise.

8. Being Too Humble or Vague

"Seeking new opportunities" or "Open to work" headlines waste valuable space.

These passive statements position you as needy rather than valuable.

Replace these with confident statements about your expertise and the specific value you offer.

For example: “Project Manager | Delivering complex initiatives on time and under budget”

hook: A very long time ago, I was the Thought Police.
text:
A very long time ago, I was the Thought Police.

I worked at a credit union data center, and I was one of the IT administrators. One of the rather unpleasant tasks I had was to monitor the Microsoft Exchange email server for sensitive data like account numbers, credit card numbers, OFAC data, etc. Microsoft provided administrators the ability to browse and inspect every mailbox in the system, looking for unintentional or purposeful leaking of protected information.

This was just after 9/11, which meant we're talking decades before AI. The server had some basic keyword scripts that flagged messages for review, and those filters were overly broad on purpose because missing ONE non-compliant email was a failure that would incur massive penalties for the company. So a human - me - had to review hundreds of emails a week for data exfiltration.

Cybersecurity has advanced considerably since those days (thankfully) but exfiltration of data has a new problem: runaway agents. And I don't mean the obvious hacks like hostile prompt injection, I mean unbounded agents trying to be helpful.

Here's an example. An agentic flow is given an ERP/CRM dataset and told to optimize it to reduce customer churn. Improperly bounded, it does a web search for tools that can perform this task, finds a third party MCP or API that's free and accessible, and begins to inject customer data into an untrusted tool to get answers that legitimately solve the problem posed to it.

It's not TECHNICALLY doing anything wrong. It's being helpful, and with lazy prompts like "Analyze this spreadsheet and give me the simple answer" (I have seen people type that literal prompt), an agent will interpret the lack of boundaries as fair game to help the user accomplish their goal.

And lots of current cybersec infrastructure is poorly equipped to handle this scenario. Most AI tools properly encrypt all their data in transit, so a network traffic inspector won't be able to see what the agent is working on; some agent tools like Claude Cowork even spin up their own virtual machines that are secure enclaves.

There are a few different ways to handle this scenario. First, training users on properly bounded, thoughtful prompts helps. Second, system-wide configurations can help at least warn the user they're about to do something dumb. And third, dedicated systems with local AI, properly bounded, can prevent an agent from calling any tool or service not on a pre-approved list.

There's obviously a lot more than just this, but this gives you a sense of the scope and scale of the problem, that "helpful" can turn into a security nightmare if AI isn't given boundaries AND sandboxed appropriately.

Photo of one of my servers from back in the day.

hook: Most first-time startup founders I talk to set themselves up to fail. Here are the 7 biggest mistakes I see nearly EVERY
text:
Most first-time startup founders I talk to set themselves up to fail. Here are the 7 biggest mistakes I see nearly EVERY founder make (myself included):

1. You spend too much money on things you don’t really need

People love getting offices, hiring salespeople, getting VA’s, expensive video equipment, software, and even setting up an entity pre-revenue. In 2013, I bought a VOIP phone system a year before we had a customer! Cash will be EXTREMELY tight at some point, even if it’s not now. Remember that.

2. Hiring people before $1m ARR

This is a hot take. I think there should be a technical co-founder building and a business co-founder doing sales, marketing, and support until $1m ARR - just like Klaviyo did. If you have that discipline, you will be profitable, control your destiny, and emerge with product-market fit.

3. Thinking you are an “ideas guy” and can find an operator

I spit out my drink when I hear this. Just like when I hear someone talking about “stealth mode”. Thinking someone will do the hard work for you at this nearly impossible stage is delusional. Once you get to $10m ARR with under 10 people, you earned it, but until then, no way.

4. Not “doing things that don’t scale” under $1m ARR

First-time founders don't understand how manual getting to $1-$3m ARR is. It’s face-to-face conversations, however you can get them, taking the feedback, and improving product as quickly as possible. Nothing will work until the product is great, so all that “growth hacking” will be a waste of time and money.

5. Thinking seed funding means you have a good business

If you were able to raise money for your idea pre-revenue, it means nothing more than you could sell a vision to investors. The hard part is making a business out of it. Keep that in mind and avoid funding at all costs. You’ll thank me later.

6. Not posting on organic social media starting TODAY

This one took me a decade to realize, and a year after I started to master. Nothing is more powerful in today’s world than being able to create great organic social media content that your prospects have demand for independent of what you’re selling. If you start today, you’ll get zero engagement, followers, or leads, but that’s not the point… You’re one day closer to finding your voice.

7. Thinking you’ll be in and out in 3-5 years

Founders should have a decades long time horizon when they start. People wildly overestimate what they can accomplish in a year, but wildly underestimate what they can accomplish over a decade.

TAKEAWAY:

Being a first-time founder is hard.

Literally everything is working against you.

If we knew how hard it was, most would never start.

But here’s the good news...

As Alex Hormozi so elegantly put it:

Every successful person started with:

0 revenue
0 subscribers
0 customers
0 fans

And the only difference between them and everyone else is they actually start.

But that’s not REALLY the secret.

The successful ones not only start…

They keep building.
