text:
#AI capability, AI-company valuation and an operating company’s ability to capture value are three different questions. 

Treating them as one is where bad decisions begin.

I believe deeply in AI.

I also don’t believe every dollar chasing it is going to earn a return.

On Monday, AI-linked stocks sold off after Anthropic’s Dario Amodei — and then Sam Altman and Elon Musk — said the industry needs to slow the pace of frontier development.

That wasn’t the market’s only problem. Oil was up. Bond yields were up. Rate expectations were changing.

Still, the reaction felt telling. We’ve spent the last few years treating three very different questions as if they were the same.

1. What can AI do? - A capability question. Answered by using the tools, not by reading about them.
2. What are AI companies worth? - A pricing question. It moves on sentiment, rates and supply of capital — not on what the models can do for you.
3. How much of that value can the rest of us actually capture? - An operating question. It is decided inside your workflows, your data and your decisions.

I don’t have a clean answer to all three. I don’t think anyone does.

But I’ve used these tools enough now to know this: even if the models didn’t improve much from here, there is already more than enough capability to change how a lot of companies work.

What I’ve watched happen — both ways

Where it worked.
AI shortened research, prepared decision briefs, flagged pipeline risk and took hours out of recurring executive work. Nothing exotic — the same tasks every week, done to a defined standard, with someone reviewing the output.

Where it didn’t. Companies bought the tools and changed almost nothing else. No outcome named, no workflow redesigned, no owner. The license renews. The operating model is identical.

That’s the gap I keep coming back to.

The technology really can be extraordinary. That doesn’t mean every investment assumption around it makes sense.

Where we start instead
At MPS, we start with the outcome someone wants to improve, then work backward. Five questions, in this order:

1. What outcome are we trying to move?
2. What has to change in the workflow?
3. Who owns it? 
4. Which data can be trusted? 
5. Where do people need to stay in the loop? 

And then the one that settles the argument: how will we know it actually worked?

That part is less exciting than a new model release, but it’s where the value actually shows up.

The question I’d put to you
If AI didn’t get materially better from here, what could your company still change with what already exists?

Market price, model capability and operating adoption are three different questions. Treating them as one is where bad decisions begin. 

If you have a view — including the view that the whole category is overbuilt — tell us where you land.

text:
The biggest AI risk in your business isn't a hallucination. It's an agent that can actually do things.

A truly capable AI assistant needs access to emails, calendars, credentials, CRM systems, and internal tools. That's what makes it useful. And that's exactly what makes it risky.

One unsafe instruction can become a real business action, instantly.

I explored how the most forward-thinking AI architectures are solving this, and the answer is isolation by design.

Each agent runs inside its own sandbox. A research agent can browse the internet but cannot touch private data. An action agent can access sensitive tools but has no internet connection. Credentials live in a vault, so agents can use them without ever seeing the secrets themselves.

hook: We only scroll social media now.
text:
We only scroll social media now.

We don't follow or like. We mindlessly flick our thumbs to watch the next TikTok, barely even considering giving any recognition to the piece of content we just watched.

That's not hyperbolic, that's data-driven reality. 

Take these numbers from Anthropic Social Analytics Manager 💾Gabriel Davis. He pulled 2.5 million Instagram posts from Jan 2025 to May 2026:
  
- Carousel likes: down 73%
- Reel likes: down 81%
- Carousel comments: down 39%
- Reel comments: down 46%
  
Even the top 1% of content saw engagement drop 54%+. Socialinsider's 2026 benchmarks (70M posts) confirmed it: "Average comments per post fell on TikTok (24%) and Instagram (16%), suggesting a shift toward more passive engagement."
  
That's a fundamental change in how people use social media.
  
Yet most social media professionals are still hyper-focused on likes and comments. I genuinely think we're moving to a post-engagement era, and Social Media Marketers need to revisit their strategies and metrics for a world where people scroll without engaging.

🤔 SO WHAT DOES ENGAGEMENT EVEN MEAN?
  
Likes, comments, engagement rates... they're not the best metrics anymore. Even Adam Mosseri's told us: it's all about views, watch through, and shares.
  
We've gotta shift likes and comments to secondary status. Nice to haves, not the goal.
 
📱 TIKTOK DOESN'T EVEN NEED THE LIKE BUTTON.
  
TikTok now weights watch time, completion rate, and replays as its strongest signals. They're tracking micro-watches (when you rewatch a segment).

Instagram measures dwell time on carousels.

LinkedIn's engineering team said time spent reading a post is now a primary rank signal.
  
If I watch 30 seconds of an emo band's TikTok, I don't have to like or follow to get more of their content, because TikTok caught those 30 seconds and will serve me more.
  
⚡ WHAT METRICS & STRATEGIES DO WE FOCUS ON?
  
Watch time and completion rate. Did they finish it? Did they rewatch? Those numbers decide if the algorithm pushes your content.
  
Hooks. You're not trying to earn a like, you're trying to earn attention. No hook, no retention, no algorithmic push.
  
THE GOOD NEWS?

The interest-graph era means our content can reach FAR MORE PEOPLE than the Follower era ever allowed. The algorithms are brilliant at putting content in front of the right eyeballs.
  
All you gotta do is become an expert in video best practices, and stop worrying about the validation of likes and comments.

creator: Damien Benveniste
hook: RAG retrieval is not one search algorithm! Sparse search, dense search, hybrid search, and reranking solve different par
text:
RAG retrieval is not one search algorithm! Sparse search, dense search, hybrid search, and reranking solve different parts of the evidence-finding problem.

Imagine an internal support assistant receives:

"ACME-ERR-431 after too many login attempts"

One useful passage contains the error code. Another says "recover access after repeated authentication failures" without repeating the user's words. Which one can the retriever see?

- Sparse lexical retrieval, often implemented with BM25, turns the query and documents into mostly empty term vectors. An inverted index finds matching terms, then BM25 scores them using term frequency, term rarity, and document-length normalization. Exact identifiers and rare phrases become powerful signals. A passage using different words may never become a candidate.

- Dense retrieval encodes the query and each passage independently. Passage vectors are computed ahead of time; at request time, the query becomes a vector and nearest-neighbor search returns similar representations. This can match "too many login attempts" with "repeated authentication failures." But one vector can weaken a rare token such as `ACME-ERR-431`, and quality depends on the embedding model and domain.

- Hybrid retrieval runs lexical and dense search in parallel, then fuses their ranked lists. Reciprocal Rank Fusion ignores incompatible raw scores and gives each document credit from its position in each list. Both the exact-code passage and semantic paraphrase can survive. But hybrid search runs two paths and only helps when their misses are complementary.

- Reranking is a second stage, not a replacement for retrieval. A cross-encoder takes the query and one candidate passage together, lets their tokens attend to each other, and emits a relevance score. That richer interaction can move the best passage to the top, but it is too expensive to apply to every document in a large corpus. More importantly, it cannot rescue a relevant passage that the first stage never retrieved.

That last distinction is the one I would use to diagnose a weak RAG pipeline:

- If the needed passage is absent from the candidate set, improve recall: fix chunking, add lexical or dense retrieval, or improve the retriever.
- If the passage is present but ranked below the context cutoff, improve ordering: fuse rankings, tune the first-stage scorer, or add a reranker.

I would not start by stacking every technique. Build a labeled set of representative queries, run sparse and dense baselines, and inspect their misses. Use hybrid retrieval when the two candidate sets recover different relevant passages. Add reranking when the candidate recall is already good but the top positions are not.

When a RAG answer is wrong, I would inspect the candidates before touching the generation model: was the right passage missing, or was it merely buried?

The New Kingmakers  

It's become clear that revenue scale no longer matters - or is correlated - with raising a round.  It's important but not sufficient.  Besides team caliber, what ACTUALLY matters to fundraising is how many top AI-native companies use your products, love your products, embrace your products and profess undying loyalty to you (i.e. say they won't replace it at the drop of a hat).  

Why?  
AI-native companies are the hardest customers to win. They have the engineers to build it themselves. They have the taste to know when something is mediocre. They try every new tool the week it launches and rip it out the week after. If one of them pays you and stays, your product survived the toughest evaluation there is. 

Investors know this.  Revenue can be bought. Pilots, services, discounts, a heroic enterprise sales team. ARR built from Fortune 500 pilots proves you can sell. The product might still be mediocre. Loyalty from a kingmaker can't be manufactured.  These companies are the leading indicator. Investors are underwriting where the market will be in 5 years, and the AI-native companies are already living there. Their workflows today are everyone else's workflows in 2029. If they picked you, you've been chosen by the buyers everyone else will copy.  

The last reason is distribution. Kingmakers talk. Their engineers post what they use. Their founders compare notes. One of them begets the next three.  

Who  
There are probably ~50 AI-native companies that are perceived as kingmakers for startups.  I've seen $50M+ rounds raised on the backs of just having one of these as a customer. (not pilot, but actual paying customer using the product as a core part of their infra and workflows).  

Meanwhile, I see early-stage founders spending 12 months chasing CVS, Walmart, and Pfizer. Long procurement cycles, security reviews, a pilot that never converts. Even when it lands, the logo proves you can survive procurement. That's the wrong thing to prove in 2026.

creator: Brij Kishore Pandey
hook: An LLM does not generate a sentence.
text:
An LLM does not generate a sentence.
 
It generates one token.
 Then another.
 Then another.
 
But a lot happens before each token reaches your screen.
 
Here is the simplified inference pipeline:
 
Your prompt is split into tokens.
Each token is converted into a numerical embedding.
Transformer layers use attention and feed-forward networks to process the context.
The model produces a probability distribution across its vocabulary.
A decoding strategy selects the next token.
That token is added to the context, and the cycle repeats.
Tokens are converted back into text and streamed to you.
 
The most interesting part is that inference has two very different phases:
 
Prefill processes the input tokens largely in parallel.
 
Decode generates tokens sequentially, making memory movement, KV-cache size, and bandwidth increasingly important.
 
This is why:
 
 → Longer prompts increase prefill work
 → Longer conversations grow the KV cache
 → Quantization can reduce memory requirements
 → FlashAttention reduces expensive memory reads
 → Speculative decoding can improve generation speed
 → Temperature, Top-K, and Top-P change how the next token is selected
 
The model may look like it is "writing."
 
Underneath, it is repeatedly performing numerical operations, selecting a token, updating its context, and doing it all again.
 
I mapped the complete flow in one diagram.
 
Save it if you are learning how LLM inference actually works.

hook: “I should be further along by now”You've said it. Maybe this week. And it feels like a timeline problem, like you're beh
text: “I should be further along by now”You've said it. Maybe this week. And it feels like a timeline problem, like you're behind schedule on some map you drew in your head. But it's not about the timeline. It never was. Strip it back, and the real sentence is: "I'm not sure this is going to work out.” That's what's underneath. The urgency isn't fuel. It's doubtful to wear a clock. Here's why that matters neurologically: Your brain doesn't distinguish between "I'm running out of time" and "I might fail." Both activate the same threat circuits. Same cortisol. Same narrowed thinking. Same erosion of the exact prefrontal function you need to execute at the level that would actually close the gap. So the founder who's obsessing over the timeline is literally degrading the cognitive machinery that would solve the timeline. You're not slow. You're anxious. And the anxiety is eating your hours from the inside. One of our founders was stuck in this loop for months. Building. Executing. Getting better every week. But waking up every morning with this low hum of "it's taking too long." Then he asked himself one question: "If I knew with certainty that I'd get there, would I still be stressed about how long it takes?" The answer was no. Which meant the timeline was never the problem. The doubt was. So he resolved the doubt, but not with random affirmations. With actual data: Tracked his execution daily. Watched his own output climb. His journal entries reflect the transformation he was experiencing. He saw, in black and white, that the person he was six months ago couldn't do what he does on a Tuesday now. And then something shifted. He stopped rushing. Started executing cleaner. Dropped the low-leverage panic tasks. Protected his ring fence sessions instead of cramming more into the day. His words: "I let go of the timeframe because I realized the fear of timing was really just self-doubt. If I know I'm going to get there, why does it matter how long it takes?" That's not passive. That's the most aggressive thing a founder can do, remove the emotional drag that's costing you 30% of your cognitive capacity every single day. The founders who break through aren't the ones who have the best strategy. They’re those who execute the one they have, best.

Instinct read my emails and Airbnb receipts and made the list. 

Then it asked, "Did I miss anything?"

It had all of them.

I sent a photo of my passport and a photo of me.

It sent back my visa on arrival as a PDF.

Bali immigration is strict. If one detail is wrong, they can deport you fast.

And if Instinct made the mistake, I had no one else to blame.

I put all my trust in Instinct.

At the gate, I scanned my passport and sweated a little.

The gate opened.

How to Build GPT-6 Astra Automations (that don’t eat your usage limit)

Codex scheduled tasks are useful, but they run inside a chat thread and use your subscription allowance.

For recurring deterministic business automations, I would rather use Codex to build the workflow, then host the predictable parts somewhere like Trigger.dev.

I broke the decision into three buckets:

→ Scheduled automations
Run the same workflow at a defined time, like a weekday morning brief that reads your calendar, does limited research, and sends you a ClickUp DM.

→ Webhook automations
Run when something happens, like a form submission, a new CRM record, or an inbound email.

→ Codex SDK automations
Use this when the workflow needs a real agentic loop that can decide what to investigate, check its own prior work, and loop back for more context.

Most business workflows are closer to the first two. The flow is predictable, so the agent does not need to choose every next step.

I also tested each hosted automation before turning it on. Local success was not enough because the deployment still needed the right environment variables, the correct delivery destination, and a real proof run.

I just dropped a YouTube video walking through all three patterns, including the Trigger.dev setup and hosted testing.

Link to the full video is in the comments 👇

You ask an AI to summarize a report. It hands back a confident answer. You read the source and notice it missed a detail that changes the conclusion.
 
You point it out. It agrees, and gives you a corrected answer.
 
The new answer is better. But you handed it a different report with the same kind of gap tomorrow, would it catch it on its own?
 
Two separate questions live inside that one correction.

hook: 214 million people saw this AI warning. So we called an emergency debate.
text:
214 million people saw this AI warning. So we called an emergency debate. 

The warning came from someone who had worked at both Anthropic and OpenAI.

Then a current Anthropic employee backed it publicly.

It had spread so far beyond the tech world that a friend of mine who cuts hair and has never really cared about AI messaged me asking, “What the hell is going on?”

I then realised a lot of people were probably asking the same question.

The problem is, when you speak to people who have spent years studying AI, you get completely opposing answers.

So I brought four of them around the same table.

Roman Yampolskiy is a computer scientist who coined the term “AI safety” and has spent years studying whether increasingly intelligent systems can remain under human control.

Nate Soares leads the Machine Intelligence Research Institute and has spent more than a decade working on AI alignment. He believes we are moving too quickly towards systems we don’t yet know how to reliably control.

Ed Zitron thinks much of the AI conversation has become detached from what the technology can actually do today. He believes the industry is overhyping it while distracting us from financial, environmental and social consequences already happening.

Andrew McAfee is an MIT researcher and economist who takes a very different view. He thinks we spend so much time talking about what could go wrong that we barely talk about what AI could make better.

And that disagreement is what made this conversation so interesting to me.

We discussed things like:

- How do you control something that eventually becomes smarter than you?
- Are the biggest warnings about AI based on evidence or assumptions?
- What happens to work and human purpose if AI becomes better at more cognitive tasks?
- Are we ignoring problems AI is already creating because we’re obsessed with hypothetical future ones?
- Why have Sam Altman, Elon Musk and Geoffrey Hinton all warned us about AI?

The question I kept coming back to was simple:

What is actually true?

Depending on who you listen to, AI is either one of the greatest opportunities humanity has ever created or something we’re racing towards without understanding the consequences.

Both claims deserve to be challenged.

There were moments in this debate where I genuinely found myself moving between the arguments. That’s the value of putting people who fundamentally disagree in the same room.

I didn’t want four people telling me the same thing. I wanted each of them to explain where the other side was wrong.

If you’ve watched the last few months of AI news wondering what you’re actually supposed to believe, this conversation is for you.

Our emergency AI debate with Ed, Roman, Nate and Andrew is out now ❤️👊🏾

hook: A few former colleagues have asked me, “Where have you been?”
text:
A few former colleagues have asked me, “Where have you been?”

Apparently, I’d gone quiet on the Medical Affairs front. I hadn’t disappeared. I’d just become slightly obsessed with AI.

A few years ago, I probably would have laughed at that.

I’m not from a technology background. I’ve spent my career in Medical Affairs, compliance and signatory work. That is the world I know and still care deeply about.

Then, in December 2024, I joined a webinar organised by Dr Nick Broughton . Listening to Heather Murray talk about what AI could do made something click. I didn’t suddenly understand the technology. I just started seeing familiar Medical Affairs problems differently.

Could AI help us make sense of clinical papers more quickly? Support parts of copy approval? Reduce repetitive work and give experienced people more time for the things that need their judgement?

I remember finding Heather Murray during the lunch break and throwing some ideas at her. I had more questions than answers, but I left genuinely excited.

That feeling stayed with me.

I started reading, took courses, tested tools and got things wrong. What surprised me most was how much I enjoyed being a beginner again.

The more I learned, the more I looked at familiar processes and thought: could this be simpler? Could we give people some time back? Could AI do some of the heavy lifting while people keep control of the thinking?

That is where my passion for it comes from.

I don’t love AI because it is clever technology. I love seeing a frustrating process people have learned to live with and realising there may be another way.

I also understand the caution. Can we trust the output? What happens to sensitive information? And where do people fit if AI starts doing more of the work?

I’ve asked some of those questions myself.

The more I’ve learned, the less interested I’ve become in AI replacing people. I’m more interested in how it can help good people do their jobs better.

Use it where it helps. Put the right controls around it. Keep people responsible for the decisions that matter.

AI can help with the preparation. People still own the judgement.
That thinking has taken me into my role as Chief Medical Affairs Officer at OllieDx, where we’ve been working on an AI-supported platform for neurodivergent assessment. 

More recently, I sat down with Maneeze Jahangir and Elsie Cunliffe from The Contrarians to talk about the real barriers people face when bringing AI into everyday work.

I’ve attached a short clip because it touches on something I care about: helping people understand where AI could help without losing the judgement and responsibility that matter.

So, for anyone wondering where I’ve been, I’m still in Medical Affairs. I’ve just found something that has made me look at it with fresh eyes.

I haven’t felt this curious about a new area of work for a long time.
If you’re exploring the same questions, message me. I’d genuinely enjoy comparing notes.

text:
AI agent is becoming the label of choice for almost any AI workflow. But autonomy is more than a name on a product page.

Forget the label for a moment. Look at what the system does.

If every step is predetermined and the software follows the sequence, that is automation, even if AI is inside it.

Agency begins when the system can pursue a goal and use what happened to choose what to do next.

The agent is not the model. It uses a model for reasoning. The surrounding system keeps track of the goal and current state, then gives the model access to tools when action is needed.

For organizations, that distinction matters.

A system that can choose its next action needs a mandate and boundaries. Accountability still belongs to people.

So before buying the word agent, ask a more useful question: can the system change what it does next because of what just happened?

Marketing can rename a workflow. Agency has to appear in the behavior.

#AIAgents #AgenticAI

text:
One of my biggest takeaways from Fast Company’s Innovation Festival: No, AI won't kill us. When you use AI as your thought partner, you can remove all the tedious, mundane work and get back to what makes us human: our ability to THINK—strategically, creatively, and innovatively.

Stop using AI like it is Google to ask questions, and start by adding your work as context, then have the AI ask you questions.

Before asking, “Which AI should I use?” understand what you actually do.

I love the 5P Framework from TrustInsights (https://lnkd.in/eivrsnKP):
Purpose, People, Process, Platform, Performance.

🎯 PURPOSE
- Why are we doing this?
- What problem are we solving?
- What outcome are we trying to create?
- How will we know it worked?

👥 PEOPLE
- Who performs the work?
- Who has the institutional knowledge?
- Who makes decisions?
- Who approves the output?
- Who will be affected?
- Do they have the skills, authority, and bandwidth?

⚙️ PROCESS
- How does the work actually get done today?
- What triggers the process?
- What are the steps?
- What information is required?
- Where are the handoffs, decisions, and approvals?
- What is repetitive or tedious?
- Where does human judgment matter?
- Could someone else follow the documented process without asking you how?

Now you have context AI can work with.

Maybe AI reads and summarizes emails while you're having your morning coffee or exercising. Maybe it prepares drafts for you to review instead of sending them. Maybe it handles repetitive administrative steps while keeping you at the approval points that matter.

The goal isn't to remove humans from work.

It's to give humans more time to think strategically, creatively, and innovatively.

And when you need AI to pull more knowledge out of your head, combine 5P with Geoff Woods' CRIT prompting framework from The AI-Driven Leader (https://lnkd.in/eXvybFip): Context → Role → Interview → Task.

My favorite part is Interview:

“Interview me. Ask me one question at a time, up to three questions, to gain deeper context.”

Then give your AI tool of choice the task.

Those questions AI asks can uncover assumptions, requirements, and knowledge you didn't think to put into your original prompt.

YOUR expertise + YOUR documented processes (SOP) + AI = a powerful combination.

Start with the work.
Document the work.
Then decide where AI belongs.

And if you're building your AI literacy, add the podcast The Artificial Intelligence Show (https://lnkd.in/eEmdDBci) with Paul Roetzer and Mike Kaput to your weekly listening and learning routine.

Become a forever student. Learning insights and perspectives from other humans will always make you reimagine how we want to live, work, and continuously be adaptable to whatever new challenges or obstacles you face in YOUR life.

Your number one priority shouldn't be to have all the answers.

It's to build a team that doesn't need to ask you the questions.

Remember, you build the people and they build the business.

text:
The Economist published a headline on September 4th saying the AI jobs apocalypse is postponed. Maybe, but the unemployment rate will never reveal it either way: AI layoffs are too small to see next to everything else going on.

American companies lay off about 1.7 million workers in a normal month. Companies blame AI for about 16,000 cuts a month this year, says the consultancy Challenger, Gray & Christmas. That is less than 1% of the layoffs that happen anyway, so the unemployment rate, 4.1%, cannot register them.

If you run a company, ignore those national numbers. They tell you nothing about your business.

The better move is to pick one job in your company, like an order or a new feature, and follow it from first step to last, writing down at every step how long someone works on it and how long it sits waiting for the next person. Whatever it waits on is your bottleneck. No jobs report counts that waiting, so nobody will find it for you.

I watched a large tech company give every engineer an AI assistant, and each engineer produced about 20% more. But the company still shipped new features at the same speed. The engineers wrote faster, yet the features kept sitting in testing and sign-off, and nobody gave those teams any tooling.

16,000 cuts a month disappear inside an economy that lays off 1.7 million people monthly. Your company is different: one slow step can hold up everything. At Nokia, engineers had to wait 48 hours for their code to compile, and nothing any engineer did individually could fix that.

P.S. I wrote the long version of that lesson; it's in the comments.

Harvard's Amy Edmondson coined the phrase "psychological safety" in 1999.

Google's Project Aristotle studied 180 of its own teams over two years.

I coach my CEO clients to begin one sentence at a time:

Most AI agents don’t (actually) learn.

And you pay them to repeat the same work every session.

New session. New model. New tool. Back to zero.

I’ve been testing SenseLab in a multi-agent development workflow across Claude Code, Codex, and MCP.

The problem was familiar:

→ Agents repeated research already completed
→ Technical decisions had to be explained again
→ Switching models meant losing accumulated context
→ One agent couldn’t build on another agent’s findings
→ Successful and failed approaches disappeared after each run

SenseLab treats this as an infrastructure problem, not a prompting problem.

It provides a shared memory layer called Rooms, where agents can store context, commit decisions and outcomes, and reuse previous findings across sessions, tools, and models, without changing the underlying agent framework.

So instead of every agent starting from scratch:

1. One agent investigates the problem and commits its findings
2. Another agent reads that context and continues the work
3. The outcome is stored for future sessions
4. Effective approaches are reinforced, while ineffective ones are corrected

Over time, work across multiple agents and tasks compounds into proprietary training data rather than disappearing inside closed context windows.

A longer prompt isn’t a persistent memory.

It’s just more context that eventually gets discarded.

As teams move from single-agent scripts to multi-agent and multi-session workflows, a shared memory layer starts looking less optional.

Curious how other builders are handling this: custom memory infrastructure, aggressive summarization, or simply accepting the repetition?

If you are a B2C company, I think you should study this picture very, very closely...

Everybody knows Will Smith and The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air, but the guy next to him, Geoffrey the butler, was one of the most lovable characters in the show and probably got around 75% of the screen time that Will got.

So what does that have to do with marketing?

I think there is a massive opportunity for B2C brands to work with more Geoffreys. 

Geoffreys are the side characters beside the main character, and because they aren't the main star, they are much cheaper to work with... but they still have a pretty decent amount of pull.

One of the companies in my portfolio, which I can't name, is working with a side character from one of the biggest TV shows in the US right now. Spoiler: it's set in a hospital... and it's working incredibly well!

They get the cultural cachet of the show, but they are able to work with one of its characters at a fifth of the cost.

I call this "The Geoffrey Effect": take something people already recognise, leverage the clout of a side character and pay much less than you would for the main star.

Everybody wants the Will Smiths, but the Will Smiths cost a lot... and very few people think about the Geoffreys.

If you're a brand doing influencer marketing, this is an absolute game changer... especially if you want to do the high-profile stuff without the high-profile price tag.

I think the gap between those two creates a sea of opportunity for brands that are smart and aren't dazzled by the biggest names!

hook: Your business gets easier to run when everyone knows the numbers.
text:
Your business gets easier to run when everyone knows the numbers.

I use a simple CEO Scorecard to make that happen.

Here’s how:

1. Pick the 7 numbers that tell you how the business is actually doing

For us, that could be:

- Cash in bank
- Cash collected
- Workshop sign-ups
- Meetings booked
- Sales closed
- Qualified leads
- Close rate

If you need 30 metrics to understand the health of your business, you probably haven’t identified the important ones yet.

2. Put them in one document

For every metric, track:

- Last week
- This week
- Target
- Delta

The team owns updating the data.

3. Create a weekly rhythm

Friday afternoon: team updates the scorecard.

Friday evening: I review it.

Monday: we make decisions.

No digging through dashboards 5 minutes before a meeting.

4. Run leadership meetings from the numbers

We start with the scorecard.

If something is green, great.

If something is off, we know exactly where to focus the conversation.

5. Step out of operations

This is the real goal.

I don’t want to know everything happening inside the business.

I want to know the few numbers that tell me when I need to look closer.

That’s how you go from operator to architect.

The business gives you the signal.

You decide where to apply attention.

—

I’m teaching you how to build a simple CEO Scorecard that gives you clarity on what actually matters in your business.

hook: You've tried AI automation but all of the outputs feel "meh."
text:
You've tried AI automation but all of the outputs feel "meh."

My D.O.S.A. Method fixes that in 4 steps (#2 is what everyone skips):

You've probably seen some sweet AI automation on YouTube or LinkedIn and thought, "man, I gotta try that!"

Then you set it up for yourself and, well, it kinda sucks.

Sure, maybe it technically did what you asked, but it didn't do it well and it probably didn't blow you away.

That's 90% of people's experience with AI.

The reason that happens is because most people are trying to automate things they've never seen results with on their own.

They tell AI to “draft cold outreach” or “personalize my resume” but they’ve never run a successful cold outreach campaign on their own, or manually drafted a resume that got them an interview.

That means they’re relying on AI to do the strategy side, which is what everyone else is doing and it leads to average outcomes.

That's where D.O.S.A. comes in!

I’ve been building systems and automations in my business for 10 years. I’ve been doing it with AI for the last 20+ months.

I created D.O.S.A. as a framework to help me know when to automate things with AI, and to to make sure I automated them the correct way.

Here’s the letter-by-letter breakdown:

D is for Do It Manually

Before you even THINK about automating something, you need to do it yourself - manually.

Every system has nuances, quirks, and gotchas that you’ll never be able to coach AI on if you haven’t done it yourself.

Ideally, the processes you’re automating are things you’re doing so often they drive you crazy so this should be easy.

But there’s one, little catch!

O is for Get The Outcome

Simply doing it manually isn’t enough.

If you automate a process that you personally haven’t seen outcomes with, you’re just scaling a broken system.

Before you automate, you need to actually achieve the desired outcome from your own manual work.

Why? Because that’s the only way you’ll know what version of the process - the exact inputs, tweaks, and strategies - are the ones that get results.

Which is exactly what you do next.

S is for Systemize It

Once you’ve gotten the outcome?

Build a system around it and document that system.

Write it out step-by-step in a Google Doc. Record a Loom of you talking through it and copy the transcript. Have everything mapped out to a tee.

A is for Automate It

Finally, once your system has been running and generating outcomes?

It’s time to automate! But when you do?

You feed AI the system you documented. You tell it all the quirks and nuances you found that make this process work.

That’s what’s going to make your AI automation make your jaw drop vs. cranking out “meh” slop that makes you sad.

🛠 Before you automate, you need a system that actually works.

Start here 👉 https://smallmachine.co

hook: Zuckerberg says AI labs don't need to slow down together, because buyers will pick the better aligned model. There's a p
text:
Zuckerberg says AI labs don't need to slow down together, because buyers will pick the better aligned model. There's a problem with that: Nobody can tell which model is safer, and the market only finds out after something goes wrong.

Yesterday Zuckerberg, joining Jensen Huang, broke from Dario Amodei, Sam Altman, Elon Musk, and Demis Hassabis, who all backed a plan for the top labs to deliberately pace themselves. 

His argument: 

"Any lab that doesn't focus on alignment will fall behind," because "people won't want to use agents that are misaligned with them and that don't do what they ask." 

And listen, he's right, and I and other have made this case: The incentive to build safely is already there. It's why cars advertise safety features, not speed.

Jensen Huang said the same thing a day earlier. 

"Safety is an engineering problem, not a legal one." Build, test it, hold it back if it's not ready. The market handles the rest.

But they're saying this as if the big labs aren't already doing this - they are. And here's where the market falls down.


THERE ARE TWO KINDS OF ALIGNMENT

Zuckerberg's example is an agent that doesn't do what you ask. You'd notice that in a week and switch. He's right about that kind.

But nobody is losing sleep over agents that ignore instructions- that's life.

They're losing sleep over what a model does in a situation nobody tested. 

You CAN compare a model's price, its speed, and its benchmark scores. 

You CANNOT compare risk. It's invisible right up until the day it isn't, which means the buyer Zuckerberg is counting on is choosing blind.


WHAT THE MARKET ACTUALLY REWARDS

Self-driving cars are statistically safer than human drivers. But when one crashes, it's on the news that night.

The market doesn't reward being safe. It rewards not being in the headlines. 

Those are not the same thing, and a company optimizing for the second one will underinvest in the first, right?


WHY DARIO'S SIDE IS WORRIED

Markets learn from failures that are small and repeated. Cars crash one at a time, so the feedback loop eventually works.

Dario's essay argues that frontier AI failures might not come in that shape. 

If the first real failure is the big one, there is no second buyer to learn from it. 

That's why he wants outside evaluators inside every lab before the failure, not liability after it. Sam, Elon, and Demis all signed on. (These are people who sue each other.)

Look at who's in which camp. 

The four asking to slow down have the models at the very front. 

The two saying no are the guy who sells the chips and the guy who gives his models away. 

Doesn't make one side wrong, just tells you their current position.

WHAT THIS MEANS FOR THE REST OF US

Nothing changes on Monday. Whether the frontier paces itself or not, the models your team has today already do far more than your team is using. This debate is about the ceiling, and almost every company I talk to is nowhere near it.

Just sayin'.

hook: Stop chasing revenue. Chase profit. 💰
text:
Stop chasing revenue. Chase profit. 💰

Payam Zamani took his first company public at a $1.2 BILLION valuation.

Today, he runs One Planet, where he owns, operates, and invests in companies.

And when I sat down with him on How We Profit, he told me he sometimes doesn't even know the revenue of his businesses.

But he ALWAYS knows the margins. 😳

(Watch the FULL episode on YouTube: https://lnkd.in/ghJAiUJN)

Your margin is basically how much money you have left after the costs it took to make that revenue.

And when Payam bought AutoWeb back, its margins were just 17%.

So he stopped chasing revenue that wasn't profitable.

Revenue went DOWN at first.

Today, AutoWeb has 50%+ margins.

As Payam put it, “Stop chasing dollars. Chase profits.”

Here are key 3 financial points every entrepreneur should be evaluating 👇🏼

💰 Find out which revenue is actually worth having
👉🏼 Go client by client, service by service, product by product. A $100K client sounds GREAT, but if it costs you $95K to serve them? You have a $5K client. 😅

🧹 Find the expenses nobody questions anymore
👉🏼 Old software. Duplicate vendors. Contracts nobody uses. Payam says this stuff piles up as companies grow. At Inspirato, his team cut $45 MILLION in expenses within months.

🏗️ Know how you'll become profitable from DAY ONE
👉🏼 You don't need to make money immediately, but you should know HOW you're going to get there. Payam avoids businesses that need to keep raising money just to stay alive.

A lot of entrepreneurs can tell you EXACTLY how much revenue they made last month.

But ask them how much they actually KEPT?

That answer gets a little harder. 😅

Before you chase another $1M in revenue, make sure the revenue you already have is actually worth having.

What’s one part of your business you need to run the numbers on? 👇🏼

creator: Brij Kishore Pandey
hook: Your AI agent gives the right answer.
text:
Your AI agent gives the right answer.
 
It also takes 15 model calls, retries the same failed tool three times, and costs more than the task is worth.
 
Would you ship it?
 
The engineering around the model is what decides that outcome. These are the concepts worth understanding.
 
𝟭. 𝗔𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗰 𝗹𝗼𝗼𝗽𝘀
 Plan, act, observe, adjust. Without a clear stopping condition, a failed attempt turns into an endless loop.
 
𝟮. 𝗠𝗖𝗣
 A standard way for agents to connect to tools and data. It does not decide which actions each agent is allowed to take, that part is still yours.
 
𝟯. 𝗦𝘂𝗯𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗺𝘂𝗹𝘁𝗶 𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝘀𝘆𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗺𝘀
 Delegate bounded tasks with clear inputs, context, and outputs. Each added agent also adds coordination overhead.
 
𝟰. 𝗔𝗜 𝗴𝗮𝘁𝗲𝘄𝗮𝘆
 A shared layer for authentication, model routing, rate limits, and usage controls. Without it, every application ends up building the same plumbing on its own.
 
𝟱. 𝗜𝗻𝗳𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲 𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗼𝗺𝗶𝗰𝘀
 Cost per completed task, not cost per call. Token counts, caching, model choice, and repeated calls all show up on the bill.
 
𝟲. 𝗘𝘃𝗮𝗹𝘀
 A definition of what a successful result looks like, tested against realistic tasks, edge cases, and failure modes before a change ships.
 
𝟳. 𝗚𝘂𝗮𝗿𝗱𝗿𝗮𝗶𝗹𝘀
 Checks on inputs, tool actions, and outputs. A model requesting an action should never be the only thing authorizing it.
 
𝟴. 𝗢𝗯𝘀𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗮𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗶𝘁𝘆
 A complete trace of the run: model calls, tool responses, latency, errors, spend. When something fails, this is the evidence you need to explain why.
 
𝟵. 𝗔𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗵𝗮𝗿𝗻𝗲𝘀𝘀
 The runtime holding everything together: state, memory, tool execution, checks, recovery.
 
These concepts connect in practice, not just in theory. A repeated tool call shows up in your traces. It drives up cost. An eval can expose the pattern. A limit in the harness can stop it. Each step is testable on its own.
 
If you are learning this stack, take one small agent and follow a single task from request to completion. Then deliberately break a tool call and watch what the system does next. That single exercise teaches more than reading about any one of these nine concepts in isolation.
 
Which of these nine layers do you think gets skipped most often when teams move agents into production too fast?

text:
The biggest news in tech this week:

- Dario Calls to "Pace the Frontier"
- Instinct Raising $1BN at $10BN & Meta Launches Muse
- Miro Sells for $1.35BN After a $17.5BN Valuation
- Mistral Raises €3BN

My notes below with Jason Lemkin and Rory O'Driscoll:

1. Summary of the Problems and the Solutions

Cyber risk is real, mass economic unemployment feels overblown, and losing control of recursive agents is difficult to assess. Meanwhile, proposed solutions range from unlikely to practically impossible to implement.

2. Why Is It Overblown and Not Nearly as Dramatic as Anthropic Makes It?

If the government truly believed a San Francisco lab had a 10% chance of destroying humanity, it would intervene immediately. The lack of intervention suggests authorities do not view extreme existential risk claims as an imminent threat.

3. Why Is It Bullshit, Dario, to Think We Will Have International Alignment on AI?

Global coordination on frontier AI ignores geopolitical reality. Getting democratic allies to agree is difficult enough, while expecting enforceable alignment with China and Russia makes international pacing agreements even harder to imagine.

4. Is the Personal Assistant Market a Market Where You Can Build a Standalone Company?

Standalone AI assistants face a fundamental question: can they build durable businesses while valuations race into the billions and platform incumbents pursue the same market?

5. Why Meta Might Just Win With Muse

Meta has a structural advantage because it owns the infrastructure and underlying LLM. While competitors spend $3 to $4 per user on compute, Meta can deliver fast, capable agentic workflows without the same infrastructure burden.

6. Is Dario Simply Being Strategic Ahead of an IPO With His Pacing Argument?

One interpretation is that Anthropic’s pacing argument is effectively an S-1 risk factor discussed in public. By addressing existential risk now, leadership can make it a debated, understood issue rather than a roadshow problem later.

7. Why I Would Not Invest in the New Instinct Round

Standalone AI assistants face brutal economics when incumbents have their own models, infrastructure, and enormous resources. Subsidising $5 to $10 per user can turn millions of users into a massive annual compute bill that venture capital must keep funding.

Instead of generating free-form text, you define the possible outputs upfront and Jev returns probabilities and confidence that your software can directly act on. 

Traditional LLM approach: “What is the capital of America?”

The LLM answers "Washington DC"

Jev can't answer the same question. But you can reframe it as "Which one of these is the capital of America?"

Then , you pass choices: Washington DC | Philadelphia | Boston | San Francisco

And the result looks like:

Washington DC: 0.94
Philadelphia : 0.04
Boston : 0.01
San Francisco: 0.01

Jev input is always Context + Questions. 

It can’t generate text back like traditional LLMs. So forget about using it as an interior decorator which is my fav ChatGPT use case these days.

Traditional LLMs evaluate next token based on current token which makes it sequential and slow. Where as Jev can work parallelly to determine the probability and confidence for each choices. Hence it’s faster.

It excels in determining the confidence of answers, hence will be suitable to evaluate LLM output with Eval

Most robotics demos show a machine completing a task. Almost none show what happens when the task goes wrong.

That gap is the whole problem.

A robot folding laundry in a lab handles one clean item, presented the same way every time. A robot folding laundry in a hotel handles items that are damp, tangled, wrinkled, and never positioned twice the same way.

I went through how the advanced systems actually close that gap, and the answer is architectural rather than one smarter model.

Several layers run at once. One interprets the instruction. Another plans the physical sequence. A separate control layer manages movement roughly one thousand times per second. Vision, touch, and proprioception feed back continuously, so the system notices when something has slipped and corrects mid motion instead of failing and stopping.

That last part matters more than the rest. Adaptation, not execution, is what separates a demo from a deployment.

For leaders evaluating physical AI, the question to put to a vendor changes. Not "can it do the task," but "what happens on attempt two hundred, when conditions have drifted." Repetitive workflows in laundry, hospitality, logistics, food service, and factories are bottlenecked by the same thing: variance.

hook: Jerry Seinfeld earned $66 million in 1997 with the biggest show on television. He earned $225 million in 1998, the year
text:
Jerry Seinfeld earned $66 million in 1997 with the biggest show on television. He earned $225 million in 1998, the year he shut it down.

NBC offered $5 million an episode for a 10th season, about $110 million, and by the network's charts the show was still growing. Season 9 was the highest-rated of the run. Warren Littlefield, who ran NBC Entertainment, said there was "tremendous confidence that no one could walk away from it."

Seinfeld walked anyway. He said he quit because the timing felt right, but turning down $110 million made him richer than taking it would have. He already owned a piece of the library: 180 episodes sold into syndication for an estimated $1.7 billion by 1998, and the back catalog stayed valuable because the show never had a season people wished it had skipped.

Forbes reported that his $225 million in 1998 came from those rerun deals. TBS paid a record $1 million an episode that September. Hulu paid nearly $180 million in 2015. Netflix paid north of $500 million in 2019. Not one new episode was made to earn any of it.

He told the New York Times, "I wanted the end to be from a point of strength." Twenty years later he told Harvard Business Review, "I realized that I was the steward of that magic and that I had to try and preserve it."

Only an owner had a reason to make that call. Seinfeld and Larry David, as creators, held the syndication back end; the three co-stars had asked for a share and been denied, so another season was pure salary to them. The man who would collect the rerun checks for decades decided when to stop, and he did.

text:
I spent a day with 1400 of the best product leaders from around the world at Lenny and Friends’ Summit in San Francisco, and I came out feeling energised and buzzing with new insights (and too much coffee  ☕ ).

My takeaways:
 👉 The product craft is here to stay. Claire Vo presented “The last roadmap”, where no roadmap needs to exist because with AI, there is no backlog. In a world where you can build and ship everything, vision, taste and judgement become king. 
 👉 Pricing is more of a challenge than ever. With AI products, cost is becoming a larger and more unpredictable variable. In a roundtable with Danielle M. Leasure, we discussed the two sides of the problem: pricing models should be clear and as predictable as possible for customers, but also ensure that our costs do not exceed our revenue.
👉 As development speeds up, user overwhelm becomes a real concern. In a roundtable with  Vikas Bhagat, we discussed the challenge of ensuring that users are made aware of and adopt new feature releases. Tara Seshan predicted that “Self-driving” product behavior is what’s coming next: intelligent defaults that guide users without requiring them to learn the tool.
 👉 Everyone continues to face a technology adoption barrier with AI. In a roundtable with Marily Nika, Ph.D, we discussed how AI adoption in companies follows the same trend as for all new technologies: the early adopters are making the most of it, and most others are left behind and wondering where/whether to start. 
 👉 We need to be creative with product validation techniques. In a roundtable hosted by Lukas Goetz-Weiss, we talked about how discovery and validation is changing. How can validation keep up with the speed of feature releases and not become a bottleneck? When is validation needed vs not needed? When can we just release a product feature as opposed to test it? We kept coming back to the theme of taking bets based on conviction and judgement, with testing as a tool to reduce uncertainty when needed.
 👉 As technology change speeds up, a tension arises in how far out we plan. Ami Vora highlighted this fundamental tension that exists at most companies: financial plans still need to be made for a 1-year horizon but the product horizons are becoming much shorter - 1-3 months. Hold a vision and direction, but plan the detail on a shorter timescale.

The tech world is the place to be right now. Each day brings new possibilities, new innovation and new ways to better serve customers. 

Thank you, Lenny Rachitsky, for bringing all these amazing product leaders together, and for creating a brand and community that attracts a certain kind of person - I found everyone to be warm, transparent, thoughtful and keen to meet new people and explore new ideas. 

To all the people I met in the last week - it was so nice meeting you, let’s keep in touch! And if you were at the summit and we didn't get to speak, I'd still like to - reach out and say hi!

hook: BatchNorm, LayerNorm, GroupNorm, or RMSNorm? Neural network normalization becomes much easier to understand when you ask
text:
BatchNorm, LayerNorm, GroupNorm, or RMSNorm? Neural network normalization becomes much easier to understand when you ask one question: which values share the same statistics?

They all rescale hidden activations. The important difference is the tensor slice used as the reference, because that decides whether examples affect one another, whether training and inference use the same rule, and whether the layer subtracts a mean.

For BatchNorm, LayerNorm, and GroupNorm, the common recipe is easy to picture: choose a group of values, compute its mean and variance, standardize it, then usually apply a learned scale and bias. The output keeps the same shape. What changes is the group.

- BatchNorm takes the same channel from multiple examples. For an image tensor N x C x H x W, one channel's statistics come from N, H, and W. Training examples therefore affect one another. With the usual configuration, training also updates running averages that are used at inference.

- LayerNorm stays inside one example. In the common Transformer case B x T x D, it takes one token and computes statistics across its D features. It does not depend on other examples, and it uses statistics from the current input during both training and inference.

- GroupNorm also stays inside one example. It splits image channels into groups, then computes statistics across the channels and spatial positions inside each group. This removes the dependency on batch statistics; the number of groups becomes an architectural choice.

- RMSNorm uses the same kind of per-token feature slice as the common LayerNorm setup, but the operation changes. It divides by the root mean square instead of subtracting the mean and dividing by the standard deviation. It then applies learned scale, without LayerNorm's explicit re-centering.

That is why swapping one normalization layer for another is not cosmetic. It changes the reference population for “normal,” the communication between samples, and sometimes the rule used at inference.

My starting point would be the architecture and the per-device batch size. For a CNN whose established recipe uses BatchNorm and whose batches provide stable statistics, I would keep it as the baseline. If memory constraints force very small batches, I would test GroupNorm. For token models, the relevant comparison is usually LayerNorm versus RMSNorm, and I would evaluate the swap inside the actual architecture rather than assume they are interchangeable.

Before changing the layer, draw the tensor axes and circle every value used to compute one statistic. That drawing usually predicts the behavior before the training run does.

creator: Kirk Borne
hook: Roger Penrose, the Nobel Prize-winning physicist who's spent decades challenging conventional thinking, just articulated
text:
Roger Penrose, the Nobel Prize-winning physicist who's spent decades challenging conventional thinking, just articulated something Silicon Valley doesn't want to hear: there are truths about reality that pure computation can never reach. In an age when AI enthusiasts promise that sufficiently powerful algorithms can solve any problem and answer any question, Penrose reminds us that the deepest mysteries of existence operate on a different plane entirely.

What is consciousness? Why does anything exist rather than nothing? What makes meaning meaningful? These aren't engineering problems waiting for better algorithms. They're existential questions that require something beyond pattern recognition and information processing. An AI could theoretically simulate every atom in a human brain, yet still fail to explain why subjective experience exists at all—the so-called "hard problem of consciousness."

This doesn't mean algorithms are useless. They're phenomenally powerful for specific domains: optimization, prediction, pattern matching, data analysis. But there's a category error in believing they can address all forms of truth. A sufficiently advanced calculator still can't tell you if life is worth living. A perfect simulation of the universe still wouldn't explain why the universe bothers to exist.

Penrose himself proposed that consciousness might involve quantum processes that transcend classical computation—suggesting that understanding human awareness requires physics we haven't yet discovered, not just better programming. Whether or not he's correct about quantum mechanics, his core insight holds: computational models have limits, and those limits are precisely where the deepest questions live.

The universe contains mysteries that demand more than silicon and mathematics.

hook: I just came out of the Slack Keynote at Dreamforce, and I got to spend time with Rob Seaman, CEO of Slack, Ryan Gavin, C
text:
I just came out of the Slack Keynote at Dreamforce, and I got to spend time with Rob Seaman, CEO of Slack, Ryan Gavin, CMO Slack, Zach Ciliotta-Young CRO, talking through the announcements. Thank you both for the time and the candid conversation. It helped me see the bigger picture behind the product news. #ad #salesforcepartner
 
First, what Slack announced:
 
- Slackforce Surfaces. Ask Slackbot in plain language for a dashboard, report, deck, or calculator, and it builds a live, interactive one inside Slack. Built on Salesforce and your connected data, under your own permissions, and shared with your team right in the channel. Live data refresh rolls out in October.
 
- Slackbot in channels. Tag it in and the whole team works from the same answer. Now in early pilot.
 
- Slackbot in Salesforce Lightning. Your AI teammate sits right next to the record, so you never leave the page.
 
- Big mode. A full-screen AI workspace in Slack for deep research, writing, and analysis.
 
- Two-way voice and video generation. Talk to Slackbot, hear it respond, and have it take action. Coming later this year.
 
- Slack Code. Code channels where people and agents write, review, and ship together, with 11 new agents including Snowflake, Datadog, Replit, and Lovable.
 
- Slack Frontline. A mobile-first preview for the people who do not sit at a desk.
And Slackbot has crossed 1.5 million monthly active users, up 145% quarter over quarter.
 
Now, my thoughts.
 
Slack is where companies communicate. So it was always going to become the place where the systems show up. This week, that stopped being a theory.
 
The second thing I keep coming back to. Every dashboard ever built has had the same flaw. It is a photograph. The moment you export it, it starts aging. And the decision it was built for usually happens somewhere else, in a conversation, using a number that was true last Tuesday. Surfaces flips that. The decision and the data finally sit in the same room, and the data stays alive while people debate it. The real win is not faster reports. It is fewer stale decisions.
 
The third shift is quieter, and it may matter most. AI at work has mostly been a solo activity. One person, one chat window, one private answer nobody else learns from. Bringing Slackbot into channels makes AI social. You see how a colleague asked the question. You build on their answer. The team gets smarter together.
 
This is outstanding work by the Slack and Salesforce teams. Shipping this much at once is hard. Making it all feel like one coherent idea is much harder. They did both.
 
After the keynote and my conversation with Rob and Ryan, one thing is clear to me: Slack is just getting started. Voice, video, frontline teams, agents shipping code next to engineers. The conversation is becoming the layer the whole company runs on, and we are only reading the first chapter.
 
Loved all the announcements!!!!
 
#dreamforce #slack #salesforce #slackbot #ai #futureofwork #leadership #theravitshow

text:
FOUNDERS: If you don’t have confidence in yourself as an entrepreneur, it’s normal. I didn’t believe in myself AT ALL as a Founder until my SECOND startup took off. Why? The first startup felt like it was cheating. 

We scraped 250k paying customers from a community page of a unicorn pioneer of our space, cold called them all, got 5k to switch over, and from the day that list was completely burned I did not figure out a SINGLE OTHER WAY to acquire a customer for that product. It was devastating. I had no idea if I could create something that would work in the “Real world”, or how long this would last before it just straight up died. 

After YEARS of banging my head against the wall, I finally got traction with something COMPLETELY NEW. Well, not completely new. It was an website-ID feature in our original app that I thought was so unique it would get people to use the original app. Which it did not. 

BUT, when we spun it out as its own company, I made a VSL from digitalmarketer(.)com’s template, got someone on upwork to make word art out of it, spent $1k on ads, and got $5k MRR back in a WEEK (see video below). 

3 years later it was at $13m ARR and we only had 6 people. Somewhere between when I launched that and when we hit $13m I felt validated as a Founder, because I actually created something from scratch that thrived in the real world. 

That one is over $20m now (Retention.com), we did another one (RB2B), and now I’m highly confident that we can make MoltSets a VERY nice business.
 
But that confidence wasn’t always there and took a LONG time to bulid.
 
If you’re struggling with self doubt, there’s really only one thing you CAN do …
 
Keep building.

hook: Here are 8 things my should steal from our Multiplayer AI Setup at MKT1:
text:
Here are 8 things my should steal from our Multiplayer AI Setup at MKT1:

1. GitHub repos: Have a repo for your team and one for yourself, both installed as plugins. Whatever one person builds, everyone else has next time they open Claude. And with your own repo you can work off any computer and build cloud routines.

2. Let everyone build: Pick an owner, but let everyone build, even if they're just shipping small improvements. And before a skill goes to anyone outside the team, have someone who didn't build it test it.

3. Skill building: Start by creating skills for repetitive work, think beyond writing use cases, and just get started.

4. Context layer: Keep the tools you already love, just make sure agents can use them too vai MCP or CLI. Build a sources-of-truth skill to tell Claude where to find everything.

5. Maintenance skills: We have a skill that runs at the end of a session where Claude proposes updates to the skill we just used—based on the corrections and feedback we gave Claude—so skills are constantly improving.

6. Form routines: Our job board submission form gets reviewed on its own, and only pings us if information is missing. You can use a workflow like this for any form submission.

7. Make your own MCP: Don't be afraid of making an MCP. It might be a better option for your internal team than a plugin, or a great sidecar product for your audience.

8. Steal skills from MKT1 MCP: 40+ of our skills are in the MKT1 MCP, built by me, made for B2B marketers.

I cover our full setup in today's newsletter, including details on 38 skills we run (that's where all those words come in, feel free to skim!) https://lnkd.in/gnKBYy5M

text:
What makes Claude Projects so interesting is that it handles teams of agents really well, you talk to a main orchestrator agent and it spins up specialists. Basically it creates an organization to solve your issue, mixing expensive and cheap agents depending on your preferences.

For example, I asked Fable in Claude Projects to select famous historical mysteries that it could try to resolve. It initiated research agents, selected the mysteries based on data it could access, and spun up eighteen separate threads, each with an agent each focused on one mystery. Then each thread launched additional agents (simulating avalanches, breaking codes) before summarizing those and passing them to still more agents for write up and another set of skeptical agents to fact check. It did this over a day of work, with the central orchestrator agent organizing it all. 

The results were interesting if you like historical mysteries. They are also for fun and certainly not definitive or guaranteed error-free (but they are also mostly reasonable & grounded in the literature). https://lnkd.in/gsJjPASe

hook: This ONE GPT-6 Astra Skill Replaces Your Higgsfield Subscription
text:
This ONE GPT-6 Astra Skill Replaces Your Higgsfield Subscription

I connected Codex to Higgsfield's API to generate images and videos, but paying per generation doesn't automatically make it cheaper.

If you're consistently using all your subscription credits, keeping the subscription might make more sense.

But if you generate 15 videos this month and nothing next month, I'd look at the API.

1. Figure out how often you'll actually use it.

If I'm still experimenting, I'd start with pay per use so I can figure out my cadence before committing to a plan.

I'd count all the paid generations, including the attempts I don't end up using.
Making five versions to get one usable clip still costs money.

2. Work out where the subscription becomes cheaper.

In my Higgsfield comparison, the API made more sense below roughly these monthly clip counts:
→ Plus, billed monthly: 19 clips.
→ Plus, billed annually: 16 clips.
→ Ultra, billed monthly: 50 clips.
→ Ultra, billed annually: 39 clips.

Those numbers apply to that comparison, so I'd recalculate them for the model, settings, and prices I'm actually using.

The rough calculation is the subscription's monthly cost divided by the API cost per comparable generation.

That's the number of generations where the spending meets, provided the subscription includes enough credits to cover them.

For annual plans, I'd use the equivalent monthly price, but I'd also consider whether I'll keep using it throughout the year.

3. Check whether you need the API for what you're building.

If I want generation built into my own website or internal tool, I need a way for that software to send requests automatically.

That's where API access matters beyond the price per clip.

For occasional use, I'd start with the API and track my spending.

If I'm consistently hitting the break-even point, I'd compare the subscription again using my actual usage.

I walk through the Codex setup, model comparisons, and break-even examples in the full video.

Link to the full video is in the comments 👇

text:
Claude now "leads" 26% of Anthropic's AI R&D work.

In February of this year, it was under 1%.

To be clear, Claude is not building the next version of itself fully autonomously today.

Anthropic defines "leads" as completing most of a task from a high-level prompt while a human supervises. They also reported that none of the R&D work they measured has reached full autonomy yet.

But going from under 1% to 26% in six months scares me.

I spend every day learning these tools, building with them, and teaching other people how to use them. I see how much good they can do.

But I keep thinking about what happens if that number eventually reaches 100%.

At that point, one model could help build a smarter model, which then helps build an even smarter model. Progress would no longer move at a pace set by human researchers.

My biggest concern is the human role shrinking from builder, to supervisor, to someone approving work they can no longer meaningfully understand.

What does human oversight look like when the systems being overseen can research, experiment, and improve faster than the smartest humans can follow?

I don't think the answer is to stop building, and Anthropic is clear that fully autonomous self-improvement is not inevitable.

But our ability to audit, understand, and control these systems needs to improve as quickly as their ability to build themselves.

If we wait until AI is doing 100% of the work to figure out how humans stay in control, we waited too long.

text:
Almost nine years after starting Vulcan Cyber, a Tenable Company, and more than a year and a half after Tenable acquired us, I’m leaving Tenable.

To cut a long post short: I have absolutely no clue what I’m doing next. The only thing I know for sure is that I’ll build again.

The ambition is to find something worthy of a ridiculously big swing and build it at a scale that sounds unreasonable today.

Vulcan started with an idea and a small group of people willing to bet we could build something that mattered.

Then came a pandemic, a market collapse, a war, and all the normal startup chaos in between. We made plenty of mistakes, changed course, lost deals we were sure we’d win and won some we probably had no business winning.

In the process, learned how to build a winning company and, more importantly, a winning team. We had exceptional people with the determination to keep going and win, no matter the odds. That’s what I’ll carry into whatever comes next.

There are far too many people to thank properly in one post, but I can’t write this without mentioning my co-founders Tal Morgenstern and Roy Horev, our key investors and board members John Brennan, Mark H., Henry Mason, Eric Elalouf, Ido Hart, Glenn Chisholm, Yasmin Lukatz, Andy Ellis, Biplab Adhya, our core team members, who stuck with the company and believed through thick and thin Noy Sinai, Guy Bratman, Noa Kremer, Anat Shimoni, Tal Marom, Rhett Glauser, Inbal Avital, Gal Gonen, Frederic SAULET, Wes Wharton and of course, to the one and only, who put up with all the startup shit alongside me, my wife, Michal Becher 💙. I’m grateful beyond words to each of you, and to everyone who was part of the Vulcan journey.

Now, for the first time in a very long time, I don’t have a company to build tomorrow morning.

I’m traveling around the world with my family focusing on what matters most, and doing something I’m historically terrible at: taking a break. Which I must admit is both odd and satisfying…

I’m not totally switched off - I’m learning new things, meeting new people, and going down new rabbit holes, but I’m deliberately not rushing to decide (or imagine) what I’ll do next. Right now, I’m just living the moment and looking for inspiration.

So if you’re thinking about an important world class problem, know a market full of broken things most think are unsolvable, or are obsessed with something I should know nothing about, hit me up.

The obvious comparison is Clubhouse. Invite-only with a giant valuation and no revenue model.

But Clubhouse was clonable, and it died the day Twitter cloned it. Instinct compounds. Every task teaches it your preferences, your people, your accounts. Meta launched Muse this week with the same feature set, built by Nat Friedman's team, and it hasn't mattered yet.

You can clone the features. You can't clone six months of someone's life inside the product.

She self harmed, was suicidal, eating disorder, depression and anxiety. 

Year 8 she didn’t attend school at all. 

As parents, with two businesses, another younger child, managing all the appointments, the upset and trying to see your daughter through this has been super hard.

hook: AI can still amaze you, but remember that beneath every fluent answer, there is software doing a great deal of mathemati
text:
AI can still amaze you, but remember that beneath every fluent answer, there is software doing a great deal of mathematics.

Ask an AI model a question.

Your words are converted into numerical representations. During inference, the model performs vast numbers of matrix and tensor operations to estimate what should come next.

The fluency appears on the screen.
The computation stays underneath.

A general-purpose CPU can run AI workloads, but large-scale AI benefits from processors designed for parallel computation. 

Graphics processing units, or GPUs, and tensor processing units, or TPUs, can execute many of these mathematical operations at the same time.

That difference helps explain why specialized compute has become such an important part of AI infrastructure.

None of this makes AI less impressive.

Quite the opposite.

Understanding what happens underneath helps us appreciate the engineering without imagining magic where there is computation.

AI can still amaze us.
Awareness simply lets us admire it with our eyes open.

#AI #AIComputing

hook: Micromanagers are insecure.
text:
Micromanagers are insecure.

They schedule check-ins because they're worried they'll lose control.
They'll ask for updates because they need to feel involved.
They'll require approvals because they're scared someone will make a mistake.

None of that is about helping the team. It's about managing their own anxiety.

And their team knows it.

Here's what real leadership looks like: "What's blocking you? What do you need? Put me to work."

Not "What's your progress?" Not "Can you walk me through your approach?" Not "Let me just stay involved."

Your job as leader is to remove everything stopping the work.

Get them resources. Unblock processes. Handle the admin bullshit. Clear the path.

Then step back and let your people do what they were hired to do.

Your designer doesn't need you questioning their creative choices.
They need you getting feedback faster.

Your engineer doesn't need you in their sprint planning.
They need you unblocking the API access they've been waiting on.

Your salesperson doesn't need another strategy session.
They need you handling contracts so they can get back to selling.

Talented people don't need oversight. They need autonomy.

If you hired well, trust them. If you didn't hire well, that's a different problem.

But micromanaging good people is the easiest way to you lose them.

Stop managing your team's work. Start clearing the path for it.

-DM

hook: Your coding agent can read the whole repo.
text:
Your coding agent can read the whole repo.
 
It still cannot see what happens when that code hits production.
 
I keep seeing the same pattern.
 
Someone asks the agent to add retries.
 
The patch looks fine. Tests pass. It gets merged.
 
Then one dependency slows down.
 
Retries stack. Queues grow. The connection pool dies.
 
“Add retries” was never the hard part. The hard part is knowing what that change does to the system around it.
 
If you are going to let an agent touch production paths, give it runtime evidence first:
 
a trace that shows where the request actually waits
metrics for latency and errors under load
logs that tie a failure back to one request
 
Then the prompt changes.
 
Not: “add retries.”
 
This: “Under load, retries are amplifying pressure on this dependency. Look at the trace and propose a bounded retry strategy.”
 
Same agent. Much better job. You still review the diff.
 
Dynatrace wrote this up well , including how agents can pull that telemetry through tools like dtctl. Worth reading if your team is past the “first generated commit” stage.
 
Link in the comments.
 
Which signal do you hand the agent first: traces, metrics, or logs?

hook: Agentic AI in 2026: What’s actually under the hood?
text:
Agentic AI in 2026: What’s actually under the hood?

Two years ago, I would explain the stack mostly like this:
Data → AI Agent → Automation
Useful, but too simple now.

Today, I believe the production agent usually needs 7 layers:
1️⃣ Experience
Where the agent meets the user: chat, voice, email, Slack, APIs, background jobs.

2️⃣ Models + Tools
The model is the brain. The tools are the hands.
Search, files, code, databases, APIs, computer use, MCP.

3️⃣ Context / Knowledge
Documents, CRM, company data, policies, customer history.
Without context, even a great model is still a smart stranger.

4️⃣ Orchestration
What should the agent do next?
Search, call a tool, retry, ask for approval, hand off, or wait.

5️⃣ Memory / State
What already happened?
What is finished? What should continue tomorrow?

6️⃣ Evals / Observability
Did the agent actually succeed?
Where did it fail? How much did it cost? Did a human have to rescue it?

7️⃣ Security / Governance
Permissions, approvals, audit trails, sandboxing, secrets, access control.
The biggest shift?

Agents are moving from answering questions to completing work.

And that means the model alone is no longer the product.
Context + tools + orchestration + memory + evaluation + security are what turn intelligence into reliable action.

Also worth noting:
You do not need reinforcement learning for every agent.
And you do not need 10 agents talking to each other.

Sometimes one well designed agent with the right tools beats an entire “multi agent system.”

That is Agentic AI in 2026. wdyt?

hook: What actually happens between a query and an AI citation?
text:
What actually happens between a query and an AI citation?

I spent some time going through the latest AirOps research with Kevin Indig, based on 16,851 queries and more than 353,000 pages.

What I found interesting is not one isolated metric, but how the different pieces connect.

In 88.6% of the cases analyzed, ChatGPT generated exactly two additional fan-out queries before producing the final answer.

So the question a user types is not necessarily the only query your content needs to be relevant for.

Then comes retrieval.

A page in the first retrieval position had a 58.4% citation rate. By position 10, that dropped to 14.2%.

Being found is clearly important, but it is only part of the process.

Pages with headings that closely matched the original query reached a 41% citation rate, compared with around 30% for weaker matches.

Another result I found particularly interesting: more coverage was not automatically better.

When strong relevance to the main query was kept constant, pages covering 26-50% of the related fan-out topics had a 38.2% citation rate, compared with 34% for pages trying to cover all of them.

That reinforces something I've been seeing more and more in content work:

A page does not need to answer everything.

It needs to be very clear about what it answers, structured around that intent and strong enough to be retrieved in the first place.

The report also found supporting signals around structured data, content length and page structure, while traditional metrics such as Domain Authority and backlink volume did not show a positive relationship with citation probability in this dataset.

For me, this makes the AI visibility process easier to understand:

The user asks a question.
The system expands it.
Pages are retrieved.
Relevance is evaluated.
A small number of sources are cited.

And each of those stages creates a different optimization problem.

I've pulled the findings I found most relevant 👇

#AISearch #AIVisibility #SEO #ContentStrategy
