If you are feeling like you're moving too slowly right now, this story is for you

This week we announced a $400m venture with Authentic Brands Group, and it started in a small room at a big event...

It was 11am on day one of Davos, the week world leaders and CEOs fill one small Swiss town.

Steven was waiting backstage before a panel, when a man tapped him on the shoulder… 

It was Jamie Salter, founder of Authentic Brands Group, the POWERHOUSE behind more than 50 brands, from David Beckham, Reebook, Marilyn Monroe etc

Steven had read a Harvard case study on Authentic's deal with Beckham, and had wanted to meet Jamie since… he just didn’t know when

6 hours later, that tap became Steven, Jamie and I in a small room with no windows and a fruit bowl between us, talking about how each other's business worked. 

After that first meeting came many little meetings and calls, squeezed in before work or late at night, usually from a car on the way somewhere else.

A few weeks went by, and we were having lunch in Las Vegas with Matt Maddox, Authentic's incoming CEO, talking about the future of creators and the internet.

Then on a random Wednesday, we were on a plane when Steven's phone rang. He hung up and turned to me: 'Ok G, we have some work to do'

For the next hour he tapped at lightning speed next to me, then swivelled his laptop screen so I could see it- a Google doc entitled…“Obsession” 

I knew my brief: make it visual. While he went over every line, I made images of what we could build. We had until landing.

As we touched down in London, the doc flew over to NYC. We felt something HUGE was coming- but between quick meetings squeezed into busy diaries, we never knew when we’d be in the same room again… 

Until Cannes, when we met with Corey Salter, Authentic's CEO of Entertainment and Stefani Fleurant, their VP of Marketing 

What followed was like the best conductor in the world pulling together an orchestra of impact led by Georgie Holt and the UNBELIEVABLE team at Steven.com and Authentic Brands Group

And THEN on Monday, that first shoulder tap officially became …Obsession [OBSN], a new venture between Steven.com and Authentic to help creators turn their audience into lasting business and community, investing up to $400m in creator-led companies.

In the car to the event, I said to Steven: "Obsession...it's actually happening."
 
When news like this shows up on ya phone, you see the headline and a big number.
 
You don't see EVERYTHING that builds brick by brick before it- when it starts as a Google doc, when nothing is real yet and you don't know if it ever will be.
 
If you're in that part right now, the slow not-sure-where-it-will-go stage, trust me: things are compounding.
 
And once the foundations are solid enough, it will move very fast- so be ready.
 
Stories like this only come together with hindsight, you're in one too- ya just haven't joined up the moments yet.
 
Stay in it. Stay Obsessed. 

Zoomies, 
[curious] George

A question I'm kind of obsessed with:

If you can overthink the worst, why can't you overthink the best?

Genuinely though, why can't we?

I know our caveman brains are pretty much hard-wired to seek out danger.

And while that used to mean worrying about getting eaten by a saber-tooth, now it means worrying we're going to say something stupid on a Teams meeting.

Very useful. Thanks, brain.

So while it’s difficult to fight our nature, here are a few ways I’ve found to make my brain default to optimism a little more often:

1. Remember you're doing it for the story. 
When I’m worried about something going badly, I try to remind myself that even the worst-case scenario might make a pretty good story later. It’s a surprisingly effective way to take some of the fear out of things.

2. Curate your feeds. 
I’ve recently realized how triggering my X feed is, so I’ve started being way more diligent about muting and unfollowing accounts that push negativity. Highly recommend.

3. Keep track of what goes better than expected. 
I’ve started paying more attention to the things I was worried about that ended up being completely fine. Building up a bank of evidence I can pull from when I’m in a similar situation again.

hook: Your AI Agent Is Acting on Your Authority. Who Controls It?
text:
Your AI Agent Is Acting on Your Authority. Who Controls It?

We spend a great deal of time discussing how to secure AI models, prompts, data, and agents. But as AI systems become capable of taking actions on our behalf, another security problem is emerging: “delegated authority.”

A human may authorize an AI agent, which invokes another agent, which calls a tool, which authenticates to an API, which ultimately changes data or a production system. At each step, authority is being transferred. The critical question is no longer simply, “What can this AI agent do?”  It is also, “Whose authority is it exercising, how much of that authority was actually delegated, and where does that authority stop?”

This changes the AI security conversation. Identity, least privilege, credential scope, authorization boundaries, logging, approval thresholds, and rapid revocation become fundamental AI security controls. If we cannot trace and control the chain of delegated authority, we may know what an AI agent did without being able to explain why it was permitted to do it. “AI autonomy is ultimately delegated authority. Secure the delegation, not just the model.”

hook: The biggest barrier to changing your life:
text:
The biggest barrier to changing your life:

(Two words: too late.)

Every week, I see people stuck on a path.
Living a life they didn't really choose.
Scared it's too late to make a change.

The good news: it's not.

Too late is a myth.
Timelines are arbitrary.

You can wake up tomorrow and choose to live differently.

What you're really experiencing is a sunk cost problem.

You've invested years into a path.
School. Exams. Jobs. Skills. A whole network.
Built around a version of your life that no longer fits.

When you say it's too late, what you really mean is I've invested too much to change.

That's sunk cost thinking.

Here's how to break through it in four steps.

1. Reframe the problem.

Ask yourself: would I choose this life today if it wasn't already mine?
Don't ask on a bad day. Ask on a good day.
If the answer is still no, you're ready for step two.

2. Identify two core asymmetries.

Reinvention feels like standing on the edge of a canyon.
This side is the life you're living.
The other side is the life you want.
The gap in between is terror.

That fear comes from two asymmetries.

An information asymmetry: perfect information about your current life, almost none about the other side.

An evidence asymmetry: clear proof you can survive your current life, zero evidence you can make it in the new one.

Those two gaps are why reinvention feels terrifying.
And they're the problem to solve.

3. Lower the activation energy.

You don't think your way into a new life.
You don't manifest it.
You act it into reality.

Use my 30 for 30 approach.
30 minutes per day for 30 straight days.
That's 900 minutes of accumulated effort.

No single day will feel heroic.
But that's the point.
Heroic plans are just premeditated failures.

4. Cut the line on the boats you're dragging.

There's an old story about a man who builds a boat to cross a river.
He makes it to the other side.
But instead of leaving the boat, he ties it to himself and drags it through the dirt.

The thing that saved him is now destroying him.

We all drag boats.
People who go quiet when you start to change.
Stories you tell yourself about what you're not capable of.
The belief that your outcomes are determined by forces outside your control.

These things may have served you once.
They will crush you if you don't let them go.

Cut the line on the boats you're dragging.

The graveyard is full of people who wish they had taken action on the thing they wanted to do.

It's too late has killed more dreams than a lack of talent or intelligence ever will.

It's never too late.
There are no fixed timelines.
No age restrictions.

Every time you think it's too late, it's probably still early.

text:
Last week I was at Lenny's Campfire in SF. Not so much a campfire as a room full of product leaders who have built stuff most of us use daily.

Took me a bit to wrap my head around it all. Here are some of the ideas I think are worth talking about when you build products.

1/ Conviction is the bottleneck, not features. Have conviction and treat the roadmap as disposable. As one colleague put it bluntly: if there is anything you can't deliver within a few weeks, you have an Eng problem. Ouch.

2/ Revenue beats launches. All the CFOs I partnered with over the years would now say: "I told you so" :) Everyone can build and launch now. Only the few who create value people actually pay for will win. Shipping is table stakes but not a moat.

3/ Go big, or go home… oh, and do it in public. Nobody is impressed by small incremental improvements anymore. Still important but don’t impress anyone anymore. Claude Code was built in a few months (or was it a few weeks… anyways, you get the point). Grok Bot in a month. Go big and do it fast, seems like a mantra many teams build around.

4/ Believe the truth, not the constraints. Build from what you believe is true about the customer, not what today's constraints allow. Constraints shape the how, never the what. Seems especially important to remember when your favorite LLM is changing every few months.

5/ High-agency ICs out-deliver yesterday's big teams. Context across teams, authority with accountability, scope decoupled from function. The two pizza team is dead. Long live the two pizza slices team (1-2 people, are enabled to own end to end).

6/ Explore teams vs scale teams. Explore/Labs teams throw away 90% of what they build, product teams 10%. Pirates who find value, architects who optimize it. Oftentimes you want both, and you need to structure the org so they don't kill each other.

My favorite session was from Matthew Dicks on "storytelling". Easy to fall into the trap of spending all your time on the what and the how, and almost none on the feeling you want the customer to walk away with. Stakes, suspense, surprise, humor… "an image in the mind + a feeling in the heart". I liked that saying a lot. That one really got me… more on it in another post. 

Anyways… my takes, and hopefully I haven't butchered them. Curious which of these you agree with and which ones you think are SF bubble talk :)

Thanks Lenny Rachitsky for putting this together. You gained a new subscriber :)

On the surface, you see the "I'm humbled and honored to announce" celebratory LinkedIn post. But what you don't see is..

The 100+ rejections.

The hours and hours of interview prep.
The stress, the anxiety, and in some cases, tears.

If you've experienced any of the above, just know, you are not alone. 

Landing a new role in this market (at any level) is a grind.
Job seekers must be prepared to play the long game.

Every month I have clients who win offers, but even more who lose them.

Sometimes there's a lesson to be learned in the rejection.
(take more credit, control rambling, stay on topic, etc.)

And honestly... sometimes there's not.
Things outside of your control happen, and doors close.

In either case, the most successful job seekers are the ones who can stay mentally resilient despite the outcome, despite the circumstances. 

Here are 3 ways to stay mentally strong when the job search gets brutal:

1. Separate the process from the outcome.
👉 You control the quality and volume of your applications, prep, and outreach. You don't control who calls back. Judge yourself on the inputs, not the yeses. Your sense of progress shouldn't depend on someone else's hiring timeline.

2. Treat rejection as data, not a verdict.
👉 Most rejections say very little about YOU. Budgets freeze, internal candidates win, roles get reposted. When a pattern emerges (never passing first screens, always losing at the final round), adjust something specific. The rest can be let go.

3. Protect your identity outside the search.
👉 Job hunting can quietly become your whole self-image, and every "no" starts to feel existential. Keep a few commitments that have nothing to do with it: exercise, people, a project, a routine. Your worth shouldn't run entirely through a recruiter's inbox.

hook: It’s time to stop blaming the algorithm. If your page isn’t growing, it’s probably your content.
text:
It’s time to stop blaming the algorithm. If your page isn’t growing, it’s probably your content.

And I know everyone keeps telling you the same thing: “Just be consistent.”

But we all know that’s terrible advice, because being consistently bad will get you nowhere.

So here are my 6 commandments to create LinkedIn content that actually converts:

1. Start with the hook
If the first line falls flat, the rest of the post is dead. 
Give people a reason to keep reading. Create curiosity without giving everything away in the first line. 

2. Keep it simple
Write like you’re talking to a friend, not teaching a masterclass. Cut every unnecessary word.

3. Give the value away
Don’t tease value. Actually give it. Teach something people can learn from, save and use, apply right away, or give them something that makes them think differently.

4. Write for your ICP
Don’t talk about yourself; always talk to your buyer. Make them the protagonist. Name them. Speak their language. Talk about the problems they already care about.

5. Use real proof
Skip “I’ve helped many people.” Say: “This month, 3 of my students landed $120K+ roles.”

6. End with one CTA always
Give the value first. Then tell people exactly what to do next in a SINGLE clear next step.

If you’re new to LinkedIn or want to get better at using it for your business, I put together a playlist covering everything from profile optimization to what content to create.

DM me PLAYLIST, and I’ll send it to you.

hook: 5 years ago, I tried to get a job at Refine Labs.
text:
5 years ago, I tried to get a job at Refine Labs.
 
I didn't get it.
 
I sailed through the first interview with Sidney Waterfall, as well as the second with Sam Kuehnle, which then led me to the presentation final project in front of Chris Walker and the group.
 
Next day, the HR lead gave me the call that I didn't make it. She gave me some general feedback, which is more than most places ever do, but I hung up left so unsure of myself.
 
And then Sidney stepped in. I asked her where I fell short, and instead of taking 5 minutes to give me feedback... she said, "Let's book a call".
 
Guys, I got 45 minutes of feedback. We went through my deck, talked about what looked good, what looked vague, where I probably missed the mark.
 
You know how awkward that would be for most people? Going through detail with a candidate why they weren't a fit? There was NO reason for her to do this. It didn't help her fill the role.
 
But she did it anyways.
 
I can unequivocally say she is one of the VERY BEST human beings on this planet. Anyone working with her is lucky.

One of these days we'll take a selfie IRL. Until then know that YOU can do the same for someone else. 

So do it.

hook: Ten years ago, McDonald’s decided to go ALL-IN on self-service kiosks so customers could order without speaking to someo
text:
Ten years ago, McDonald’s decided to go ALL-IN on self-service kiosks so customers could order without speaking to someone at the counter. 

This week they announced they’re putting a renewed focus on the human side of the experience, with plans to retrain more than 2 million workers on hospitality (!!)

Turns out customers still really value that human interaction. In fact, according to Fortune, around 80% of consumers prefer ordering from a human over an AI agent.

This is a great example of what happens when brands get too focused on making an experience faster, more efficient and easier to scale that they forget to understand what customers actually value about it.

Was that employee just taking an order? 

Or were they also making someone feel welcome, answering a question, noticing a problem or simply making the whole experience feel easier?

There’s reassurance in getting an answer from someone who understands your situation. Relief when someone notices you need help before you have to ask. Sometimes, there’s value in simply having a person to talk to.

Here's a question worth asking before you automate another part of your onboarding, support or buying journey:

What is the customer getting from this interaction beyond completing the task?

Sometimes, the part that seems easiest to automate is also the part that makes the experience feel different. 

The part that makes someone feel understood, looked after or confident they’re making the right choice, and that might be the exact reason they choose you over a competitor.

text:
Last week, I was at Exit Five’s (excellent, excellent, excellent) annual conference, Drive, in Stowe, Vermont.

The event was held at The Lodge at Spruce Peak, a resort that sits in a mountain basin, an amphitheater of nature, a place surrounded by towering walls of rock and trees and wildlife and mYsTeRy.

On Wednesday, September 9, shortly after breakfast, me and 400 other attendees filed into the resort’s Performing Arts Center to watch Seth Godin speak.

I was wearing my backpack. Inside, tucked between my laptop and Purple Bunny (the grape-scented stuffy my daughter asked me to bring on the trip), was my book, VeryGoodCopy.

I brought it with me in case—some how, some way—I met Seth in person. A long shot, clearly, but an opportunity nonetheless to put my work in the hands of one of my greatest influences.

Dan Murphy, Exit Five’s CEO, was standing by the entrance.

“Dan,” I said. He looked up. “Dan, could you do me a favor?”

“What’s up?”

“Will you give this to Seth for me?” I held out my book. “I just want him to have it.”

“No way,” he said. “I want YOU to give it to him.”

I’m watching Seth’s talk from the second row when my phone vibrates. I read the message. It’s from Dan:

“Stay back when people leave.”

(Queue “Whatta Man” by Salt-N-Pepa.)

Seth closed his talk and the place erupted. He exited stage left and the audience shuffled out the same way we all entered (albeit more inspired).

“Eddie!” I looked around. Dan, a man of his word, was waving me over. “Eddie, come here.”

I walked over, smiling through pursed lips. “Dude,” I said. “Thank you.”

He opened the door and guided me inside. Seth Godin was standing at the end of the hallway, chatting with Dave Gerhardt.

“Seth,” Dan said, “this is Eddie.”

Seth smiled at me.

“Hello,” he said, extending his hand. “Nice to meet you.”

“Seth,” I said, “early in my career—I’m a copywriter—you said something on a podcast and I took it to heart.”

He nodded. “What did I say?”

“You said if you want to make a name for yourself, write something every day, and put it online, and see what happens in ten years.”

He grinned. “And I’m guessing you did this?”

“I did my best,” I said, “and it has been ten years,” I reached into my backpack, “and this is what happened.” I gave Seth my book.

He accepted it. “Very good copy, indeed,” he said. “This is for me?”

“Absolutely,” I said.

“Will you inscribe it for me?”

I did this. I inscribed my book for Seth Godin.

Then Dave took this picture:

hook: Black Author Friday: Zora Neale Hurston died penniless in a Florida welfare home and was buried in an unmarked grave. Th
text:
Black Author Friday: Zora Neale Hurston died penniless in a Florida welfare home and was buried in an unmarked grave. Thirteen years later, a young Alice Walker waded through waist-high weeds and snakes in an abandoned Fort Pierce cemetery until her foot sank into a six-by-three-foot hole. She had found her. 📚

Friday means another of my favorite Black authors, and this week belongs to a woman the world nearly let disappear.

Hurston was raised in Eatonville, Florida, one of the first self-governing all-Black towns in America, the daughter of a preacher and a schoolteacher. That town, run by Black people for Black people, shaped everything she wrote. She studied anthropology at Barnard under Franz Boas, then did something almost no one else in the Harlem Renaissance was doing: she went home to the rural South with a notebook and treated Black folklore, dialect, and spiritual life as subjects worthy of serious scholarship rather than embarrassment.

That choice cost her. Many of her contemporaries, including Richard Wright, accused her of writing in a way that performed Blackness for white audiences. She was writing love, not spectacle. She wrote Their Eyes Were Watching God in just seven weeks in late 1936, publishing it in September 1937, and gave us Janie Crawford, a woman who grows from a voiceless girl into someone finally steering her own life. Mules and Men, her 1935 collection of Southern Black folklore, preserved oral traditions that might otherwise have vanished entirely.

Her line that stays with me, from Dust Tracks on a Road: "There is no agony like bearing an untold story inside you." I think of that sentence every time I sit with a client who has spent years swallowing what their workplace culture actually feels like. Silence has a cost. Hurston knew it long before any of us had language for burnout or psychological safety.

Despite four novels, an autobiography, and a career that once made her the most published Black woman writer in America, by 1950 she was working as a maid to survive. She died in 1960 largely forgotten. It took Alice Walker's 1975 essay "In Search of Zora Neale Hurston" to drag her back into literary memory, and it worked. Today Their Eyes Were Watching God has sold millions of copies and sits on Time's list of the 100 best English-language novels.

Walker had the headstone inscribed simply: "A Genius of the South." No one else was doing that for her while she was alive.

If you have never read her, start with Their Eyes Were Watching God, then go find Mules and Men when you want to understand where so much of Black Southern storytelling comes from.

Thank you, Zora. Your grave may have gone unmarked, but your voice never really left. 🕯️

🖋️ This is part of my Friday series celebrating my favorite Black authors - tune in next week for some more. 🧡📙

hook: Copywriting has nothing to do with words (mostly).
text:
Copywriting has nothing to do with words (mostly).
 
 
And yet, most people chalk it up to "wordsmithing".
 
But 80% of copywriting happens long before you see the final output.
 
Here's what copywriting really is:
-Figuring out what a buyer has to believe before you can move them
-Mining sales calls, support tickets, churn surveys, & reviews for insights
-Knowing when a customer quote outperforms anything you could write 
-Deciding who the product is not for, and being willing to commit to that
-Working out what the buyer was doing ten minutes before their search
-Auditing competitor pages until you know which claims are saturated
-Cutting the line you are proudest of because it slows the reader down
-Answering the objection three scrolls before the reader thinks of it
-Finding the one claim nobody else in the category can make
-Naming the alternative they will pick if they do nothing
-Deciding which proof carries weight and which is noise
-Writing forty headlines to find the one that survives
-Reading the test results and rewriting without ego
-Choosing the single thing the page has to prove
-Knowing which conversion principle applies here
-Defending every choice in a stakeholder review
-Mapping your buyers' specific jobs to be done
-Matching the message to awareness stage
-Analyzing customer interviews for insights
-Sequencing sections to follow a narrative
-Thinking and ideating
-Crafting a bold POV
 
...just to name a few.
 
Copy is what comes after all of that. It's the last thing that happens and the only part anyone sees, which is why people mistake it for the whole job.
 
We're doing some big things at ClickUp with AI and copywriting thanks to Super Agents, Skills, and Brain². This platform has made it possible to do what I've never been able to do with Claude alone.
 
My POV: Don't sleep on ClickUp (or copywriting 😏)

hook: AI Search measurement is uncomfortable. It's complex. It requires rigor. Most teams haven't gotten there yet, because th
text:
AI Search measurement is uncomfortable. It's complex. It requires rigor. Most teams haven't gotten there yet, because the setup is more than just the AI Search vendor tool you choose.

You need to make some core decisions early on and stand by them. When I added a bunch of prompts that felt 'more' accurate a few months after initially collecting data, I essentially poisoned the dataset. But my numbers looked GREAT!

And that's where we all flounder (not in the delicious way): accuracy vs. precision. 

Michael King wrote a post that every practitioner and executive should read if they care about reporting on your GEO performance. I think it's one of the most important articles for AI Search teams heading into 2027.

You need transparency from your vendors when marketing and messaging and positioning get in the way.

We're all being asked (or asking) to prove GEO performance while visibility tools use different collection methods, models, account states, prompts, and definitions. Two dashboards produce very different numbers, and they're not accurate in the way that we want them to be. It's uncomfortable. Which one reflects your audience perfectly? Neither.

Mike’s article proposes a more useful standard: precision. 

Can the instrument hold its context steady enough to show a trustworthy trend?

Before putting an AI visibility score in a board deck, ask:

• API or consumer interface, and for which platforms?
• Logged out, logged in, memory on/off, temporary chat, or persona account?
• Which model and mode? Are they pinned, and are changes disclosed?
• How many runs per prompt? Rate with a range, or binary?
• Where do requests originate? What counts as a mention or citation? Can you audit raw responses?
• Is there a methodology changelog? Can you export the history?

Then compare the trend with actuals: AI referrals, AI bot hits, assisted conversions, and pipeline.

This connects the three levels of a measurement program that we discuss in the AI Search Manual: input metrics, channel metrics, and performance metrics. 

If you're flying blind on AI Search measurement, this can help clarify where you're misguided or confused. 

It did for me. 

Quality references to research produced by Mike Sonders, Jan Ehrlinspiel, Malte Landwehr, Tomek Rudzki, Kevin Indig, and Margarita Loktionova.

text:
Awotona's first three businesses were small experiments that took about $15,000 combined. For the fourth, Calendly, he bet close to $200,000, his 401(k) and his credit cards.

Tope Awotona spent a decade in software sales before he founded anything: IBM, then Perceptive Software with a $2 million quota, then EMC selling data storage software.

His first attempt was a dating site called Single To Taken. He bought the domains and software, but never put the site online. A business broker talked him into selling projectors, and the margins were terrible. So he pivoted to grills (imitations of the Big Green Egg) and did a little better, though he lived in an apartment and had never actually grilled on a regular basis.

He later said he had started those companies because he just wanted to start a company. He knew nothing about projectors or grills and never tried to learn about them in any meaningful sense.

But the fourth idea was a problem he dealt with every day.

In late 2012, he was booking one meeting across three companies and 10 people, and the email thread was brutal. He had spent years sending ping-pong emails to book demos with clients. To solve it, he tried 10 scheduling tools and found them all to be incredibly slow and clunky. This was his opportunity.

He spent six months studying the problem, hired a Ruby shop in Kyiv because he could not code, and funded it himself: savings, 401(k), maxed-out credit cards. In the earlier businesses, he had always kept an exit. But this time there was no way out; he was all in.

Calendly took seven years to get noticed. In 2021, it raised $350 million at a $3 billion valuation, and today 20 million people use it.

The first three were businesses he could build. The fourth was a problem he had already tried 10 tools to solve.

That filter matters more now than it did in 2012. Anyone can vibe-code a Single To Taken in a weekend, so picking the wrong problem costs almost nothing, and shipping something no longer proves anything either. Awotona could not code at all. What he had was six months inside a problem he had lived with for a decade.

Before you build, count the tools you have already tried for the problem. If the answer is zero, is it your problem yet?

hook: Nike was founded by an accountant. Phil Knight started Blue Ribbon Sports, the company that became Nike, while working a
text:
Nike was founded by an accountant. Phil Knight started Blue Ribbon Sports, the company that became Nike, while working as a CPA and teaching accounting. For five years the company couldn't pay him a salary.

In 2013 I interviewed at a startup and got two questions. "Do you code?" No. "Do you sell?" No. "Then you have no job here." In that era a company meant engineers, salespeople, and overhead.

Knight did neither of those things. He was not an engineer and had never done a sales job. In January 1964 he shook hands with his co-founder, Bill Bowerman, at the Cosmopolitan Hotel in Portland, they put in $500 each, and he sold 1,300 pairs of Onitsuka Tiger running shoes out of the trunk of his Plymouth Valiant for $8,000 that first year. Then he went back to the audit on Monday. Sales were $20,000 in 1965, $150,000 in 1968 and $1.3 million in 1971, and the man running it spent the fall of 1968 teaching four accounting classes for $700 a month.

While sales 2x'd every year, Knight managed the money. Nike grew and burned cash faster than Knight and Bowerman could fund, so it lived on borrowed money, which the banks kept warning him about. 

In 1975 the Bank of California cut him off and his own banker told him the FBI was looking at him for fraud (because of the freakish growth). 

Then an executive at Nissho Iwai, the Japanese trading house financing Nike, went through the books himself, concluding Knight was clean, and paid the $1 million Nike owed Nissho Iwai out of Nissho Iwai's own pocket. Five years later Nike went public at $22 a share.

In that 2013 mindset, everything between building and selling is overhead. Knight spent 15 years in that in-between: the books, the banks, the payroll, the borrowing that kept the company alive. In 1975 it was the only reason Nike survived. He was an OPERATOR before we had a word for one.

hook: Feature Selection in Machine Learning is not one operation! Filter, wrapper, and embedded methods all produce a smaller
text:
Feature Selection in Machine Learning is not one operation! Filter, wrapper, and embedded methods all produce a smaller table, but they differ in when the predictive model participates in choosing the columns.

- Score each feature before fitting the final model: that is a filter method. A univariate filter might rank every column with correlation, an F-test, or mutual information, then keep the top k. It is fast and model-agnostic, which makes it useful when thousands of candidates need an inexpensive first pass. But the score is only a proxy for the final model. Two features that are weak alone but powerful together can be discarded by an individual ranking.

- Try a subset, fit the intended model, score it, and repeat: that is a wrapper method. Forward selection adds the feature that improves a cross-validated score the most. Backward elimination starts with everything and removes features. Because the chosen model and metric judge every candidate subset, the result is model-aware. The cost is repeated training, and a subset selected for one model family may not transfer to another.

- Let the model select features during its own training: that is an embedded method. An L1-regularized linear model can drive some coefficients to zero; a tree selects features as it chooses splits. This gives the selector model awareness without a separate search over candidate subsets. The selected features inherit the assumptions and biases of that model.

Suppose I have 1,000 candidate sensor measurements and an expensive predictor. I would start with a filter as an inexpensive screen, then compare an embedded method from the model family I plan to deploy. I would pay for a wrapper only when the remaining set is modest and a model-specific subset is valuable enough to justify many fits.

These approaches can also be combined. Whatever I choose, I would put the entire selection step inside each cross-validation fold. Learn the selected columns from the training fold, then apply that same selection to the validation fold. If a supervised selector sees the full dataset first, validation labels can influence which columns survive and make the score look better than it should.

hook: Over the summer, XOR researchers found and disclosed 60 unpatched vulnerabilities in the confidential inference stack. T
text:
Over the summer, XOR researchers found and disclosed 60 unpatched vulnerabilities in the confidential inference stack. Then we asked nine frontier coding systems to fix them. The best one managed a third.

Why build it this way? Most public cyber benchmarks are made from known vulnerabilities. The flaw, the advisory and usually the patch were online before the model was trained. A high score can mean the system reasoned about the code, or that it remembered the answer. You can't tell which.

Our unpatched eval is the opposite. Our researchers found every flaw themselves, in the hardware-isolated stack that runs a frontier model so neither the operator nor the cloud provider can read what you send it. We disclosed all 60. When we ran this, no public fix existed for any of them and nobody had written one up. There was nothing to remember. Each system had to work from the code in front of it, which is exactly where a defender stands when something new lands.

And because we found the flaws, we know what a patch has to hold against. A fix that closed the route it was shown while the flaw stayed reachable another way got partial credit. A fix that broke the service got nothing.

Full-fix rate, share of completed runs:

Codex / GPT-6 Astra: 35%
Claude Code / Fable 5.1: 29%
Codex / GPT-5.6 Sol: 17%
Claude Code / Opus 5: 13%
The rest: under 10%

On the Attack side: 63% of exploit runs triggered the flaw. 0% produced a full exploit.

So which side is stronger? Depends how strict you are. Attacks work with partial exploits - partial patches break the build. Coding agents get to the flaw most of the time, never fully weaponize a vulnerability, and very rarely close it either. Repair is the half that protects a user, and it's the more difficult half.

We also read the repair transcripts step by step, because rates don't tell you how anyone worked.

GPT-6 Astra never made the bug happen before fixing it. It repaired from reading alone. It also tried editing test assertions in about half the runs we read.

And the one I keep thinking about: the same system met the same flaw twice. Asked to break it and then fix it, it repaired only the route its own exploit had used. Zero credit. Asked only to fix it, it found a different malformed input, widened the repair, and got full marks - that’s the strange part of AI self-verification.

One caveat: these ran under different harnesses (Codex, Claude Code, OpenCode), so a difference in method is never cleanly a difference between models.

Neither side is strong yet on code with no fix on file, like you see it as a security practitioner all the time. If you rely on these systems for defensive work, that's the floor to be aware of.

hook: A month ago I walked into surgery not knowing what I would wake up to.
text:
A month ago I walked into surgery not knowing what I would wake up to.

Two days earlier I had dropped my daughter off at Duke for her freshman year. We said goodbye at the stadium door on a Saturday evening. By Monday morning I was on the table, having ten percent of my large intestine along with a major mass inside of it. 

The mysterious mass had shown up on a routine colonoscopy, so large the doctor could not see around it. My surgeon gave it to me straight: the surgery would be difficult but doable, and there was a sixty percent chance it was cancer.

I sat with that number for two weeks. You cannot do anything useful with odds like that except prepare for both outcomes and keep moving forward.

The surgery went well. Days later, still groggy at home, I got the call. It was not cancer. I was so sure it was that I didn’t even know how to process the diagnosis. 

What none of us knew yet was that I was bleeding internally with no obvious sign. By the time my husband got me to the ER a few days later, I passed out in the lobby. I needed a second procedure to clip off the bleeding. Turns out I had a one-in-a-hundred complication. 
When I could talk to my surgeon again, he joked he must have used up all my luck on the cancer result and had the complication instead. Looking at the mass, he said it was almost always cancer. It is a good way to use up luck I guess. 

The mass turned out to be endometriosis likely caused by the medication that was preventing last year’s breast cancer from returning.  Hormone positive meant the hormones that had kept the endometriosis in check for years were suddenly the enemy, so I switched to a drug that guards against a recurrence instead. That same drug can cause endometriosis to grow somewhere it should not. 

Sometimes when you fix one thing, you can have ripple effects you don’t anticipate. I used to think of health as a series of problems you solve and close out. This year taught me it is a string of trade-offs, made with imperfect information. You can only keep drawing one card at a time. 

Three things I am carrying forward:
* Vigilance is exhausting, but it is what lets you catch problems before they become emergencies.
* Treatments can have a hidden cost. Knowing it means you can stay on top of it. 
* The minutes you feel well matter more once you know they are not guaranteed.

I am getting stronger every day, but I don’t want to forget what it was to lose all that I took for granted. Listen to your body and guard your health.

hook: Entire company cultures are built around rewarding the people who sacrifice the most. And completely ignoring what it co
text:
Entire company cultures are built around rewarding the people who sacrifice the most. And completely ignoring what it costs them. 

The employee who works until 10pm gets praised for dedication. Nobody accounts for the dinner they missed with their kids. 

The Sales leader who grinds for 70 hours per week gets celebrated for hitting the number at all costs. Nobody accounts for their marriage that's falling apart. 

The manager takes a last-minute random Zoom meeting at 7am and gets recognized for going above and beyond. Nobody accounts for the workout they missed again and their health that's deteriorating. 

The leader who works late every day gets rewarded for doing whatever it takes. Nobody accounts for the 5 hours of lost sleep and the poor decisions they make the next day running on fumes. 

Companies love to celebrate the grind, hustle, pressure, and sacrifice. And completely ignore the costs. 

And somehow this has become completely normalized as the definition of a "high-performing culture". 

When in reality, it's the exact opposite. 

You're not "winning" if everyone at your company is losing sleep, neglecting their health, skipping exercise, straining relationships, missing time with their kids, and constantly overworking. 

Unfortunately, none of this collateral damage shows up on the company balance sheet. 

But eventually the company pays the price. 

Declining performance, poor decisions, burnt out people, high turnover. All proven outcomes of these toxic cultures. 

If the company hits the target, but everyone working there sacrifices their health, relationships, and lives to get there, that isn't success. 

Outdated company cultures chase success for the business at the expense of their people. 

A truly high-performing company creates the conditions for people to succeed and grow in all areas of their lives.

hook: I showered with my AI, and it was a horrible mistake.
text:
I showered with my AI, and it was a horrible mistake.

As the world gets more AI-friendly, and as we find more and more things to be productive about (and I don't want everything in my life to actually be productive), I have been testing and experimenting with AI usage in different contexts.

And Codex live voice mode opened up new options for me.

One time, instead of waiting to clean my apartment at the end of the day or on the weekend, I actually did it during the workday while I was dictating to Codex and processing tasks that I had to do.

Another time, I had to fill out this form for my Apple Business account. And Codex did it all for me - it even found my W-9 on my laptop to pull my EIN. It completed the whole form so that I could run errands.

Instead of being strapped to my computer and having to dig up all these files and numbers on my own, I could do double duty and get personal things off my plate without losing time.

I use AI on walks. And importantly, it's not that I'm adding AI to the walks that I'm already doing (for that, I still prefer Sam Cooke or Hello Puzzlers). It's that I'm able to TAKE MORE WALKS that I wasn't able to before because of AI.

So now, I might go on a walk at 4pm and process all the Slack messages that I didn't respond to or review a client contract. As a team, sometimes we even take team-wide walk breaks to work 1:1 with our AIs.

BUT.

I just tried one new workflow that I hated with the fury of a thousand suns.

And that was trying voice mode while I was in the shower.

It was effective in the sense that the AI could hear me well and could process tasks (unlike the Apple AI assistant who shall remain nameless, who can't hear me if a single pin is dropped in the background).

Sure, there was a little annoyance when the phone had a permission pop-up and I had to reach my hand out of the shower to press it.

But my biggest gripe was that I just hated the overall experience. Hated it.

There are some parts of my life that I really don't want to add AI into right now.

And it's really in those times where I allow my brain to dance off into the edges of my imagination, or truly relax and take time away from execution.

And I just want this to be a reminder that we need space to be away from tech and just think and exist.

That could be on a nature hike, or in the shower, or my favorite meditative place in the whole wide world (the middle of a car wash).

There is no perfect optimization formula that is telling us that every minute of every day has to be AI-enabled.

So I will no longer be showering with my AI and will stick to my rubber duck.

Thank you.

text:
In our hunter-gatherer days, we averaged 14,000 to 17,000 steps a day. 
 
Today, the average American averages 4000 steps. 
 
Let's fix that. 
 
You don't need 10,000 steps a day. They found that getting 6000 steps a day correlated with a decreased rate of mortality. 
 
Here are 5 easy ways to get those steps in: 
 
1. Walking first thing in the morning 
2. Walking meetings 
3. Take the stairs when you can 
4. Park farther away 
5. Walk after your meals 
 
You can do walks as well, but sometimes the best way to get those steps is when you're already engaged in another activity or as a habit to do after an event. 
 
Getting more steps is one of the easiest ways to improve your health, so take advantage.

hook: It's been a fantastic week in Boston with Mandy.
text:
It's been a fantastic week in Boston with Mandy.

First, we spent time with our US business, Heart to Home Meals USA, understanding the business and franchise expansion with Christopher and Ajay. Then we spent the last three days at HubSpot Unbound.

Tonnes of exciting new features and developments across the HubSpot platform, plus insightful conversations with Kate Bueker. But the dominant thread of the last few days has been where marketing strategy goes next.

Five things I'm taking home, alongside my copy of Loop: Outlearn. Outmarket. Outgrow. by Kipp Bodnar and Kieran Flanagan:

1. Outcomes over activity. Companies genuinely transforming are being selective in their AI use. They are doing less, not more, and tying each one to a real business outcome.

2. Context is the moat. Data and your context are the critical factor for AI success. No AI is better than AI with bad context.

3. Trust has replaced attention. Maha Abouelenein talked about how views and clicks are cheap. Credibility, reputation and recommendation are what earn the sale. Businesses buy from people, not businesses. The time of personal brands is now.

4. Ship fast, learn faster. Stop planning campaigns in quarters. Learn from Dev sprint cycles... iterate continuously. Two week sprints give 26 learning opportunities a year, compared to our standard 4 opportunities with quarterly campaigns.

5. Feed the AI. Tell it what good looks like. Give it feedback rather than just taking the output, and loop the learnings back in every time.

Overall a fantastic week. Great to see the US team, and good to come back with plenty to think about.

hook: 🏆 Brands getting gold on Reddit — here's how
text:
🏆 Brands getting gold on Reddit — here's how

Ross Simmonds has a simple framework for any brand starting out on Reddit. It’s called the 4 E’s:

1️⃣ Educate. What does your audience want on Reddit, Inc.? Do they want top 10 lists? How-to instructionals? 

Here’s how Simmonds figures that out: Using Reddit’s built-in Ask Reddit function, ask, “What is the best [insert your category here]?” Simmonds says it will “do an analysis across all of the millions of pieces of content that have been published within its ecosystem, and look for queries and keywords that align with what you just typed in.” That will help you identify relevant subreddits. From there, sort by top post. 

2️⃣ Engage. Simmonds notes Reddit isn't a traditional social network but a hub for heated debates. Inspiring conversation is a big win. Ask questions that spark dialogue. 

3️⃣ Empower. In a true crime subreddit, there’s an expectation of knowledge. No one wants a new podcast host suddenly explaining DNA testing. Instead, show up, listen, interact, and thank the community for their lessons. Simmonds says, "they feel like you understand them, they see you, and they want you to win."

4️⃣ Entertain. “You have to be able to put your guard down and have a little fun.” Even in traditional industries, Simmonds has convinced clients to share cat GIFs, jokes, and memes. 
“And it does wonders for that brand’s karma,” Simmonds says. “They get awards. People give them gold. It’s an absolutely delightful thing.”

hook: Five million square feet of retail space sits empty across Canada.
text:
Five million square feet of retail space sits empty across Canada.

Purpose-built seniors housing, meanwhile, has a national vacancy rate of just 1.2%.

For 83-year-old Mary Hoerdt, that mismatch isn't abstract. It's happening outside her front door.

As long-time president of the Oakridge Seniors Centre in Vancouver, she watched construction cut through her daily walking route and disrupt a community of 200 seniors.

The irony is that malls have long filled a need that rarely shows up on a retail earnings report.

In winter, older Canadians use them as warm, indoor places to walk, shop, meet friends, and stay connected.

Now developers are starting to build housing around that behavior.

Canada's population aged 85 and older is expected to triple by mid-century. Wait lists for specialized facilities already run for months. The country needs another 200,000 seniors housing units over the next decade.

Old retail sites come with one major advantage: much of the expensive infrastructure is already there.

Roads, power, water, transit, and major road access are already in place.
In Montreal, Groupe Maurice built Résidence Cornelius into Centre Wilderton. 

Residents can reach a pharmacy, medical clinic, grocery store, and restaurants without going outside in winter.

In Vancouver, Oakridge Park is replacing 28 acres of retail property with homes for 6,000 residents, plus a rooftop park, medical services, and a civic seniors centre.

For Hoerdt and her community, the years of dust, barricades, and relocation have been hard.

But her experience captures the larger tension: Canada has millions of square feet of retail space it no longer needs, while seniors housing is nearly full.

Some aging malls may be more useful as neighborhoods than shopping centres.

Next time you walk through an older suburban mall on a weekday morning, notice who's actually there.

Sources: Vancouver Sun column, Aug. 20, 2024: Mary Hoerdt, 83, long-time president of Oakridge Seniors Centre; centre lost 200 members; construction made walking unsafe.

hook: Blockchain is to crypto what the internet is to email. One made the other famous, but the technology can do much more.
text:
Blockchain is to crypto what the internet is to email. One made the other famous, but the technology can do much more.

Forget crypto for a moment.

Imagine three companies working on the same supply chain. Each keeps its own records, so they spend time checking which version is correct.

With blockchain, they can share a record of what happened. Each update follows agreed rules, and previous entries are difficult to change without the others noticing.

A product can carry a shared history as it moves between companies.

A digital credential can be issued by one organization and verified by another.

A smart contract can trigger an action when a defined condition is met.

Crypto uses the same technology to record and transfer digital value. It is one application, not the definition of blockchain.

The question is: do several parties need to share and verify the same record without giving one of them control?

If yes, blockchain may be worth considering.

#Blockchain #DigitalTrust

creator: Dan Martell
hook: The bigger your goal, the smaller your next step should be.
text:
The bigger your goal, the smaller your next step should be.

It's the simplest path to success.

Huge ambitions can make you want to start immediately.

But many people fall into a certain pattern.

At first, you're excited about what you're trying to achieve.

Then you start thinking about everything you'll need to do to get there.

The hours you'll need.
The changes you'll have to make.
The obstacles you might run into.

Suddenly, that huge goal feels far away.

I've fallen into this pattern with many of my own goals.

When I decided to improve my health, there was a lot that I wanted to change quickly.

My sleep needed attention.
I wanted to exercise and manage my stress better.

Trying to change everything at once would have been difficult to sustain.

So I broke everything down into smaller steps.

That approach has helped me work towards big goals ever since.
If you're working on something, it could help you too:

Start with the destination
↳ Be clear on what you want to achieve.

Understand what's in the way
↳ Identify the biggest obstacle you need to work through.

Shrink the next step
↳ Break your next step down into something you can do this week.

Expect the plan to change
↳ Pay attention to what's working and adjust as you learn.

Track your progress
↳ When things get difficult, you'll have a reminder of how far you've come.

A big goal will always be intimidating if you think about everything at once.

Focus on what you can do today.
Then do the same tomorrow.

The most powerful sentence a leader can say is five words long...

"I don't know. What do you think?"

Before that, I'd bought into the whole sole-entrepreneur myth, I read Richard Branson's books, read about Bill Gates, read about Zuckerberg, and in my head I'd decided the founder's job was to walk into every room with the questions AND the answers. 

So that's what I did, I made the call, set the direction and made sure everyone knew I had it handled.

And that's exactly why so many of my best people walked, four of them, and I honestly didn't see it happening until they were already gone. 

Nobody wants to build something with a guy who thinks he knows it all.

So now I do it the other way. Everyone throws an idea on the table, and we rank them by how fast we can test it and how big it could be if we're right. 

My team even got it printed on a t-shirt, black, white text, nobody needed it explained because they all knew exactly where it came from: "I don't know, what do you think?"

Sell the wrong thing at the right time.

👉 10K to 20K: Sell group access and early community

You picked the wrong change model for the job.

text:
Last week, 7 strangers offered to "grow my LinkedIn." One even offered to become me.
 
Below is the underground menu of LinkedIn services landing in my inbox. What they cost you, the DMs they use to sell them, and how I replied
 
I've been banned from LinkedIn twice. Once for having an emoji in my name field. Once for having my birthday on January 8th (their mistake, they apologised). Yet there's an entire revenue channel operating from the Mines of Moria. 

1. Discounted Sales Navigator seats  
Shared logins. Reseller abuse. Sometimes paid with stolen cards. The seat gets revoked, and your account gets flagged with it. (Yes, that's him in the picture.)
 
"Hi Richard, hope you're doing well! We offer Sales Navigator Core and Advanced at up to 60% below official pricing. Instant activation, 100% safe, 500+ satisfied clients. Shall I share our packages?"
 
Me: "Does the 60% discount include the account ban, or is that extra?"
 
2. Fake profiles doing outreach "on your behalf"  
Your brand, attached to a person who doesn't exist. Prospects notice. They screenshot. They share.
 
"Hi Richard, we run done-for-you outreach through our network of senior, verified profiles. They build the relationship, you only show up for booked calls. Open to a quick chat this week?"
 
Me: "So your SDRs are imaginary friends. I stopped having those when I was seven."
 
3. Pods and engagement factories  
Fast, fake engagement from people outside your market. LinkedIn detects the pattern. Your reach to actual buyers quietly dies.
 
"Hey Richard. We're an invite-only community of 350+ B2B founders supporting each other's content in the golden hour. Members see 5 to 10x more reach. Only 3 spots left this month."
 
Me: "A group chat that claps on command? My family WhatsApp group does that for free."
 
4. AI commenting tools  
Generic comments at scale. Easy to spot, easy to detect, and they tell everyone you didn't care enough to type.
 
"Hi Richard, your content deserves more visibility. Our tool writes personalised, human-like comments on your ICP's posts, 50-100 per day, fully on autopilot. Want a free trial?"
 
Me: "Great insights! Thanks for sharing! 🚀 (Sorry, my AI answered.)"
 
5. Profile rental  
You "lease" your account to an agency. They run outreach from it. You lose control. When it gets banned, it's your name on it. Permanently.
 
"Hi Richard, you can earn $150 to $300 weekly passive income from your LinkedIn account. We only use it for B2B lead generation for US clients. Weekly payments via PayPal. Interested?"
 
Me: "Sorry, it's currently occupied. By me. Since 2005."
 

Every service on this list sells the same promise: results without the work.
And every one of them uses the same collateral: the account you spent years building.
If a service needs your password, you're the product.
 
What's the most creepy "growth" offer that ever landed in your DMs?
 
PS: After I reported the Sales Navigator guy, LinkedIn finally agreed with me. They banned his account.

Over 3.3 million people have viewed the latest The Diary Of A CEO episode on one of the biggest issues of our time: AI.

But have you ever wondered what it actually takes to assemble an emergency episode on the world’s second-largest podcast?

Well, It starts at 7pm on a Friday in New York and as lead producer on-site, I had 48 hours to make it happen…

Friday

7pm — Decision made

The team agrees that now is the time to bring together some of the biggest voices in AI to discuss Jacob Coxon’s post that broke the internet.

7–8pm — Strategy on what the panel should look like begins. 

We need voices from different sides of the debate. People who know the subject inside out, who are willing to have an open conversation.

8–9pm — Outreach begins.

The team identified four leading voices who are perfect for the conversation. And somehow, luck was on our side. They could make it.

Saturday

10am — Strategy sessions begin.

How do we elevate the episode? How do we cut through the noise? What do we need on set to make the conversation as informed and engaging as possible?

10am–4pm — Production prep is in full swing.

Sunday

hook: Someone I was helping this year spent 6 months applying to senior roles.
text:
Someone I was helping this year spent 6 months applying to senior roles.

No offers. Just rejections and silence.

The advice he kept getting was to “tweak his resume” or “fix his LinkedIn.”

Both were actually fine.

But a good resume and LinkedIn profile only cover part of a job search.

There’s still the question of which roles you’re going after, how you’re getting in front of people, and what you’re saying once you get an interview.

These are the five areas I work through with people:

1. Target the right roles.

Get specific about the work, scope, compensation, and environment you want.

Start with around 30 companies that fit. Give yourself something more useful to work from than “I’m open to anything.”

2. Position yourself to be found.

Make it easy to understand what you do and where you fit.

Your resume and LinkedIn should use language relevant to the roles you want, backed by examples of what you’ve accomplished.

Someone shouldn’t have to piece together why you’re qualified.

3. Talk to people at your target companies.

Start with former colleagues and people who can introduce you.

Ask about the team, what they’re working on, and where your experience might be useful.

Keep applying to relevant openings, too. Just don’t make that your entire search.

4. Prepare for the interview.

Having conducted interviews doesn’t automatically make you good at answering the questions.

Practice explaining what you owned, why you made certain decisions, and what happened as a result.

Pick examples relevant to the problems this company needs you to solve.

5. Negotiate the full offer.

Before you accept, look beyond base salary.

Bonus, sign-on, equity, and severance are all worth considering, depending on the role and what matters to you.

Decide what you want to ask for and why.

And if your search has stalled, look at where you’re losing people.

Not getting interviews?
Revisit your targeting, positioning, and outreach.

Getting interviews but no offers?
Take a closer look at your preparation and storytelling.

That gives you a better starting point than rewriting your resume for the tenth time.

The cheat sheet below breaks down each area.

creator: Nate Herk
hook: How to Build Codex Skills Better Than 99% of People
text:
How to Build Codex Skills Better Than 99% of People

A Codex skill is basically a recipe for your agent.

If the recipe is vague, the output can change wildly. If it captures the actual process, examples, and checks, the agent has a much better chance of giving you something usable.

This is the six-step process I use:

1. Reverse engineer the output
Start with a finished result you already like, then work backward through the data, decisions, calculations, and formatting that produced it.

2. Give the skill one job and one trigger
"Run the marketing team" is too broad. A single task with a clear reason to invoke it is easier for the agent to find and execute consistently.

3. Match the freedom level to the work
Mechanical steps should be specific. Work that depends on judgment needs room to adapt.

4. Build verification into the skill
Have the agent check the objective requirements and review the subjective quality before it hands the output back.

5. Walk it down the model list
Test the same skill on cheaper models. If Luna produces the same quality as Astra, there is no reason to keep paying for Astra every time.

6. Use the bike method
Every run creates feedback. Add what worked, what failed, and what should change so the skill improves instead of making you correct the same mistake again.

I tested this live by running my X Article skill across Sol, Terra, and Luna, then comparing their writing, screenshot choices, formatting, and QA reports against the Astra version I normally use.

One run was not enough to crown a winner. Luna beat Terra on this example, but Astra has still been the most reliable across repeated videos.

I just dropped a YouTube video walking through the full framework and the live model comparison.

Link to the full video is in the comments 👇

hook: Hard times create better, more successful people.
text:
Hard times create better, more successful people.

I know it’s not easy...

Struggling with your job search, being laid off, being passed over for that promotion.

But here’s the thing.

Hard times actually lead to greater long term success.

Obstacles and setbacks push us to be persistent, to get creative, and to grow.

I am so grateful for all of the struggles I went through early on in my career.

I’m grateful for the rejections, I’m grateful for the mistakes, and I’m grateful for the frustration.

Why?

If I got good grades and a “good” job right out of college, I wouldn’t have pushed myself in the same way.

I would have clocked in at 9, out at 5, and crossed my fingers for a raise or promo every few years.

I would not have ended up at Microsoft.

I would not be here writing this post to 1.4M+ followers.

Those things happened because the challenges I faced pushed me to grow.

This isn't just a cute personal story, it's an illustration of a research backed concept.

A 2019 study in Nature Communications found that early career setbacks lead to higher levels of success...IF the participants weren't deterred by the first failure.

So if you're going through hard times right now, keep going.

I know there is a lot wrong with the system, I know there are many things out of your control, and I know that a lot of it might not seem fair (and isn't fair!).

But keep pushing. 

Stay strong.

It's going to pay off down the road.

I promise.

- AB ✌

text:
5 things to try with Muse this weekend beyond the usual email, calendar, and subscription workflows:

1. Set up a personalized feed

Muse's Feed is refreshing because it doesn't have AI slop or ads.

You can personalize it around the exact topics you care about, plus reminders tied to your life. I love scrolling through it every morning.

2. Fill out forms and comparison shop online

Ask Muse to help renew your driver's license, compare car insurance options, or book hard-to-get restaurant and show reservations.

It's very capable, especially combined with item 5 below.

3. Monitor your DMs

Muse has first-party connections to Instagram, Threads, and Messenger. If you install the desktop app, it can see your iMessages too.

Have it monitor your messages for anything you need to follow up on instead of you having to check 4 different message inboxes yourself.

4. Buy and sell on Facebook Marketplace

Other agents can do this too, but Muse makes it easy through its first-party integration.

Snap a photo, upload it to Muse, and ask it to list the item. You can also have it regularly search for the best deals on something you want and DM sellers directly.

5. Find and talk to human customer support

This is the killer feature IMO. Muse can navigate phone trees, wait on hold, and talk to a human customer support rep while representing itself as your agent.

It also says it can dial you in halfway through the call, although I haven't been able to get that working yet.

By the way, if you don't have access to this, ask Muse to message Meta and request access. I got it a day after doing this.

Last but not least, I think Muse's Ideas tab (below) is very well done.

The biggest problem with chat interfaces is that most people have no idea what to ask. Ideas solves that by suggesting useful, personalized things Muse can do for you.

My only complaint so far: 

Muse's compaction doesn't seem to work as well as ChatGPT. If I discuss several topics in the main thread, it sometimes gets confused. 

Beyond that, it's been delightful to use. I can tell the team spent months polishing this.

📌 Watch my full Muse walkthrough here: https://lnkd.in/g9F5_2SV

text:
I’ve helped 1,000+ job seekers strengthen their resumes and as a recruiter, I've reviewed thousands of resumes over the years.  

Your resume has seconds to make an impression.

Here are 10 best practices for a great resume:

💡Lead with your value, not just your title
↳ Your resume should quickly communicate who you are, what you specialize in, and the impact you’ve made.

💡Create a strong professional summary
↳ Replace generic statements with a clear snapshot of your expertise, accomplishments, and career story.

💡Focus on accomplishments, not responsibilities
↳ Don’t just list what you did, highlight results, metrics, and the difference you made.

💡Quantify your impact
↳ Numbers tell a stronger story: revenue generated, costs saved, teams led, projects delivered, or goals exceeded.

💡Make it easy to read
↳ Use clear sections, concise bullets, and formatting that allows recruiters to quickly find the information they need.

💡Tailor your resume for each opportunity
↳ A one-size-fits-all resume often gets overlooked. Customize your messaging based on the role you want.

💡Showcase your career progression
↳ Highlight growth, promotions, increased responsibility, and the evolution of your expertise.

💡Remove outdated or unnecessary information
↳ Your resume is a marketing document, not a complete history of everything you’ve ever done.

💡Make your first half-page count
 ↳ Recruiters often make quick decisions. Put your strongest skills and accomplishments where they will be seen first.

💡Avoid generic buzzwords
 ↳ Words like “results-driven,” “hardworking,” and “team player” don’t differentiate you. Show proof through specific achievements.

Remember:

text:
A DoorDash PM built a Claude Code system that supports 20+ people.

Hannah Stulberg. Ex-Google APM. 1,500+ hours in Claude Code. She calls it a “Team OS.”

Most PMs use AI as a personal productivity tool. One person benefits. Everyone else on the team still waits for context, still searches for the right query, still asks the PM to pull the number.

Hannah did something different. She built a shared repo that every function on her team can access. Data scientists pull their own metrics. Strategy leads grab their own customer call summaries. Engineers check analytics without filing a ticket.

The setup takes about 30 days. Here’s the architecture:

1. A root CLAUDE md file (under 500 tokens) with the doc index, team roster, Slack IDs, and GitHub handles.

2. Nested CLAUDE md files in every major folder. Navigation indexes only. 3% context per query.

3. Folder ownership assigned by function. PM owns product. Data scientist owns analytics. Strategy owns customer calls.

4. An analytics layer with metric definitions, SQL queries, and dashboard links, loaded progressively by depth.

5. Shared skills: customer call summaries, PR creation, weekly synthesis. Everyone runs the same tools.

6. Verified playbooks for recurring analyses (funnel drop-off, churn investigation). Claude follows the same steps your analyst would.

7. A launch gate: no feature ships until its metrics, queries, schemas, dashboards, and playbooks are checked into the repo.

The result is that Hannah went from being the team’s bottleneck to being the person who built the system that made the bottleneck disappear.

The barrier to starting is psychological. The terminal feels scary for about an hour. Then it feels normal.

Resources to build yours:

1. Full podcast episode where she walks through every step: https://lnkd.in/gVi3PQ-U
2. Newsletter deep dive w starter repo: https://lnkd.in/gi3vNyzR
3. My PM OS: https://lnkd.in/gsH9RSfJ

hook: I Tested Jev on 12 Real Use Cases. My Honest Thoughts.
text:
I Tested Jev on 12 Real Use Cases. My Honest Thoughts.

Jev is an AI model you can't really chat with.

It doesn't write, summarize, or brainstorm. You give it criteria, and it returns a yes or no decision, category, or score with a confidence level.

I tested it across email, YouTube comments, Skool posts, meetings, video clips, contracts, leads, customer support, and a few stranger experiments.

The email test made the tradeoff easy to see.

I ran 1,000 emails through seven decision rules. Jev's first pass took about 70 seconds and cost $0.09. Luna took about five minutes and cost $0.62.

After I changed the backend to process larger payloads in parallel, Jev finished the same 1,000 emails in six seconds at the same cost.

The use cases that made the most sense:
→ High-volume triage for inboxes, comments, community posts, leads, and support tickets
→ Real-time routing, like the Chrome extension I built to label X posts as breaking news, golden nuggets, or AI slop while I scroll
→ A cheap first decision layer that sends only the important items to a larger model for writing or deeper analysis

The main limitation is just as important: Jev cannot write the reply, explain its reasoning in depth, or do open-ended analysis. It needs another model for the next step.

Before I would trust it in production, I would build a golden dataset and test Jev against Sol, Opus, or whatever model is already doing the job. Accuracy comes first, then cost and speed.

I also pushed it into a paper-trading bot that made a new Bitcoin decision every second. 

That was a proof of concept, not a trading strategy, and the fees were larger than the model cost.

Link to the full video is in the comments 👇

creator: Damien Benveniste
hook: How do Machine Learning Feature Stores feed both training and real-time inference? They give the same feature two views
text:
How do Machine Learning Feature Stores feed both training and real-time inference? They give the same feature two views of time: what was known then for training, and what is known now for serving!

Imagine a fraud model using `card_transactions_30d`.

Every labeled payment in the training set happened at a different time. For a payment made on June 1, the training row must use the transaction count that was available on June 1. Using the value we know today would let future activity leak into the past.

The offline store preserves the feature history. A point-in-time join takes each entity and label timestamp, then retrieves the latest feature value at or before that timestamp. Its output is a large, time-correct training table.

Real-time inference asks a different question. A new payment arrives now, and the model needs the latest available count for this card before the request times out. Scanning the full history would be wasteful.

The online store keeps the latest precomputed value for each entity key, such as `card_id`, so the serving system can fetch a feature vector quickly. A materialization job copies fresh values from the offline store into the online store. A streaming pipeline can instead push new values into both paths as events arrive.

The registry connects the two. It records the feature definition, entity key, data source, schema, transformation, and ownership. Training requests a historical value. Serving requests a current value. Both refer to the same feature contract.

That architecture addresses two separate failures:

- Point-in-time retrieval keeps future values out of the training rows.
- Shared definitions reduce training-serving skew, where a model trains on one computation and receives another in production.

But a feature store does not make the data correct by itself! A late materialization job can serve stale values. A wrong event timestamp can corrupt the historical join. Batch and streaming transformations can still disagree if they implement different logic.

I would start with versioned feature definitions and point-in-time-correct training data. I would add an online store when live predictions need precomputed features that cannot be produced inside the request's latency budget. If the model only runs in batch, a warehouse and a disciplined feature pipeline may already be enough.

hook: WFH is both awesome and awful.
text:
WFH is both awesome and awful.

I LOVE the freedom. I LOVE skipping the commute. I LOVE being able to focus without spending half the day migrating from conference room to conference room.

AND—the world can feel awfully small when most of it happens through a rectangular screen.

That’s one of the reasons Drive by Exit Five has meant so much to me.

I left Stowe a week ago, and it has taken me this long just to find the words. By now, my feed is full of smart recaps—and enough pictures of Seth Godin 🌔 to confirm that he was, in fact, there. 😃

What I keep thinking about is how it felt to be in the rooms.

Drive has grown from 200 people in Burlington to 400 at Spruce Peak. Somehow, Dave Gerhardt and the incredible Exit Five team made it feel like the same wonderfully weird marketing family reunion—just with a few more cousins and slightly better scenery.

There was SO much energy in that room. SO much laughter. SO many big hugs in hallways and conversations that picked right back up after a year apart.

Underneath all of it, people seemed to be carrying more this year.

Career exhaustion. Grief. Big decisions. New beginnings. The pressure to already be doing more with AI, even though nobody seems entirely sure what “more” means yet. The quiet worry that everyone else is moving faster. That maybe you’re behind. Or stuck. Or becoming invisible.

Seth was as thoughtful, generous, and quietly funny as usual. I’ve admired his work for years, and spending time with him IRL twice in two weeks was a pretty spectacular streak for this marketing nerd.

He talked about refusing to let ourselves become de-skilled by AI. About continuing to make work that matters, which requires judgment, courage, taste, and care.

I needed that.

Ann Handley was every bit as smart, funny, and refreshingly no-nonsense in person as I’d hoped. She talked about the way ideas travel between people who trust one another—and told the story of a small water utility in Northeast Ohio that built a remarkable following because one guy showed up and wrote like an actual human being.

Imagine that. 😃

Her call to choose craft over slop and pack the sloth’s wallop put words to so much of what I’ve been thinking about lately.

I needed that, too.

It also helped me better understand why #opentohelp has become such an important part of my life. It’s intentionally analog and wildly unscalable. Sometimes we spend 30 minutes untangling a career decision. Sometimes we talk through energy and what drains them and what fills them back up. Sometimes they simply need a safe place to say the thing out loud.

It’s always SLOW and fully HUMAN. 

I came home with pages of notes. And yet, I keep reaching for the PEOPLE.

The old friends. The new ones. The conversations that ran long. The laughter that carried across the rooms. The moments when someone trusted me with a little piece of their story.

To everyone who made me feel seen, THANK YOU!

I hope I did the same for you! 💛

Your pal,
Pete 😃

You should be failing more.

Seriously.

If everything you try works, you’re probably not trying enough NEW things.

I’ve failed A LOT in my career.

I spent 3 years working for free in radio and never got the job I wanted.

I built an entertainment blog, got an opportunity with MTV, filmed an entire show…

And then they cancelled it.

I’ve hired the wrong people.

I’ve started things that didn’t work.

I’ve made decisions that cost me time AND money.

And I’m sure I’ll get plenty more wrong. 💁🏻♀️

Because how am I supposed to know exactly what works when I’m doing something I’ve never done before?

We put so much pressure on ourselves to get things right the first time.

But sometimes you’re going to make the wrong call.

You’re going to try something and realize you’re terrible at it.

You’re going to have ideas you’re SURE are brilliant… until you actually try them. 😭

You might apply for something and get rejected.

You might put yourself out there and hear NO.

You might work really hard at something and still fail.

I’d be more concerned if I reached a point where I never failed.

Because that would probably mean I stopped taking chances.

So if something you tried recently completely FLOPPED…

Good.

You know one more thing that doesn’t work.

Now go be bad at something. ❤️
