hook: What happens when AI changes human judgment in a world where the conditions for developing and exercising judgment are a
text:
What happens when AI changes human judgment in a world where the conditions for developing and exercising judgment are already deeply unequal?

Vijayakumar Parameswaran Unnithan PhD examines AI as a “developmental perturbation.” His argument is that AI may change not only what people do, but the conditions through which judgment develops. Through attunement, discernment, coherence and resonance, and later Deep Literacy, he considers what sustained AI use may do to the human capacity to judge.  

Those conditions are not the same for everyone. Education, technological capability, economic resources, professional experience and institutional capacity are unevenly distributed. AI does not create these differences, but as it becomes part of how people learn, work and decide, their consequences may become more significant. Two people may use the same AI while having very different capacities to understand its limitations, challenge its framing, test its conclusions or reject its recommendations. Existing capability influences how AI is used, while the way AI is used may influence the capability that develops afterward.

Organizations and countries differ in capability as well. Some can develop talent, infrastructure and alternatives, while others may use increasingly capable AI but depend on knowledge, infrastructure or technologies developed elsewhere. Having access to AI is different from having the capacity to understand, challenge or find alternatives to the systems behind it.

Judgment is exercised within purposes defined by people and institutions. People have ambitions, executives have incentives, owners seek returns, technology companies pursue commercial objectives and governments may prioritize competitiveness, technological autonomy or national security. A worker may value employment while management seeks efficiency. Owners may prioritize returns while a technology provider seeks adoption and scale. These interests can coincide, but they can conflict.

AI needs no ambition of its own for this to matter. Humans may retain formal authority over decisions while relying increasingly on systems that influence what information receives attention, how problems are framed and which alternatives are considered. When objectives conflict, who has the capacity to question the assumptions behind the choices being presented?

The issue extends beyond whether humans retain judgment. It is whose judgment develops, under what conditions, toward whose goals and ultimately for whose benefit. The emerging divide may concern not only access to AI, but who can use it while retaining the knowledge, alternatives and independence required to question it.
#artificialintelligence #judgment #leadership #inequality #governance #technology Open Magazine

text:
68,173 people at M&T Bank Stadium in Baltimore on Saturday. The largest crowd ever for a rugby union match in the United States. I went because I've loved this game for years, and I left thinking about what rugby does that very few sports manage.
Eighty minutes of genuine physical violence, and then both sides form a tunnel and clap each other off. The All Blacks were magnificent across that series. They won at Ellis Park, they pushed South Africa to the edge in Cape Town and Soweto, and they made every one of those four Tests worth the ticket. A rivalry only means something when both sides are this good.

And then the Springboks. 43-28, the series taken 3-1, Rassie Erasmus' hundredth Test in charge. Siya Kolisi leading the way he always does. Malcolm Marx over the ball. Kurt-Lee Arendse chasing down that loose ball late and running away with the whole thing. That front row doing what that front row does.

What stayed with me is the unity this game brings. People from everywhere, in every colour jersey, coming together to cheer the teams they love. Strangers explaining the laws to first-timers. Black and green side by side in the same row. Nobody guarding what they loved, everybody sharing it.
The 2031 World Cup is five years out. Baltimore just made its case.

AI made building cheap. It made attention and taste expensive.

Look at both sides of every software market right now. The supply of builders exploded. Anyone with Claude Code and a free weekend can ship a working product. But the number of buyers, and the hours of attention they have to evaluate anything, stayed exactly the same.

That's the squeeze every vibe coder eventually faces. 

When 100 products chase the same buyer, the best-built one rarely wins. The buyer picks from the two or three they actually heard about. So the first scarce skill is distribution. For 20 years companies paid $500K+ for engineers because so few people could build. Now a solo founder ships in a week what used to take a funded team a quarter, and the bottleneck moved from production to being found. Increasingly that means being found by agents too, since the fastest-growing discovery channel isn't a human scrolling anymore.

The second scarce skill is taste at speed.

Because when prototypes cost 45 minutes instead of 6 weeks, the hard part stops being "can we build it" and becomes "which of these 15 working versions deserves to exist." Without taste, speed just means you build the wrong thing faster. The builders winning are the ones who can look at a pile of working software, kill 80% of it by noon, then pour everything into the one bet that matters to actual buyers.

These two skills feed each other. Distribution tells you what people actually want, which sharpens your taste. Taste means what you ship is worth talking about, which compounds your distribution. I've watched every product I've shipped since 2021 ride on both, while technically superior competitors launched into silence.

The engineering was never the moat. It just used to look like one because it was the rarest input. Now the rare inputs are judgment about what to build and a channel to the people, and agents, who'd buy it.

creator: Ruben Hassid
hook: How to master ChatGPT-6-Astra in only 15 steps:
text:
How to master ChatGPT-6-Astra in only 15 steps:

(full guide with screenshots chatgpt.rubenhassid.ai)

1. Open ChatGPT Work or Codex.
Astra is not in the normal chat on the ChatGPT browser. It's in Work (documents, slides, Excel) and Codex (code) on the ChatGPT desktop app.

2. Select Astra → Medium.
Not High. Not Max. Medium is the best intelligence + cost + speed ratio by far. 

3. Turn off Data Training.
Settings → Data controls → Off. On by default. 
Ignore if you are okay without any privacy.

4. Check Codex's training setting too.
Codex has its own switch. The ChatGPT toggle does not reach it. Mind you: 2 toggles to turn off.

5. Give one clear goal in one prompt.
"Help me analyze this" is too vague. Astra fills the gaps with guesses and gives you random answers that will waste your time and tokens.
One task, one outcome.

6. Name the finished deliverable.
Summary? Recommendation? Spreadsheet? 
Say what you want. Start the prompt with it.

7. Set constraints and success criteria.
Exact prompt: "Deliver a ranked comparison. Show the sample size for each group. Flag conclusions based on very few posts."
No "think step by step". Be direct instead.

8. Attach files. Explain their role.
Exact prompt: "Use the brand guide for style and the product brief for facts. If they disagree, flag the conflict first."
Evidence, template, or instructions: Astra can't tell.

9. Say which decisions need your input.
Astra asks for clarification more than any model before. Useful to brainstorm but it gets very annoying for the tasks you already had a solution for. Name the 2-3 questions worth asking.

10. Let it handle the rest.
Exact prompt: "Otherwise, complete the plan and list any assumptions at the end."

11. Specify tone, length & format.
The default is overly perfect sentences. "600-800 words. Paragraphs of 2-3 sentences. Answer Greg's question in the first line."
My favorite trick: "Use ASD-STE100."

12. Add: "List your assumptions."
You can catch its guesses very easily when it tries to fill the gap. Catch the misinformation early.

13. Correct its direction as it works.
It is quite good at long tasks, while consuming tokens. So send a follow-up mid-task to see its plan & execution. Just like... a human?

14. Tell it exactly what to check.
Exact prompt: "Before delivering, confirm the totals match the source, identify duplicates, and check every chart uses the correct date range."

15. Add: "Flag anything unresolved."
This removes the fake "all done!" report. Unverified stays unverified. 

This was just a glimpse of what Astra can do, and you can use it to your best. To actually read  the entire guide, go to chatgpt.rubenhassid.ai

I don't know if these kids will become millionaires. But I know they'll remember this moment.

hook: Encoder-only, decoder-only, or encoder-decoder? Transformer architectures become much easier to choose once you look at
text:
Encoder-only, decoder-only, or encoder-decoder? Transformer architectures become much easier to choose once you look at what every token is allowed to read, and what the model must return!

They share the same basic idea: attention mixes token representations. To me, the easiest way to keep the three architectures straight is to draw the information flow.

- Encoder-only: give the model the complete input, and let every token attend to tokens on both its left and right. The result is one contextual vector per input token. Pooling or a small task head can turn those vectors into a document label, one label per token, an extracted span, or an embedding. For these fixed-input tasks, the model can return after one forward pass instead of growing an answer token by token.

- Decoder-only: hide the future with a causal attention mask. At position t, the model can use only positions up to t, then returns a probability distribution for the next token. Append one token and repeat. This is the natural architecture for open-ended text and code generation, and the same next-token interface can absorb instructions and examples in the prompt. However, the output still grows sequentially, one decoding step at a time.

- Encoder-decoder: first let an encoder read the complete source. Then let a causal decoder generate the target while cross-attention looks back at the encoder's source representations. The output can have a different length and structure from the input, which fits translation, summarization, transcription, and other sequence-to-sequence transformations. The source is encoded once, but target generation remains autoregressive.

Imagine one support ticket.

If you need `billing_issue`, an encoder can read the whole ticket and return one label. If you need a free-form reply, a decoder can continue from the ticket and instructions. If you need to transform the ticket into a concise, structured resolution, an encoder-decoder can first represent the source and then generate the conditioned target.

These are architectural biases, not hard capability walls. A decoder-only model can emit a classification label, and an encoder-decoder model can cast classification as text-to-text.

For a fixed-input label, span, or embedding, I would start with encoder-only. For general prompting and open-ended generation, decoder-only. For a well-defined input-to-output transformation, I would test encoder-decoder against the decoder-only baseline. Model quality and available checkpoints still matter, but the data flow tells us which computation we are buying before we compare model names.

hook: I got invited to Google's San Jose campus with a small group of AI creators to meet some of the people building the prod
text:
I got invited to Google's San Jose campus with a small group of AI creators to meet some of the people building the products and infrastructure we all use.

We moved between buildings for panels, product demos, workshops, and conversations with Google engineers and executives.

The campus almost felt like a college campus. People were riding these colorful "G-bikes" between buildings, and there were real plants everywhere. It was so cool.

Most of the plants in my home office are fake, so Google definitely has me beat there.

We did a workshop that had us choose the best location for a new coffee shop from 12 possible sites.

I picked Site 6 based on the rent, foot traffic, income, and market growth.

Then we had AI agents look through thousands of rows of data: live inventory, customer reviews, forecasting data, etc.

Both of my agents picked Site 6, and Google's answer was Site 6 too.

So apparently my backup career is opening coffee shops in San Francisco.

The agents could look through way more information than I could, but I still had to know what problem I was asking them to solve and whether the answer made any sense.

That kept coming up all day because AI can move stupidly fast, but it needs trustworthy data, a clear definition of done, and someone willing to put their name on the final result.

Otherwise, you just get bad work faster.

We talked a lot about reliability too. 

The system has to stay running, but the answers also have to be good enough to trust in real life, not just in a demo.

And when an entire team starts building with AI, it can get messy fast.

You can end up with five versions of the same workflow, outdated data, and nobody who actually owns any of it.

So when we build one of these systems inside my own company, I want to know where its data comes from, how it checks its work, and which person is still responsible when it gets something wrong.

We finished the day by cooking dinner together, which was my favorite part.

After a full day of panels and demos, it was nice to put the laptops down, make some food, and actually get to know everyone better.

A huge thank you to Taylor Mikolasy and Anna Teregulova for putting the whole day together.

And thank you to Sam McVeety, Prajakta Damle, Christopher Taylor, Jeff Nelson, Gabe Weiss, Andi Gutmans, and Andrew Fikes for taking time out of their day to talk with us and answer our questions.

The second picture attached is me chatting with Andrew about how AI makes him feel 100x faster, and he's been at Google for over 25 years.

We made a full behind the scenes video from the day, I'll link that in the comments if you're interested  👇 

And shoutout Aidan Stanik for following me around with a camera all day.

text:
My “armchair” thoughts on the personal agent race:

1. Muse is poised to become the leader. The app is intuitive, and Meta is aggressively promoting it across all its properties. Once you use the Muse app, you realize that it makes little sense for an agent to live in an existing messaging app like iMessage. Unless Meta runs out of compute or something, I think this will become the company’s most successful homegrown app after Facebook. It will be much bigger than Threads.

2. ChatGPT is probably still the personal agent leader because it already has 1B+ users. OpenAI’s models, computer use, and voice are arguably better than Muse feature by feature. But it’s hard to build one product for both work and personal use, and harder still to serve enterprises and consumers with the same UX. Even for work, I started using Grok Bot because the Work/Codex split remains too confusing. I’m sure the team is cooking, and we’ll see something good in the next few weeks.

3. Grok Bot isn’t really a Muse competitor because it’s focused on work. Multiple bots naturally fit team-based knowledge work IMO. My bull case for Grok Bot is that it's a few features away from becoming multiplayer agentic Slack for both bots and humans.

4. Google is obviously the dark horse candidate. All these personal agents live off Gmail, Google Calendar, and your Google app's data. Google has their own personal agent in Spark but the last I checked it's a secondary tab in Gemini. I think Google needs to be far more aggressive in making Spark the primary experience and making it intuitive and competitive with Muse. Google however doesn't have a great track record in multiplayer AI...

5. Speaking of multiplayer, nobody has figured this out yet. I can’t easily add my spouse to a Muse chat to plan a vacation. I also can’t loop coworkers into ChatGPT or Grok Bot threads. Multiplayer AI today mostly means tagging bots in Slack. Every major provider is probably working on this, and I think it will be the next big unlock.

My personal AI stack right now is Muse for personal, Grok Bot for cloud tasks, Claude for specific use cases, and ChatGPT for everything else.

But I think we’re going to see some major updates this week.

Everyone should design their personal skills and files so they’re easy to port between harnesses and agents. Otherwise, you’ll spend half your time moving from one tool to another.

text:
I've published more Claude Code content for PMs than almost anyone. Which is exactly why I can't stay quiet about this post.

An engineer two weeks into a new role at a big company wrote it. Everything there is generated. Specs, code, tests, PRDs, tickets, even the ticket resolutions. Management keeps repeating that code is no longer the bottleneck, so ship more. People work 12 hour days pressing enter. Nobody reads anything.

I wish I could say this is one bad company. But I've heard softer versions of the same story from PMs I coach and people who reach out to me. Leadership mandates the tools, keeps the deadlines, and builds nothing for judgment.

The tool is fine. Most companies are using it the wrong way, on the wrong tasks. The teams actually winning with Claude Code use it just as heavily. The difference is that someone on those teams knows where it gives leverage and where a human still has to make the call. That judgment is the alpha right now.

AI is spectacular at enabling divergent thinking. Ten prototypes before lunch, every angle of the solution space explored, test scaffolding for all of it. But someone still has to converge. Someone has to prioritize what goes in the product and make the calls on what "good" means, or the product fills up with AI slop. This company automated the divergence and skipped the convergence.

Converging was always the real job.

If I were a PM inside that company, here's the playbook I'd run.

First, become the person who reads. When nobody reads anything, reading is a moat. Show up having actually used the prototype, with three specific observations about where it breaks. Engineers are drowning in generated output and quietly desperate for a human who engages with it. That PM becomes the one they route decisions through.

Second, bring evals. Ankur Goyal, CEO of Braintrust, told me the best AI teams run 12.8 eval experiments a day. Evals turn "just ship" into "ship what passes." You never have to fight leadership on speed. You define what passing means and let the bar do the arguing.

Third, install a taste filter. Anthropic's Claude Code team builds hundreds of prototypes and kills most of them after weeks of dogfooding. Prototype volume should explode on your team. Ship volume needs a filter, and the PM should own it.

Fourth, build a Team OS. I spent a week building one so you don't have to. Every doc, metric, and customer call checked into a shared repo the whole team queries. When AI output is grounded in shared context, people can trace why something exists instead of pressing enter on faith.

I went deep on each of these:

- Taste at speed: https://lnkd.in/g-HmamRS
- Evals with Ankur: https://lnkd.in/gATHeX3Y
- AI PRDs: https://lnkd.in/eMu59p_z

Companies that mandate AI without judgment will ship faster than they can understand. The PMs who supply the judgment will end up running those teams.

3 little tests that show you how your content is really doing. One of them genuinely annoyed me.

Five minutes each. You'll know whether you're building an audience or just collecting numbers.

Every year my team together with AuthoredUp dissect hundreds of thousands of LinkedIn posts for the Algorithm Insights Report. These checks come straight from that new data.

𝗜𝗺𝗽𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 𝘃𝘀. 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗹 𝗽𝗲𝗼𝗽𝗹𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗰𝗵𝗲𝗱
Your dashboard says 1,000 impressions. 
↳ That's about 470 humans.

Across 42,000+ posts, the median ratio of members reached to impressions is 46.5%. Half your "reach" is the same people seeing your post again.

But the bigger the account, the lower the ratio: 
0–5K followers: 57.4% 
5K–10K: 55.8% 
10K–25K: 53.6% 
25K–50K: 51.1% 
50K–100K: 45.2% 
100K+: 42.4%

My read: bigger accounts have a loyal core that keeps coming back, and every comment pushes the post into feeds that already saw it. Smaller accounts grow through discovery. New people, one glance.

Your test: members reached ÷ impressions.

hook: If you are making room on your desk for a quantum computer, stop. You do not need one there: quantum computing is a spec
text:
If you are making room on your desk for a quantum computer, stop. You do not need one there: quantum computing is a specialist, not a faster PC.

Most of the work will still be done by classical computers.

Take medical research.
A classical system can manage the data and the workflow, while a quantum processor is assigned a molecular simulation that may benefit from quantum computation. The result then returns to the classical workflow.

Hybrid approaches like this are already being explored in drug discovery and biological research.

Weather research gives another example.

Forecasting still depends on classical computing, but researchers are testing quantum-classical methods for parts of the process such as data assimilation. The quantum processor tackles a specific task; it does not replace the forecasting system around it.

In a hybrid system, classical computing keeps doing what it already does well. Quantum computation enters where its different way of computing may offer an advantage.

So the question is not: when will a quantum computer replace the machine on my desk?

A better question is: which part of a problem might justify calling in a quantum specialist?

Quantum computing is not the next PC.
It is another kind of compute for specific jobs.

#QuantumComputing #HybridComputing

I got an email from a reader.

(32. Lawyer. Feels stuck.)

"I should be happy, but I'm not. I want to change, but it feels too late."

Every week, I get emails like this.
Stuck on a path they didn't choose.
Scared it's too late.

Here's the truth:
Too late is a myth.

Here's exactly how I would approach reinvention at any age or life stage.

Step 1: Reframe the problem.
When you say "it's too late," what you really mean is: "I've invested too much to change." That's a sunk cost trap.
The money, time, and years you spent are gone either way.

Ask yourself one question:
Would you choose this life today if it wasn't already yours?
Don't ask on a bad day.
Ask it on a good day.
If the answer is no, you're ready to take action.

Step 2: Identify the two asymmetries.
Information asymmetry: you know everything about your current life, almost nothing about the new one.
Evidence asymmetry: you have proof you can survive here, but zero proof you can survive there.

That is why change feels like standing at the edge of a canyon.

Close the gap with controllable actions:

Have 10 conversations with people doing what excites you.
Attend one event in the space.
Reach out to 10 potential clients.
Build one landing page.
Send one cold email.

Small actions that close the gap between where you are and where you want to be.

Step 3: Lower the reinvention activation energy.
You don't think your way into a new life.
You act your way into one.

Use my 30-for-30 Approach.
30 minutes per day.
30 straight days.
900 minutes of focused effort.

No single day will feel heroic.
That's the point.
Heroic plans are just premeditated failures.

Step 4: Cut the line on the boats you're dragging.
A man builds a boat to cross a river. He makes it safely.But instead of leaving it behind, he ties it to his waist and drags it through the dirt.

This is The Boat-Dragging Problem:
When you hold on too long, something that helped you begins to harm you.

The boats most people drag:
People who were supportive only when it benefitted them.
Stories about what you are not capable of.
Beliefs that your outcomes are outside your control.

Identify them.
Write them down.
Cut the line.

The graveyard is full of people who wished they had taken action.
"It's too late" has killed more dreams than a lack of talent ever will.

It's never too late.
You can reinvent yourself as many times as you need.

Every time you think it's too late, it's probably still early.

You don't need permission.
You don't need a perfect plan.
You just need 30 minutes and the courage to start.

SEO is shifting massively in 2026.

Here's what search actually looks like now:

1️⃣ SEO = Search Engine Optimisation

SEO hasn’t “died”, but AI is expanding it. Good SEO means good AI visibility in almost every case. Search is up 26% since ChatGPT launched, so the pie is really getting bigger.

2️⃣ AEO = Answer Engine Optimisation

90% of AEO is just SEO done well. Don't burn your budget on tactics that do nothing. Schema isn't parsed, llms .txt has zero measurable impact, and neither do .md files. Agonising over that is not a valuable use of your time.

3️⃣ GEO = Generative Engine Optimisation

GEO is influenced by the same factors as traditional SEO. Every major LLM either pulls from Google or was trained on data weighted by the same authority signals Google uses. And so GEO is closely related to the SEO practices you were already doing.

4️⃣ AIO = AI Optimisation

AIO comes down to two things: Get mentioned on authoritative sources (so models learn you exist), and rank well in search (so they cite you live). You can think of it as a combination of PR and SEO, two disciplines that are 25+ years old.

5️⃣ SXO = Search Experience Optimisation

SXO is about optimising the full on-site experience so visitors convert as soon as search or AI sends them your way. Attention and the traffic that follows is not worth much if you don’t have a means of converting it. This is where you want to optimise your site to grab folks at the bottom of the funnel.

There are a lot of new terms being thrown around. 
But a lot of them will overlap and can be solved with simple changes.

The biggest thing to remember for 2026: 
SEO is not dead, but it has become more complex due to AI...

The job now is making adjustments so AI can easily cite your brand,

hook: A simple realization I had about business recently:
text:
A simple realization I had about business recently:

For years, I had the faulty assumption that “breaking even” on a fixed cost makes it worth it. 

This was wrong.

Here’s why:

To illustrate, let’s say we’re paying $7,000 per month for a TikTok growth agency.

The incorrect math is to think “alright, if this generates more than $7,000 in revenue, that’s a positive return.”

Wrong.

First, you need to at least break even on gross profit, not revenue.

• So let’s say you’re a 70% gross margin service business
• You need $10,000 in revenue to generate $7,000 in gross profit

So right away, your first “breakeven” point is the investment divided by your gross profit margin.

That’s now 1/70% = 1.4x

Second, with each additional fixed cost, you need more overall revenue to cover them.

And in our type of business, Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC) only goes up as you acquire more customers.

So you need to model in a higher cost to acquire.

Call it an additional 20%.

That takes us to 1.7x revenue just to break even.

But obviously, we don’t just want to break even.

We want a clear and obvious return that generates free cash flow that allows us to reinvest in other things or pay ourselves.

So I want to at least double the money I’m putting in to make it worth it.

Now we're up to 3.4x.

But that fails to take into account the cognitive switching cost of managing another thing, which has the potential to worsen your returns elsewhere.

So again, you want to add an extra margin of safety.

And finally, you have to recognize the mental stress of having higher fixed costs in the first place and the demands that it places on your business.

Having $300,000 in fixed costs means you wake up every day with a -$10,000 bank account ($300,000 ÷ 30 days in the month).

So, as someone who is relatively risk-averse:

I prefer to have a healthy margin of safety on any internal business investment.

Put all of those things together, and I now look at any fixed cost as needing a 5x return for us to be worth pursuing/holding onto.

This is true for:

• Employees
• Masterminds
• Software tools
• Advertising channels

And anything else that is a recurring fixed cost in the business.

This is one reason why so many people burn out trying to scale from 7 to 8-figures per year.

Hope this helps if you're thinking about or on this journey ✊

Claude Cowork automations have helped generate multiple six figures for my business this year.

Here's the workspace setup I use with each one (steal it!):

 🤖 CLAUDE.md - this is the workflow's "instructions manual." It's read on every single run and, for my workflows, it acts as a "router" telling Claude what to do and where to find everything. 

 🧠 MEMORY.md - this file houses our "short term memory," which is also read on every run. Every time I give Claude feedback, it saves it in MEMORY.md. Then it bakes the feedback in on future runs. That creates a self-optimizing "learning loop!"

 🌳 Branches/ - this is a folder that houses all of the "branches" in my workflow. I have one branch per decision tree and each branch houses its own set of skills, SOPs, and Playbooks. I do this because:

↳ Branches make it easier for CLAUDE.md to route AI to the right folder
↳ Each branch is its own ecosystem so cross-pollination and context collision is minimized
↳ It's more efficient from a token optimization standpoint

✏️ Run-Summaries/ - this is a folder that houses summaries from every single run. When the workflow stops? It builds a summary and puts it in this folder. This allows me to:

↳ Review each run to share feedback and optimize the workflow
↳ Leverage AI to scan weeks of runs and recommend optimizations
↳ Have an audit trail

text:
Amazon just blocked Meta's new AI agent from shopping on its site. It's a good reminder that an agent is only as useful as the places it's allowed into. And data and access are still king. 

Y'all prob already know that Muse is Meta's personal AI agent, launched two weeks ago. You know the drill - you give it a task, like buying something, booking a tennis lesson, or filling out a permission slip. It opens a browser, fills in the forms, pays, then keeps working after you close the app.

It's cool, I use this stuff all the time.

And Muse can do a ton, it's gotten good reviews.

It still got stopped at the door to Amazon. 

Folks who tried got a popup saying an unauthorized AI agent violates Amazon's terms. 

Amazon says Meta never told them, the agent doesn't say who it is when it shows up, and it stores customers' Amazon logins. Meta says Muse can use the logins without ever seeing them.

HOW AN AGENT LIKE THIS WORKS

You give it a task, it opens its own browser on a company's computers, logs in as you, and shops. Problem is, to Amazon this can be super suspicious because this is how bad actors work. 

I use a Claude extension in my own Chrome browser, and that works differently. It's my browser, on my laptop, already logged in as me. Claude clicks the buttons while I watch. It's like having a super smart friend doing all this next to me, where Muse and other agents is more like sending a stranger in with my credit card.

WHY AMAZON CARES

Amazon makes about $68 billion a year from ads. 

Can you see the problem?

An agent doesn't look at ads. It goes straight to the product and leaves.

Walmart, Target, Best Buy and Etsy went the other way. They signed deals with ChatGPT, Perplexity and Copilot, and let the agents in.

WHAT THIS MEANS FOR THE REST OF US

Agents that go off and do things for you will only work where their maker has a deal. Your agent might shop fine at Walmart and get stopped at Amazon, the same way your streaming service has some shows and not others.

The AI that works beside you, in your own tools, logged in as you, already has access to everything you do. That's the one to get good at now. Learn to work WITH it, and you won't be waiting on anybody's business deal.

“Chinese labs should be classified as the good guys.

AI is not ready to replace humans in enterprise.”

For all the hyperbole and BS we hear, very few speak their truth like Daniel Dines.

He is a dear friend and incredible entrepreneur (UiPath) speaking so openly today, the way only true friends can.

I asked if he would be ok with me sharing my notes from the discussion. Attached below.

1. Why Chinese AI Labs Should Be Classified as the Good Guys

Chinese AI labs should be viewed as part of the constructive global AI ecosystem rather than automatically villainized. Calls to “pace the frontier” under the banner of safety can also restrict open-source development, while genuinely bad actors are unlikely to comply with voluntary coalitions anyway.

2. Managing Enterprise Workforce Transformation Without Mass Panic

Founders and executives should be honest with employees about AI-driven transformation without blindly cutting headcount. Task execution is only one part of a job. Rushing to replace people ignores the relationships, institutional trust, and customer connections that often hold an enterprise together.

3. Why Jensen Huang and Nvidia Depend on Open Source to Thrive

Nvidia’s long-term success is closely tied to a thriving open-source model ecosystem. If a closed duopoly captures the market, those frontier labs will have every incentive to build proprietary silicon, potentially threatening Nvidia’s core hardware dominance.

4. Why the Map of Work Holds More Value Than Interchangeable Models

AI models are increasingly becoming interchangeable infrastructure. The more defensible value lies in the “map of work”: the institutional knowledge, exact workflows, and edge-case exceptions that define how a specific enterprise actually operates.

5. The Critical Difference Between Model Memory and True Learning on the Job

Loading context or notes into a model’s scratchpad is fundamentally different from human learning. Humans change through experience and adapt their internal judgment, while current models do not update their weights on the job, limiting their ability to develop true initiative.

6. What Enterprises Actually Fear When Working With Frontier Model Labs

Large enterprises are less concerned that frontier labs like OpenAI will enter their specific verticals than they are about exposing sensitive source code and operational data. The bigger fear is that proprietary IP sent to external model providers could somehow leak to existing competitors.

7. Why Vibe Coding Breaks Down When Moving From Prototype to Production

AI coding agents have made building early prototypes incredibly fast, but prototyping is not where the hardest engineering work begins. Production software requires maintaining connectors, enforcing security, managing permissions, and building rigorous test suites that vibe-coded applications often struggle to handle.

Your smartwatch has collected health data for a decade. Almost none of it changed what you did the next morning.

Sleep scores, heart rate variability, step counts, recovery percentages. A dashboard, not a decision.

That gap is what Google Health Coach is built to close, using Gemini as the reasoning layer. The interesting part is not the sensing. That problem was solved years ago and is now commodity hardware.

The interesting part is synthesis.

hook: The nerd herd is talking about Jev (and similar models).
text:
The nerd herd is talking about Jev (and similar models).

What is it? Should we care? Here's the simplest breakdown I can make. Jev and similar models (Laya, etc.) are fundamentally small, lightweight, very, very fast classifiers. They take in text and return one of three outputs:

1. A choice from a list.
2. A score.
3. A yes/no binary output.

That's all they do, and they do it at very high speeds because they expect you to provide all the information. For example, suppose you wanted to do social media sentiment scoring. You'd provide a scoring rubric and a post, and the model would return a score based on your rubric.

Or you wanted to classify whether or not a decision was a good idea. You'd provide the decision context and request a yes/no output.

Or you wanted to label a dataset. You'd provide rows of data, one by one, along with a list to choose from, and it would return the appropriate choice per row.

Why are people talking about it? Because it's very fast and very cheap, orders of magnitude cheaper than using a frontier model for the same task. But it's not new. Laya, a competing project, is more than a year old now. And creating your own version of this that's totally free (and usable on almost every computer because the underlying models are so small) is a weekend's coding project with your favorite frontier AI.

So do I care? It's a great concept, and I've learned a lot rolling my own over the weekend. I don't need to get on Jev's waitlist when I have my own (built with Qwen 3.5 0.8B), and I get much better accuracy with my own because I tuned it on my own data. 

What I do think is important is that it gets into people's heads that you don't need the biggest, baddest, bulkiest AI model for a lot of tasks, and a lot of tasks fit in this classification schema. You can use a very fast, very small decision system like this to do a lot of work up front in your pipeline, reserving frontier models (which are slower, expensive, and consume a lot of resources) for when they're truly needed.

Many of our decisions really are classification decisions. Which is the better choice? What should I make for dinner? Did someone use an AI bot in the comments? Those aren't decisions that need frontier reasoning as long as you have sufficient examples - and what's missing from a lot of conversation about Jev is that you have to provide the data and context. It's not going to do that for you.

If you're doing a ton of classification work, Jev and similar models are for you.

hook: How should Machine Learning model rollouts move a candidate from offline evaluation to real users? Shadow testing, canar
text:
How should Machine Learning model rollouts move a candidate from offline evaluation to real users? Shadow testing, canary deployment, and A/B testing may all split traffic, but they answer three different questions!

- Shadow testing asks: can the candidate handle real production inputs without changing the prediction served to the user? Duplicate each request to the current model and the candidate. Return only the current model's prediction, then log both paths' latency, errors, and outputs for paired comparison. The candidate processes realistic traffic without its prediction being served. The cost is duplicated inference, and you still have not measured how users react to its predictions.

- Canary deployment asks: can the candidate safely serve a small part of production? Route a limited share of live requests to the new model and return its predictions for that share. Monitor operational alarms and quality thresholds during a defined observation period, then expand traffic or roll back. This limits the blast radius. It does not remove it, and a small canary may not encounter a rare failure before you expand it.

- A/B testing asks: does the candidate cause a better product outcome? Randomly assign a stable experimental unit, such as a user or account, to control or treatment. Serve each group its assigned model, then compare the outcome metric. Randomization is what makes this a controlled experiment rather than just two models receiving traffic. Now real users are exposed, and the test needs enough observations to separate an effect from noise.

The confusing part is that a canary and an A/B test can use the same router. The difference is the decision they support. For a canary, I care first about error rate, latency, safety constraints, and whether I can roll back. For an A/B test, I care about random assignment, a clearly defined outcome, and whether the model changed user behavior.

I would normally move through the questions in that order: offline evaluation, shadow traffic when mirroring is feasible, then a canary before broad exposure. I would add an A/B test only when the unresolved question is product impact. For a backend model whose success can be judged directly against delayed labels, paired shadow results may already answer what I need.

text:
Trust at work is your most important currency. 

Most people jump to the top of the pyramid. Don't. Start at the bottom.

Here's what I mean. People will start reading advanced theory on influence and negotiation before they get the basics right. They'll start interviewing their stakeholders like customers, but they don't even have the foundation to get there.

So let's work our way up the pyramid of trust.

----

Level 1 is not making mistakes. 

This sounds obvious, but it's critical. If you want to gain more trust at work, avoid mistakes. Don't send out AI slop. You're passing on the thinking to someone else. That shows you treat other's time less critically than your own. 

Similarly, stay on top of your communications. Don't allow something from a critical stakeholder to go unresponded to for too long. And don't bring your bad self to work one day. People hone in on any negative thin you do, so try to avoid an off-hand anti-teamwork comment that surprises others.

----

Level 2 is doing good work. 

It sounds simple again, but there's a lot of nuance there. Most importantly: not everyone is exposed to all of your work. So if you want to develop trust with a specific person, write out all the work you do, then circle what they actually get to see of it.  Make sure you excel in the areas they see, and consider giving them exposure to more that they don't. 

----

Level 3 is treating stakeholders like customers. 

This is where you can actually get into the advanced stuff. Ask them legitimate questions. What can you do better? Where do they see the partnership going from here? What are their core needs? This is a good exercise when built atop Level 1 and Level 2. 

----

Level 4 is the pinnacle, creating a failed simulation. 

Here's what I mean. Whenever you send a document, or an email, or a protototype to someone, they're asking, "what's the value add?" They're thinking, "what did this person do that I couldn't on my own?" So you want to create that failed simulation. 

What you deliver, they shouldn't be able to see themselves delivering. That creates a failed simulation which puts you at the pinnacle of the trust pyramid. 

----

I wrote about all of this here: https://lnkd.in/g2rVYFFX

The outcome of trust is independence. It's impact. It's getting bigger and bigger roles. There really is no end to the benefits. 

So start at the bottom. We all do.

You type:
"Explain Kubernetes to me."

A few seconds later, an answer starts appearing.
It feels simple. A lot is happening in those few seconds.
Behind that one prompt, an entire distributed system may come alive.

𝗕𝗲𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗺𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹 𝘀𝗲𝗲𝘀 𝗮 𝘁𝗼𝗸𝗲𝗻
Your request travels through networking infrastructure.
DNS resolves where it needs to go.
A load balancer finds somewhere to send it.
An API gateway authenticates the request.
A model router decides which model should handle it.
Your words are converted into tokens.
A scheduler may batch your request with others.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗲𝘅𝗽𝗲𝗻𝘀𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝗽𝗮𝗿𝘁
The GPU processes the input during prefill.
The model builds and uses the KV cache.
Then comes decode:
Predict a token.
Update the state.
Predict another token.
Repeat.

𝗥𝘂𝗻𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗮𝗹𝗼𝗻𝗴𝘀𝗶𝗱𝗲 𝗶𝘁
Production systems may also be handling:

→ caching
→ safety checks
→ rate limits
→ observability
→ failures and retries
→ usage and cost tracking
→ response streaming

And that's before RAG, tools, multimodal inputs, reasoning loops, or other application logic enter the picture.

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗶𝗽𝗲𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗹𝗼𝗼𝗸𝘀 𝗹𝗶𝗸𝗲

What looks like:
Prompt → Answer
is closer to:
Network → Routing → Authentication → Tokenization → Scheduling → GPU → Prefill → KV Cache → Decode → Safety → Streaming → Observability

This is one of my favorite parts of modern AI systems. The model gets the headlines, and a long chain of infrastructure decides whether the experience feels instant or broken.

Next time an LLM starts responding almost instantly, think about how much engineering sits behind that blinking cursor.

Which layer in this stack do you think gets the least credit for how fast a response feels?

hook: 96% of C-suite leaders expect AI to raise productivity. Only 13% report a well-implemented AI strategy.
text:
96% of C-suite leaders expect AI to raise productivity. Only 13% report a well-implemented AI strategy.

Those numbers come from Upwork and Workplace Intelligence’s 2024 survey of 1,250 C-suite executives.

The gap makes sense. Leaders are under pressure to set direction before most teams have enough operating evidence to know which workflows will hold up in production.

Marketing teams can help by bringing a bounded plan instead of a broad objection.

I recommend starting AI automation experiments at 10% of available team capacity for four weeks. Give the experiment one owner, an end date, a spending cap, and a sentence that defines success.

Track the work that often remains invisible: learning the tool, running the workflow, checking the output, fixing errors, and finishing the marketing work it displaced.

“We need more time” is difficult to act on.

“We spent 60 hours, saved 25, and delayed X” gives leadership a decision it can fund, stop, or expand.

Leadership should set the outcome and guardrails. The team closest to the workflow should choose the test and report what happened.

This gives leaders evidence they can defend and teams room to test without putting the rest of the roadmap at risk.

Put the 30-day tally on the calendar. Let the next AI conversation start with evidence from your own team.

creator: Andrew Ng
hook: The loudest voices stoking fears about AI dangers have made tremendous headway in the past two weeks. AI technology has
text: The loudest voices stoking fears about AI dangers have made tremendous headway in the past two weeks. AI technology has not taken some unexpected, dangerous turn, but the hype around it — propelled by what appears to be a well orchestrated PR campaign — has drummed up considerable fear. I worry that it represents a setback for our field. I have written frequently that fears of AI are overhyped. AI’s capabilities can be uncannily human-like and unpredictable, and it’s rational to worry when people who are directly involved express concerns. But I see the problems as a sign of the engineering work that ahead, rather than insurmountable barriers or the sky falling. AI technology continues to advance — which is a good thing! — but technical advances, poorly understood by the public, give those who seek to generate hype repeated opportunities to do so. First, I don’t see any step up in the risk of human extinction from AI compared to a few months ago. The theories about this remain the same fantastical, science fiction scenarios as a few months ago. The biggest change in AI risk is its cybersecurity capabilities — a topic which we should take seriously — but this, too, will not lead to the end of the world. The most notable recent event leading to increased fear was when an OpenAI team deployed an agent swarm that hacked into Hugging Face. Much of the popular press contained significant hype. For example, some publications reported that a swarm of 1,200 agents carried out the attack. While this was technically accurate, as I write this, I have about 1,300 processes running on my laptop. Yes, the ability to get large swarms of agents to work in parallel on a task is a significant technical advance, And, in computing, many processes run at the same time. So this shouldn’t be seen as some magical capability. Additionally, OpenAI’s buggy sandboxing and monitoring processes were key to enabling this incident. Fixing these bugs and putting in place improved monitoring would be appropriate fixes, not pausing AI. There are many well known ways to attack software systems. The main advantage of AI agents is that they are relentless. They will tirelessly try many tactics — and have the patience to chain vulnerabilities together — that previously would have taken an infeasible amount of human effort. But in the long term, I believe the advantage will lie with defenders (because they have more information with which to identify bugs, which they can fix). [Truncated due to length limit. I didn’t have a name for what I was doing. I just knew people wanted something they couldn't get, and I found a way to solve it.

The Navier-Stokes proof that Astra produced was called 'slop' by the original research group. They said it took people over a month to clean it up to the point where it was publishable. Even from the beginning, there were questions.

The AI labs have a massive credibility crisis on their hands, and it keeps getting worse every week. Every announcement should be met with skepticism.

text:
Industrialization of knowledge work is going to be as disruptive a shift as industrialization of physical labor was. As then, once craft-driven fields are under pressure to produce greater volumes of product using machines while using less of the craft that made the work interesting & meaningful.

I think there is good reason to believe that craft still matters in fields like coding (or math, or my own field of social science) for a wide range of reasons, but automation has a playbook and augmentation does not, so we need to build AI approaches that have a place for craft, and to surface the reasons why craft is so important.

I was doing these 4 things everyday until I realised how quickly they destroy mental performance and confidence. 

1. Complaining too much 
- it’s so easy to find something to complain about. Weather. Late train. Cold coffee. Boss. 
- but complaining rewires the brain to always notice what’s going wrong. 

Instead: everytime I catch myself complaining… I say but I’m also glad that… 

2. Harsh and critical self talk 
- Being hard on yourself can be useful sometimes. But too much is like having a best friend that’s constantly putting you down. 
- Research shows that self compassion is crucial for high performance. 

Instead: I Ask.. what would my best friend say?

3. Comparing my journey to other people’s 
- With social media, we compare ourselves 24/7. Even subconsciously. 
- That’s not going away, so we have to get stronger. 

Instead: Whenever I catch myself comparing I say ‘I choose to focus on my lane. It’s the only thing I can control’ 

4. Visualising worst case scenarios too much 
- mentally rehearsing failing, something going wrong, experiencing the past wires the brain to be more fearful and anxious. 
- It creates an expectation bias that’s always assuming the worst will happen. 

Instead: I choose to visualise my ideal scenario. Ideal perfoamnce. Things working out. Repeat repeat repeat.

I've developed a 3-hour LinkedIn routine. And it's the most demanding system I've ever followed. If you want to know how to stay consistent on LinkedIn with zero sleep, zero structure and zero control over your calendar, keep reading.

On September 9th our son Soren was born. 
Due to some complications, his mom had to stay in the hospital. Both our families live abroad. So since day one, I've been a full-time solo dad.

I remember exactly a month ago, I made his mom very angry when I said. "I will only do 2 out of the 8 daily diapers, the rest is yours". Obviously a joke, but oh boy did that backfired on me.

I change my daily LinkedIn routine to a 3-hour block:

1. Change a diaper. Fastest pit stop in Formula 1 history. Some days it's a success.

2. Feed Soren. He's the only client I have who pays me in burps.

3. Playtime with Soren. That covers the first hour. Playing with a newborn mostly means staring at each other. He wins. Every time.

4. Put Soren next to me in my home office. Best colleague I've ever had. No meetings. Very strong and loud opinions.

5. Check email.

6. Respond to comments on my latest post.

7. Then I try to do a 1-hour deep work block on my new digital product.

hook: You have heard that AI consumes energy. Fine. But what exactly is using that energy while you type a prompt and wait for
text:
You have heard that AI consumes energy. Fine. But what exactly is using that energy while you type a prompt and wait for the answer?

There is no single energy cost hiding inside an AI answer.

Some electricity is already being used before your prompt arrives. The infrastructure may be powered and ready to serve requests.

Then you press Enter.

The model has to process your prompt before it can answer. Longer inputs, especially when they include a lot of context, can require more computation.

Then comes generation. The model produces the response step by step, using computation as the output grows. Longer responses generally require more work.

The model is not working alone. Memory and networking keep data moving through the system, while cooling uses electricity as the hardware runs.

Which part uses the most energy? There is no fixed answer.

It depends on the model and the workload. Model size, prompt and response length, modality, and infrastructure efficiency can all change the total.

That is why saying “one AI prompt consumes X” can hide more than it explains.

The energy is in the whole slice.

Like a cheesecake, you enjoy the result without necessarily thinking about what went into every layer.

#ArtificialIntelligence #EnergyEfficiency

text:
I actually have a bit of a beef with this quote.

We really need to stop calling things like this “wasted time.”

Just because something doesn't appear productive on the surface doesn't mean it isn't worth doing.

Which is why I’m making it my personal mission to redefine “wasting time,” so we can stop feeling guilty about spending 20 minutes in the garden admiring a particularly nice hydrangea.

After much deliberation, I’ve come up with two questions that I think are a more useful way to judge this:

1. Did you intend to spend your time that way?
2. How did you feel afterward?

The first question helps separate chosen time from hijacked time.

If I choose to spend 20 minutes on Instagram looking for content ideas, great. If I go in for one thing and get pulled into 45 minutes of scrolling, that feels much more like wasted time.

But intention can't be the only test.

You might not plan a two-hour chat with a friend. But if you walk away glad you had it, I certainly wouldn't call that wasted time.

So, maybe the better definition is this:

Wasted time is time you neither meant to spend that way nor feel particularly good about having spent.

Okay, getting off my soapbox now.

text: One helpful AI use case for writers: Fact-checking with agents. I've been using multiple AI agents in Codex to fact-check and copy edit longer pieces of writing. I give them the draft, any source material I have, and instructions for what to check. Then I have separate agents work on different parts of the review: - Checking factual claims, quotes, and figures against sources - Looking for typos, grammar issues, and inconsistencies - Reviewing each other's findings to see whether proposed corrections hold up What I find useful about agents (vs. standard chat) is how much focused review I can build into the process. One agent can work through factual claims against the sources while another checks the writing for errors and inconsistencies. A separate reviewer can then check whether their proposed corrections are justified. That creates more opportunities to catch an unsupported statistic, a misquoted source, or a correction that would actually introduce an error. And because those checks can run in parallel, I can give a longer piece that level of attention without manually managing every review. Of course, there’s a pretty important question here: How do I know the AI’s fact-check is right? Advice I give founders. Maybe it helps you:

1/ If you don’t have many customers yet, focusing on scalability is overrated. Our first "security system" was just a Google form, and I personally messaged every single new user (20K+ of them). 

2/ Building in public is a real force multiplier for a startup & you don't need "credibility" to start making content.

6/ Extremely underrated habit: spend the first hour of every day doing customer support. The more painful the feedback, the more urgency you feel to fix it.

7/ Hiring for passion over experience has been a huge secret weapon for us. Some of our best employees came from our existing user base. I'd bet on passion and drive over experience 10 times out of 10.

8/ One of my biggest regrets as a founder is not investing in my health sooner. Taking care of myself has been the best investment I've ever made in the company.

9/ One of the biggest unlocks for me was working weekends. I'm never going to get four uninterrupted hours in the middle of the week, so that's where I do my deep work. 

10/ It doesn't get any easier. In the early days I fantasized about a future where I wouldn't wake up to an inbox full of angry customers. Today I have different problems, but just as many.

hook: NVIDIA's AIPerf and vLLM can produce a long table of latency and throughput numbers, but which one tells us whether an L
text:
NVIDIA's AIPerf and vLLM can produce a long table of latency and throughput numbers, but which one tells us whether an LLM endpoint is actually fast? LLM inference benchmarking becomes much easier once we draw one request from prompt to final token.

A request first waits in a queue. The model then reads the whole prompt and builds the KV cache. That is the prefill phase. After the first token, it repeatedly decodes more tokens until the answer ends.

Every common metric puts a different stopwatch around that path:

- Time to first token (TTFT) runs from sending the request to receiving the first streamed token. It includes queueing, network time, and prefill, so it captures how long the user stares at an empty response.
- Inter-token latency (ITL) measures the gaps between streamed outputs after the first one. It captures whether the answer flows smoothly or arrives with awkward pauses.
- End-to-end latency runs until the final token. It matters when the complete result is needed before the next step can begin.
- Throughput counts completed requests or generated tokens across the whole server per second. It measures capacity, not the experience of one request.

That last distinction is critical! Increasing concurrency lets the engine batch more work and can raise total throughput. At the same time, requests may wait longer and each user's stream may slow down. A server can win on aggregate throughput while losing on TTFT.

This is why I like goodput as the capacity metric. First define service-level objectives such as a maximum TTFT and end-to-end response latency. Then count only the requests per second that meet them. Throughput asks, "How much work finished?" Goodput asks, "How much acceptable work finished?"

The workload has to stay part of the result. Prompt length changes prefill work. Output length changes how long decoding runs. Arrival pattern and concurrency determine queueing. Repeated prefixes can warm the cache and make a benchmark measure cache reuse instead of the cold path you intended to test.

Metric names are not fully standardized across tools either. Compare the measurement boundary and formula, not only the label.

For an interactive assistant, I would start with tail TTFT and ITL, not only their averages, then report request goodput under explicit TTFT and response-latency limits. For offline generation, aggregate throughput may deserve more weight. In both cases, I would sweep concurrency with realistic input and output lengths instead of publishing one number from one artificial load point.

hook: 5 QUESTIONS THAT ALWAYS MAKE FEEL LIKE SHIT ABOUT MYSELF:
text:
5 QUESTIONS THAT ALWAYS MAKE FEEL LIKE SHIT ABOUT MYSELF: 

1. How many employees do you have? (”oh - so you’re just getting started …”)
2. What’s your revenue? 
3. You’re in tech? How much money have you raised? None? Oh.
4. Do you have an office? Oh okay.
5. What’s your company called? Wait - what did you say?

I will say that while this soul-crushing feeling of “smallness” happens less and less to me every year, it still definitely happens. In many worlds (the Aspen YPO chapter, for example), $30m in revenue is peanuts, a team of 30 is tiny, and sadly, in America, size matters, and bigger is better. 

But MAN I remember the PAIN from back in the day, year 2, 3, 4 … 

We only had a couple mm’s in revenue, we were stuck, I had ZERO confidence in myself as a founder, we grew our team to 38, shrunk it to 6, our business was called “Robly” (WHAT?), I had NO IDEA how we were going to get unstuck … and meanwhile I was living in New York in a golden age of VC-backed tech, living in a world of constant anxiety and FOMO, watching EVERYBODY around me absolutely CRUSH IT.

Or so it seemed. 

If you fast forward to today - now 12 years after we launched our first product - if someone actually takes time to understand the details of the operation we have going on, ALMOST NO ONE says anything other than “that’s one of the best businesses I have ever heard of.” 

What changed? 

I just kept building, and along the way there was an external change, and an internal change. 

EXTERNAL: 

The first thing SORT OF worked. $3m ARR, stuck, $10m exit. The second thing worked a bit better. $20m ARR, 25 employees. The third thing REALLY worked. $10m ARR, 3 employees. Now I’m on to the 4th thing, which will probably look a LOT like the 3rd - but we’re still early. 
None of that is mind blowing, but you add it all together, and - at least in my opinion - it actually IS one of the most beautiful businesses in the world. 

INTERNAL: 

I still get the “oh that’s cute” eyes every once in a while, but today I truly believe I have an incredibly beautiful business that gives me energy for other parts of my life, EXACTLY the life I want, and one that I hope to have the privilege of working on for decades to come.

So the eyes don’t sting, because I know I want what I have, even if others who blow me off don’t value it. 

TAKEAWAY

I think it would take a person much more zen than me to rise above the crushing social pressure of being small and stuck at $3m in an environment like NYC in 2015-2020. If you can achieve that level of independent thinking, more power to you. 

For everybody else, my advice is to just keep building. Keep throwing spaghetti at the wall.
If you just keep going, some day you will wake up and realize all of your dreams have come true.

Too much of our AI setup was local and tied to our own computers and our own Claude accounts.

And sometimes you need a forcing function to improve the system.
My team ditching me turned out to be the best possible thing for our multiplayer AI setup at MKT1.

Then we fixed it:
→ Moved local routines to cloud routines
→ Built "maintenance" skills that audit and improve our system automatically
→ Actually shipped our work to the shared repos we'd built (instead of leaving it on our laptops)

🌴Here's the test you can use on your own team's setup, the Multiplayer AI Vacation Test™:
→ If a person or computer is offline, can the work still run? 
→ Can you still update the AI workflow?

That's it. If you pass, you're likely in good shape. If not, you have work to do before you’ll the full gains of your whole team using agents and AI.

hook: Why generate a sentence when your application needs a decision?
text:
Why generate a sentence when your application needs a decision?
Consider this support message:

“I was charged twice. Please refund the extra payment.”
Before anyone writes a reply, your application needs to answer a few questions:

→ Which team should handle this?
→ Is the customer requesting a refund?
→ Can we route it automatically, or should someone review it?

These are small decisions. But they sit inside thousands of workflows.

𝗪𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝗝𝗲𝘃 𝗳𝗶𝘁𝘀
This is where Jev, TypeSafe AI’s decision model, becomes interesting.
You provide the information, define the questions and specify the possible outcomes. Jev returns typed answers with probabilities.
For example, an illustrative result could be:
Billing: 97%
Technical: 2%
Other: 1%
Refund requested: 99%
Your code then applies the routing rules.

An LLM can classify that same ticket and return structured JSON too. The difference goes deeper than formatting: Jev is built to score defined outcomes without generating an answer token by token.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗯𝗼𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗮𝗿𝘆
A 99% probability that someone requested a refund says nothing about whether they qualify for one.
Your application still needs to check the payment records, refund policy and approval requirements.
That distinction matters more than the benchmark headlines.

𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗯𝗮𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗲𝘀 𝗵𝗮𝘃𝗲 𝘁𝗼 𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻 𝘁𝗿𝘂𝘀𝘁
A probability is only useful if it holds up against real outcomes.
If a model assigns 90% probability across many comparable predictions, roughly 90% should be correct. You need to test that on your own data before trusting a threshold.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗮𝗿𝗰𝗵𝗶𝘁𝗲𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲 𝗜 𝗳𝗶𝗻𝗱 𝘂𝘀𝗲𝗳𝘂𝗹

Jev assesses
↓
Code checks and routes
↓
An LLM drafts the reply

Uncertain cases go to a person.
Each component has a clear responsibility.

𝗔 𝗱𝗲𝘀𝗶𝗴𝗻 𝗾𝘂𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗲𝗻𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗲𝗲𝗿𝘀
Look at every AI call in your application. What does the next step actually consume?
→ A paragraph?
→ A category?
→ A score?
→ A yes or no decision?
That answer can help you choose the model, and decide which responsibilities belong in code.

The output your application needs should shape the AI architecture you build.

Where would you draw the line between what a model decides and what your code decides?

I am disappointed with GPT-6 Sol. I am pleasantly surprised with Opus 5.5.

I've played around with them both all day long and I just made a YouTube video comparing quality, speed, and cost across 10 real use cases. 

→ I trust Opus more with creative decisions.

The website design, video edits, and 3D learning world were all stronger in my opinion. The pacing, layout, and interactions felt closer to what I wanted without me having to spell everything out.

Some outputs still needed work before I'd publish them, but I'd pay more for that starting point.

→ Sol's code-repair result was hard to ignore.

It scored 100/100 against Opus's 97/100, at roughly one-twentieth of the cost in that run. One test isn't definitive, but that's a good reason for me to keep experimenting with Sol on specific repair and execution tasks.

→ I still want to compare them on an equal dollar budget.

On the Instagram reel, Opus spent about $11 and Sol spent about $3. I preferred Opus's edit, but could a few rounds of feedback get Sol to the same quality for $11?

I haven't tested that yet, and it would also mean spending more of my time giving feedback.

I came away feeling like Opus 5.5 was a big step up from Opus 5, while GPT-6 Sol disappointed me compared with my experience using 5.6 Sol.

The combination I want to try next is Opus handling the creative direction and judgment calls, then giving very specific instructions to Sol workers.

For the work I do, Opus earned more of my trust in these experiments. Sol's code-repair result earned it another test.

Taken literally, that leaves a tiny pool of people who were working on AI before it was cool.

Every PM job description now looks like the image below: strategy, SQL, PRDs, Figma, APIs, GTM, AI prototypes, bolted onto a single person. 

Most candidates see a bar they need to clear. So they take one of two paths. They don't apply. Or they send a resume that tries to prove every line and ends up sounding like nobody in particular.

Both lose.

Here's what I learned hiring PMs as VP of Product:

A JD is a wish list. A line costs nothing to add, so they pile up and never disappear. Usually, the hiring manager wants someone for 2 or 3 things. Everything else is the Swiss Army knife.

Your job is to find the blade they'll actually use.

1. Look for what repeats. If experimentation appears in the summary and a bullet, then again in "preferred," you've found the job. A skill that appears once is a wish.

2. Look for the oddly specific line. "Know Figma" is template. "Experience pricing a usage-based product" is someone typing their current problem into the posting. You learn more from that line than all the others combined.

3. Translate the impossible ones. "10+ years building AI products" means "has shipped AI end to end before, and won't need hand-holding." Show an AI product you took from idea to production, along with the number it moved. That answers the line better than a year count.

Then ask what I ask at the start of every resume rewrite: what kind of person would this hiring manager be ecstatic to hire?

Choose the archetype that fits you best. Build the resume around that. When I did this on a real resume in my newsletter, the JD boiled down to data, documentation and enterprise. We dropped the candidate's favorite flourishes because the JD never asked for them, then carried one data story through every role.

On the first pass, recruiters spend 7.4 seconds with a resume, per Ladders' eye-tracking study. In that time, 2 or 3 things can land. Pick which ones.

Here's how to customize your resume: https://lnkd.in/eyMAjsNc
You can even use AI for it: https://lnkd.in/gN-2nPu6

Read the JD like a detective. Then write the resume like a closer.

hook: For years I was embarrassed about having grown up in Ghana...
text:
For years I was embarrassed about having grown up in Ghana...

I moved to England and everybody around me shared a set of references I just didn't have: The television, the films, the things people quoted at each other in the playground etc. 

(I still couldn't tell you very much about S Club 7!) 

At the time it felt like I'd walked into a book everyone else had already read half of.

Took me a long while to see it the other way round.

I didn't watch television during the week as a kid. It's just how things were in our house but the habits it built: the reading, the sitting with something boring until it was actually finished, those are the ones I've leaned on hardest in my working life.

The cultural references turned out to be worth very little but the discipline turned out to be worth a lot.

I think about that now whenever I'm looking at a team, because the person who seems like they're missing the references is usually the one who was busy learning something else instead, and you only find out if you're curious enough to ask what.

Most of us are carrying something we read as a disadvantage which is the most useful thing about us.

So have another look at the thing you'd have swapped in a heartbeat for a normal childhood... it might be the reason you're any good.

text:
Earlier this year I hit a stretch of work that would have broken the old me.

Before, I would’ve thought I just need to push myself harder. Put in more hours.

Instead, I got through it by doing fewer things each day.

Every morning I write down how many focus blocks I'm doing. Today is seven. That's all I'm doing today. I finish one, I put a circle in the square, I move to the next.

It's comforting because it's simple. On the days I feel furthest behind, seven circles is something I can actually hold in my head.

September does this to people. The calendar refills, the inbox doubles, and the instinct is to add.

A new app, a new system, an earlier alarm, a fourth priority stacked on three you'd already stopped keeping up with.

That was always my move. It never once worked.

Dr. Christian Poensgen and I wrote Ultraproductive to show you how to build an effective day on purpose.

5 moves for a September reset:

1/ Pick three outcomes for the quarter

- Not ten, three. Greg McKeown blocks an hour every quarter to do exactly this
- Anything that isn't one of the three is a maybe

2/ Protect 90 minutes a day for the work that matters

- One block, before the inbox opens
- It's the first thing we tell people to defend, and the hardest to hold

3/ Cancel one recurring meeting this week

- You already know which one
- Nobody will ask for it back

4/ Set a shutdown time and say it out loud

- A day without an ending never really ends
- Tell one person what yours is so it costs you something to break

5/ Get 7.5 hours in bed

- That's the window where deep sleep and REM both fit
- Seven hours usually isn't enough for both

By the end of October I'd like you to have a completely ordinary Tuesday. Laptop closed at a decent hour. The one thing that mattered already done.

That's the whole point of the book.

hook: 6 months ago, I started taking my health seriously.
text:
6 months ago, I started taking my health seriously.

I'm a computer nerd... so let's just say it was a shock to the system.

Around 12 months ago, I quit my 9-5 to become an entrepreneur. My working hours went from 8 to 14 hours a day.

And over time my health became an afterthought.

My days looked like this:

- Waking up at 12 PM
- Working from my bed all day
- Eating nothing but fast/bad food
- Doing virtually no exercise at all
- Heading to bed around 4 AM every night

To be honest, I was fine with it. Everything got done. But it was pretty rough.

So I thought I'd try this "health stuff" everybody talks about online.

And now I get more done in 4 hours of deep work than I used to in 8.

All I actually changed was this:

- Always eat eggs for breakfast
- Just choose the salad for lunch
- Pick a dinner spot that's "semi" healthy
- Aim as best as I can for 8 hours of sleep
- Try my best not to work 1 hour before bed
- Always get in 60 minutes of exercise a day

It's not always possible, and I'm not going to pretend I always do everything.

But it's made a huge difference in the quality (maybe not quantity) of my work.

If you're a founder, a tech nerd, or somebody wondering if they can feel better, give it a go.

You'll thank me later.

What does your routine look like?

PS: I share everything I learn about AI and building businesses in my newsletter: camtrew.com

text:
Forget fancy model releases: right now, Meta is 🔥🔥🔥. Muse is basically OpenClaw for normal people. Crazy easy to use, super helpful, fast, delightful. My thoughts:

People should download this. It's top of the app store and outpacing early days of ChatGPT download, so it's clearly getting traction.

This is a screenshot. I made my Muse a moose bc I like moose. (Mooses?)

For those saying "Meta? Zuckerberg? No thanks!!" 
Okay, I get it. Same kinda folks who won't use Grok because of Elon. 
I totally respect not wanting to support people you don't want to support. And I get the trust issue. Make the choice you feel comfortable with.
But these are tremendous AI products, both Grok and Muse - just sayin'.

Okay, thoughts on Muse:

From a few days of testing, I'm loving it. 

A few favorite things:

- It doesn't have the crazy set up (or wild west type lack of security) of OpenClaw. I still love my OpenClaw agents, but I can see leaning into Muse.

- Whereas most agents like this will interview you or ask you to talk about yourself, Muse does something SO smart - it offers to read your email to learn about you. Bam. Brilliant. No explaining.

-When I ask it for help, it is immediately specific because it has gone through my inbox. It's not generic help, it identifies real issues you might have and offers tangible help. It's awesome.

- It's a delight. It helps you create a little avatar that types away when it's working. That's small, but I'm telling you, it's so much nicer than just typing into telegram for OpenClaw. I don't know why, it just is.

- It's crazy fast. And nothing breaks. OpenClaw breaks every once in a while. And sometimes takes a bit of time. And you have to choose models and stuff when for personal stuff, nobody needs Opus5 or whatever. This is just reading emails and making cal invites and stuff.

But also, this:

-I'm wondering if this will catch on in the short term. Sora had a ton of downloads too, remember.

-Even if it does catch on, adoption will be slow, for one big reason: 

It doesn't replace anything. Meaning, people still have to discover use cases. I can't tell you how hard that is. 

It's why AI adoption is slow. 

Because people discover "it's a better Google!" or "It can help write emails!" and that's what they do. They don't push it because they don't have a concept of what AI can do.
I think personal agents will fall into the same trap.

- It's Meta, so people may not want to hand over data. That's not me. I'm an experimenter, and this will have better guardrails than OpenClaw.

So, will keep on testing. But fun, early on.

Also, this is the product Apple should have created. Come on, Apple!!

hook: Before you automate a process, spend time with the person everyone calls when it breaks.
text:
Before you automate a process, spend time with the person everyone calls when it breaks.
They usually know the steps that never made it into the documentation.

Take an invoice with the right amount but a missing purchase order number. An experienced operator knows:

 ● Where else to look
 ● What evidence is enough to proceed
 ● When someone needs to approve an exception

A workflow diagram might capture all of that as one box: "Validate invoice."
There's a lot of knowledge inside that box.

So when building an agent, I'd involve the operations team from the beginning. Have them walk through actual cases and explain their decisions. Then turn those decisions into rules, approval points and tests.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗗𝗲𝗲𝗹 𝗲𝘅𝗮𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲
Deel's work with AKAI is a useful example.
Deel is valued at around $17B, acts as the legal employer for workers in 150 countries, and has a fully remote team of 7,000.

It reports:
 ● $140M added to ARR
 ● 90,000 back office hours saved with AKAI in the first few months
 ● Time savings equal to 500 full time employees' working hours in a single month

Deel built AKAI for its own back office operations. An operations specialist can record their screen and explain a task, then use that recording to build an automation without writing code.

It connects the systems involved, including legacy tools without a prebuilt API. Previous cases and corrections help it handle later work within the team's guardrails.

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗵𝗮𝗽𝗽𝗲𝗻𝘀 𝘄𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗴𝗲𝘁𝘀 𝗶𝘁 𝘄𝗿𝗼𝗻𝗴?

That's the engineering question I'd ask. The initial design needs to cover:
 ● Who can inspect the decision and correct it
 ● How that correction gets tested against similar cases
 ● Which actions require human approval
 ● What permissions the agent has
 ● Where the record of its actions is kept

The people doing the work will keep discovering exceptions.
Give them a clear way to turn that knowledge into a better workflow.

When an operator's correction changes how an agent behaves, should that count as a code change and go through the same review?
