text:
If Anthropic disappeared tomorrow, my entire AI system would still be on my laptop.
 
Because I build and run everything locally (here's why you should too):

Building "locally" means your AI systems live in folders on your computer.

Those folders include all of your instructions, skills, context, outputs, etc.

Then you just point your AI to the folder and let it go to work!

The alternative is housing everything in your AI company's cloud.

Here are 7 benefits to doing things locally:

Benefit #1: You Own Your Files & Workflows

In Anthropic disappeared tomorrow? All of my AI systems would survive untouched on my laptop.

Same if the price doubled, a model got nerfed into oblivion, or a critical feature got removed.

The AI (Claude in my case) runs my workflows, but the files are all mine.

I can keep building on them no matter what happens to any one AI company.

Benefit #2: You Can Leave / Switch Any Time

You might use Claude but OpenAI just dropped GPT-6 Astra and everyone's raving about it.

You want to switch, but Claude knows everything about you and ChatGPT doesn't so you feel stuck.

Building locally fixes that! When your context lives on your machine, you can switch tools at any time.

Just unplug from one and plug the new one into your local system. 

Benefit #3: Easy Editing & Access

Want to change how a workflow runs or edit a playbook?

All you have to do is open the markdown file and make the edit.

No asking your AI to update it and hoping it listens, no digging through screens, no re-explaining yourself.

All of my AI systems are built in plain text docs I can edit any time.

Benefit #4: Tighter Access & Security

I choose what folders AI can access.

If a file isn't in that folder? AI can't access it.

I have full control over what AI sees and what it can impact. That means I sleep well with no worries about a rogue AI in my system.

Benefit #5: Full Transparency

I can see exactly what the AI has access to, what it edited, etc.

I don't need to ask the AI to show me files or changes, I can go open the files and read them for myself.

My judgement stays in the loop and I don't have to blindly trust my AI's word.

Benefit #6: Works Across Multiple Tools

It's not just great for switching tools, local folders can be plugged into many tools!

You can open the same files in Claude Code, Google Drive, and Obsidian.

Edits in one place automatically map across the other tools plugged into that folder.

Nothing gets trapped inside one app, one company, etc.

Benefit #7: Backups & Version History

You've probably read some story about AI deleting files or a codebase.

If that was in the cloud? You're cooked.

But I can back up my local AI systems.

So if my AI deleted everything? It's all good, I can restore it in 5 minutes.

text:
Nearly all marketing leaders I talk with have been asked to reduce the size of their team. Do more with less. But the data shows they are doing something different and changing their team's shape instead.

Let’s talk about marketing shape vs. shrink.

Gartner’s 2026 CMO survey says 39% of CMOs plan to cut labor and agency costs. The same survey showed companies are spending more on marketing headcount (21.9% to 24.5% of their budget) and less on marketing tools, which fell to 19.4%, a five-year low.

It’s not the size of the marketing team that’s changing; it’s shape. Three core changes:

1. The 0-1 marketer: We built marketing teams out of specialists because humans can only hold so much context. AI removes that limit. I'm now seeing super generalists build a personal AI stack (Context, Connections, Skills, Artifacts) and take an idea from nothing to a shipped v1 on their own. Research, positioning, page, campaign, analysis. Way more productive.

2. Depth of craft matters more than ever: Sounds counter to the first point, but because of the above, standing out is harder. You’ll still need people with true depth of craft. Positioning is an art. Design is an art. Brand is an art. My take is these people will be in more demand than ever. Authenticity is a winning formula.

3. Pods, not trees: The first org chart was drawn in 1855 to run a railway, because moving information was so hard. It was shaped like a tree. Most functions still use it, including marketing. That doesn’t scale for an AI-native team. Information moves through shared context in seconds so that shape can change often. Small pods that include 0-1 marketers and craft experts, with a clear outcome, one owner, and weekly shipping, work better.

The best marketing teams will change shape, not shrink.

P.S. I did a full breakdown in my Substack, along with a starter kit to move your team in this direction.

hook: Use AI at the peak of the previous best.
text:
Use AI at the peak of the previous best.

If you want to get the most benefit out of AI without expending the most resources (and cost), here's a simple rubric for you to remember: use AI at the maximum level of the previous generation.

For example, Anthropic released Opus 5.5 yesterday. Record-breaking performance, faster, better, etc. etc., the usual marketing copy we've all heard. But what's useful from their benchmarks is the generational chart. 

On their chart, they have the best of the best from the previous generation, Fable 5.1 (the green line). You can see that Fable 5.1 tops out around a score of 55 (vertical axis).
What does that correspond to in the new model? Opus 5.5 at medium effort. Not high, not xhigh, not max, but medium.

Why? Because as brains increase, effort decreases. Today's state of the art models are so much better than previous generations that you can use them at lower, faster, cheaper settings than the previous generation at full blast.

Likewise, if you're used to GPT-5.6 Sol at full blast, you can get away with Opus 5.5 at low setting and still get equivalent results.

You don't need to operate AI dialed all the way up to 11, not all the time. If you want great performance AND lower costs/environmental impact, choose the model effort settings that correspond to the previous generation's best efforts. As brains go up, effort goes down, and you'll get faster, better, AND cheaper results.

hook: Recently, we took one of my most commonly used scriptwriting frameworks... ... and applied it to a 6m subscriber kids ch
text: Recently, we took one of my most commonly used scriptwriting frameworks... ... and applied it to a 6m subscriber kids channel. This is not a niche I've worked in before but the results were very interesting. And they reassured me that this scriptwriting framework is a no-brainer for pretty much any channel! So... what's the framework? Well, the most important part of any YouTube script is structure. But deciding how to progress from A to B to C is the easy part. It's how you signpost that structure that matters most. The viewer needs to understand your video's structure in two key places: 🔷 Hook - right at the outset, set the expectation of the video's structure. 🔷 Setups - when a new segment begins, remind the viewer where in the structure they are so they don't lose track. While I've spoken about this before, I'd never applied it to kids' entertainment. Part of me wondered whether an 8-year-old would have the patience to sit through an extra 5-10 seconds of structural explanation. But once we saw the retention (it stayed above the average for over half the video), not only does it seem like they do... ...but it turns out they were actively more engaged because they understood the video's structure better from the word "go". Now I don't want to oversell it... this was just one video. But it's an early signal that the exact same framework I've spent 5 years screaming about might truly be niche-agnostic. Spending an extra 5 seconds signposting that structure at the start... ...might buy you an extra 50 seconds of their attention later!

If you're a founder struggling with product marketing, 
there's one place you should look: 
the mirror! 

Founders are often their own worst enemy.

Most of them reach out and say, "I'm struggling to succinctly explain our product!"

And we'll poke and prod and inevitably, we always find the same root cause:

The founder is trying to communicate their whole vision to their customers. 

To be fair, this comes from a good place. 

Their vision is why they decided to build the startup in the first place. 

But messaging lives on a spectrum. 

On one end is the founder's vision. 

On the other end is what the product does today.

These two messages are almost always mutually exclusive. 

(There are some exceptions with mission-driven companies, but 99% of B2B companies don't qualify for this exemption.)

Pre-product-market-fit companies need to be focused on one goal:

Get to:
• one million ARR, from 
• one customer segment, with
• one use case, from 
• one channel 

Everything you do needs to be aimed at winning these customers over.

And getting a customer requires them buying your product. 

Not your vision. 

Your PRODUCT.

The hardest part of AI images was never generating them. It was changing one thing without breaking everything else.

You approve a layout. Then a product name changes, a headline needs trimming, or the background has to shift for a different market.

With most generative tools, that means regenerating the whole image and hoping the parts already signed off on survive. Often they do not.

Luma AI's Layers, built on its Uni 1 model, takes a different route. It separates an image into individually editable components: text, fonts, objects, backgrounds.

Each element can be pulled out with a transparent background and reused elsewhere. Layouts can be rearranged for different aspect ratios. The same creative can be localized for multiple markets without starting from zero.

The detail I keep coming back to: this works on images that have no source file at all. Old assets. Files from tools nobody on the team still uses. One off exports from a vendor who moved on years ago. Those become editable again.

That reframes what a creative archive is worth. For marketing and design leaders, the constraint has quietly shifted from how fast assets get produced to how cheaply they can be revised at scale.

Everyone’s really mad about iced coffee right now. 

“Don’t bring it to job interviews!” one Fortune 500 recruiter said. 

“Shut up, you bootlickers!” Starbies fans everywhere slammed their cold, clinky, sweaty cups on their desks.

The iced coffee debate is currently all over my Threads feed, governed by an algorithm that spits out post after post on life’s tiny indignities and the lowest stakes debates you’ve ever seen. And it is, unfortunately, an algorithm that I myself built brick by brick.

Because algorithms don't just happen to us. We train them through our behavior.

That got me thinking about something Wil Reynolds said when he joined me on the Zero Click Marketing podcast:

"Google and AI are just proxies for human trust."

Social media algorithms are also trying to understand human behavior. Different systems, same general problem: machines trying to understand people based on the signals we leave behind.

Meanwhile, marketers spend an extraordinary amount of time trying to understand the machines: How do I rank? How do I show up in ChatGPT? How do I please the LinkedIn algorithm?

I get it.

But these aren't durable questions. Better to think through first principles:

• Why would a person keep swiping to read your carousel?
• Why would someone cite your research?
• Why would a coworker send your article in Slack?
• Why would a customer voluntarily tell someone else your product is amazing?

Those are the human behaviors worth earning. Some will create signals algorithms can pick up. Some won't. Sure, learn how the proxies work. How to rank in Google. How to show up in AI tools. How LinkedIn serves up content.

But most of all, get better at understanding the people the proxy is trying to understand.

Much more on this on the SparkToro blog and the Zero Click Marketing podcast.

hook: How does speaker diarization know who spoke when? NVIDIA's new Nemotron 3 Diarization supports live audio with up to eig
text:
How does speaker diarization know who spoke when? NVIDIA's new Nemotron 3 Diarization supports live audio with up to eight speaker channels, including overlapping speech. If you build meeting summaries or voice agents, understanding how those channels are made helps diagnose a transcript that gets every word right but credits the wrong person!

Imagine three turns in a meeting:

Alice: “We can ship Friday.”
Bob: “After the review?”
Alice: “Yes.”

Speech recognition gives us the words and their times. Diarization adds a timeline of speaker activity: speaker 0, speaker 1, then speaker 0 again. Those are anonymous labels, not verified names.

How do we build that timeline? There are two useful approaches:

- Cut the recording into short windows and detect the local voices, including times when two voices overlap. Represent each voice with a numerical vector called a speaker embedding. Then group similar vectors across windows to give the same voice one label. This is a modular pipeline, as in pyannote. Its stages can be adjusted separately, and clustering need not impose a fixed number of output channels. The problem is that a bad segment can produce a bad embedding and send later segments to the wrong group.

- Pass audio chunks to one model and predict which speaker channels are active in each short frame. Two channels can light up simultaneously! This is end-to-end diarization. Nemotron 3 Diarization orders its channels by when voices first appear and carries speaker context across chunks, so “speaker 0” can remain speaker 0 after a pause. A shorter live-audio buffer reduces waiting, but also gives the model less context to resolve speaker turns.

Finally, align the speaker timeline with the speech recognizer's word timestamps. This is where an apparently good system can still fail: during an interruption, two people may be active at once, while a word recognizer may provide only one stream of words. Assigning each word to whichever speaker is active at its midpoint cannot tell which of the two said it.

For a recorded conversation where I can process the whole file and may have many speakers, I would start by testing a modular pipeline. For a live conversation with a bounded number of speakers, I would test a streaming end-to-end model and measure the whole transcript on real overlapping audio. The choice depends on the audio and latency budget, but the diagnostic is the same: check word errors and speaker errors separately before trusting “who said what.”

Five big pieces of Zero-Click Marketing news this week:

1) Google's new UI manipulations (ain't no way I'm calling them "upgrades") inside AI Mode, AI Answers, and Discover are all clearly designed to limit tracking, keep people in Google, and encourage extra searches. 

2) Meta's new pay-for-links in organic posts scheme might be the most aggressive and obvious Zero-Click nudge I've seen yet. Creators are trying to end-around it with nudges to search rather than click, but I suspect this will further compound social's anti-link bias (unless you pay).

3) 2023 appears to have been the height of referred traffic to the open web (with a slight caveat for the 2024 election traffic surge in the US). It's been declining ever since, with the most rapid fall in the last 2 years. Most of that is Google, no surprise, but every other traffic source (social, email, referral links) are declining, too.

4) The (raw, purely traffic) value of a branded subReddit appears to be 3-4X what the traffic opportunity of all AI tools combined is. That's a combination of the fact that subReddits can get a lot of reach in search, that more users are searching directly in/on Reddit, and that AI tools send a vanishingly tiny amount of traffic (avg. of 0.5% of referrals).

5) 85% of brand mentions by AI responses come from third-parties, not the brand's website. Publishers are the biggest source. Like I've been saying for a while, PR is the future of AI visibility; IMO everything else is just temporary tricks.

p.s. Zero Click Marketing, our book, is now on Amazon 😉

I Tested Opus 5.5 vs. GPT-6 Astra on 12 Real Use Cases. Here's What I Learned.

Astra spent 45% less time and came in about 38% cheaper on estimated API cost.

These are my judgments based on my work and my taste, and a lot of the tasks involved creative decisions.

→ Opus gave me more of what I wanted when I left the creative direction open.
I preferred its website designs, video edits, and 3D learning world.

Its business spreadsheet also had more formulas and references, which matters when I want to change inputs and have the report update.

→ Astra earned its four wins on the museum game, trip planner, coding challenge, and Instagram carousel.

I liked how quickly I could get into the game, how clean the trip planner was, and the editorial choices in the carousel.

So I wouldn't say Opus wins every creative task, either.

→ The comparison I still want to run is an equal-budget test.

I preferred Opus's learning world at roughly $60, but Astra's first version was roughly $12.

Could I get a better result by giving Astra feedback and letting it use the same budget?

I haven't tested that yet, and it would also take more of my time.

For now, I'd lean toward Opus when I want it to help figure out the creative direction, and Astra when I can give it a very specific outcome to work toward.

Both are capable, but I still need to communicate what a good result looks like for me.

text:
Muse, Instinct, OpenClaw, Claude Code…
All successful agents have 3 key components: 

🧠 Brain → model, harness (logic)
👐 Hands → tools, computer, browser
🗃️ Files → memories, skills, repos

The 'easy' way is to throw all these in 1 stateful computer (a Mac Mini)

Like, you run 𝚌𝚕𝚊𝚞𝚍𝚎 or 𝚏𝚡 in your mac, you keep it running all day with 𝚌𝚊𝚏𝚏𝚎𝚒𝚗𝚊𝚝𝚎, it has storage, and CLIs and apps installed.

But if you want to cost-efficiently run agents in the cloud, you actually start breaking down these parts.

🧠 The harness can run in Fluid compute. To make it reliable across restarts, rollouts, crashes, you make its event log durable using Workflow.

👐 The hands can be a dedicated browser fleet like Browserbase/Kernel, a computer like Sandbox, and even more efficient lightweight tools like just-bash. 

🗃️ 🆕 What was missing was a way to also decouple storage. Imagine you want to run a memory consolidation cron job every night ("dreaming"). You can read/write to the files directly without 'booting up' the agent's full computer.

Today we're introducing the perfect companion to Sandbox: Drives. We shipped the computer for agents, now we're giving you the 'external disk' you can attach at will. It's early, and we'll be expanding capabilities here quickly.

Btw, breaking apart the agent into these independent parts not only optimizes costs in a big way, it also *massively* improves security and auditability. I'd argue you can't even run a secure agent otherwise!

hook: Jev came out this month and I've been mapping where it fits in an agent.
text:
Jev came out this month and I've been mapping where it fits in an agent.
Quick background if you missed it. 

Jev is a model from TypeSafe AI that doesn't generate text. 
You give it context and a set of questions, and it returns a typed answer for each one with a confidence score. 
Three answer types: yes or no as a probability, one choice from a list you define, or a position on a scale.

Once I started listing the decisions inside an agent loop, the list got long fast. 
Is this input an injection attempt. Does this question need retrieval. 
Is the task done. Should this tool call run. 
Should this fact go into memory. 
Today a lot of us send each of those to a general LLM and parse whatever comes back.
So I drew the nine places I'd try it first, grouped by where they sit in the loop.

𝗕𝗲𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗰𝗮𝗹𝗹
1.Input screening for injection and off policy requests
2.Retrieval decision, so you skip vector search when no context is needed
3.Composite scoring: four narrow scores in one call, weighted in your code

𝗜𝗻𝘀𝗶𝗱𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗹𝗼𝗼𝗽
4. Tool call gating: allow, ask, or deny
5. Stop check: is the task complete
6. Model routing for each step of the plan

𝗔𝗳𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗮𝗻𝘀𝘄𝗲𝗿
7. Grounding check, one question per claim
8. Memory write filter
9. Confidence handoff: act, confirm, or send to a person

𝗪𝗼𝗿𝘁𝗵 𝗸𝗻𝗼𝘄𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗯𝗲𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗯𝘂𝗶𝗹𝗱

It answers every question in a single pass. 
TypeSafe's own numbers put 13 questions in one call at about 12x cheaper than 13 separate calls. That makes composite scoring practical. When priorities shift, you edit a weight in code and leave the prompt alone.

I spend a lot of my time on guardrails and oversight for agentic systems, so the confidence scores are the part I care about most. 

In regulated work someone eventually asks who approved an automated decision and on what basis. A calibrated score, with thresholds set in code and every decision logged, is something an audit team can actually review.

It has limits. The docs say it can't reliably count, do arithmetic, parse dates, or write text. It also reads instructions literally, so negations need to be spelled out in your criteria.

On speed and cost, all we have so far are vendor numbers: about 100 ms for a typical call and $0.042 per million input tokens, with output free. 

LiteLLM ran a small routing benchmark on 80 synthetic prompts and got 95% tier agreement for Jev against 73.75% for Haiku, and they were upfront that their labels weren't independently reviewed. Test it on your own labeled decisions before you trust any of it.

For those of you building agents: where do you draw the line between a decision that belongs in plain code, one that belongs in a classifier like this, and one that still needs a full LLM?

hook: Total compensation is the worst number to negotiate on.
text:
Total compensation is the worst number to negotiate on.

It tells you what an offer pays if everything goes perfectly. You stay all four years, and the stock ends up worth exactly what the letter says. For most PMs, neither of those turns out to be true.

Look at an Amazon Director offer. Using Levelsfyi medians for L8 this month (sign-on left out), it pays about $423K in year 1 and $1.19M in year 3. Amazon vests 5/15/40/40, so 80% of the stock shows up in years 3 and 4. Average it all out and you get around $860K, which is what people call the TC. Amazon usually pays a sign-on over the first two years to cover some of that gap.

Leave after two years and you only ever see 20% of the grant.

So when I work with PMs on an offer, we set TC aside and figure out Effective Compensation, or EC. It's basically what you'll actually get paid each year, for as long as you'll actually be there.

Here's the math.

EC per year = cash per year + (equity value × % that vests while you're there ÷ years you stay) + (sign-on ÷ years you stay)

Here's how I'd run it on your own offer.

1. Pick your real tenure

Everybody plugs in 4 years because the vest is 4 years. Put in the number you'd actually bet money on.

2. Figure out what the equity's worth

Public company RSUs are easy. Take face value. Private stock is harder, because it depends on whether there's ever a payout and how long you wait for it, so your inputs move the answer a lot. With the assumptions I use, a $400K private grant can be worth anywhere from about $80K (Series C, 40% odds of an IPO in 5 years) to about $216K (late stage with a yearly tender). Run your odds, then run worse ones.

3. Spread out the one-time money

A $40K sign-on is $20K a year if you stay two years. Stay four and it's $10K.

4. Push where your EC moves most

Base counts dollar for dollar, and every future raise builds on it. Equity only counts for whatever you got in step 2. So if you're thinking 2-3 years, go after sign-on and front-loaded vesting. If you're thinking 4+, go after base and equity.

Here's how big the gap gets on a Series C offer with $200K base, a $30K bonus, a $40K sign-on and a $400K grant. The recruiter's going to call that $370K a year. Stay two years with those Series C odds and your EC is closer to $270K a year. That $100K is what you should be negotiating around.

The gap gets bigger as you go up, since more of the offer is equity. When I was interviewing at Apollo, my ask added $350K a year, and almost all of it was equity.

The full playbook has the formula for every equity type (RSUs, options, PPUs and PE profits interests), plus 5 real negotiations from PMs we coached this year. None of them had a competing offer, and every one came out ahead without losing the offer.

Full guide → https://lnkd.in/eRtd453e

Your recruiter is always going to quote the four-year number. You just need to know yours before you answer.

Most of that is pattern matching against data I already own. 
Which makes it a textbook case for an agent.

So why have I not built it yet?
Because the report is the smallest part of what it needs.

It needs to know which findings I have revised since publication and which still hold. 
> Stale advice is worse than no advice.

It needs to separate a founder with 2,000 followers from a creator with 200,000. 
> Identical advice breaks one of them.

It needs the rules the data does not explain on its own. 
> Links go in the post body, and never into the first comment.

Then there is the trust question, which is the hardest one. 
I can accept an agent that misses something. I cannot accept one that answers with confidence in a case it has no data for. It should say "ask Richard" and stop.

Every one of those is more a context problem than a building problem, at least to me.

Now that is the premise behind HubSpot's Fall Spotlight.

hook: JEV founder just dropped a Gem!
text:
JEV founder just dropped a Gem!

We spent the last few years making AI better at answering questions.

The next big shift might be making AI better at making decisions.

That’s why Jev caught my attention.

It’s not really trying to be another LLM.

Instead of generating text token by token, Jev is designed to take messy state in and return structured, probabilistic decisions out.

Think:

→ Which tool should this agent use?
→ Should this action be allowed?
→ Does this output pass?
→ Should we retry or escalate?
→ Which workflow should run next?

That sounds simple.

But it could change how we architect agents.

Today, we often ask one big LLM to do everything:

understand → classify → reason → route → act → judge

A more efficient stack may look like:

Jev → decide
Code → compute
LLM → reason + generate
Jev → verify
Tools → execute

In other words:

LLMs generate. Jev decides.

I made this cheat sheet to break down where Jev fits, where it doesn’t, and why “decision models” could become an important new layer in the AI stack.

The bigger question:

Are we moving from an LLM-centric world to a world of specialized models for different types of intelligence?

Most people know Druski as one of the funniest people on the internet. His videos have been watched over a billion times, and more than 40 million people follow him.

But it all started in Georgia, making funny skits on his phone.

Those videos eventually went viral and eventually caught Drake’s attention. Since then, Druski has gone from making people laugh online to building his own production company, hosting major awards and working alongside people like Kevin Hart.

As we spoke, I realised he was doing the same thing with me.

He would notice tiny changes in my expression, stop mid-answer and ask what I was thinking.

- The message from Drake (@champagnepapi) that transformed his career.

- Why his brother’s life went in a very different direction.
- Having a gun pointed at his head and deciding to change.
- Netflix and Amazon rejecting him but then came crawling back.
- How comedy saved him from prison.

There’s a moment in the conversation where I tell Druski that our dark sides are often connected to our light sides.

I think his story is an extraordinary example of that.

The awareness that helped him navigate difficult moments as a child became part of the thing that millions of people now find funny.

Behind the person you see online is someone far more thoughtful, ambitious and complicated than I expected.

This conversation changed the way I see Druski.

For years I was the first person in the room with an answer.

Someone would bring me a problem and I'd have a fix before they finished the thought.

It felt like leadership. It was actually just impatience.

Now I try to speak last. It's hardest when I'm sure I'm right.

A CPA firm owner in my accelerator came in after a full year of zero growth. About $4M in revenue with 17 employees. Their projections showed more of the same.

Her read was that she needed more leads.

We worked through it properly and the leads were fine. The sales process in general was strong.

What was hurting her was onboarding. New clients would sign, then wait, and the excitement drained away. A few of them tried to back out of their packages.

She rebuilt onboarding into five steps and gave one person ownership of it.

The problem she almost solved would have cost her another year and a sales hire she didn't need.

This is exactly why asking the right questions matters.

1/ What's actually not working?
- Name the thing underneath the symptom
- Ask three people who sit closer to the work than you do

2/ What's changed around us?
- Inside the business and in the market
- Something usually shifted before the problem showed up

3/ What does success look like here?
- Write the number down
- If you can't write it, you're not ready to choose

4/ What haven't we tried?
- List at least six options before you judge any of them
- Include the one you'd pick if you couldn't fail

5/ Can we test it small?
- What's the cheapest version that proves this works?
- What does it cost us if we're wrong?

Slowing down at the start is what keeps you from solving the wrong problem for a year.

How I stay in my zone of genius:

(and what exactly I delegate to AI):

There are four types of work in everyone’s life:

1. Zone of Incompetence: 
Tasks you are not good at, and AI can do way better.

Examples: cleaning up messy data, summarizing a contract, transcribing meeting notes

Lesson: Give this to AI. Include an example of what “good” looks like and the mistakes to double-check for.

——

2. Zone of Competence: 
Tasks you’re good at, but AI can do just as well as you.

Examples: proofreading, spreadsheet formulas, doing monthly accounting

Lesson: Give this to AI. Make sure you include 2-3 samples of your past work, specific instructions on what you want them to do next, and a word limit.

——

3. Zone of Excellence: 
Tasks you are exceptionally good at and get rewarded for, but that drain your energy.

Examples: creating detailed project plans, responding to emails, creating slide decks

Lesson: Give AI 70% of this work. You finish the last 30% with your magic touch. Make sure you give it context on who is reading it, what the specific goal is, and things to avoid.

——

4. Zone of Genius: 
Things you are uniquely suited for, deeply love, and can happily do for hours.

Examples: writing my book, writing newsletters, setting the strategy for our business

Lesson: Do this yourself. Protect all of your time for your superpowers. Not using AI for these things will give you a competitive advantage.

The mistake I see so many people make?

Not giving AI enough context on the tasks you can delegate. 
So it comes out with generic AI slop and you keep doing all of it yourself.

text:
One of my favorite lines from Jurassic Park is, “Your scientists were so preoccupied with whether or not they could, they didn't stop to think if they should.”

And I think about that when I look at how we’re using AI these days.

Even in my own businesses, sometimes I’ll see someone spin up an AI solution that probably didn’t need to exist in the first place.

Worse still, those solutions don’t always work well anyway.

One of our companies spent a boatload of money getting an AI agent set up to do screening calls. The voice sounded human, and it had been trained on all the greatest sales scripts and objection handling techniques known to man.

But when the AI went live, the numbers tanked.

Calls were running short, people weren’t booking the next call, and overall it was a huge waste of time and money.

Meanwhile, my own sales department has an agent so good at booking calls and managing the dialers, we named it Zig, after Zig Ziglar.

So what’s the difference between Zig and the dysfunctional AI?

Context.

Being able to connect to existing data bases to create connections and streamline processes is what separates great AI tools, like the ones we use from HubSpot, from subpar white label builds.

Zig had been connected to the customer base, the CRM, and everything it needed to see who the customer is, where they’re at in their journey, and see everything happening on the board.

The other agent… hadn’t.

It didn’t matter that it had all the training and scripts you could ever ask for, without the appropriate context, it couldn’t make the right choices. You have to integrate your AI agents, or they’re just like really smart biologists at a robot convention… Useless.

Remember 6th grade math? It’s time to learn the order of operations.

1. CUT

Stand at the door of every workflow and ask why it exists. You're not the CEO here, you're the bouncer, and everything you automate has to have a reason.

2. STANDARDIZE

Write down how everything actually works, why it exists, what a good outcome looks like, what a bad one looks like, and the rules something has to follow.

3. AUTOMATE

Now hand it all the context.

An agent inherits whatever you give it, so give it a clean picture of your customers, your process, and your use cases. Make sure it’s able to see any context a human would need to make good choices.

↓↓↓

@HubSpot built their Fall Spotlight on this idea. AI works best when it knows your business. After all, you wouldn’t expect a consultant to know your customer until you give them the data, right?

If you want to network effectively, you need to:

 - Have a way to keep the engagement going

2. Make A List Of Job-Related Keywords

Think of keywords, skills, phrases, and jargon that align with your target role.

Start with one keyword (or the job title itself).

Run a search for it on LinkedIn.

From the “Filters” option, select “Posts.”

Then change “Date Posted” to “Past Week.”

4. Filter By “Author Company”

Click on “All Filters” to find the “Author Company” filter.

Add all of your target companies to this filter.

This will give you a list of all the posts related to your target role, written by people at your target companies, posted in the past week!

5. Analyze Posts & Authors

Scroll through the posts.

When you find one that resonates? 

Click the person’s profile and check to see if they post consistently (at least once / week).

If they do?

Bookmark their profile in your browser.

6. Leave A Value Driven Comment

For each author you find that posts regularly in your target space?

Leave a comment on their post recent post that is:

 - Supportive
 - Postive in tone
 - Offers your own take / value
 - Is more than one sentence

Repeat for each author.

7. Rinse & Repeat Daily

Every day, click through the author profiles you have bookmarked.

See a new post?

Leave a new comment.

Repeat this process every weekday if you can.

But aim to leave at least one comment / week at minimum.

Content creators love engagement.

hook: New IBM study of 1500 CHROs and 8800 employees: 43% of employees say THEY get blamed when AI gets it wrong. Yet 41% of C
text:
New IBM study of 1500 CHROs and 8800 employees: 43% of employees say THEY get blamed when AI gets it wrong. Yet 41% of CHROs think their people may not feel safe challenging AI. You see the HUGE problem here right? And you see why it's happening?

This is from IBM's study, "Designing the Thinking Organization: 5 focus areas for CHROs as AI reshapes work."

And this is why CHROs have to help lead AI adoption. Because this is a people challenge, not a technical challenge.

Think about it:

People are afraid to question the AI… and fear they will get blamed when it's wrong.

This is completely understandable if you've spent even five seconds using AI. 

AI speaks with complete and total confidence. 

As an employee, you're like 'okay, clearly this genius thing has to be right.'

Yet the single most valuable thing in the era of AI is...say it with me...YOUR JUDGMENT. 

It's why a huge part of our AI training at large organizations focuses on trusting your own judgment. Not because it's "the right thing to do" but because that's how you get good results.

When we don't push back against AI, we get AI slop, bad decisions, regression to the mean. And worse, we destroy all the experience and critical thinking you bring to the organization.

THE PROBLEM IS THAT PEOPLE DON'T UNDERSTAND WHAT AI IS

Most people see AI as software, and software either can do something or it can't. 

Your calculator doesn't have good days and bad days. So if the AI gave you an answer, it must be right. And if it's wrong, you must have done something wrong.

AI works much more like a brilliant colleague. Usually right, sometimes wrong, and how well it performs depends a lot on the people around it.


WHY THIS IS GETTING HARDER

Critical thinking doesn't disappear when a tool is unreliable. Back in 2023, we were great critical thinkers because ChatGPT hallucinated all the time.

Critical thinking DOES disappear when a tool is right almost all the time.

That's where we are now. AI's mistakes today are about context: the client history, the team dynamics, the thing you never told it. And those mistakes sound exactly as confident as the right answers.

BACK TO THE IBM STUDY...

71% of CHROs say the most essential skill now is being able to supervise, validate and override AI, but only 38% of employees agree. 

On handling exceptions, the exact skill you need when AI misses context, it's 32% of CHROs and just 14% of employees.


WHY THIS IS HR'S JOB

We already know how to help people work with brilliant, imperfect colleagues. It's called psychological safety: the freedom to say "I think this is wrong" without getting punished for it.

Where the CHRO shares responsibility for deciding which decisions stay human, 76% of employees feel safe questioning AI. Where HR is only advisory, that drops to 43%.
And yet 46% of organizations don't involve the CHRO when they set AI strategy.

AI is a brilliant helper. Your people's judgment is what makes it valuable.

Prompt quality matters less when the system already has the right context.

That gives us three interesting changes:
• From prompting → steering
The human spends less time explaining context and more time reviewing direction and judgment.

• From individual knowledge → institutional knowledge
What one consultant learns about a client can become useful to the rest of the team.

• From generation → grounded generation
The value isn’t just producing content quickly. It’s producing something based on the organization’s actual files, records and approved context.

text:
The hardest problem in autonomous driving was never recognizing the world. It was deciding what to do when the world stops making sense. 

A car that identifies a pedestrian, a cone and a stopped truck has solved the easy part. The hard part arrives when those three things show up together in a configuration nobody trained for.

Reasoning models are changing that calculus. They take camera feeds covering the front, sides and rear of a vehicle and build a single understanding of the full scene. From there they decide whether to stop, yield or change lanes, generate a safe trajectory, and produce a reasoning trace explaining why that decision was made.

That last part matters more than it sounds. A decision you can inspect is a decision you can audit, challenge and certify. Interpretability stops being a research nicety and becomes a regulatory asset.

There is a second effect I find just as significant. These models can connect decisions to specific regions in camera images and turn raw fleet footage into labeled training data automatically. Teams can test rare road situations, inspect failures, validate driving behavior and train smaller models for deployment inside the vehicle itself.

I spent time digging into how this actually works, and the shift is hard to miss. Autonomy is moving from pattern matching to reasoning. The technology behind it is NVIDIA Alpamayo 2 Super.

2. Why Muse and Instinct are the biggest credible threats to ChatGPT

Autonomous agent interfaces like Muse act as a Trojan horse against ChatGPT by bundling solid consumer LLMs with free autonomous agent execution. Offering daily conversational AI and action-taking agents for free with higher token limits makes paying $20 monthly for basic chat hard to justify.

4. What should the API policy be for every big company?

Aggregated consumer demand dictates tech adoption far more than theoretical payment protocols. When platforms like Meta aggregate massive user volume against backend systems, incumbents like Amazon, OpenTable, and Resy must immediately formulate agent API policies. Demand aggregation remains the ultimate driver of enterprise urgency.

5. Why I would make the investment into Factory at 5 billion

Investing in Factory at $5 billion is a high-conviction bet on data sovereignty and model choice. C-level executives deeply distrust frontier labs with confidential codebases, fearing competitive data leaks through shared LLMs. As coding inference surges, air-gapped, model-agnostic enterprise platforms will capture massive market share.

6. Why would Rory invest in Factory at $5 billion?

text:
Alright, here’s all my best personal branding advice.

Totally free, right here, for you.

Build influence over entertainment: Content should prove expertise and answer “why hire you,” not just entertain — especially for service businesses or high-ticket offerings.

Consistency over frequency: No single required cadence; more posts = more opportunities, but sustainable rhythm matters most; focus on getting 1% better each post.

Authenticity beats polish: “Yapping” content (one-cut, unscripted perspective videos) performs well; highly produced content is not required to build an audience.

Hook is critical: Write the hook and body content separately; the opening one-liner should be the most compelling, standalone statement possible.

Repurpose relentlessly: Tell the same story in as many different ways as possible; repetition with new context is a feature, not a flaw.

Success stories as content: Any example of your business solving a problem makes strong, credible content.

CONTENT IDEATION FRAMEWORKS

50-idea exercise: Write 50 content ideas on paper without self-editing; the first 20 are easy — the real, niche ideas emerge after pushing past that threshold.

Calendar as content source: Every meeting or appointment can generate at least 3 content ideas.

AI as collaboration partner: Use AI to brainstorm by feeding it context about your business and asking it to surface story angles — not to generate content from scratch.

Crowdsource ideas: Family, young employees, and peers are valid sources; social media natives offer algorithm insight unavailable to older users.

PLATFORM AND FORMAT DECISIONS

Short-form vertical video: Single most important format for the next decade; same video can post to TikTok, Instagram Reels, and YouTube Shorts simultaneously.

LinkedIn specifics: Best for B2B and professional audiences; I-statements and personal perspective outperform generic tips or meme content; text, image, and carousel (PDF) formats perform best.

Instagram: Best for combining fandom-building and new business acquisition.

Batching & scheduling: Batching is strongly recommended for busy owners; scheduling does not hurt algorithmic performance.

hook: I'm going to attempt to tie three disparate concepts together into a prediction of the future (which I rarely make, but
text:
I'm going to attempt to tie three disparate concepts together into a prediction of the future (which I rarely make, but IMO warrants an exception):

1) After ~12 years of operation, Google's most important ranking factor switched from links to user behavior
2) AI tools and AI-powered answers within existing platforms (Google, Amazon, Instagram, FB, Twitter, etc.) are currently reliant on model training data + live web/index searches
3) A huge amount of marketing time + budget is going toward influencing places marketers hope/believe will affect AI answers (probably 10X more than is warranted by potential ROI, but that's a different discussion)

Here's what I believe will happen:
 - The AI systems (native tools like Claude and ChatGPT, but obviously Google/Bing, and eventually the social and e-commerce players, too) will exhaust the value of text in their training corpora and get diminishing returns from live web search
 - Like Google before them, they'll turn to weighting by usage... i.e. did a lot of real humans read this article? Then we should heavily use it in our responses. Did some marketer post this listicle hoping to influence AI, but no one ever visited it? Then we should ignore it.
 - A metric ton of AI-influence work will be useless and a surprising amount of PR-to-influence-real-people work will become valuable.

This might already be starting. It wouldn't surprise me at all to find the correlation between AI visibility and which products/services have huge engagement/go viral/get covered on social and by well-read press is way higher than the correlation between AI visibility and the most common content creation + distribution tactics the field's currently employing.

I seriously doubt it will take AI companies 12 years this time; I think it's coming soon if it isn't already here. And if you're not trying to influence *people* in the places they pay attention, you're gonna have a bad time.

Across all six runs, the agents asked me one question total, and none of them used a subagent.

For normal knowledge work, Medium is still fine for most tasks.

It wasn’t the workshop I thought I was doing. 

I just finished up my fourth workshop with the wonderful Laboratory Products Association, and it wasn’t the workshop I thought I was doing. 

Months ago I had proposed an agenda and that’s what got published online. A week before the workshop, a survey went out to registered attendees with questions like "What is the ONE thing you need to learn at this workshop to make it worth your investment?"

This isn't a new question or a new idea. Asking your audience what would make an event a success is always a great idea.

When I looked at the responses that came in, 6 days before the workshop, I realized I had a serious problem. What I wanted to teach, no one wanted to learn. Despite how we marketed it, none of the agenda items were the attendees' burning questions. What attendees really wanted, I could teach, but it wasn't what I planned.

So the entire thing went in the trash a week out from the event.

I fired up my speaker second brain that I talked about in my newsletter a couple weeks ago to see what I had in stock. And I had a gap, a sizable gap. 5 days before my workshop, I decided to write down my thoughts about those gaps, and that became last weekend's newsletter.

Then last night at the opening night reception, I talked to some of the folks who hadn't filled out the survey, and over ravioli and prosecco, I finalized the agenda. The night before the workshop. Granted, there weren't a ton of tweaks, but some of the material got more focused on very, very specific needs and use cases.

And today? The workshop went off without a hitch. I got to all the material I wanted, I hit my times exactly, and in side conversations, attendees told me they were getting exactly the value they'd need to judge the event a success.

The big thing I learned from this is that the jagged edge of AI is INCREDIBLY jagged. Some folks had deep skills in one part of AI but never touched others, and one aspect in particular that's been in market for a couple of years now is still absurdly underutilized - Katie Robbert and John J. Wall talked about that today on the Trust Insights livestream, deep research. In the workshop, I showed a deep research report that half the attendees wanted to take home because the information was immediately usable by their sales teams.

For both speakers and events, the faster we can pivot to meet the needs of our audiences, the happier they'll be and the more they'll recommend our events as "can't miss" value. With things like second brains, you can build to order in hours instead of weeks, and make your audiences deliriously happy.

AI fluency.

A lot of that traces back to one rubric. Wade Foster, co-founder and CEO of Zapier, published it, and hundreds of companies have used it to screen candidates and grade their teams.

It has 4 levels: Unacceptable, Capable, Adoptive, Transformative.

So I asked Wade what it takes to reach the top one. I didn't want the theory, so I brought 3 of my own PM work products and had him grade each one live, on camera.

→ Artifact 1: a PRD written in ChatGPT. No prototype, no customer evidence. In 2024, Capable. In 2026, Wade called it "a little old-fashioned." His instinct was to throw my PRD into Cursor and build it himself.

→ Artifact 2: a working prototype first, then a markdown PRD with customer evidence. "Very solidly" Adoptive. Then he pushed on my Q4 timeline: "Shoot, you've got five weeks. What are we doing for five weeks?"

→ Artifact 3: a system. Agents cluster customer signals overnight, the PM decides what to promote, and an auto-build chain produces the PRD, prototype, evals and draft code before a human gate. "Starting to get into transformative territory."

Three things surprised me.

1. The top rating is meant to be rare. I assumed 20-30% of a strong team. Wade: "Transformative means you are an n of one. You're the first of your kind doing this new thing." Across Zapier's 30 to 40 PMs, maybe one a half.

2. He caught my shortcut. I can't see Zapier's Gong calls, so I told the model to "pretend you looked at Gong calls." Wade noticed the evidence named exactly the tools he'd cited minutes earlier: "AI just has that hyper-specificity to it."

3. The CEO rates himself Adoptive. His rule of thumb: in your discipline, you should be ahead of your CEO. "If I'm spotting things that are obvious to me and not to you... that makes me nervous."

He also opened up his robot staff: a 6am brief, a 5pm scribe that took his end-of-day cleanup from two hours to 15 minutes, an agent that writes his exec agenda, and a CEO CRM that drafts 10 to 20 customer emails every Saturday night. He describes each one to Cursor and runs it on Zapier.

Boston Dynamics’ Atlas has gone from performing backflips to preparing for factory work.
And that evolution says a lot about where humanoid robotics is heading.

Seven years ago, Atlas was a hydraulic research robot best known for parkour, jumps, and impressive demonstrations of balance.

Today, the electric Atlas is being designed around practical industrial work.

It has 56 degrees of freedom, tactile hands, 360° vision, and can repeatedly handle loads of up to 30 kg.

That shift is important.

The question for robotics is no longer just, “Can a humanoid robot move like a human?”
It is becoming, “Can it reliably perform useful work inside environments already designed for humans?”

For manufacturers and technology leaders, that changes the conversation from robotics research to workforce augmentation, factory automation, safety, productivity, and operating economics.

The biggest opportunity may not be replacing traditional industrial robots.

It may be automating tasks where flexibility, mobility, and human-like manipulation matter more than fixed automation.

From research demo to potential real-world worker in seven years.

What will humanoid robots look like inside factories by 2030?

hook: The OpenAI-Medicare incident, where an AI agent gained unauthorized access to files in Australia’s Medicare statistics p
text:
The OpenAI-Medicare incident, where an AI agent gained unauthorized access to files in Australia’s Medicare statistics portal, raises a much bigger question than the breach itself.

For years, cybersecurity has largely been about stopping people from doing things they shouldn’t do, or stopping software behaving in ways we already understand.

AI agents are different.

They can explore. They can improvise. They can try another route when the first one doesn’t work. And increasingly, they can take actions that nobody explicitly told them to take.

That changes the security equation quite dramatically.

The big risk is no longer simply bad people using AI to attack us.

It is also perfectly legitimate AI systems doing unexpected things at enormous speed.
And I’m not sure our security infrastructure, governance or incident response processes are ready for that yet.

We are racing to make AI agents more autonomous, more capable and more useful. I’m excited about that.

But every step forward in capability also increases the importance of containment, permissions, monitoring and control.

Because if AI can operate at machine speed, our defenses cannot continue operating at human speed.

For me, that is the real warning from this incident.

We are entering a world of autonomous digital actors, and cybersecurity is going to have to change much faster than many organizations currently realize.

What do you think? Are we building the security infrastructure for AI agents as quickly as we are building the agents themselves?

text:
You and your AI do not need to split the work 50/50; what matters is the right contribution at the right moment, not an equal share.

In practice, the balance can shift from one task to the next.

A procurement team may let AI scan thousands of supplier records and flag unusual changes. Most of the volume sits with the machine.

Then one case reaches a buyer who knows that a supplier is going through a temporary production change. Context changes the interpretation, and one human judgment can outweigh hours of machine processing.

AI may then return to the workflow and handle the next batch.

No symmetry required.

Responsibility follows a different rule. If an AI-supported recommendation affects a supplier decision, the organization still owns the outcome.

So do not measure collaboration by how much work each side does. Ask whether AI is handling the work it can do well and whether people enter where judgment is needed.

A 50/50 split looks neat on a slide.
Real collaboration follows what the work requires.

#HumanAICollaboration #FutureOfWork

text:
If you chase after money, it has a funny way of avoiding you.

At least, that's what I've found in my career.

Instead, I'd much rather focus on something better:

Big, painful, miserable problems.

I started learning how to solve these problems back in 2009 in my startup days, and quickly figured out how valuable that was.

Solve one painful problem? Here's some money.
Solve another one? Here's more.
Keep solving them? Here's a boatload.

When you can save people money or time (or both) AND help them sleep better at night, you have incredible earning potential.

So work on that skill ferociously.

Here's how I do it:

1. Hypothesize

When you see a big problem, try to write down every single reason you think it might be happening. Guess. Jot every single thing you can think of.

2. Rank

Stack rank them from most likely to least likely to be the culprit. Start by cutting everything except the top 2 or 3.

3. Isolate

Starting with your most likely, figure out how to isolate your hypothesis and measure it effectively.

4. Prove or disprove

Don't guide the data. Let the data guide you. Were you right? Wrong? Talk to people as well. Qualitative and quantitative feedback are useful.

5. Install

Once you've figured out the actual fix, install it. Then move on to the next problem.

Congrats...you're on your way to being hyper valuable.

This is just one of seven incredibly important skills in entrepreneurship.

I break down this one even more, and six others, in a free guide to building valuable businesses.

Everything I learned in a decade building my one-person business to $15M in profit, compressed into a short 30-minute read.

text:
Do the AI labs have any credibility left? Anthropic’s enzyme system discovery is equal parts hype and reality. The reality is that AI is really well suited to this type of work. Give it a pattern and a massive dataset, then tell it to find everything that matches the pattern.

AI scales access to information, so finding needles in a haystack is where AI can shine. But that’s the simple part of the process. Anthropic’s model wasn’t able to help determine what the enzyme does. The next step is where value gets created or where a lot of work ends in disappointment. Such is science.

Most biologists and geneticists agree that the way the work is being presented far exceeds what the model really did. It’s unnecessary hype. The model did something really useful that we can deploy today, but someone in marketing didn’t think it sounded interesting enough, so they juiced up the language.

Every time that happens, the entire industry loses a little more credibility. At some point soon, AI will do something truly amazing. The only question is, will anyone still believe us when it does?

A man who can no longer speak thought the words "I love you".

His wife heard them out loud, in his own voice.

Terry Mandable has ALS. 

The disease has taken his speech, but his mind is completely sharp.

He's part of Neuralink's VOICE trial, using his implant to help fine-tune a brain-to-voice interface for himself and others who can't speak.

The training ran in two stages:

1. Miming
↳ Terry mouthed words as best he could so the decoder could learn the brain patterns behind each one

2. Thinking
↳ He then simply imagined the words and heard them spoken aloud

The voice you hear is his own, rebuilt from recordings made before ALS took it.

Earlier this year I covered Brad Smith, Neuralink's third patient and the first with ALS who couldn't speak.

Brad types with his brain and an ElevenLabs clone reads the words out in his voice.

Terry skips the keyboard entirely. The words go from his brain straight to the speaker.

Neuralink has now implanted more than 20 people worldwide, and VOICE is its first trial built around speech rather than cursor control.

Sure, there’s still a delay of a few seconds between thought and sound.

But we're taking the fiction out of science fiction one month at a time.

All that engineering, and the first thing he chose to say was "I love you."

That’s what technology is all about: restoring a person’s ability to reach the people they love.

And that’s about as good a use of human ingenuity as I can think of.

Arthur C. Clarke wrote that any sufficiently advanced technology is indistinguishable from magic.

This is what it looks like when it arrives.

Some founders care more about feeling validated as visionaries than actually growing a business.

Having a storied venture capital firm hear your pitch how you’re going to change the world, and then giving you their blessing.

Raising a round isn’t a “means to an end.” 

It’s the end.

You get the TechCrunch article. 

You get to announce it on LinkedIn. 

You get the gold star. 

After working with hundreds of B2B founders, I kept trying to understand why the VC validation mattered so much more than the customer validation. 

Why did so many founders have seemingly little interest in getting CUSTOMERS to want their product? 

Why wouldn’t growing revenue matter more than growing your funding? 

And it comes down to this: 

VCs invest in the vision, but customers don’t care about it at all. 

They don’t give a shit about your “why.”

They just care about your “what” and your “how.”

“What is this product and how can it help me?”

It’s like the movie that wins an Oscar, but flopped at the box office. 

The founder that raised (but ultimately fails) still has the acceptance from the academy. 

The public wasn’t ready for their visionary movie, but that’s because they are too pedestrian. 

They’d rather go see some Marvel slop. 

Failure in the box office was THEIR fault, not mine. 

Because I know my movie was good, and I have the awards to prove it.

hook: Before you automate a process, spend time with the person everyone calls when it breaks.
text:
Before you automate a process, spend time with the person everyone calls when it breaks.
Ask them to walk you through a normal case. 

Then ask them to show you one that needed extra work.
Take an invoice with the right amount but a missing purchase order number.
The person handling it might check another system, look through an email thread, or contact someone who approved a similar exception last month.

The documentation probably just says "Validate invoice."

So I'd involve the operations team from the beginning when building an agent. Have them explain their decisions while doing the work. Include the cases where they stop and ask for help.

Deel built that idea into Akai: people can record their screen and explain a process to build an automation.

It started with Deel's own back office. For context, Deel is valued at roughly $17B, acts as the legal employer for workers in 150 countries, and has 7,000 fully remote employees. It reports making $500M in three months without additional hiring.

With AKAI, Deel reports 90,000 hours saved in the first few months, including a month with savings equal to 500 full time employees' working hours.

For any team trying this, I'd want to understand what happens to the difficult cases.
 ↳ Does the agent recognize missing information?
 ↳ Does it know when approval is needed?
 ↳ How much time does someone spend checking and correcting its work?
Those questions should shape the first version.

𝗪𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝗜'𝗱 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗿𝘁
Pick one process.
Capture the exceptions.
Agree on the approval rules.
Measure the time saved after reviews and corrections.

And have the person who taught the process review the first runs. They know which mistakes to look for.

Where should the line sit between what an agent handles on its own and what still needs a person to sign off?

Thanks to deel for sponsoring this post.

 Most headlines are just job titles.

text:
I interviewed 5 billionaires at my live book launch last weekend and asked them how they build companies and make decisions.

Here are 7 things they said that I can’t stop thinking about:

1- Keep a written list of your failures

Before making a new bet, compare it against the ways you've lost before.

If the setup looks familiar walk away. Or decide what will make you pull out. Otherwise you’ll end up funding the same mistake because of sunk cost.  

2- Deliver the bad news before you know how to solve it

If you make a mistake, tell your team immediately.

Waiting until you have a solution just gives the problem more time to grow. And bad news never gets better with time.

3- Doing nothing is riskier than taking a wrong bet

Waiting feels safe because nothing immediately breaks.

But while you wait:

- competitors keep moving
- employees get bored
- you miss out on opportunities

Taking small consistent bets > waiting for certainty.

4- The cheapest way to grow revenue is upselling your existing customers

A new customer costs more than one you already have.

You should spend less time chasing people who don't know you yet and more time selling deeper into the ones who do.

5- Turn price objections back into questions

When customers complain about raises, ask them back if they'd raised their own professional rates that year.

That helps you explain the raise without getting defensive about it.

6- Let your employees make decisions without going through you

Give your team direct access to the data, tools, and context they need to do their jobs.

If every decision has to go through layers of managers, you’ll create bottlenecks that slow everyone down.  

7- Get distribution before margins

You can improve margins after you’ve captured customers but you can’t always recover attention, momentum, and market share when you’ve lost it.

First get the engine running; then make it more profitable.

text:
Companies aren't seeing ROI from AI for two reasons. They're measuring the tool instead of the people, and they're encouraging AI use instead of building it into processes that drive how work gets done.

This is why we say stop encouraging use cases and start embedding AI into daily processes - and have those processes created from the bottom up, held accountable by team leaders.

Okay, here's what we see:

MISTAKE #1: MEASURING THE TOOL

A traditional tool comes with its measurement built in: more leads in the CRM, more tickets closed, stuff like that. 

AI doesn't, because its power runs through your people. Counting how many times Copilot got opened, I mean, it tells you nothing because that could be people just using it as a better search engine, which gives you zero ROI.

We know the gains are real. Anyone using AI well knows they can do 5 or 10 times what they did before. 

But - and this is critical - those gains are in individuals who choose whether or not to use AI, so of course there's no consistent ROI.

You can't measure AI, but you can measure a process. How did this work run before, and how does it run now? Decide what good looks like before you start, on your own numbers, and then count.

MISTAKE #2: ENCOURAGING INSTEAD OF EXPECTING

Most companies rolled out AI by giving Copilot to everyone and waiting for everyone to get efficient. That's like putting a treadmill in every house in America and expecting to cure heart disease.

Leaders see what AI can do and confuse that potential with people actually using it. Imagine installing Excel on every computer in finance and then just *encouraging* people to try it. Nobody would do that. Excel is simply how the work gets done.

The same goes for use cases, and we've been saying this since 2024. A use case lives in the person, so when your best AI user leaves, everything they figured out leaves with them.

THE FIX: BUILD AI INTO THE PROCESS

Stop relying on will power to get people using AI. Build it into their processes for them.

You can tell everyone to walk 5,000 steps a day, or you can put the parking lot 5,000 steps from the building. Then nobody has to remember. It's just how you get to work.

AI works the same way. When a team rebuilds a process around AI and their manager holds it as the standard, nobody can avoid using it, and nobody has to rely on willpower.

That's how you get a million little hockey sticks: every team rebuilding its own processes, one at a time, with each gain locked in. Add those up and you get the curve the CFO (or the consultant) has been looking for.

hook: Google just made Gemini 3.8 Live with Live Avatar generally available. Voice agent architectures are easier to choose wh
text:
Google just made Gemini 3.8 Live with Live Avatar generally available. Voice agent architectures are easier to choose when you can answer one question: where does the caller's speech become text before the reply is spoken?

Imagine someone says, “Move my appointment to 3 pm.” The agent has to understand the request, check the calendar, make the change, and confirm what happened. I would draw three possible paths through that job:

- Transcribe the speech, send the words to a text agent, then turn its text reply into speech. This is the cascaded STT → LLM → TTS pipeline. The transcript and reply give you places to inspect errors, apply rules, and swap components. But the text agent no longer hears vocal cues, and each handoff can add delay. Streaming partial transcripts and speech can overlap some of that work.

- Send the audio to a real-time model and stream audio back. This is native speech-to-speech, the path used by Gemini Live. There is no separate transcription or TTS stage in the main response path, so the model can use vocal cues and avoid those handoffs. It can still call tools! The trade-off is less control over the exact words spoken and no guaranteed text record at every intermediate step.

- Let a real-time model hear the audio, but have it produce text for a separate speech generator to read. This is a half-cascade. It keeps audio cues on the input side and gives you explicit control over the spoken reply. It still has a TTS handoff, and it does not automatically give you a transcript of the caller's words.

The architecture choice does not remove the turn-taking problem. A pause after “move my appointment...” may mean the caller is thinking, not finished. Wait too little and the agent cuts them off; wait too long and the conversation feels slow. If the caller interrupts a reply, playback and conversation state should reflect what they actually heard.

For a booking agent that must call tools and confirm exact details, I would start with the cascaded path because I can inspect both sides of the text workflow. For free-flowing conversation where timing and vocal expression matter most, I would test speech-to-speech. I would try a half-cascade when I want audio-native understanding but need to control the wording or voice of the answer.

Then test all three on the same noisy, interrupted conversations. Measure the first audible response *and* whether the appointment actually moved to the right time!

The Atlantic profiled a UC Davis grad with a close-to-perfect GPA who applied to 200 jobs and heard back from none of them. Around the same time, LinkedIn said it was absorbing 11,000 applications a minute, up 45% in a year.

I've coached PM job seekers through this market every week for two years, and I think most people are misreading what broke.

For about 70 years a résumé did two jobs. It told the employer what you'd done, and it told them how badly you wanted this particular role, because tailoring an application took a real evening. A hiring manager reading a good cover letter was also reading the fact that someone sat down and wrote it.

ChatGPT took that evening down to a few minutes.

Once a polished application costs nothing, everybody sends hundreds, and you get the numbers Annie Lowrey reports. One HR consultant she interviewed pulled a remote posting after 1,200 applications came in. BCG surveyed chief HR officers and found companies using AI to screen résumés, schedule interviews, and even run avatar-led video screens where software scores your tone.

Michael Spence wrote this up in 1973 and eventually got a Nobel for it. A signal only sorts people while it's costly to produce. The moment it goes free, employers can't tell who tailored and who bulk-sent, so they stop reading either one closely. Your résumé still says everything it said in 2019. Employers just quit trusting it.

I see the fallout constantly in coaching. Candidates with strong backgrounds send 300 applications and get nothing, while candidates with weaker résumés land three onsites in a month. The second group moved their effort out of the application form and into places a hiring manager can still see it.

Here's what that looks like for PMs.

Get the referral before you apply. A referral costs the referrer some social capital, which is why hiring managers still trust it. Most of the offers my students landed at OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta AI this year started with a warm intro.

Write to the hiring manager directly. A three-sentence note that mentions something their team shipped last quarter can't be bulk-generated, and they know it.

Show work they can click. A portfolio, a GitHub with one real project, a teardown of their product. Those take hours, and hours are what employers are trying to detect.

Get into the first 50. Greenhouse co-founder Jon Stross has said recruiters see candidates in the order they applied and often stop once they have enough good ones. Apply the day it goes live.

1. Get recruiters coming to you: https://lnkd.in/egeXb7Sc

The candidates getting hired this fall put their effort where a hiring manager can still see it. The UC Davis grad put his where nobody was looking.

hook: Knowing 20 Product Management frameworks doesn't make you a Product Manager.
text:
Knowing 20 Product Management frameworks doesn't make you a Product Manager.

Knowing which one to use, and when, does.

Most aspiring PMs I talk to can recite:

→ RICE
→ MoSCoW
→ Kano
→ AARRR
→ JTBD
→ SWOT

Then they get a real product problem and freeze. Which one do I use?

Here's the shortcut. Each of these was built to answer one question. Figure out your question, and the framework picks itself.

1. What problem are we solving? → JTBD
Ask what job the customer is hiring your product to do. Start here, before you have any ideas.

2. Where are users getting stuck? → AARRR
Acquisition, activation, retention, referral, revenue. Find the stage where people drop off before you fix anything.

3. Is this a must-have or a nice-to-have? → Kano
Some features people expect. Some delight them. Missing a must-have hurts far more than missing a delighter.

4. What should we build first? → RICE
Reach, impact, confidence, effort. Great for ranking a long list. Be honest about confidence. That's where most scores get inflated.

5. What fits before the deadline? → MoSCoW
Must, should, could, won't. Use it when the date can't move. Watch out when everything becomes a Must.

6. Should we do this at all? → SWOT
Strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, threats. It only helps if it ends in a decision.

Notice the order. You understand the problem before you rank solutions. You rank solutions before you cut scope.

And there's one question no framework answers for you: what are we saying no to?

My rule for that one: if it isn't a clear yes, it's a clear no.

I wrote in 2022 that frameworks are easy to learn and the execution takes time. Still true. And the execution starts with knowing which question you're answering.

Learn frameworks.

Just learn the question each one answers first.

If you're working toward your first PM role, start here:

1. Breaking into PM: https://lnkd.in/gHFdYmkn
2. Becoming a PM with no experience: https://lnkd.in/gj2ppv_G
3. Finding the real problem: https://lnkd.in/gtDjdkWX
4. Prioritizing a roadmap: https://lnkd.in/gkjG4mpN
5. Saying no: https://lnkd.in/g_qqRAGa

The best PMs don't ask "Which framework should I use?"

They ask "What question am I trying to answer?"

hook: Digital technology expands what healthcare can do, but to make the most of that potential, different systems need to und
text:
Digital technology expands what healthcare can do, but to make the most of that potential, different systems need to understand each other.

Think of a lab result moving from one healthcare system to another.

Sending the number is not enough.
The receiving system also needs to know what the result refers to, which unit was used, when it was recorded, and which patient it belongs to.

If that context is missing or interpreted differently, the data has travelled, but part of its meaning has not.

This is what interoperability helps solve: different systems can exchange information and interpret it consistently.

Standards provide a common language.

HL7 FHIR (Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources), developed by Health Level Seven International, defines ways to structure and exchange health information.

DICOM (Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine) does the same for medical images and related data.

The same principle applies when information moves between clinical systems and connected devices. Data should not need to be manually “translated” every time it crosses a boundary.

And understanding each other does not mean giving everyone access to everything. Privacy and authorization still determine who can see and use the information.

Good interoperability lets health data move without leaving its meaning behind.

#DigitalHealth #Interoperability

hook: The best salesperson I ever hired was also the worst person I ever managed.
text:
The best salesperson I ever hired was also the worst person I ever managed.

He could walk into any room and come out with a signed contract. He found a customer's pain point faster than anyone I have worked with, and he made them feel like we were the only company on earth who could solve it. Number one on the leaderboard every month without fail.

He was also a nightmare to have in the building.

He was arrogant enough that the rest of the team stopped asking him questions. They stopped learning from him. They started walking on eggshells. The energy in the office changed the moment he arrived, and not in a good way.

For months I told myself he would grow out of it. That the numbers justified it. That I was being oversensitive about something as vague as atmosphere.

He did not grow out of it. And I was not being oversensitive.

Here is the lesson it took me far too long to learn.

Protecting your culture is not the soft decision. It is the bravest one you will make as a leader, because it costs you something immediately and only pays you back slowly.

The moment you let one brilliant, difficult person set the temperature of the room, you have quietly told everybody else that results matter more than how people are treated.

And they will believe you. They will believe you for years.

If you have one of those people on your team right now, you already know the call you need to make.

The only real question is how much longer you are going to put it off.
