hook: Stop telling ChatGPT “Take a deep breath.”
text:
Stop telling ChatGPT “Take a deep breath.”
Stop telling ChatGPT "Think step by step."
Stop telling ChatGPT "right?" & "maybe."

That’s how you end up with generic slop AI answers.

“Give it more context.” Fine. But WHAT context? That's what I get into in this free article on 11 prompting rules: https://lnkd.in/eG6kpMHt

Use these 11 prompting rules instead:

1. Don't direct in one direction in your questions.

“Renting is a waste of money, right?”

You've already told it which side you're on.
Try “Compare buying and renting for my situation.” Give it room to disagree.

2. Tell it who YOU are. Instead of random prompting rules you read in a guide.

“I'm an engineer. I understand the technical side, but I've never sold anything.”

That's useful context. Much more useful than another “think step by step.”

3. Click the links it gives you. Yes, actually open them. AI sounds pretty confident while lying.

An answer can sound great & still be wrong. Check whether the source says what ChatGPT claims it says. A link isn't proof by itself.

4. Start with (only) 3 rules in one prompt.

“3 paragraphs. Under 150 words.”

Easy to check. Start there before adding another 12 requirements.

5. If you have more than 3 rules for one task, ask in 2 different prompts.

Get the draft first. Then:
“Now check your draft against these rules.”

Give the checking its own turn. You don't have to squeeze the whole job into one message.

6. Say what you want help with.

“My open rate dropped. Help me figure out why.”

Start with the problem. Otherwise, you can spend 20 mins writing the email good enough, when the email wasn't the issue at all.

7. Let it ask YOU questions.

“Ask me what you need before you answer.”

The audience, the budget, the thing you already tried. It's all in your head. You haven't told it any of it.

8. Don't settle for yes or no.

“Is A better?” gives you very little to work with.
“Which is better for me, A or B? Here's what matters to me.”

Now there's something to compare.

9. Give it the numbers.

“My emails aren't working” could mean almost anything.
“My open rate went from 40% to 25%.”

Same problem. Much more useful starting point.

10. Tell it what DIDN'T change.

“Same day. Same time. Same format.”

People explain what changed & leave this part out. But it helps narrow down what to look at next.

11. Forget the old prompting rules. It doesn't work on the new models anymore.

“Take a deep breath.”

Fine. But what's the task? Who's it for?
What does a useful answer need to include?
Put that in the prompt.

Start with prompt rule 7. It's the one technique I use in almost all my chats with ChatGPT and Claude, no matter the task I am working on.

Let ChatGPT ask. Spend a few minutes answering. It helps you to think more about the task and give better context.

This is the stuff I write about in how-to-ai.guide.

You can spend 20 mins correcting ChatGPT. Or take the annoying prompt you & check it against these 11 rules: https://lnkd.in/eG6kpMHt

hook: I recently came across the idea of “unclenching.”
text:
I recently came across the idea of “unclenching.”

Basically, becoming aware of the tension you hold in your body, and finding ways to let some of it go.

I think this is a crucial step on the journey to create a "softer" life.
One where your nervous system isn’t jacked up 24/7.

A few ways I’ve been trying to “unclench” lately:

1. Do things (a bit) slower. Walk a bit slower. Eat a bit slower. Turn your podcast back to normal speed. The more you rush through everything, the harder it becomes to switch out of that mode.

2. Practice the “unclenching loop.” A few times a day, I’m trying to notice where I’m holding tension, make one small physical adjustment, and see if anything shifts. Relax the jaw. Drop the shoulders. Exhale a little longer. Basically, catch the clench and soften it.

3. Sauna a few times a week. I always feel noticeably calmer afterward. Which makes sense, because research suggests sauna recovery can shift the nervous system toward a more parasympathetic, “rest and recover” state.

4. Put a curfew on social media. Mine is 8pm. After that, I’m off everything until the next morning. I’ve realized it’s very hard for me to fully unclench when some part of my brain is still waiting for the next notification, message, headline, or thing to respond to.

5. Drink less caffeine. This one is purely personal, but I’ve become much more aware of how physically clenched I feel on high-caffeine days. More jaw tension. More restless energy. So I’ve been experimenting with less.

text:
I think I'm having a Reverse Midlife Crisis.

(And I couldn't be happier about it.)

A few weeks ago, a friend said something at dinner that caught me off guard.

"I think I'm having a midlife crisis."

He's married with two kids.
He lives in the suburbs outside New York and commutes into the city for work.

Good job. Good family. Good life.
In many ways, the archetype of the dream.

But he'd been growing jealous of younger colleagues' freedom.
Scrolling Instagram, his feed filled with a life he felt he was running out of time to live.

In my view, the midlife crisis isn't driven by ego, vanity, or lust so much as fear.

Fear of a door permanently closed.
Fear of a road not taken.
Fear of a season past.

As I reflected on my own life, at a roughly similar stage, I had to be honest:

I think I'm having a Reverse Midlife Crisis.

A Midlife Crisis is about action that chases feelings from the past.
Re-living the things your 18-year-old self would find impressive.

Fast cars. Fancy stuff. Status symbols. Limited responsibilities.

A Reverse Midlife Crisis is about presence that compounds meaning for the future.
Building the things your 80-year-old self will find impressive.

Deep relationships. A healthy body. A grounded mind. Meaningful responsibilities.

Same fear.
Same anxiety.
Same grief over time lost.

The only difference is the direction of the response.

Don't cling to spring.
Stay interested in the changing seasons.

creator: Brij Kishore Pandey
hook: One Architecture Diagram That Explains Every AI Agent
text:
One Architecture Diagram That Explains Every AI Agent
 
Strip away the framework names and every agent you have ever used is the same seven components wired into a loop.
 
Not LangGraph specific. Not CrewAI specific. The pattern holds whether you built it yourself in 200 lines or bought it as a platform.
 
Here is the anatomy.
 
𝗣𝗲𝗿𝗰𝗲𝗽𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗹𝗮𝘆𝗲𝗿
 Input arrives as user text, API calls, sensor data, events, or scheduled triggers. This layer normalizes all of it into something the model can reason over. Most teams underinvest here and then blame the model for bad outputs.
 
𝗥𝗲𝗮𝘀𝗼𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗲𝗻𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗲
 The LLM, running some structured reasoning pattern: chain of thought, ReAct, plan then execute. Its real job is one decision, made repeatedly: can I answer this directly, or do I need to act first?
 
𝗣𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗺𝗼𝗱𝘂𝗹𝗲
 When the answer is no, the goal gets decomposed into ordered subtasks. This is the component people skip when they prototype, and the one they retrofit painfully once tasks stop fitting in a single hop.
 
𝗠𝗲𝗺𝗼𝗿𝘆 𝘀𝘆𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗺
 Two distinct systems that get collapsed into one far too often. Short term holds conversation context and working state. Long term holds vector stores, episodic memory, and learned patterns. Different write policies, different retrieval logic, different failure modes.
 
𝗧𝗼𝗼𝗹 𝗲𝘅𝗲𝗰𝘂𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗹𝗮𝘆𝗲𝗿
 Where the agent touches the world. MCP servers, API calls, code execution, database queries, file systems, external services. Results flow back into reasoning, and the loop asks again: goal achieved?
 
𝗚𝘂𝗮𝗿𝗱𝗿𝗮𝗶𝗹𝘀
 Permissions, approval gates, content filtering, rate limits, human checkpoints. Notice in the diagram that guardrails run vertically alongside everything rather than sitting at one entry point. That placement is the whole argument. A gate at the input does nothing about what the agent decides to do on step four.
 
𝗢𝗯𝘀𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗮𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗶𝘁𝘆
 Traces, logs, metrics, cost tracking, latency monitoring. It spans the full width because you cannot debug a loop by inspecting one node in it. You need the trajectory.
 
The interesting part is not the boxes. It is the two diamonds: "can I answer directly" and "goal achieved". Those are the only places the agent actually decides anything. Everything else is plumbing. When agents misbehave in production, the fault is almost always in how those two checks were specified, not in the model doing the reasoning.
 
Where do you draw the line between an agent and a workflow that happens to call an LLM? 

My working definition is whether the system chooses its own next step rather than following a predetermined path, but that gets blurry the moment a planner writes the steps in advance.

I have a weekly reminder in my phone:

To tell my sons how proud I am of them.

I try to do it every Sunday night and I share specific examples.

Occasionally, they’re big things:

- Making it through the first day of school.
- Going with a new teacher for an activity with no parents.

But most of the time, it’s the small stuff:

- Giving their brother a hug when they're having a hard time.
- Saying thank you to the waitress at the restaurant.
- Trying again when he makes a mistake (sometimes a few in a row).
- Asking his Mom how he can help when she’s doing something.

Growing up in my family, the word “proud” was shared sparingly by my Dad.

It was saved for major milestones and achievements.

That put me in constant approval seeking mode.

And it made me overlook the journey in favor of the outcome.

I think most men have a similar experience.

I want to break that cycle in my family.

I want my boys to know that I’m ALWAYS proud of them.

Not because they got an A+, made the varsity team, or scored some big name job.

But because they are working to be kind, thoughtful, and to make the world better for the people around them.

So, if you read this far…

Think of one man in your life today.

And tell them you’re proud of them. 

They’ll appreciate it more than you know. 

- AB ✌

text:
Trust is a competitive advantage for agents and AI. I see a lack of trust block a buying decision at least once a week. “We can’t use it if we don’t know what it does with our metadata and our customers’ data.” My clients usually default to building agents internally, leveraging open-source models they control.

We realized that using frontier models internally for client work was a nonstarter. I can’t be sure I wouldn’t be violating our NDAs and DPAs, so everything we do with agents leverages Nemotron and runs on hardware we control. Transparent architecture can be audited to earn clients’ trust.

Using agents and AI means we must trust the company behind the agent with some of our most sensitive and valuable data. We must trust them to build models that are accurate and agents that put our best interests above theirs.

I think Meta has one of the most interesting and promising product roadmaps for AI and agents, especially on the hardware side. But adoption requires trust. It must be architected into every agent and AI product. So far, most are architected to put the company that makes them ahead of the people paying for them.

Today, I run an $8,000,000/year writing business.

8 insane (even dumb) things I did to get here:

1. No internet.

When I was in my early 20s, I didn't allow myself to have Internet in my apartment until I finished writing my first book, Confessions of a Teenage Gamer. 

It took me 4 years. 

But I did it.

2. Started my first company with only $5k.

I started my first company at 26 years old with $5,000 in savings and no back-up plan.

3. I convinced one of my best friends to quit his job and build a ghostwriting agency with me. 

And when he said it was too risky, I removed the risk by:

• Working double-time
• Paid him a "salary" out of my savings for 4 months

I did this until we figured out how to land more clients.

4. I got put in the hospital.

When our agency took off, I pushed myself so hard I ended up in the hospital with shingles.

Instead of stopping, I popped painkillers for a month and continued taking sales calls, client calls, and interviews with new hires.

5. Had multiple side projects.

While working 60+ hours/week, I took on side projects helping crypto companies with their messaging and getting paid in tokens. 

All of them went to 0. Learned a lot though!

6. Took on investors.

We sold 20% of our ghostwriting agency to 2 angel investors, knowing there was massive risk in this being the wrong decision for the company (it was) but also knowing we'd learn a ton in the process (we did).

7. Took hardly any vacation.

When I finally took a vacation in 2019 (my first real vacation in years), I realized I was on the wrong path.

I also realized nobody could get me off the Ferris wheel except me.

Came home & fired 20+ people on 1 Zoom call, shutting down my agency.

8. Building Ship 30 for 30 on nights & weekends. 

When I started Ship 30 with Dickie Bush, I was still ghostwriting (to pay the bills) and he was still working at BlackRock. 

We both worked:

This guy helped create ChatGPT. His new startup is in talks at a $10 billion valuation.

Meet Diogo Almeida.

He worked at Google Brain. He worked at OpenAI. He was a co-author on the RLHF training paper behind ChatGPT.

Then he left.

He spent two years in stealth with his co-founders, Erik Gafni and Sasha Sheng, on a $40 million seed led by DCVC at a $200 million valuation.

On September 15, they finally came out of stealth and launched their first model, Jev.

The launch video has 38 million+ views on X. And Jev became the fastest-adopted model in the history of Vercel's AI Gateway, with 13% of paid teams using it in the first 24 hours.

That's both viral success and adoption, which is pretty insane in an AI market that's incredibly crowded and has pretty much been dominated by two players for much of the last three years.

We've seen lots of new model launches from big names, including Mira Murati. But Diogo Almeida seems to have shaken up AI the most with Jev.

I spent the last week with it, and I haven't been able to stop using it.

Here are just a couple use cases that are pretty interesting.

First, it can do browser use much more cheaply. We all know browser use is one of the most expensive tasks we're doing with models like Opus and Fable right now. Fable charges $10 per million input tokens and $50 per million output tokens.

Jev charges $0.042 per million input tokens, and doesn't even charge for output.

So it can very, very cheaply use browsers, and it's actually quite accurate. It doesn't hallucinate anything because of the architecture it's built on. It can only pick from the answers you define.

Another interesting use case is doing any sort of instant evals, which is really important for product teams. You can instantly get live evaluations of things at almost no cost.

In fact, in the last week I've been using Jev, I haven't even blown past the $5 in free credits they start you with. That's how cheap it is.

And it's basically instantaneous. It's much faster than an LLM because an LLM writes its answer one token at a time, and every token waits on the one before it. Jev doesn't write anything. It answers every question you give it in parallel and hands back a decision with a probability attached, in 70 to 500 milliseconds.

Madhu Narasimhan, CIO at DaVita, on what has to be true before you scale AI in healthcare, and what turns employees from trying AI into trusting it.
Sohrab Rahimi, Director of AI/ML at Google, on agent protocols. His sharpest point: the transport layer is solved, the semantic layer is wide open. Two agents can speak perfect A2A, return a success code, and still disagree about what a customer is.

None of these are about model quality.

They own the context layer. Indexed once, served everywhere, so agents stop rediscovering the company on every request.

Permissions travel with the work. Shared threads answering under each person's access is harder than it looks, which is why most tools avoid them.

MY TAKE
We spent 2 years benchmarking models. In 2026 we benchmark systems. That is a category growing up.

hook: How can Qwen3.5-35B-A3B have 35B total parameters but activate only about 3B for each token? Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) ro
text:
How can Qwen3.5-35B-A3B have 35B total parameters but activate only about 3B for each token? Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) routing explains the computation, and it changes how we should think about serving the model!

Picture a transformer layer with a bank of feed-forward networks instead of one. Each network is an *expert*. The token's current hidden state goes to a small router, which scores the experts and sends that state to a selected few. Those experts each transform it; their outputs are combined and passed to the next layer. The choice happens again for the next token and at the next MoE layer.

That is the source of the “active” number. Qwen3.5-35B-A3B has 256 routed experts per MoE layer and selects eight for a token, alongside a shared expert. The token uses a fraction of the expert bank in that pass. It still goes through the model's other shared computation. Active parameters describe work along one token's path, not the number of weights in the checkpoint.

The serving consequence is easy to miss! Different tokens may choose different experts. For low-latency serving, the full expert bank needs to be ready in accelerator memory. Quantization can reduce its size. CPU offload saves accelerator memory but makes the engine transfer chosen weights when it needs them.

Put different experts on different GPUs and you have *expert parallelism*. The serving engine sends a token's hidden state to the GPUs holding its selected experts, runs their feed-forward computation, then brings the outputs back together. One token may need several GPUs. This spreads weight memory across devices, while dispatch and return traffic enter the inference path. If many tokens select experts on one GPU, that GPU can become the bottleneck even when the expert counts look evenly divided.

I would size an MoE deployment from the total stored weights, the runtime state, and the intended batch and context length. If the weights and runtime state fit on one accelerator, I would start there and avoid cross-GPU dispatch. If they do not, I would test compression or expert parallelism, depending on the memory shortfall and available GPU links. A 3B active label tells me how much of the model runs per token; it cannot size the serving hardware for me.

hook: Before you add another LLM call, look at what your application actually needs back.
text:
Before you add another LLM call, look at what your application actually needs back.
A lot of the time it needs a category, a score, or a yes or no.

I've been looking at Jev, the System One model from TypeSafe AI, for exactly that kind of work. You pass it context and a set of defined questions. 

It returns typed answers with probabilities attached, and your code can route, classify, or score on them directly.

LLMs can already return JSON constrained to a schema. Jev gets there differently:
An autoregressive LLM writes the answer out token by token.

Jev scores the defined outcomes in parallel and never writes prose.
If your workflow makes dozens of small decisions per request, that difference is worth measuring.

𝗔 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗹 𝗲𝘅𝗮𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲
A support ticket comes in: "I was charged twice. Please refund the extra payment."

That one message holds four separate jobs:
Route it to the right team
Detect whether the customer is asking for a refund
Check payment records against refund rules
Write the reply

I'd test Jev on 1 and 2. Step 3 stays in application code. Step 4 goes to an LLM. Anything below your confidence threshold goes to a person.

I keep those jobs apart on purpose. A high probability that the customer asked for a refund tells you nothing about whether the refund should be approved. Your rules make that call.

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝗵𝗮𝘃𝗲 𝘁𝗼 𝗱𝗼
A cleanly typed answer can still be wrong. Before you trust it:
Measure accuracy on your own ticket history
Check calibration, so 0.9 means right about 90% of the time on your data
Set thresholds based on what a mistake costs you

𝗛𝗼𝘄 𝗜'𝗱 𝘀𝗽𝗹𝗶𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸
Explicit rules go in code.
Judgment calls inside a fixed set of options are where a decision model is worth evaluating.
Anything that needs language goes to a generative model.

Then judge the whole workflow on accuracy, latency, cost, and how much human review it creates. Benchmarking one component on its own won't tell you much.

Which step in your agent workflow only needs a label, a score, or a yes or no back?

text:
Most businesses put almost all their energy into winning the customer and almost none into the fortnight straight afterwards.

Facebook's growth team had a name for the thing they were hunting for. They worked out that new users who connected with a handful of friends early on were far more likely to still be around months later, and then built everything around getting people to that point quickly.

We used the same thinking at Fanbytes, and it is still one of the first questions I ask the companies I am involved with now. Not how do we sell more, but what actually happens in the first two weeks after somebody says yes, and is any of it memorable.

Usually the honest answer is that nothing happens. An invoice, a login, and silence.

So map those fourteen days properly. Find the point where a new customer first thinks this was a good decision, then work out how to get them there sooner and make it deliberate rather than accidental.

Most retention is won before anyone has had time to churn.

If you want to get paid more, you need to understand this 1 simple framework:

You can't have upside without volatility. 

The reason most jobs don't have upside is because they don't have volatility.

That's the trade.

You make "less" because what you make is consistent. 

If you want to make more, you have to build the skill of managing your own psychology to tolerate periods where what you make is inconsistent.

That's what you're getting paid "more" to do.

Your value is not just the hard skills you have.

It's the meta-skill of being able to stomach volatility and still perform at an elite level.

Here are the 3 levels of volatility:

1. Roles with performance bonuses (but a base salary) 

This is beginner mode.

Minimal upside, zero downside.

2. Sales (commission-only) 

This is intermediate mode.

More upside, more downside.

3. Entrepreneurship 

This is expert mode.

Maximum upside, maximum downside.

The older I get and the more companies I build, the more I understand why so many people don't pursue entrepreneurship.

Because it requires you to live in a constant state of risk. 

For example:

When you're in a commission-only role and performance is down, yes you make less money.

But your worst-case scenario is capped at $0. 

When you're an entrepreneur, and performance is down in your business, yes you make less money.

But your worst-case scenario is uncapped.

You don't go to $0.

You go negative. 

Which is why entrepreneurs tend to be the highest-earning category of worker.

Not because they're the "smartest," but because they are the most vulnerable.

Entrepreneurs get paid to feel the weight of the one thing everyone works very hard to avoid:

Uncertainty. 

I used to think everyone should want to become an entrepreneur.

I don't think that anymore.

I think some people's skills are much better suited and more easily maximized within an organization.

And most people perform better when they're exempt from the existential risk of:

"...What happens if it doesn't work?" 

But whether you become an entrepreneur or not, it's important to understand why some roles have more upside than others. 

Because everyone says they want more upside...

Until they experience more volatility.

And you can't have one without the other.

Starting from vagueness instead of specificity.

I've seen 1,000s of creators do this.

hook: I asked my mom & dad for advice recently from raising me and my brother...
text:
I asked my mom & dad for advice recently from raising me and my brother...

This is what they told me, maybe you’ll find it useful too:

1. Your kids are not your friends. 

They’re yours to safeguard and support, but set rules. Biggest problem with most kids in our generation, their parents wanted to be liked not respected.

2. Psy ops are underrated. 

My mom had this line for whenever I got into trouble. She’d say, “When I ask you a question like this, I already know the answer. I am giving you a chance to come clean...” 

At which point I’d sing like a canary because I’m a scaredy cat. I found out today she rarely knew the answers. Brilliant and maniacal.

3. Always on the same page. 

My mom and dad rarely fought in front of my brother and I. They would never go back on the word of the other. United front to deal with us mini terrorists.

4. Make time. 

My dad had this silly line that is actually not silly: “You can make money, you can make a cake, but you can’t make time.” So they made allllll the time for us.

5. Four chairs. 

We have these four chairs in our living room, no tv. 

Growing up, we’d sit and debate and talk for hours. Politics. Opinions. Our days. Only thing not allowed was an opinion you couldn’t defend unemotionally. We still do this today.

6. Mi Sangre mi siempre. 

They’d always say, blood comes first. They meant it. I hired my brother, my dad, my mom, my cousin at times. We stick together and we may fight like hell but never in front of others.

7. Once you decide, you don’t quit. 

We could play any sport or instrument BUT if we committed we had to play the full year all out. No 3 lessons and quit. Taught us to choose thoughtfully and keep going even when it hurt.

8. Always call. 

They still pick up the phone nearly every time it’s family. My dad in a meeting will pause to answer my mom. My husband taught me this too, and I try to do the same. If they’re your first priority this is an easy way to prove it.

9. You’re not a princess, you’re a president. 

My dad always used to say that line. 

He told me recently that I lived up to it. Gutted me. He taught us we didn’t need to be saved, instead we could save ourselves and help others.

10. Hug often and seriously. 

If you’ve ever hugged my parents, they mean it when they do it. 

Such a simple, free gesture. My mom always gives you a hug and says vaya con dios… go with God. How can you not do big things with parents that hold you like that?

Just some Lessons from the Road from parents I happen to think are some of the best in the world.

Moms and dads everywhere, I’m in awe of you.

Hardest job I’ve ever seen.

*This is one of my favorite pics of me and my dad. Doesn’t get old.

To become an AI PM, you need six skills on top of core PM. Here's the order to learn them.

The pay gap is why it's worth it. Glassdoor puts the average AI PM at $198K in total pay, against about $151K for PMs overall.

Most AI PM learning maps I see are generic PM concepts with "AI" in the title. They skip what hiring managers screen for, which is proof you've done the work.

So in this map, every stage ends in something you can show.

1. Learn how the models work

Tokens, context windows, embeddings, tool calls, agents. You don't need to train a model, but you should be able to sketch everything that happens between a user's prompt and the reply. A PM I coach hit exactly this depth check in technical screens at both Nvidia and Glean.

2. Engineer the context

Everyone rents the same models, so the edge is what you feed them. Climb only as far as you need. Prompting first, RAG when answers depend on your data, fine-tuning when a style has to stick. Your proof is a Claude Project loaded with your past PRDs that drafts a spec your team would sign off on.

3. Hand work to agents

Chat answers a question. An agent finishes the whole task, as long as your brief has a goal, the right context, the tools it can touch and a clear definition of done. Your proof is one recurring task, like a weekly competitor recap, running on Claude Code or Codex while you only review the output.

4. Prototype it yourself

Alex Danilowicz, CEO of Magic Patterns, said on my podcast that the classic mistake is spending two hours debugging a database when all you needed was a clickable mockup to show five customers. Reach for Bolt.new when you need real data and logins, and Magic Patterns for flows on your design system.

5. Ship it to real users

AI fails in ways no demo shows. Before launch, instrument task success rate, human handoff rate, cost per successful task and how often users hit regenerate. Then put your prototype on a live URL and synthesize feedback from 20 real users.

6. Prove it with evals

A vibe check is an eval. You're using your own brain as the scoring function, which works right up until you're the bottleneck. Hamel Husain and Shreya Shankar walked me through the sequence I'd copy. Read 100 real traces, name the failure modes, add cheap code checks, then build one LLM judge per failure mode and check it against your own labels.

Your proof is your top five failure modes, each with an eval that catches it.

Stack all six proofs and you have an AI PM portfolio.

creator: Damien Benveniste
hook: How should AI agent model routing choose which LLM gets the next turn? NVIDIA's NeMo Switchyard is an open-source router
text:
How should AI agent model routing choose which LLM gets the next turn? NVIDIA's NeMo Switchyard is an open-source router for agent requests, making that choice as a job moves from routine file reads to a difficult failing test. The key is what evidence the router has *when* it chooses.

Picture a coding agent asked to fix a failing test. Its first request reaches a router, which chooses a model and forwards the conversation. The agent reads files, edits code, and runs tests through its tools. Its next model request includes those results. The router can keep the same model or choose again. That is where it gets interesting! We can make the choice from three different kinds of evidence:

- Look at the task before work begins. That is task routing: a rule or classifier maps the request to a model tier. “Summarize these files” may go to the efficient model; “investigate this intermittent failure” may go to the capable one. The choice is quick when the task is recognizable, but the opening request cannot reveal every complication the agent will encounter.

- Look at execution as it unfolds. A stage router reads recent tool results: repeated errors or stalled exploration suggest the capable model; steady progress may favor the efficient model. This can change the target on each turn without paying for a separate judge call, but it needs tool signals that actually reflect progress. A file edit by itself does not prove the hard part is over!

- Start efficiently, then escalate. In escalation routing, a separate judge checks the agent's progress and moves a struggling task to the capable model after enough bad turns. This can rescue work whose difficulty was invisible in the first request. The judge call and the cheap model's failed attempts are part of the bill, though, and escalation cannot undo time already spent.

I would start by testing a fixed efficient model and a fixed capable model on a set of *complete agent tasks*. Then compare routing with both baselines. Measure accepted outcomes, elapsed time, model calls, retries, and judge cost. If the cheap model already finishes almost everything, a router may add complexity without much value. If failures cluster in turns that your tool trace can identify, stage routing is worth testing. If difficulty appears only after several attempts, escalation is the more natural experiment.

LangChain's 145-task Deep Agents evaluation of Switchyard illustrates the trade: escalation cost 74% less than its frontier-only baseline, but task accuracy was about six points lower, and the judge consumed 21.2% of routed spend. On that suite, routing was not clearly better than the efficient model alone. I would want to see all three results before choosing a router for my workload.

text: I've been building The Rundown for 3.5 years, and we've grown to 20+ people. And until last week, we'd never all been in the same room! This was our first-ever team retreat, in Lisbon. People flew in from Canada, Switzerland, Seattle, San Diego, Chicago, Florida, Greece, France, India, and Hong Kong. One person traveled over 27 hours to be there. I'll be honest, I was a little worried. Put a bunch of people who work on the internet all day in one room, and I figured it'd be quiet. Lots of introverts. Lots of awkward small talk. I was wrong. The one thing everyone kept saying all week: they were shocked at how open and friendly everyone was. You'd never guess it was our first time meeting. Some context on how this happened. Earlier this year, I sold a stake in The Rundown AI and partnered with Electrify to take us from newsletters to multi-platform media. If you don't know them, they run some of the biggest tech YouTube channels on the planet: Veritasium, Fireship, Mentour Pilot, Astrum, and many more. They're fully remote too, so every 6 months they bring everyone together. Sessions on feedback, improving our media, and where we're all heading next. I'm super grateful they included The Rundown. It meant we could finally all be in one place. Being fully remote and async is a big reason we can deliver AI news this fast. I wouldn't change it. But a few days in person did something Slack never could. I know it's small. But for my first company, getting everyone together is a big deal. Can't wait to do the next one.

text: If you're an AI power user who wants to adopt new models and tools sooner rather than later, the best way to decide what earns a place in your work is a personal AI benchmark: a small set of your own real requests, given to several AI options side by side, with the names hidden. Last week I ran mine on seven models and five tasks from my own work. The model I use every day came last. I would not have guessed it, and I would not have believed a leaderboard that told me. Nathaniel Whittemore and I ran a Frontier Lab on how to build one, in five steps: 1. Find your tasks. Four to six real requests that cover what you really do: daily habits, rare high-stakes moments, and one thing you wish AI did better. Pick work where you can spot a weak answer fast. 2. Choose your options. Two to four models or tools, including what you use today. I tested seven, and that was too many to judge well. 3. Run the tryout. Same request, same settings, a fresh chat each time. 4. Hide the names and pick. Read every answer before you judge any. Brand preference is louder than most of us expect. 5. Decide: Switch, Split, or Stay. A clear win on tasks that matter moves you. A close call goes to cost, speed, and habit. 💡 Three things my own run taught me: - Write down what good looks like before you see a single answer. - An AI judge can score alongside you, and it needs checking too. My first one gave top marks to almost everything. - The best-looking result was also among the slowest and most expensive, so cost and speed belong in the decision. You build it once and reuse it for months: when the next release lands, rerun the same requests and see whether it earns a place in your lineup. hook: I spent 48 hours in SF with billionaires, data labs and AI founders running $1B to $100B companies. Here's what stood ou
text: I spent 48 hours in SF with billionaires, data labs and AI founders running $1B to $100B companies. Here's what stood out: 1. So many stories of data brokers making $2M a week selling company data to AI labs. I can't tell if it's the beginning or a bubble, and I'm still figuring out which niches are left. 2. At dinner, someone asked the table: "If a new model drops next month, does your company get better or worse?" Half the table went quiet. Best question to ask any AI startup right now. 3. The new bar is $1B in revenue in 12 months. What nobody talked about was retention. I think we'll see a lot of AI companies with huge revenue and terrible retention. 4. We're living through the reinvention of the computer. The model is the CPU, the harness is the operating system, and skills and plugins are the apps. Seeing it that way makes the whitespace easier to spot. 5. Agent harnesses are the new GPT wrappers, in a good way. The best teams treat the model as swappable and route different models to different jobs. One founder told me the model is maybe 20% of the product. The rest is industry data, expert-written evals, permissions and a clean review screen. 6. Software is getting easy to copy. Someone showed me about 10 apps worth $5B+ each that he'd cloned. If software can be rebuilt this fast, the value moves to data, and some SaaS companies are secretly data companies. 7. Every company wants to plug its internal data into agents. Then they look at the data and realize it's a mess. Cleaning that up is a big opportunity. 8. A consumer exec told me the next fight is over memory. The AI that remembers the most about you wins. 9. Physical AI came up a lot. A robotics founder told me the hardest problems in AI are now deployment problems. Their robots call a human when they get stuck, and every call becomes training data. 10. Some startups are worth more dead than alive. A shut-down company with years of Slack, email and code can get paid to license it. 11. The hire everyone wants: someone with taste who can write evals. AI can generate endless ideas. The hard part is knowing which ones are good. 12. Distribution is the bottleneck. Founders are sponsoring buses, buying billboards and throwing parties with famous DJs. It feels a bit like the dotcom era. Attention is what's scarce. Always good to get a dose of SF. Feeling inspired and lucky to have had such a fun trip. Locked in and happy to be home and building. hook: A.A. Milne's New Nib Rule for getting more done: Winnie the Pooh turned 100 yesterday. But he might never have existed I
text: A.A. Milne's New Nib Rule for getting more done: Winnie the Pooh turned 100 yesterday. But he might never have existed If A.A. Milne hadn't discovered his New Nib Rule. Milne cracked consistent creativity when working as an assistant editor at Punch. There, he had to produce a weekly 1,200-word article that packed “a smile in every paragraph and a laugh in every inch.” Under this pressure, he knew what it felt like to be stuck: "Sometimes... I sit at my desk and wonder if there is any possible subject in the whole world upon which I can possibly find anything to say". But then on other days he found, "I do not need to bother about a subject. To-day I am without a care. Nothing less has happened than that I have a new nib in my pen". The task had stayed the same. But the new nib brought more pleasure to it. James Clear would call this making the task "more attractive". So often, we think of productivity as something bleak and disciplined. When the most productive thing we can do is get back in touch with the pleasure of the act itself. I'm seeing this as I work through The Artist's Way. Small acts of self-care and tokens of indulgence (like some new pens and notebooks) can go a long way to opening up a new stream of output. The challenge: this goes against what we believe "hard work" must look like. It's far from the puritanical showdown, the wrestling match with ourselves, that we've come to believe is "being productive". At first, it feels wrong to indulge ourselves, no matter how obvious it is that we'll do more of what we enjoy. So buy yourself that new pen. Let yourself work from that cafe. Start with the task you'll enjoy most for a change. And if you feel resistance to doing this That's exactly why it's so powerful. A.A. Milne discovered this. Now you can too. What's a small pleasure that gets your work going? Share below- it might inspire else. Photo credit: New Statesman

text: I sat down with Jensen Huang , CEO of NVIDIA , to discuss one of the biggest concerns surrounding AI: safety and security, and what NVIDIA is doing to address them. Jensen has been vocal about his opposition to pausing AI development. His argument is that AI safety is fundamentally an engineering problem, and we need to build the technology to solve it. But here's where things get interesting. At GTC Berlin yesterday, NVIDIA introduced its new OpenShell Reference Architecture, designed to make autonomous AI agents safer to deploy. The idea is surprisingly straightforward: → Give AI agents only the permissions they actually need. → Isolate them from sensitive systems and data. → Continuously monitor their behaviour. → Enforce security boundaries independently of the agents themselves. → Use hardware-level controls to stop agents that violate those boundaries, potentially within milliseconds. NVIDIA is essentially building a security layer for a world where billions of AI agents could be working autonomously. And I think this represents an important shift in how we approach AI safety. For years, much of the conversation has focused on making AI models safer through training, alignment and guardrails. But as AI moves from answering questions to executing actions, model-level safety alone won't be enough. We also need to secure the environments in which AI operates. Of course, this doesn't solve every AI safety challenge. Questions around misuse, alignment and long-term risks remain. But it is a concrete example of turning safety research into engineering. hook: “SEO takes time” is probably the most repeated line in marketing. Earlier this month, Google finally put numbers on what
text: “SEO takes time” is probably the most repeated line in marketing. Earlier this month, Google finally put numbers on what “time” actually means. Google shared typical and slowest times for 23 steps between publishing a page and seeing it in search. I’ll be honest, the typical times didn’t surprise me much. The slowest ones did. A few that stood out to me (typical vs slowest): - Discovering a new page: ~20 hours vs weeks to never - Recrawling an existing page: ~30 days vs weeks to never - Indexing a page: ~1.5 hours vs months, or never - Processing a site migration: 1-3 months vs 6 months to 1 year+ - Recovering from a core update: 3-6 months vs 6 months to 1 year That word “never” comes up A LOT, and it’s often tied to quality. My takeaway: you can’t speed your way past a page Google doesn’t think is worth keeping. The 30-day recrawl is the one I’d pin to every marketer’s wall. Google can index a change in about 1.5 hours, but only once it comes back to your page. For an existing page, that’s typically a month. So when someone says “we updated it last week and nothing happened”, that’s usually why. It matters for AI search too, which is my world. Google said AI Overviews and AI Mode use the same crawler as regular search, so the same clock applies here. What I’d do with this: 1. Before deciding a change didn’t work, check when Google last crawled the page with URL Inspection in Search Console. 2. If new pages aren’t getting indexed, look at quality before you touch the sitemap. 3. If you’re migrating, plan in months and keep monitoring long after launch. 4. If you’ve been hit by a core update, give your fixes time. Recovery is measured in months. I’ve put all 23 processes into the graphic. Save it for the next time someone asks why their SEO changes aren’t showing up.

hook: We asked 441 founders, executives, and high performers to rate their life across 10 different dimensions. Here's what we
text: We asked 441 founders, executives, and high performers to rate their life across 10 different dimensions. Here's what we found: 1. Mental was scored by far the lowest. It came in last in every age group, whether people rated the rest of their lives high or low overall. 2. Health was ranked the highest. 3. People who rated their Mental low ranked all 9 other areas of their life significantly lower (p < 0.001). 4. People who rated their Mental high ranked all 9 other areas of their life significantly higher (p < 0.001). 5. Even though Mental was ranked lowest, very few people had goals related to improving it. Most goals centered around family (61%), meaningful work (59%), time freedom (51%), financial independence (47%), and physical health (46%). - We believe Health ranks highest because it's the most measurable and understood. Founders, executives, and higher performers tend to approach their physical health proactively. We believe Mental ranks the lowest because it's the least measurable and understood. Unlike physical health, most people approach their Mental health reactively. One possible conclusion is that the Mental domain may be the biggest constraint in people's lives, yet it often goes unrecognized. Most people point their goals outward to time, money, family, and physical health. The data points to something counterintuitive: That perhaps the fastest path for people to achieve their external goals like time, money, and family, is to focus on the Mental domain first. Among the people we tracked over time, those who improved their Mental domain experienced 3X more improvements across all 9 other areas of their life than those whose Mental didn't improve (p < 0.001). - Link to the full study in the comments, which includes methods, limitations, and additional findings.

text: Marketing is an “out-of-focus” skill by 2030... At least according to 1,000+ employers. I’ve worked in marketing for 10 years, so this one stung a bit. My first reaction was to argue with it. Then I looked at the top right: → AI and big data → Analytical thinking → Creative thinking → Curiosity and lifelong learning → Resilience and agility → Leadership And realised that’s basically what my days look like now. Last year I moved from Sweden to London to be employee #2 at an AI search company. I came up through community and content. But building our marketing engine from scratch looked nothing like the marketing I learned. It was systems, data, building workflows with AI and then the creative and human parts on top. So no, I don’t think marketing is dying. I think the job is splitting in two. The marketers who win the next five years won’t be the best at any one channel. They’ll be the ones who can design the system behind them. That’s what I share in my newsletter every week: the AI workflows behind that engine, and how to scale them. And the bar is moving super fast! PwC found AI-exposed entry-level jobs are now 7× more likely to require skills that used to come with seniority. What used to set senior marketers apart is becoming the entry requirement. So the question isn’t “will AI replace marketers?” It’s which half of the chart you’re building. Which top-right skill are you working on this year?

text: Every time I get excited about a content idea, I give it the Dinner Party Test.™ Here's how it works. Imagine you're a guest at someone else's dinner party. Not an intimate dinner, and not a full-on party. So there's, say, 6 of you. You're with friends, but they're primarily the hosts's friends. Not your besties. Now explain your idea to them. How do you communicate? - What jargon do you leave out, which do you make it a point to include? - What's relevant/funny/surprising/resonant? - What are the high-level details? - What's the point? And remember, this is dinner conversation, so you can't be boring. You have to get them to care at least a little. If your idea doesn't pass the Dinner Test, it needs some work. Maybe it needs a better hook, or maybe it needs additional angles. I taught this concept in my Content Marketing 201 course. And funny enough, it's a similar sort of framework my publisher has for his authors. (Only he calls it the Happy Hour Pitch!) text: Interesting data! We tracked 202 founders and leaders who completed the ENCODED mental training protocol. Here's what we found: 1. People who completed the protocol rated their lives higher in every area: time, financial, social, creative, location, purpose, relationship, health, mental, and spiritual. 2. The biggest improvements were in Mental (+2.07) and Purpose (+2.05). These were also the lowest areas to start. 3. Improvement happens fast. People reported significant improvements across all areas of life within 51 days (p < 0.001). 4. Improvements kept growing with continued training. People who trained longer reported increasing benefits over time ( p < 0.001). The ENCODED protocol combines established research principles across neuroscience, psychology, and performance research, including: -Self-concept clarity -Belief updating -Future-self clarity -Selective attention -Cognitive offloading -Identity-consistent action The initial research begins to demonstrate that converting these established concepts into a daily training routine can significantly improve someone's mental wellbeing, relationship quality, and overall life satisfaction. Despite the positive results for the people who completed the training, 239 people who started the protocol failed to build the habit and didn't complete the protocol (54%). This failure rate is similar to established research on exercise dropout rates by the NIH, where they found 63% of people quit an exercise routine within 90 days. We're still early in our research, but these initial findings are encouraging: People who commit to the ENCODED mental training protocol reported positive improvements across every area of life. And their life ratings continued to improve the longer they trained, much like how progress works with physical exercise. It's pretty obvious: in the future, mental training will be as common sense as exercise. - Link to the full study, methods, results, and limitations in the comments.

text: I told Claude to "make it better" 100 times in a row and it went too far. I gave Claude Code a hideous coffee shop website and sent it the same prompt 100 times in a row, once with Sonnet 5.5 and once with Opus 5.5. Every round was a fresh session with no skills, CLAUDE.md , plugins, or memory, so each model only had its own knowledge and built-in tools. The prompt told it to look at the site, think outside the box, make one bold change, use any tool it had, and ship something every round. I had to force that last part because when I tried this before, it would stop around round 20 and say nothing else could be done. The two models went in very different directions: → Sonnet made small, careful changes for 100 rounds, mostly to the ordering flow. It finished in under 2 hours for about $22 in API value, and the site got better without going off the rails. → Opus kept inventing: voice ordering, a chat assistant, a pumpkin you can carve, a Spanish toggle. It ran for 8.5 hours, used about $137 in API value, and ended at 21,000 lines with features breaking each other. → Neither model searched the web once in 200 rounds, even though the tool was right there and the prompt kept telling it to innovate. I really thought it would go look at award-winning sites or component libraries for ideas, but every single idea came from what the model already knew. So AI can probably get you to an 80 out of 100 on its own, but the last 20 still takes someone with taste pointing it at the right inspiration. text: It's almost 𝘯𝘰-vember. 5 minimalist habits to avoid burnout this month: 🍂 1. Make no your default. In the words of Derek Sivers, if it’s not a “hell yes,” it’s a no. No to that extra project when your plate is full. No to overgiving and stretching yourself thin. No to what doesn’t align with your goals. Every no this month declutters some space for the right yes. —— 2. Create (and keep) boundaries. If your work hours are 9am - 6pm, don’t answer that 10pm email. It can probably wait until morning. Your boundaries teach people how to treat you. If you don't respect them, no one else will either. —— 3. Understand what’s urgent vs. important. Answering that ping on your phone? Might feel really urgent. But spending quality time with your kids before bed? That’s important. The happiest people I know do the important things first. —— 4. Prioritize rest. Cutting 1 hour of sleep tonight might seem like gaining 1 hour to get stuff done… But 1 less hour of sleep actually = 2+ fewer hours of productivity tomorrow. A foggy brain moves slower. —— 5. Enjoy single-tasking. If I asked you what your priorities are right now, you could probably list them out. There are about ~5 of them, right? But there should only be 1 at a time. I love this quote from Greg McKeown: “The word priority came into the English language in the 1400s. It was singular… It stayed singular for the next five hundred years.” By definition, priority = 1 thing. Try this: Every morning, put your phone in Do Not Disturb mode for 1-2 hours and get your #1 most important thing done. This is the magic of doing fewer things, better. —— Enjoy your 𝘯𝘰-vember. Your future self will thank you. 🍂 ☕️ Save this post to re-read later ➕ Follow me (Jade Bonacolta) for daily posts on minimalism, productivity hacks, and how to build a quietly rich life.

text: Most companies have a fix that's been waiting since March. Until it ships, a workaround keeps things running. Barely. Ours is a formatting bug. hook: When I told my mum I was dropping out of university to start a business, she said she’d never speak to me again if I did
text: When I told my mum I was dropping out of university to start a business, she said she’d never speak to me again if I did. She meant it. We didn’t speak properly for two years, and that only changed when she saw the business was paying enough to cover my bills. As weird as it sounds, it never really bothered me, because I understood her story. I knew she was standing in my way out of love. She left school at 7 or 8 to work on a stall in Nigeria with her mother. After we moved from Africa to the UK she struggled to make her own business work, and she was scared I’d go through the same thing. I think this is true for a lot of people, especially the children of first-generation immigrants. The people who love you most will sometimes give you some of the worst advice about your life, and it’s usually because they care so much they can’t bear the thought of you failing. Their advice is shaped by what they lived through. If you’ve felt what it costs to lose money and security, you’ll weigh that risk much more heavily than any upside. So they push you towards comfort, the thing they probably never had, when the growth you actually need tends to come from taking risks and struggling through them... What I understand now is that her advice was a reflection of her own life. For someone who’d been working since she was a child, without a safety net, failure meant something far worse than it did for me. And because she’d already been through the hardest part, my worst case at 18 was a few rough years and a gap on my CV - a very different risk to the one she was imagining or that she would have faced in Nigeria. So when someone who loves you gives you advice, I think it’s worth asking whether they’re describing your situation or their own. And in the end it’s your life and you’re the one who lives with the consequences, so the decision has to be yours. "My parent were tasked with the job of survival and I with self-actualization. The immigrant generational gap is real. What a luxury it is to search for purpose, meaning, and fulfillment.” - Bo Ren

text: Anthropic just told investors its AI may soon double the speed of AI progress. The warning is in its revised IPO filing about recursive self-improvement. This means AI helping to build the next AI. The document is “Amendment No. 1” to Anthropic’s Form S-1, the registration statement a company files with the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) before selling shares to the public. Anthropic filed the original on 26 October to list on Nasdaq as ANT. They filed this updated version exactly one week later on 2 November. The new risk factor says Anthropic “may imminently meet” a threshold in its Responsible Scaling Policy, the rulebook it has used since 2023 to match how capable its models get with the safety measures it must have in place. That threshold is called “dramatically accelerated progress attributable to AI”. In simple terms, it means AI doing so much of the research and engineering that one year produces as much progress as two years normally would. Anthropic says the estimate is about future models, and that no current model has crossed the line. It adds that it is weighing new rules to require human review and approval of certain research decisions as its models take on more of that work. If Anthropic decides to slow down, public shareholders won’t be able to outvote it. → Shares - the seven co-founders own about 10% → Votes - one special share gives them 50.1% → Board - a separate trust elects the majority → Amazon and Google - over 5% each, with no vote The price per share in its funding rounds rose from $2.57 in the May 2021 Series A to $589 in the May 2026 Series H, 230x higher. Revenue also rose from $376m in the first quarter of 2025 to $17bn in the third quarter of 2026. The real pressure is on compute, with the amendment listing $895bn of commitments running to 2045. When ANT starts trading, the share price will look far lower than $589, because a 10-for-1 split in September turned each Series H share into ten public shares worth about $58.90 each. Investors are reportedly expecting a valuation of $1.5trn to $1.75trn, which, by my maths, works out at roughly $90 to $100 a share. That would mean public buyers pay 50% to 75% more than the Series H investors did six months ago. They’ll be buying into a company with about $70bn of compute bills due in the next 12 months, roughly what it now earns in a year at its current pace. I expect revenue to keep climbing, but the bigger change is how Anthropic gets its computing power. It started out renting almost all of it from Amazon, Google and Microsoft, then in November 2025 committed $50bn to building its own data centres in Texas and New York with Fluidstack. The amendment now lists $451bn of data-centre leases that haven’t even started yet. I think this IPO marks Anthropic’s shift from a lab that rents its computing power to a company that owns it, like Amazon and Meta, and the share price will depend on whether revenue keeps pace with this bill.

Here’s where it gets a little uncomfortable… A lot of teams sit at Level 1 because the boss trained them to stay there. Every time someone brings you a problem and you solve it for them, you’re teaching them to bring you the next one. And the next one. And the next one. So flip it. Before you clean up the mess, ask “What would you do?” Then (and this is key) give them the authority to go do it. She never needed to be the hero, wasn’t afraid to take action, and she’d look at my latest idea and say: “We can do that. text: 🤖 Could AI be getting worse because it's learning from itself? Artificial intelligence is generating an extraordinary amount of content. Articles, images, social media posts, websites and even entire datasets are increasingly being created by AI. But there's a fascinating problem emerging. 🧠 What happens when the next generation of AI models starts learning from content generated by previous AI models? It's a phenomenon sometimes described as AI inbreeding, and it could lead to something called model collapse. As AI-generated content finds its way into training datasets, models risk reinforcing existing errors, losing diversity and gradually producing less reliable or original outputs. Imagine making a photocopy of a photocopy, over and over again. Eventually, important details can disappear. ⚠️ The concern is that AI could begin amplifying its own mistakes rather than learning from the richness and complexity of the real world. Of course, carefully managed synthetic data can also be incredibly useful. The challenge is knowing how to use it without compromising quality. The future of AI might depend just as much on the quality of the information we feed it as the intelligence of the models themselves. 💬 Do you think AI-generated content could eventually make AI less intelligent? 👇 #AI #ArtificialIntelligence #AIInbreeding #ModelCollapse #GenerativeAI #ChatGPT #MachineLearning #SyntheticData #AITraining #FutureOfAI #DataQuality #AITechnology

hook: Let's talk about best practices for a moment. In a perennial trope, several presenters commented at MarketingProfs B2B F
text: Let's talk about best practices for a moment. In a perennial trope, several presenters commented at MarketingProfs B2B Forum that best practices (and/or AI) leads to average results at best and thus should be something we should spurn. As always, there's some nuance here. Let's draw a bell curve, a normal distribution, of quality of output. On the left? You suck. You're terrible. You couldn't market a life vest to a drowning man. On the right? You're a marketing deity. You could convince a die-hard carnivore that an all-chickpea diet was the way to go and they would love you for it. And then there's the great big middle. If you suck, best practices will get you to meh, and meh may be a startling improvement. If you suck, AI will get you to slightly above meh, skillfully used. Neither one currently will replace human genius, on the far right... ...for now. AI is moving rapidly towards the right side of the curve, skillfully used. (and yes, as Claude likes to say, "skillfully used" is doing a lot of lifting there) Incompetent use of AI will still land you on the left side of the curve, but AI is advancing quickly. But here's the big question, and the one that makes me doubt my fellow presenters and speakers who rail against best practices and AI as if they were the devil incarnate. Yes, human genius is the ideal, the aspiration to which we all presumably strive if we love our work (shoutouts to Lianna Patch and Michael Barber ). But where along this curve do buyers buy? If buyers only bought from our efforts at a human genius level, 99.99% of all businesses would be out of business. Very few of us have human genius-level marketing even some of the time. If buyers buy even when we objectively suck, then adopting best practices + AI will get us slightly to the right of meh, and vastly beyond what it takes to persuade a buyer. Should we continue to aspire towards the right side of the curve? Yes, if it gives you professional and personal satisfaction to do so. But if you're concerned mainly with the bottom line and being able to defend your job, best practices + AI is probably more than enough if you currently suck, and if we're REALLY honest, most marketing is squarely on the "you suck" line. Original art that sucks by me. #AI #GenerativeAI #GenAI #ChatGPT #ArtificialIntelligence #LargeLanguageModels #MachineLearning #IntelligenceRevolution

hook: Your AI agent can use an approved tool to perform an unapproved action. That is the failure mode I would put in an archi
text: Your AI agent can use an approved tool to perform an unapproved action. That is the failure mode I would put in an architecture review. Consider a deployment agent. A human approves artifact A for staging. The agent then calls the deployment tool with artifact B and production as the target. Valid identity. Permitted tool. Correctly formatted arguments. Wrong deployment. Coming from backend engineering, I care about what happens between those checks. “Can this agent call deploy?” leaves an important question unanswered: “Was THIS artifact approved for THIS environment?” A human approval needs to remain attached to the exact action it authorized. Sponsored by Amazon Web Services (AWS) . This is the problem temporal policies in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore are designed to solve. With temporal policies configured and enforcement enabled, AgentCore Gateway can evaluate a tool request against earlier actions in the same policy session before allowing the protected tool to run. For this deployment workflow, I would define rules requiring: ● A recorded approval from a trusted approval service. ● An exact match between the approved artifact and environment and the ones the agent actually requests. ● An approval that is still within its validity window. ● A fresh approval when the previous one has already been used. Those checks happen outside the agent’s reasoning loop. The deployment service still needs its own authorization and protection against duplicate execution. Every route to a privileged action needs an enforceable boundary. I would apply the same discipline across the rest of the architecture: At the model layer, configure Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to mask or block PII before it reaches the agent. Use a geographic inference profile to support throughput within the chosen geography. Enable prompt caching on supported models, and tag application inference profiles so application spend is visible in AWS Cost Explorer. Security, performance, and cost all need explicit design decisions. Explore Amazon Bedrock: https://fandf.co/4jZfuUs My test for an agent architecture is this: If the agent changes its plan after approval, does the system notice before anything happens? Where would your system catch that change: the agent, the gateway, or the deployment service?

text: There's one sentence I told my friend Blake to never say again. "I'm not good at hiring." Blake is 28 and runs a big business out of Newport Beach. We sat down at a whiteboard in Brooklyn to figure out why he still has no time. He told me he couldn't enjoy a single day of his trip to Hawaii. Design the Dream Week Before you remove anything, figure out what you want your week to look like. Blake's answer: • A 4-hour creative block most mornings • Long afternoons outside, hiking or at the gym • Soccer or tennis a couple of nights a week • A long wind-down before bed Now every decision has something to measure against. 2. Run a Time Audit Every Friday, list every task you did that week and mark whether it gave you energy or drained it. Then go task by task and look for what you can cut. Elimination is the best one. Whatever's left that you shouldn't be doing goes on the delegate list. Your delegate list is your next job description. 3. Hire for Your Time I told Blake to bring on 2 people: a chief of staff and an operations person. Their core metric is his time. My sister's whole job on my team is protecting 20 hours of creative work for me every week. Nothing gets booked on top of it. Why 2 people? If one doesn't work out, you're not back to square one. 4. Treat Hiring Like a Funnel Hiring works the same way a sales funnel does. • Post the role and sort the applications • Ask for a 5-minute Loom before any call • Interview the ones who stand out • Give finalists a real challenge, like remaking one of your offers 5. text: Company-wide AI literacy in November 2026 includes tokens, and they matter a lot. It also includes how the model thinks, what context to give it, and when to hand work to an agent. Like many companies, Check Point Software moved its AI tools to consumption-based licenses. Working with Assaf Asbag and Elad Brandes , we used that moment to teach the entire Q4 AI handbook, with token efficiency as the way in. Much of what used to be taught, like prompt formulas, has aged out. That doesn't mean "just talk to it" gets you far enough. Natural language creates an illusion that there is nothing to learn, and it works by accident for natural communicators and for people who ramble at AI, for the same reason: both hand over a lot of context. The "Work Smart With AI: The 2026 Handbook" is built primarily on six habits: 1. Know how it works: a few mechanics explain most frustrations, like every message resending the whole chat and hidden thinking being billed like writing. 2. Bring your thinking: the model reaches for the most likely answer and is tuned to agree, so your view and how sure you are is what pulls it away from average. 3. Give the right context: too little and it guesses, too much and it loses focus, which is why often more costs less overall. 4. Match intelligence and attention: a smaller model with a clear brief can beat the top model with a vague one, and deep thinking on a simple task buys a long wait for the same answer. 5. Earn autonomy per task: automated is not always better, and when it does, it still needs to be proven before you hand control over to AI. 6. Kill the spin: an automation nobody reads spends tokens on every run and saves no one a minute. What I find time and again is that even for people who already use AI heavily, understanding the why behind each habit changes how they work. The through-line is intentionality: the habits that keep a CFO calm are the same ones that raise quality, with less slop and less sycophancy. AI tools push a new version every week. When was the last time you updated the version of the AI best practices you're using?

Discovery Inc , BBC , TED Conferences THE INNOCENT: Optimistic, wholesome, genuine goodness. Dove , The Coca-Cola Company THE CREATOR: Imaginative, builds things that never existed. Apple , the LEGO Group , GoPro . THE RULER: Authoritative, polished, commands respect. HUGO BOSS , Microsoft . THE CAREGIVER: Nurturing, selfless, puts others first. Johnson & Johnson , UNICEF . GPT 5 mini got 17 of 20 cases right on its own and 19 of 20 with the skill. My harness also put the skill text into every request, so tokens rose 40 percent. Zep's team pointed out both problems: the task was too easy, and the agent should pick skills from a catalog. ⠀ 𝗧𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝟮: 𝗭𝗲𝗽'𝘀 𝗯𝗮𝗻𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗮𝘀𝗸 I ran Zep's public banking example without changes. A customer asks the bank to check April savings interest and correct any underpayment. Four savings accounts compete for two checking accounts and two cards, each source can boost only one account, some pairings are excluded, and every credit must be exact to the cent, with a report. GPT 5.1 at high effort solved one case. Zep turned that verified Trace into a skill about a minute after the Trace closed. GPT 5 mini then ran 5 fresh cases in two arms: an empty skill catalog, or the skill listed with a read_skill tool. ⠀ 𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗜 𝗺𝗲𝗮𝘀𝘂𝗿𝗲𝗱 → Correct outcomes: 0/5 without the skill, 5/5 with it → Without it, every run posted all four credits at the wrong amount → With it, GPT 5 mini read the skill once, ran 32 to 36 quotes, compared once, then credited → Median time: 172 s without, 159 s with → Tokens per run: 325k without, 505k with, mostly cached input → Building the skill, paid once: one GPT 5.1 run, 697k tokens, 299 s ⠀ 𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘀𝘂𝗿𝗽𝗿𝗶𝘀𝗲𝗱 𝗺𝗲 The skill made GPT 5 mini do more work. text: The era of System One Vision Model is here! Introducing VFlash: parsing the visual world in parallel at unmatched speeds for Physical AI. Most embodied prediction tasks like object localization, robot trajectory planning, and dense 3D motion are fixed-length float vectors. For example, a bounding box is always 6 tokens, a 10-waypoint robot arm trajectory is 54: we know these beforehand. Instead of decoding one token at a time, we can output the entire geometric shape in one go. VFlash enables up to 12x faster action decoding and a 5.1x overall robot inference speedup on edge GPUs like the Jetson Thor and DGX Spark. What’s surprising is that it ends up *even more accurate* than the VLM backbone, with up to 61% lower 3D trajectory error. The intuition is that VFlash avoids the cascading errors of autoregressive decoding, where every coordinate is written in ink and every later point loses the chance to backspace. Everything that moves will be autonomous, and everything autonomous will need to think on its own chip. The next inference revolution is physical reasoning at the speed of reflex. hook: Meta's new F3 Lightning lets ML features ship independently while sharing computation. If one invalid feature definition
text: Meta's new F3 Lightning lets ML features ship independently while sharing computation. If one invalid feature definition delays your whole release, the boundary between those two jobs matters! Imagine an ads model using click and impression counts over seven days. Both features can reuse the same event read and time filter. F3 combined feature computations into one graph, running shared operations once per request. But that graph also shipped as one unit, so an invalid definition could block unrelated changes. F3 Lightning compiles a complete configuration for each feature. Each can be validated, released, or rolled back separately. The serving process then recovers the sharing: - Give identical computations the same identity. The compiler derives identifiers from the operation, its parameters, and its inputs' identifiers. A changed time window produces a different identity. - At startup, collect the active configurations into one ordered execution plan. Keep each shared operation once and place it before its consumers. - Assign integer buffer slots at startup so requests can access results directly, without looking up identifiers. Each request gets its own buffer, and consumers share list and map results by reference instead of making separate copies. Simply separating releases had increased CPU usage. Even after removing duplicate computation, scattered intermediate results still cost CPU. The shared buffer addressed the memory layout too. Meta reports about 3.6x faster delivery of comparable extraction features, with no increase in infrastructure compute cost. Engineering details: https://lnkd.in/gT_bCf2P

text: The fastest way to kill an AI project is building a "God Agent". You know the pattern: one giant system prompt, 35 attached tools, and full read/write permissions. It's expected to classify intent, query SQL, parse PDFs, and draft emails all in a single autonomous loop. It works great in a 3-turn laptop demo. But under production load, it hits a hallucination spiral by Turn 6 because you’ve overloaded its context and attention. Instead of building a giant monolithic agent or overcorrecting into a massive, expensive multi-agent swarm , follow this strict order of operations: Start with 1 Constrained Agent + Deterministic Code: Handle your primary happy path with strict outputs and standard if/else logic. Add a Fast Router (Cost & Speed Win): Put a fast, cheap classifier upfront to route simple intents away from your heavy models. Bring in Scoped Workers: Only build specialized sub-agents when the task exceeds one clean context window. Give a SQL agent SQL tools, and nothing else. Add a Verifier Node (Reliability Win): Build a lightweight adversarial critic whose only job is to validate schema compliance and check outputs against your data before the user sees it. Don’t start with a complex swarm. Don't rely on a single overloaded God Agent. Earn your complexity. Start small and build a pipeline. text: Since GPUs accelerate AI on my computer, could I save money by buying a PC without a CPU? Not at all. The CPU still has its own job. An AI application needs more than the calculations accelerated by a GPU. On a typical PC, the CPU runs the operating system and application logic. But the CPU can perform AI computations directly, too. For some models, inference may run entirely on the CPU. Whether that is practical depends on the workload and available hardware, not on a rule that every AI task needs a GPU. An accelerator can make a system faster without replacing the processor that coordinates it. #AIInfrastructure #CPU

text: I think AI is about to create a massive resurgence in blue-collar work. Let me explain. The FT’s John Burn-Murdoch published a brilliant thread this week on AI and jobs. In US tech, output has stayed on trend while employment has fallen in a straight line since 2022. Now most people might read this as AI replacing workers (which is what media headlines want you to think). But the timing doesn’t fit quite right. The productivity jump started in 2020, two years before ChatGPT launched. Between 2019 and 2022, Meta and Amazon almost doubled their headcount, while Google and Microsoft grew theirs by more than half. A lot of today’s layoffs are pandemic overhiring being unwound, sped up by interest rate rises. The chart does show something AI will push much further, though. Software firms can sell more without hiring more, while consultancies like Accenture and Deloitte still need extra people to grow. AI is moving more and more office work onto the software model. But the physical world can’t follow, and the AI boom is making that glaringly obvious. When Microsoft’s president Brad Smith asked his team for the single biggest obstacle to building data centres in the US, they named a shortage of electricians. He thinks the US needs about half a million more over the next decade. → Electrical work - 45–70% of data centre build costs (IBEW) → Construction - 349,000 net new workers needed in 2026 alone (ABC) → Meta - $115m to train tradespeople for its own sites Replacing these roles would need humanoid robots to advance at a blistering pace over the coming decade. I thought Palantir CEO Alex Karp had a great framing for this on TBPN in March: “There are basically two ways to know you have a future. One, you have some vocational training. Or two, you’re neurodivergent.” Karp has dyslexia, and I think he's referencing specifically individuals who have unique outlooks and can frame problems in unique ways. Looking at things differently is now a core skill. AI can take what once was a hard-to-articulate thought and turn it into real-world action. Success, he argued, will favour people who are “more of an artist, look at things from a different direction, be able to build something unique.” Therefore I believe the safest careers of the next decade will need either a pair of hands or a mind that sees what others miss.
