creator: Damien Benveniste
hook: Choosing a vector search index changes which embeddings your RAG system gets a chance to find. Apple's latest retrieval
text: Choosing a vector search index changes which embeddings your RAG system gets a chance to find. Apple's latest retrieval write-up explores learned routing; let's unpack the search work saved by IVF, HNSW, and product quantization! Imagine we already have a query embedding and a million passage embeddings. We want the closest passages under a chosen distance measure. - Score every stored vector and keep the nearest results. This is an exact scan. It gives us the reference answer for that distance measure, but the work grows with the database. - Group vectors around learned cluster centers, then search only the lists whose centers are closest to the query. This is an inverted file index, or IVF. It skips much of the database, but can skip the list containing a true neighbor. Probing more lists improves recall at the cost of more scanning. - Connect vectors in a layered graph. Compare the query with linked vectors, follow closer ones through sparse upper layers, then explore more candidates at the bottom. This is HNSW. It avoids a full scan, with extra memory for graph links. Keeping more candidates can improve recall but adds work. - Split each vector into pieces and replace each piece with the ID of its nearest learned representative. This is product quantization, or PQ. Search scores these compact codes approximately, reducing vector storage and memory traffic. Compression can change the ordering of results. We can combine these operations! IVF-PQ searches selected lists and scores compressed vectors inside them. PQ can also compress the vectors stored in an HNSW index. To measure the approximation, compare against exact search on the same vectors and queries. Recall@k is the fraction of exact top-k neighbors found in the approximate top-k. Relevance labels tell us whether those passages answer the user's question. Apple's retrieval write-up: https://lnkd.in/g7FBdPVJ

hook: Subject matter experts matter more than ever. And subject matter expertise is as much experience as it is expertise (par
text: Subject matter experts matter more than ever. And subject matter expertise is as much experience as it is expertise (part of what EEAT stands for in SEO circles) these days, especially when it comes to spotting AI-generated content. Here's an AI-generated picture of my town by Gemini, based on this prompt: > Create an image, using your web search tools, of a side street with litter in [my town]. Take extra time to validate that anything shown in the scene, such as houses, vehicles, litter, etc. are geographically appropriate to [my town] in 2026. I live just outside of Boston. This photo looks pretty good, doesn't it? Could you tell this wasn't my town? I can, but it requires subject matter expertise. 1. Our street signs are blue, not green. 2. Our town's trash bins are grey and our recycling bins are black with yellow lids. 3. Our hydrants are blue, not yellow. 4. Coburn Street doesn't intersect with another street like this. (it's near my house) 5. Most of the litter is wrong. Props for getting the Dunkin cup correct, but the rest is quite wrong. Every morning, my wife and I go pick up trash on our morning dog walks, and this is not what our local litter looks like. To be clear, gone are the days where you had hilariously wrong details that stuck out like a sore thumb in AI-generated content. You have to work harder to spot the details and you need subject matter expertise, like what litter would be geographically appropriate. This is the epitome of why subject matter expertise matters, to see the nuances that help us perceive what's real and what's not. As our audiences demand more authenticity, we have to know the limits of AI and what it can and can't do - and know when to use it and when not to. Equally important, if you try to pass off something AI as something human-originated, chances are there will be at least one detail that doesn't ring true, and like a magic trick, once the first thread unravels, the entire tapestry unravels. If you misrepresent yourself, all it takes is one subject matter expert to call it out. Try this exercise over time with your own domains of expertise, be they academic or lived experience. See for yourself how much better AI has gotten, and what limits it still has. And any time someone suggests to use AI "because no one will know", remind them of this photo. #AI #GenerativeAI #GenAI #ChatGPT #ArtificialIntelligence #LargeLanguageModels #MachineLearning #IntelligenceRevolution

hook: You can scale a gRPC service to ten pods and still have one pod doing all the work. One long lived HTTP/2 connection car
text: You can scale a gRPC service to ten pods and still have one pod doing all the work. One long lived HTTP/2 connection carries every call, and an L4 load balancer only balances connections. I mapped the six patterns an agent stack depends on, with the failure point for each. 𝗥𝗘𝗦𝗧 Stateless and cacheable, so a GET behind a CDN is close to free. You pay for it in over fetching and chatty clients. Still the safest default for public CRUD APIs. 𝗚𝗿𝗮𝗽𝗵𝗤𝗟 The client asks for exactly the fields it needs, in one round trip. Add DataLoader early for N+1 resolvers, and cap query depth and amount, since neither is limited by default. 𝗴𝗥𝗣𝗖 Protobuf contracts over HTTP/2, with streaming in both directions. Fix the one busy pod problem with L7 or client side load balancing. 𝗪𝗲𝗯𝗦𝗼𝗰𝗸𝗲𝘁𝘀 One persistent connection where both sides can send at any time. OpenAI's Realtime API offers it for server side voice agents. For plain LLM token streaming, Server Sent Events is usually simpler. 𝗪𝗲𝗯𝗵𝗼𝗼𝗸𝘀 The provider calls you when a long job finishes, so nobody polls. Expect duplicate and out of order events. Verify the signature, return 2xx fast, and dedupe on the event ID. 𝗠𝗖𝗣 The standard way for an agent to discover and call tools. The July 28 spec made it stateless, with no initialize handshake and no protocol sessions, so remote MCP servers can scale like any other HTTP service. The cost to watch is tool definitions filling the context window. In the animation, each panel walks through its own flow in the order of the numbered steps. Where do you draw the line between exposing a capability as an MCP tool and keeping it a plain API call?

text: “I don’t really know what I’d use AI for” is the most common thing I hear, and I think the problem is that people are trying to answer that question alone. Turn it around. hook: You don’t need to build a database engine to use SQL. You still need to understand what happens when your query runs. I
text: You don’t need to build a database engine to use SQL. You still need to understand what happens when your query runs. I think RAG is heading in the same direction. Tools can already handle much of the ingestion, indexing and retrieval infrastructure for you. You may never write every part of that pipeline yourself. But when it returns a convincing answer built on incomplete evidence, you need to know where to look. Think about databases. Knowing SQL doesn’t automatically tell you which data model fits your workload, why a join duplicates rows or why an index isn’t helping. RAG needs that same depth of understanding. Here’s a simplified way to think about three common approaches. Classic RAG: follow a defined retrieval workflow. Question → Search → Rank → Generate. Useful when retrieving the relevant passages gives the model enough evidence to answer. It can combine multiple documents. The limitation is that a single-pass workflow won’t go looking again when a crucial piece is missing. GraphRAG: make relationships part of retrieval. Supplier → Component → Product → Customer. Useful when the question depends on how things connect, or on patterns across a collection of documents. Depending on the implementation, it can use graph relationships, source text and summaries of connected groups. The responsibility: keep entities and relationships accurate and current. A wrong connection is still wrong, even when it lives in a graph. Agentic RAG: let the system choose the next retrieval step. Search → Inspect → Decide → Search again if needed. Useful when the next question depends on what the previous search uncovered. The agent might rewrite a query, switch sources or retrieve more evidence. That flexibility comes with less predictable latency. You need limits on access, time and cost, plus a way to evaluate whether those extra steps helped. One distinction matters: GraphRAG describes how evidence is organized and retrieved. Agentic RAG describes how retrieval decisions are made. An agent can use a graph. You can combine them. As tools handle more of the implementation, I’d put more learning effort into retrieval quality, data modeling, evaluation and failure analysis. The tool can build the pipeline. You still need to judge whether the evidence supports the answer. Which RAG fundamentals should every engineer understand before trusting a managed pipeline?

hook: An "Access denied" message does not always mean something went wrong. Sometimes the system knows exactly who you are, an
text: An "Access denied" message does not always mean something went wrong. Sometimes the system knows exactly who you are, and still says no. Authentication verifies your identity. Authorization determines which applications and information you are allowed to access. Consider an employee who moves to another department. The company account remains valid, but some permissions associated with the previous role may no longer be appropriate. Those permissions should change with the work. And identity is not always the only condition. For sensitive applications, security policies may also check whether the device meets company requirements before allowing access. So an employee can be correctly authenticated and still be denied access to a particular resource. There is nothing contradictory about that. People can share the same corporate network without having the same permissions. Access should reflect what each person is authorized to do, even as responsibilities change. #IdentitySecurity #AccessControl

text: Google AI Overviews uses nearly 8x more UGC than ChatGPT. If you’ve got one AI search playbook for both, one of them is getting the wrong one. At Searchable , we looked at 3.2 million pages that 5 AI engines listed as sources between 12 and 25 October. Then we took a large sample of the forum and social pages and checked who really posted them. The gap between Google and the chatbots is wide, and it changes what you should be doing about Reddit, YouTube and creator content. It’s easy to treat “AI search” as one channel with one playbook. The data says Google’s AI and ChatGPT are reading very different parts of the internet. The way I read it, there are 3 things worth knowing: 1️⃣ Google cares what people say about you. 1 in 12 of the sources Google AI Overviews used (8.6%) were forum threads, creator videos or personal posts. For ChatGPT and Perplexity, it was 1 in 90 (1.1%). If Google’s AI is where your buyers search, what customers post about you is part of your marketing now, whether you like it or not. 2️⃣ On Google, that mostly means YouTube and Reddit. Those 2 sites supplied 62% of the user-generated sources AI Overviews used, and Google AI Mode follows the same pattern. I wouldn’t spread effort thinly across every platform because 2 sites are doing most of the work. 3️⃣ A lot of “social” content isn’t from users at all. Between 44% and 50% of the forum and social pages used by Google’s AI search, Gemini and Perplexity were posted by brands, publishers or the platform itself. That’s company LinkedIn pages and brands’ own YouTube channels. Useful, but it’s still you talking about you. Your own YouTube channel is owned content. It doesn’t stand in for what customers and creators say about you. If Google’s AI search matters in your category, I’d put genuine effort into independent creator reviews and genuine Reddit discussion. If ChatGPT matters more, Reddit is the user-generated site that counts. It supplied 90% of ChatGPT’s user-generated sources ! creator: Brij Kishore Pandey
hook: One Architecture Diagram That Explains Every AI Agent Strip away the framework names and every agent you have ever used
text: One Architecture Diagram That Explains Every AI Agent Strip away the framework names and every agent you have ever used is the same seven components wired into a loop. Not LangGraph specific. Not CrewAI specific. The pattern holds whether you built it yourself in 200 lines or bought it as a platform. Here is the anatomy. 𝗣𝗲𝗿𝗰𝗲𝗽𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗹𝗮𝘆𝗲𝗿 Input arrives as user text, API calls, sensor data, events, or scheduled triggers. This layer normalizes all of it into something the model can reason over. Most teams underinvest here and then blame the model for bad outputs. 𝗥𝗲𝗮𝘀𝗼𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗲𝗻𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗲 The LLM, running some structured reasoning pattern: chain of thought, ReAct, plan then execute. Its real job is one decision, made repeatedly: can I answer this directly, or do I need to act first? 𝗣𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗺𝗼𝗱𝘂𝗹𝗲 When the answer is no, the goal gets decomposed into ordered subtasks. This is the component people skip when they prototype, and the one they retrofit painfully once tasks stop fitting in a single hop. 𝗠𝗲𝗺𝗼𝗿𝘆 𝘀𝘆𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗺 Two distinct systems that get collapsed into one far too often. Short term holds conversation context and working state. Long term holds vector stores, episodic memory, and learned patterns. Different write policies, different retrieval logic, different failure modes. 𝗧𝗼𝗼𝗹 𝗲𝘅𝗲𝗰𝘂𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗹𝗮𝘆𝗲𝗿 Where the agent touches the world. MCP servers, API calls, code execution, database queries, file systems, external services. Results flow back into reasoning, and the loop asks again: goal achieved? 𝗚𝘂𝗮𝗿𝗱𝗿𝗮𝗶𝗹𝘀 Permissions, approval gates, content filtering, rate limits, human checkpoints. Notice in the diagram that guardrails run vertically alongside everything rather than sitting at one entry point. That placement is the whole argument. A gate at the input does nothing about what the agent decides to do on step four. 𝗢𝗯𝘀𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗮𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗶𝘁𝘆 Traces, logs, metrics, cost tracking, latency monitoring. It spans the full width because you cannot debug a loop by inspecting one node in it. You need the trajectory. The interesting part is not the boxes. It is the two diamonds: "can I answer directly" and "goal achieved". Those are the only places the agent actually decides anything. Everything else is plumbing. When agents misbehave in production, the fault is almost always in how those two checks were specified, not in the model doing the reasoning. Where do you draw the line between an agent and a workflow that happens to call an LLM? My working definition is whether the system chooses its own next step rather than following a predetermined path, but that gets blurry the moment a planner writes the steps in advance.

text: Deloitte ’s new State of AI report finds 81% of companies say AI has made them faster, but only 25% say it’s deeply transforming business. Sounds familiar, amiright? Lemme share a thought experiment here to explain why: Imagine you buy a pill for everyone in your company. It makes each of them 30% faster at their work and 30% smarter in their work. Miracle drug! You’re going to crush everyone. Everybody takes it. Day one, whole company. Six months go by. Your CFO walks in and wants to see the ROI. Did we make our money back? So ask yourself - how would you measure it? Did you make more sales? Close more deals? Ship more products? And what’s the output of the analyst whose job is to be right about the market? Or the manager keeping eight people pointed in the same direction? The pill could be working all around you, and you’d have no way to see it. Because - and here's the thing - nobody ever said what “better” would look like. Nobody defined the exact processes that, when changed, would ultimately yield that ROI. That's why AI transformation isn't about tech - I mean that. It's about process change and using AI to do that really, really well. It's also why I freakin' love Deloitte and the work they put out. What they highlight here is that the gains are real, but they don’t turn into results on their own. Deloitte’s own conclusion is that ROI comes when a company changes around the technology, “not simply when the technology is deployed.” WHAT ELSE WE LEARNED FROM THE STUDY A few other highlights: >> Only 28% report revenue gains from AI, up from 20% in January. >> 74% report efficiency and productivity gains, up from 66% in January. >> 67% expect revenue growth from AI, more than any other benefit. >> Of the 81% who got faster, only 7% call it a significant improvement. creator: Damien Benveniste
hook: Passing tests and proving a property give us different guarantees about AI-written code. Microsoft's PDD Kit prototype c
text: Passing tests and proving a property give us different guarantees about AI-written code. Microsoft's PDD Kit prototype combines both, so let's look at what formal verification adds! Let's say an agent writes a function that returns the largest value in a non-empty integer list. With testing, we run concrete examples: [3, 9, 2] should return 9, and [-5, -2] should return -2. Generating thousands more lists expands the search for mistakes. A passing run establishes the checked behavior for those executions. With a proof, we first write a contract: - The input list contains at least one element. - The result occurs in the list. - No element is greater than the result. A verifier such as Verus turns the code and contract into logical statements for a solver to establish for every allowed input in its formal model. For a loop that scans the list, initialize the candidate with the first element and keep the larger value at each comparison. The candidate is then the largest element seen so far. This is a loop invariant. Prove it holds initially and survives any next element; when the scan ends, it covers the whole list. We don't have to enumerate every possible list! The LLM can propose code and proof annotations; a separate, deterministic verifier checks them. A failure can mean a bug, an incorrect contract, missing proof steps, or a solver limit. The cost is specifying the behavior precisely and supplying enough reasoning. We still have to check that the contract says what we meant. Dependencies outside the proof need explicit assumptions. Integration tests can check their actual behavior; the verifier and its model must also be trusted. PDD Kit currently verifies Rust. Its login example combines proved application logic with tests for trusted dependencies, including database lookups and password checking. PDD Kit: https://lnkd.in/gSwKSW57

hook: 9 in 10 third-party AI citations come from outside tier 1 press. At Searchable , we analysed more than 117,000 AI answer
text: 9 in 10 third-party AI citations come from outside tier 1 press. At Searchable , we analysed more than 117,000 AI answers to see which third-party sites AI pulls from when it answers a question. Tier 1 press made up 11% of those citations. Blogs and niche sites alone made up 20%, nearly twice as much as every tier 1 outlet combined. Add trade titles, comparison sites, review platforms, social media, forums and Wikipedia, and you get the other 89%. For years the PR playbook has been fairly simple - land the big national and the rest follows. I don’t think that holds in AI search, for two reasons. 1. AI answers the specific question in front of it. When someone asks ChatGPT for the best CRM for a 10-person agency, the answer gets built from the pages that cover that exact question. That being comparison sites, G2 and Capterra reviews, and specialist blogs. 2. Tier 1 rarely covers the questions buyers ask. A national feature on your funding round is great but it will not tell ChatGPT or Gemini which tool suits a 10-person agency. To be fair to tier 1, it still has its purpose. Investors, board members and enterprise buyers still read it. If they see that big logo on your homepage, it definitely earns trust. AI just isn’t reading it very often when it answers a buyer’s question. The problem, as I see it, is budget. A lot of PR spend still goes on targeting these tier 1 sites. If I were planning PR for next year, I would split it in two. Keep a small tier 1 budget for credibility moments, like a raise or a big launch. Put the rest into the trade titles, blogs, comparison sites and review platforms your buyers read. It's definitely easier to get into a trade title or comparison list... But let me know, what's your approach?

text: Replit CEO Amjad Masad defines “self-driving companies” as businesses designed so AI agents can carry out and coordinate much of the day-to-day work across departments. The agents use the company’s data and software to pursue goals set by people, who decide what matters, make judgment calls, and remain accountable for the results. In “Rise of the Self-Driving Company,” Masad stated that, “By the end of 2030, every company in the Fortune 500 will be a Self-Driving Company.” On Ep 249 of The Artificial Intelligence Show, I expressed why I disagree with that timeline for large enterprises, but agree that self-driving companies will exist in the near future. ChatGPT was introduced four years ago this month, yet the majority of companies are still in the understanding and piloting phases of implementing basic AI assistant capabilities across their organizations. What we often see in enterprises are 5-10% of staff (at best) who are advanced users, and that’s usually within a department or business unit, not the whole organization. So, the idea that within the next three years we will see these same large enterprises somehow solve for agents and completely reimagine their organizations and workforces just seems extremely optimistic. That being said, we are seeing early glimpses of the self-driving company at SmarterX, and do believe these types of companies will become prevalent in the startup world much sooner. Just this week, we began building agent analyst prototypes in ChatGPT that could largely automate performance monitoring and data analysis across the company—and we held an internal demo session showcasing new customer success agents the team is testing that could quickly reinvent those roles. Masad wrote, “As agents take on more of the execution and coordination, companies can work more efficiently, and their people can pursue more ambitious goals. Realizing that potential will require companies to rethink how they organize and make decisions.” I agree. We’re focused on bringing that sort of company to life in the most human-centered way possible.

text: So Scott Wilson is one of the most respected CIOs in the US. He has taken WashU’s AUM from $8BN to $19BN in just 9 years. At one point, SpaceX made up over 20% of their total AUM. In his first week, he cut 75% of their hedge fund commitments. Scott does the job like no one else. He is revered for it. I sat down with Scott and have summarised my lessons from the discussion below. (Links in Comments) Huge thanks to Adam Kurkiewicz and Lee Fixel for some fantastic question suggestions. -- 1. How We Made Billions From SpaceX and Were Able to Keep Hold of It At one point SpaceX made up more than 20% of WashU's portfolio. The team had many chances to take liquidity but held with conviction, using several continuation vehicles to stay in through the IPO. Scott says that is not possible without the right governance structure. 2. What Is the Right Level of Diversification for a $19 Billion Endowment? The quantitative benefits of diversification trail off quickly beyond 20 to 30 look-through exposures. WashU targets half its portfolio in its top 50 look-through positions, which Scott still sees as very diversified next to hedge funds that hold most of their capital in their top 15 to 20 names. 3. Why Mega Funds Do Not Work for the WashU Portfolio? Mega funds do not need WashU's capital or its co-investment, unless the round is so large that WashU could go direct anyway. Scott expects it will be very hard for them to repeat the multiples they achieved on much smaller funds. 4. The Valuation Premium in Privates Is Encouraging Everyone to Stay Away From IPOs Scott believes Anthropic could have raised privately at north of $2 trillion, a price he is not convinced public markets would give. With public markets near all-time highs, he puts the lack of DPI down to too much capital chasing private champions. 5. Why Venture Investors Do Need to Be Price-Sensitive for Their LPs WashU wants discipline around valuation and does not want its capital used for deals at 100 times revenue. Scott sees Lee Fixel as pragmatic, willing to pay up for great companies but stepping away when things get too frothy. 6. How This $19 Billion Endowment Finds Direct Deals WashU asks managers which five portfolio companies they are most excited about, meets them, and offers to help lead the next round when one stands out. It has also led employee tender offers and gone direct on cap tables instead of waiting for an SPV offer. 7. Why the Biggest Mistake I Made Is Not Doubling Down on Our Winners Scott says his biggest mistake at WashU has been not adding capital to winners. The endowment had chances to put more into names that did extremely well, but held back because they were already north of 1 or 2% of the portfolio.

text: You might be doing a repetitive task by hand because explaining how to automate it sounds like more work than just doing it again. I had one of those every time I gave a talk. hook: Before choosing Qwen3-ASR or a Parakeet model for local transcription, look at which information their decoders use. In
text: Before choosing Qwen3-ASR or a Parakeet model for local transcription, look at which information their decoders use. In automatic speech recognition, that helps explain the difference between parallel frame scoring and sequential text generation. An audio encoder turns short stretches of sound into a sequence of feature vectors. We can learn to map that long sequence to a shorter transcript without labeling where every text token begins! - Predict a token or a blank at every encoded frame. Models such as Parakeet-CTC use Connectionist Temporal Classification (CTC). In greedy decoding, merge consecutive repeats, then remove blanks: h h _ i becomes hi. Once the audio is encoded, frame scores can be computed in parallel. The basic head does not read its previous text predictions; a separate language model can add text context. - Combine the current audio frame with the text already emitted. This is a transducer. In a Recurrent Neural Network Transducer (RNN-T), a token extends the transcript, while a blank advances the audio position. We gain text history, but decoding needs repeated decisions along the audio. Parakeet-TDT, a Token-and-Duration Transducer, also predicts how far to advance, skipping decoder decisions for intermediate frames. - Let a text decoder attend across audio representations and earlier text to generate the next token. This is attention-based sequence generation. Qwen3-ASR feeds audio embeddings into a language-model decoder, letting each prediction use both kinds of context. Generating the transcript requires repeated decoder steps, one per new token. For live captions, check the encoder's look-ahead: how much future audio it needs before encoding a frame. CTC and transducers can both stream with a suitable encoder; Qwen3-ASR also supports streaming. Chunk size and look-ahead add waiting time alongside the decoder's computation. CTC walkthrough: https://lnkd.in/g3kZFMCV Parakeet architectures: https://lnkd.in/gYfZaZMa Qwen3-ASR: https://lnkd.in/gfYG6nbd

text: If your AI writing sounds like everyone else’s, it might be because you haven’t told it who you are yet. Two files have helped me get AI to write more like me. One describes how I actually sound and think. The other lists the words and tones I never want to see: the corporate wrap-ups, the stock phrases, the hedging. Voice and anti-voice. The trick is not writing these yourself. Have AI interview you about your writing preferences. How do you want to sound? What words do you love? What do you hate? I write the way I talk, direct and specific, and I end with a challenge rather than a summary. It took me about ten minutes to get that into a file. It’s saved me a lot of rewriting since. text: A favorite optimistic view of the future of AI is from a pessimistic book that not about AI: "Rise and Fall of American Growth," which argues that we had a one-time explosion in living standards from 1870 and 1920 (& later outside the US). hook: BCG models a scenario where the IT budget drops by $27 million, yet total technology costs rise by $250 million. What ex
text: BCG models a scenario where the IT budget drops by $27 million, yet total technology costs rise by $250 million. What explains the difference? AI can make existing IT work less expensive, while business departments adopt AI services that generate new operating costs. Model usage and other recurring expenses grow with adoption, even if the technology function becomes more productive. One assumption matters: the productivity improvement inside IT must translate into actual savings. Completing work faster does not automatically reduce a budget. hook: Your SEO cheat sheet is lying to you! Here’s what Google actually says: I took 18 numbers that turn up on every SEO chea
text: Your SEO cheat sheet is lying to you! Here’s what Google actually says: I took 18 numbers that turn up on every SEO cheat sheet and checked each one against Google’s own documentation. Google NEVER set 7 of them, 3 are half right or out of date, and only 8 hold up. 1/ The myths - Title tags and meta descriptions have no character limit. Google cuts them to fit the screen, so the 50 to 60 figure comes from what fits on screen rather than from any rule. - There's no "one H1" rule. Google says there's no ideal number of headings, and the order doesn't matter either. - Alt text has no length rule. Describe what's in the image. - Keyword density was never a target. Google only warns against stuffing. - There's no set number of internal links per page. Add them where they help the reader. - There's no ideal word count. Google's own guide asks if you're writing to a word count because you heard it has a preferred one, and answers: no, it doesn't. 2/ Out of date - The 15MB figure everyone quotes is Google's default for its crawlers in general. Its docs now say Googlebot reads the first 2MB of a file when it crawls for Search, and ignores the rest. Keep your important content and links near the top of the HTML. 3/ Half right - Googlebot follows up to 10 redirect hops, not 5. Five is the figure for robots.txt . Either way, aim for one. - GA4 only keeps data past 14 months on GA4 360. And that setting only affects explorations and funnels, not your standard reports. 4/ The ones that hold up - robots.txt : 500 KiB, and Google ignores anything after it. - XML sitemaps: 50,000 URLs or 50MB uncompressed per file. - Disavow file: 100,000 lines or 2MB, and blank and comment lines count. - Core Web Vitals: LCP within 2.5 seconds, INP under 200ms, CLS under 0.1. - Search Console keeps 16 months of data and allows 1,000 properties per account. - Business Profile: 750 characters for the description, 30 seconds and 75MB for a video. A cheat sheet is only useful if the numbers on it are real, so please always make sure to check the source before you rewrite 200 title tags. Which of these have you been following?

But I don’t trust them blindly because the way you build effective and reliable AI is to force each system to EARN your trust. I once built a classifier to tell my two cats, Tesla and Huxley, apart. It labeled every photo perfectly. Then I noticed that every photo of Tesla had a radiator in the background. I hadn’t built a cat detector at all. I’d built a radiator detector. And even though Tesla’s obsession with a warm spot made my classifier weirdly accurate for that apartment, what happens when the cats move to another apartment (true story)? Answer: the performance plummets. Whose fault would that be? Mine (aka the HUMAN) for testing it in one world and using it in another. You trust plenty of things without knowing exactly how they work, like the pain meds you take for a headache, or a microwave to heat your leftovers. What matters is that you can check that it *does* work. AI deserves the same treatment: → If you didn’t test it, don’t trust it. → If you didn’t test it in your environment, don’t trust it in your environment. → If you didn’t test it with your users and your data, don’t trust it with them either. If you use a tool where it hasn’t been verified safe, any mess you make is your fault. AI is a tool like any other. The new SAS Data and AI Impact Report, a survey of 2,699 decision-makers across 28 countries, shows the companies getting this right are pulling ahead. 65.9% of trustworthy AI leaders run automated AI validation, compared with 0.4% of laggards, and those leaders are 15x more likely to report strong ROI (62% vs. 4%). 0.6% of decision-makers say they never override AI. Even 0.6% is too high for my liking, since blind trust is a terrible thing. When someone asks you how often you engage your judgment, pretty please never say never. And what’s even better than overrides? An ounce of prevention. As the report puts it, “Catching problems before deployment is structurally cheaper than managing overrides.” Excellent advice! So what makes AI trustworthy? Everything you do precisely *because* you’re too smart to trust it blindly. Becoming a statistician taught me that trust issues can be a superpower; after all, if everything is probabilistic, then you stop hoping it works perfectly (hope is not a strategy!) and you start doing something far better: testing and planning. The SAS report backs this up. Leaders test their AI on the actual job they need it to do, with the kind of tests that would make a statistician proud. They build safety nets around it, so when (not if) the system does something probabilistic, the mistake can’t hurt them. And where outcomes really matter, they keep a responsible HUMAN close by, ready to apply good judgment. #sponsored Read the full report here: https://lnkd.in/giaGzcWA #SASVisionary Oh, and a repost makes my heart happy. ♻️

text: We've trained over a quarter *million* people (mostly at scale, in large enterprises). I'm telling you, "use cases" are a terrible way to teach AI. Why don't they work, and what actually does? First, how do we know use cases don't work? That's easy - we're almost 4 years into the AI revolution. People talk about use cases nonstop. It's how most organizations train their people. And yet. Most people are still only using AI a few times a week inside organizations. That's not "using AI." That's using a better version of a search engine, plus an "email writing machine." No organization ever transformed their work with a better search engine and writing emails faster. Second, use cases don't work because they don't change behavior. Here's a quick thought experiment: Imagine a parallel universe where electricity was never invented. People still living in caves, cooking over fires, making their own clothes. Now you introduce electricity. People say "How do you use it?" What do you say? Because the use cases for electricity are almost infinite. Everything around you was built with electricity, you use it a million times a day. Starting with use cases of a general purpose technology is an exercise in futility. Instead you have to start with what people do, and start changing their behavior so that they instinctively use electricity. Not just name things like "it can help manufacture couches at scale." Now, before I get into what DOES work, here's a caveat: If you are already good at AI, use cases are awesome. Share them around. If you are just starting and people share use cases, expect them to try those use cases and stop, rather than applying AI to everything they do, all day long. Again - we know this is true because we are four years into ChatGPT. So what works instead? What we do - and what has been tested in published studies by Microsoft - is show that the best way to train is to focus on behavior. I mean that literally. Focus on what is happening in the brain. What people are misunderstanding about AI. Why their brain continues to push them down the wrong path. We don't teach with use cases. Or prompting. Or features. We focus on two things: How to change behavior at scale, and then how to build those behaviors into processes so that individual processes are changed, permanently, one by one, to integrate AI. That's how you transform. That's how you reinvent. By systematically changing how people work, using actual processes they work on. If you're still sharing use cases and it hasn't worked, I'd humbly suggest exploring new ways of driving adoption. +++++++++ UPSKILL YOUR ORGANIZATION AI Mindset drives behavioral transformation at scale for some of the biggest companies in the world. text: Honestly, 12 months ago I thought “sovereignty” was a BS marketing message for founders to leverage to get funding. Now I think it is a strategic imperative and will breed some of the largest companies of our time. Mistral is the poster child of sovereignty. The last remaining hope for Europe when it comes to frontier model providers. I sat down with Mistral CEO, Arthur Mensch to debunk the hype from reality and ask the uncomfortable questions. My notes from the discussion below. 1. Why Energy Is Not the Ultimate Cost That Matters Energy makes up around 10% of the total cost of ownership of compute, so it is not where most optimization can happen. The cost of energy is not the one thing that matters in the economics of a project. 2. What Would Mistral Do Differently If They Were Totally Resource-Unconstrained? Mistral would build much more capacity, with capital as the main bottleneck. Customers are running out of compute, and once one use case scales they need thousands of GPUs rather than eight. Europe does not have enough compute, so Mistral is putting equity to work to build capacity ahead of demand. 3. How the Inference Market Behaves Very Much Like a Commodity Market On-demand inference behaves like a high-margin commodity market where pricing matters a lot and demand comes from non-committed customers. Mature customers need service level agreements, reserved physical capacity and guarantees on latency and generation speed. The more precisely they describe the shape of their demand, the better Mistral can price it. 4. Models Have Gotten So Strong They Are Being Treated as Defense Systems Models are now strong enough to carry out cyberattacks, and the US began banning them outside the country in May. China is also looking at restricting exports beyond a certain threshold. As with any dual-use technology, customers now want security of supply on both infrastructure and model IP. 5. Will We End Up With a Model Landscape That Has Just Two to Three Providers? If every company relies on two or three centralized AI providers, those providers gain enormous leverage. They will use the data their systems produce to build better systems and go after their customers' business, an end game Arthur sees as priced in today. 6. The Biggest Problem With AI Effectiveness Within Enterprise Today Is... Most enterprise problems are not well defined, and ambiguous objectives with humans in the loop cannot be solved through self-improving loops. They only get solved by deploying models that interact with people, which is why Mistral uses FDEs to define problems better. (links in comments)

text: When you download a pruned LLM, what computation has actually disappeared? Amazon's latest HOPE write-up explores deleting whole expert networks, while other forms of LLM pruning leave the original matrix shapes intact. Let's start with a trained weight matrix. We want to remove connections or components while limiting the change in the model's outputs. There are three common ways to organize that removal: - Zero selected weights wherever they occur. This is unstructured pruning. We can choose individual connections, but the matrix dimensions stay the same. A dense matrix multiplication still processes the zeros! Saving memory and work requires a compressed sparse layout and kernels that can use it. - Keep two values in each supported group of four. This is 2:4 semi-structured pruning. Store the retained values plus their positions, then use a compatible sparse matrix-multiplication kernel. The regular pattern helps hardware skip work, but restricts which connections survive. Half the weights does not guarantee twice the application speed. - Remove entire neurons, attention heads, layers, or experts. This is structured pruning. Deleting a hidden neuron also removes its incoming and outgoing weights, allowing connected matrices to shrink. Standard dense kernels can then run smaller matrices, but we sacrifice a whole component at once. Removing experts saves weight memory; if we keep selecting the same number per token, the active computation can remain similar. Matrix shapes, batch size, and the serving backend still determine the speedup. Fine-tuning or distillation can help the surviving weights recover lost quality, with extra training cost. HOPE's expert-pruning method: https://lnkd.in/gDEnN2wN

hook: Someone said earlier on Threads, "I think a competitive pay rate for writers is $1 per word." One of the biggest realiti
text: Someone said earlier on Threads, "I think a competitive pay rate for writers is $1 per word." One of the biggest realities folks don't understand is that all automation devalues the individual unit of work. This is not new or news - today's combines have fully automated the harvesting of a field from what used to take 2 weeks plus 2 months (for threshing and husking) for 30 workers harvesting 30 acres to having the whole thing done by one dude riding a GPS-powered John Deere X9 1100 combine clearing the entire field in an hour. The harvesting cost of a single ear of corn has dropped from about 3-4 cents per ear of corn done manually to 0.0005 cents per ear, a 99.98% decrease in cost. In writing terms, $1 per word or even $0.05 per word is vastly overpriced in today's market. On just the $20/month ChatGPT/Gemini/Claude entry level paid plans, you get about 80 million tokens, which works out to about 60 million words, give or take. Assume half get eaten by reasoning models, etc. and the cost of a word made by AI is 67 millionths of a cent. This is why I urged people as far back as September 2023 that charging by unit of work - by word, by hour, etc. - in the age of AI is the worst possible idea. "But human writing is so much better/higher quality/more artisanal!" you argue. Sure. I don't disagree with that on principle - I still hand-write my Almost Timely newsletter every Sunday. But put yourself in the CFO's seat. Let's say a human writer costs 5 cents a word. Let's say the machine is operated by someone competent and not a doofus typing "Yo Chat, write me some thought leadership" as their entire prompt. The difference between a human per word cost and a machine per word cost is that the human at 5 cents a word is 74,627 times more expensive. Is the human's writing 74,627 times better than the machine's? That's what the CFO is going to ask. What's your answer? Yes, you're not paying for a typist, which is what per-word pricing invites as a comparison. But even when you say, "Well, you're really paying for strategy and ideas and lived experience and a unique point of view that's only human", the CFO still wants to know if that's 74,627 times better than what you get out of the machine. The bottom line is that automation is SO much cheaper that if you want to get paid as a writer, you have to find a completely different way to price and explain your value. Per word pricing loses to the robots every time, and for good reason. The only way you justify human writing costs - and something the machine can't do - is to sell outcomes rather than process. What does your writing do that a machine can't, that a CFO will care about? #AI #GenerativeAI #GenAI #ChatGPT #ArtificialIntelligence #LargeLanguageModels #MachineLearning #IntelligenceRevolution

hook: You ask LLM a question. It pauses. Then the answer starts appearing, piece by piece. There’s a lot happening between tho
text: You ask LLM a question. It pauses. Then the answer starts appearing, piece by piece. There’s a lot happening between those three moments. Nine months ago, I shared a diagram explaining how LLMs generate text. It went viral. I’ve updated it with a practical example and a clearer explanation of what happens behind the screen. Let’s say you ask: “Find the top 3 customers by total spend.” Here’s how a text-generating LLM builds that answer. It breaks your request into small pieces. These pieces are called tokens. A token might be a word, part of a word, or punctuation. The model converts them into numbers it can process. It processes the context. Your request, instructions, and the information you provide help shape the answer. In this example, that includes the names of the columns in your orders table. This initial processing is called prefill. It accounts for part of the wait before the answer starts. It calculates what could come next. The model produces scores for possible next tokens. A selection rule chooses one. For our SQL example, the answer might begin with SELECT. That becomes part of the context for the next prediction. It repeats, reusing earlier work. The model processes the selected token and predicts another. A temporary store called the KV cache keeps intermediate information from earlier tokens, saving repeated computation. This repeating stage is called decoding. The pieces become visible text. As tokens are converted back into text, the application can display the growing answer. That’s the streaming effect you see. Understanding this process helps explain several everyday experiences: • Longer prompts can add work before the answer begins. • Longer answers require more generation steps. • Keeping more context can require more memory. • Fluent output can still contain mistakes. That last point matters. The model can generate a convincing SQL query. The query still needs to be checked against your data and tested. I’ve put the process, the generation loop, and the main performance checks into the handwritten diagram. Which part of how LLM works would you like explained next?

If ChatGPT leans more on its own index, being in that index matters more. Right now a small group of sites is getting most of the attention. So what can you actually do about it? Five things I’d be looking at: 1. Allow OAI-SearchBot. Check your robots.txt file and make sure you’re not blocking OpenAI’s search crawler. 2. Check your infrastructure. Make sure your CDN, firewall and bot protection aren’t preventing OpenAI from accessing your pages. 3. Improve discoverability. Have a clean XML sitemap, strong internal linking and technically accessible pages. 4. Publish original content. Proprietary research, unique data, expert opinions and first-hand experience are all worth prioritising over generic content. 5. Build authority elsewhere. Get your brand, expertise and research referenced by credible third-party websites and publications. There is no guaranteed way to get into ChatGPT’s index. But you can certainly make sure you’re not giving it reasons to overlook you.

text: I get paid to ask CEOs questions. One of my favorites is just 5 words long. It comes from Intel in 1985. The company’s memory chip business was losing to Japanese rivals. Memory chips were what Intel was built on, and nobody wanted to let go. Andy Grove turned to Intel’s CEO, Gordon Moore, and asked: “If we got kicked out and the board brought in a new CEO, what do you think he would do?” Moore answered right away: “He would get us out of memories.” So they did it themselves. Intel left memory chips and bet the company on microprocessors. I boil Grove’s question down to 5 words: “What would my replacement do?” A new leader walks in with no history and no attachment to the old plan. This question lets you look at your decision the way they would. A few more questions worth asking before your next hard decision: 1. What happens if we do nothing? ↳ Waiting is a decision too, and it has a cost. 2. What would change my mind? ↳ Decide up front which new facts would make you change course. 3. Can we undo this later? ↳ If yes, decide fast. If no, slow down and test it first. 4. Who owns it once it’s made? ↳ Without one clear owner, the same decision comes back next month. Moore knew the answer the moment he heard the question. He just needed someone he trusted to ask it. Better questions lead to better decisions. Which question would you add to the list? P.S. text: “We’re doing more marketing than ever. So why aren’t we growing?” When growth stalls, most teams go straight to their channels. They post more often, launch another campaign or try a new tool. But in my experience, the channel is rarely the problem. It usually sits a layer or two higher up. I think of marketing as four layers (save this for your next planning session): 1. Audience: who you’re actually for, and what makes them start looking. Not “B2B companies”, but the moment in their business that sends them searching, like a new hire, a tool that stopped working or a target they’re about to miss. 2. Positioning: why they should pick you over the alternatives. If a competitor could put your homepage headline on their own site, you haven’t found your difference yet. 3. Messaging: what you want them to remember. Ask a few customers to describe you to a friend. Their words are usually simpler and better than yours. 4. Channels: where you show up. Ask “How did you hear about us?” everywhere, and check whether AI answers mention you, because that’s where more buyers start now. If you’re not clear on who you’re for, your positioning gets vague. Vague positioning turns into messaging that could belong to anyone. At that point no channel can carry it, however much budget you put behind it. So before you add another channel, go back to the top of the pyramid. Get the first two layers right and I can assure you that every channel starts working harder. Which layer do you think most teams skip?

text: If I had a dollar for every hour I've thought about "use cases," I'd have at least $1000 😊 My cofounder and I have hammered this topic to death, particularly this question: "What is a use case, and how is it the same/different from a JTBD?" Eventually we realized: they are two sides of the same coin. A job-to-be-done is something a customer is doing or one of their desired outcomes. These LOOSELY mirror the two schools of thought around JTBD, with the more activity-based JTBD being closer to what Tony Ulwick preaches, and the more outcome-based JTBD being closer to what Bob Moesta preaches. Either way, there are groups of people doing things (activity-based JTBDs) and groups of people who want things to be different (outcome-based JTBDs). Both of these groups could serve as great markets for our products. We can look at these JTBD and say, "that would be a great use case for my product!" Novo Nordisk looked at the large group of people saying, "I wish I could lose weight" (an outcome-based JTBD) and then say "Hey, that would be a great use case for our product Ozempic!" Dropbox looked at the large group of people saying, "I'm currently sharing files with thumb drives" and say "That would be a be a great use case for our file-sharing product Dropbox!" Maybe this is a bit trivial and pedantic... but THIS IS LinkedIn, so... 🤷🏻♂️

text: PwC is spending $100 million for all 85,000 of its US staff to get a certification in critical thinking. Here's why it's a total waste of money: Contrary to popular belief, the #1 factor in judgment and decision quality isn't experience, knowledge, or the number of advisors consulted. The #1 factor in decision quality is the nervous system state of the decision maker at the time they make the decision. The things that actually impair someone's judgment are all the automatic biases in their mind: "I'm not creative enough to do that" "Nobody cares what I have to say" "It's not safe to stand out" "If I say that, people might judge me" "I'm not experienced enough to be in this room" "It's smarter to ask someone else than trust my own judgement" "I can't disappoint people who are counting on me" "I need someone else to approve my decisions" "Making the wrong decision could get me fired" "I can't afford to make mistakes" "Other people out there know better than I do" -- These automatic mental biases are invisible. They don't feel like choices, they feel like facts about who they are and how the World works. When a decision-maker has some of these biases, it automatically drives their nervous system into a constant sympathetic-dominant state. Less cognitive resources are allocated to the pre-frontal cortex where higher-order reasoning and rational decision-making occur. The result is lower quality decision making regardless of how much knowledge, experience, analysis, or time the person has to make the decision. This can be measured physiologically in lower heart rate variability (HRV) and lower HRV is already demonstrated in research to be associated with lower-quality decision-making, less emotional regulation, and lower cognitive performance. -- Lots of people realize things are changing with AI. That things like human connection, judgment, creativity, and adaptability are now some of the most valuable professional human qualities. The problem is that almost nobody can tell you how to actually develop these skills. And companies, universities, and professional development programs continue to use old methods (learning) that are ineffective at developing these new skills. Trying to teach someone judgment and decision-making in a course or LMS is equivalent to having someone watch a video about pushups and expecting they're going to get in shape. The companies that realize this and get this right soonest will build massive compounding advantages in their workforce for decades.

hook: Everyone says "Work needs to be reinvented!" But they don't say HOW. You think your average employee wants to 'reinvent'
text: Everyone says "Work needs to be reinvented!" But they don't say HOW. You think your average employee wants to 'reinvent' their work? And you can't mandate 'reinvention.' So here's how we do it with companies: 1) Understand that you can't mandate AI. There's nothing to mandate - it's a new way of thinking and working. Giving people a tool doesn't mean they'll use it. You can only mandate things that replace an old way of doing things, or things that are binary. You can mandate people use a certain CRM, that they show up to work on time, that they meet sales targets. Which means that you have to get your people using AI, across the entire organization, by changing their behavior. Which is hard. But it's what we've been doing for years. 2) AI has to be an employee engagement strategy. We approach this as helping people live in this new world. Not to "speed up mundane tasks" but to discover the magic of AI and how it will help them think bigger, enjoy work more, do the impossible, and also become a better parent and spouse and cook and gardener. We train them to benefit their own careers first. That's how you get people using AI. (We do this for tens of thousands of employees at a time.) Which in turn sets them up to figure out how to reinvent their work with AI. 3) Reinvent process in partnership with the people doing the process. There are two things that we find drive actual process transformation. First, have your people own the change in their process. They know it better than anyone, they know the bottlenecks and opportunities and how they would do it differently. So let them help define it. That drives a sense of ownership and enthusiasm. Second, you must hold them accountable once they have reinvented that process (using AI). Because the 'hackathon high' wears off. People are excited in the moment, and then they slip back into old ways of working. Somebody has to do that. Which means... 4) Focus on leadership development for team leaders. This level of management is critical. They have to hold their people accountable for applying the new AI-driven process. It's boring. And it's a bit painful at first. And it pays off. Obviously there's more to it. But it sure isn't just rolling out tools and holding hackathons. +++++++++ UPSKILL YOUR ORGANIZATION AI Mindset drives behavioral transformation at scale for some of the biggest companies in the world. Microsoft independently validated our approach in their WorkLab research - 30 minutes of our training doubled the quality of people's work. DM me, or check out our website at ai-mindset[.]com

creator: Damien Benveniste
hook: A ticket router can score the teams you give it without generating a JSON answer token by token! Hugging Face now suppor
text: A ticket router can score the teams you give it without generating a JSON answer token by token! Hugging Face now supports decision models, adding another option for text classification alongside fixed classifiers, entailment models, and prompted LLMs. Let's say the message is “My parcel never arrived.” We want Billing, Delivery, or Technical support. - Train on examples of each department. A fixed-label classifier turns the message into a vector, then a learned classification head produces one score per department. Return the department with the highest score. This fits a stable taxonomy with labeled data. Adding a new department requires adapting the head. - Turn each department into a statement, such as “This request concerns delivery.” An entailment model scores how strongly the message supports each statement; we select the department whose statement scores highest. This is zero-shot classification through natural language inference: new labels can arrive at inference time. More candidates mean more pairs to evaluate, even when batched. - Put the message, instructions, and departments in a prompt. A generative LLM predicts successive tokens until it has written the answer. It can also write a reason or a reply, but those tokens require decoding. A supported constrained-output schema can restrict the answer to an allowed department while retaining that generation process. - Supply the message, question, and described options to a decision model. It scores the options, normalizes those scores into probabilities, and returns the top option plus the distribution. Direct scoring removes response-token generation; ordinary code can serialize the results as JSON. Runtime labels already existed in zero-shot classifiers. The shared decision interface also supports ratings and yes/no probabilities. Its implementations vary, so the interface alone establishes no speed or accuracy advantage. Hugging Face's explanation: https://lnkd.in/gEyJPh6C

text: “My order says delivered. There’s nothing at my door.” That one message is a useful way to understand the AI agent stack. Imagine an online store has an AI support agent. Here’s how the pieces in this diagram could help it handle that message. 𝗥𝗔𝗚 It needs the store’s missing package policy. Retrieving the relevant information is RAG. 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗲𝘅𝘁 Your message, order number and the information available in this conversation form its context. 𝗠𝗲𝗺𝗼𝗿𝘆 If you contacted support yesterday, saved details from that conversation can be brought back through memory. 𝗧𝗼𝗼𝗹𝘀 + 𝗠𝗖𝗣 To check the delivery status or open a support case, it needs tools. MCP is one standard way to connect the AI to those external systems. 𝗔𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁 The agent can choose a permitted action, use a tool and inspect the result. 𝗔𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗰 𝗔𝗜 Suppose the tracking says “delivered,” but the delivery photo shows a different front door. The system needs to reconsider its next step. That ability to choose actions and adjust based on results is part of what we mean by agentic AI. 𝗦𝗸𝗶𝗹𝗹 A skill can provide the instructions and resources for investigating a missing delivery. 𝗛𝗼𝗼𝗸 A hook can run a configured check at a specific point, such as checking required details before a tool creates a support case. 𝗦𝘂𝗯𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀 + 𝗢𝗿𝗰𝗵𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 For a complicated case, subagents could take on focused tasks. Orchestration coordinates the steps, results and handoffs. 𝗘𝘃𝗮𝗹𝘀 Evals test whether the system actually performs the job correctly. Did it use the right policy? Did the tool call succeed? Did it make a promise it wasn’t allowed to make? These terms become easier to follow when you connect each one to a job. They also aren’t twelve mandatory steps. A simple tracking lookup may need only a small part of this setup. For the customer, the result should be clear: what happened, what action was taken, and what happens next. The agent noticed the wrong front door and changed its plan. Is that enough to call a system agentic, or should the label require more?

text: AI labs are bulk-buying second-hand books, training models on the contents, then destroying them. Booksellers fear rare and out-of-print titles are being pulped in the process. The practice traces back to a June 2025 court ruling. Judge William Alsup found Anthropic's approach of buying physical books, cutting off the bindings, scanning the pages and training on the text was “fair use”. The $1.5 billion settlement only covered the pirated digital copies. Buying and scanning print was declared perfectly legal. That ruling handed AI labs a legal roadmap for a supply chain: buy physical books in bulk, scan them, train on the contents. ISBNdb, a database company that once helped libraries and bookshops move inventory, advertised bulk sourcing of 1,000 to one million books per order "tailored to your LLM training needs". Its pitch promised buyer anonymity because, in its own words, "the optics problem is real" and "'AI company destroys two million books' is not a headline that generates sympathy". One second-hand seller went from shifting 20 books a week to hundreds, with orders unified only by the fact that every title has an ISBN. Rare booksellers in the Netherlands, Germany and Spain report the same pattern of random titles, bulk volumes, and buyers with no interest in resale value. Nine days after the report, ISBNdb deleted the pages and denied the service ever launched. There’s an important detail worth understanding: why pre-2022 print commands a premium. It is the only text structurally guaranteed to be free of AI-generated writing, which has already seeped into the open web and newer publishing. That makes the clean pre-LLM corpus a finite asset, and the labs destroying it are also the ones actively bidding its value up. text: Planning your 2027 PR budget? Tier 1 press gets just 11% of AI citations. At Searchable , we analysed more than 117,000 AI answers across seven AI search tools, including ChatGPT, Gemini and Google AI Overviews, to see which third-party sites they pull from for the average consumer brand. Blogs and niche sites were the biggest single source at 20%, nearly twice as much as tier 1. Smaller press outweighed tier 1 too, with regional, trade and specialist titles making up 17%. The rest came from review platforms, ranking sites, social media, forums and reference sites like Wikipedia. For years the PR playbook has been fairly simple - land the big national and the rest follows. That worked because a tier 1 feature did two jobs at once. It got you found, and it made you look credible. I think AI search is pulling those two jobs apart. Getting found has moved. When someone asks ChatGPT for the best running shoes for flat feet, it doesn’t care whether a source is a national newspaper or a specialist running blog. It wants the page that answers that exact question, and that’s usually a review site, a niche blog or a forum thread. Looking credible hasn’t moved. Investors, board members and big retail partners still read tier 1, and that logo on your homepage still earns trust. The problem is that a lot of PR budget is still spent as if one placement does both. If I were planning PR for 2027, I’d split it to match. Keep a small tier 1 budget for credibility moments, like a raise or a big launch, and put the rest into the trade titles, blogs, comparison sites and review platforms your buyers actually read. The good news is that the coverage AI uses is also the coverage that’s easier to get. A trade title or a comparison list is a much smaller ask than a national feature. If you run PR, how much of your 2027 budget is going on tier 1?

text: Your AI coding agent can explain a function. Can it explain what depends on it? That's what I'd want to know before handing it a change request in an enterprise application. Imagine a simple request: "Add a 'Needs review' state to the invoice approval workflow." The implementation might look straightforward. Add the state, update the screen, adjust the logic. But I'd want the agent to investigate a few things first: • Which applications consume that approval status? • Does the ERP integration expect only "Approved" or "Rejected"? • Which roles can move an invoice out of review? • What happens to notifications, retries and existing invoices? A change can look correct inside one application while breaking an assumption somewhere else. And if the tests never covered that assumption, a green test run won't settle the question. Application context is what I look at when evaluating AI coding tools. I want the agent to inspect the relevant data model, existing logic and dependency relationships before proposing changes. I also want it to distinguish what it found from what it inferred. hook: Get skilled at slower AI. I'm prepping for a newsletter issue this weekend on the state of the AI industry. One of the b
text: Get skilled at slower AI. I'm prepping for a newsletter issue this weekend on the state of the AI industry. One of the big threads tying it all together though is that compute capacity remains highly constrained, and in the arms race to make better and better models, AI companies are hitting walls fairly quickly. Combine this with some deep financial instability, and you have a recipe for 2027 that looks a lot like AI with capacity constraints that flow to us, the users. You already see this to some degree - there's a fair amount of "shrinkflation" in our monthly subscriptions. Usage limits have typically been opaque - "you have 57% usage for the week" is meaningless if we don't know the underlying metric - and that allows AI companies to change what that percentage is arbitrarily. On top of that, savvy tech folks over on Reddit have spotted hooks in popular AI tools like Claude that allow the harness (app) to serve up experimental models or nerfed (dumber) models when capacity gets tight. This makes predicting AI performance fairly difficult - one day things seem fine, the next day Claude behaves like it got hit on the head with a mallet. There's an antidote to this, which is open weights AI, running AI models on your own infrastructure or through inference providers like DeepInfra . For those providers, there's also batch pricing available. If you've got a large job that doesn't need near-realtime results, you can submit it and the provider will take up to 24 hours to process it and hand you back the data. For open weights AI, models like Qwen 3.8 27B or similar are reliable, predictable workhorses that get the job done. They aren't as fast or as theoretically smart as their frontier brethren, but most tasks don't need state of the art intelligence, and if you invest the time in building/customizing great harnesses, a midrange local, open weights model is often just as smart as a frontier one when tuned to the task. Here's what this means: if you're good at planning and project management, working with slower but more reliable AI will serve you very well in the next year. If you think through and plan well, you can queue up jobs to be done by your open weights AI that may take hours, but left overnight can bake and be ready for the next day. Now granted, we're talking about BIG stuff here - entire presentations, codebases, books, etc. Open weights AI models are still just fine to use in real-time for small stuff like light research, editing, etc. But if you want to reap the benefits of open weights AI, get good at planning and scheduling, and you'll be able to delegate more and more to AI under your control. #AI #GenerativeAI #GenAI #ChatGPT #ArtificialIntelligence #LargeLanguageModels #MachineLearning #IntelligenceRevolution

hook: If you're testing Amazon's Mitra-v2 against XGBoost, the models use your labeled rows differently. Let's compare gradien
text: If you're testing Amazon's Mitra-v2 against XGBoost, the models use your labeled rows differently. Let's compare gradient-boosted trees with tabular foundation models from training to prediction! Imagine predicting delivery time from distance, parcel weight, and service type, using historical deliveries with known durations. One option starts with a base prediction, then grows trees that split rows using feature thresholds. Each leaf supplies a correction. Under squared-error loss, the next tree is fitted to the same features with the remaining prediction errors as its targets. This is gradient boosting. To score a new delivery, follow the saved trees and add their leaf contributions to the base. We don't reread the training rows. Another option feeds labeled deliveries AND the new delivery into a pretrained network. Attention combines information across features and examples; the output gives a prediction for the new row. This is in-context learning, and the network's weights stay fixed during the prediction! That ability comes from pretraining across prediction problems. Models such as Mitra and TabPFN practice on synthetic tables: hide some targets, predict them from the visible examples, and update weights from the errors. They learn a reusable prediction procedure before seeing our delivery data. Pure in-context prediction avoids task-specific weight updates, but the labeled context still costs inference memory and computation. Caching can reuse some context work across requests. The two modes can coexist: Amazon says Mitra-v2 fine-tunes on each new table by default, updating weights and averaging predictions from several copies. Its full workflow includes both task-specific training and in-context prediction. Mitra-v2's design and default workflow: https://lnkd.in/g2XapAut

text: Took a look through the new Reddit Reviews for headphones to see how this new feature turns posts and comments into pages (thanks to Elvis Masinde for finding it so quick and sharing it with the team). It appears Reddit only lists one when a brand or retailer catalog supplies it. - Mentions come from a wide range of subreddits: The Philips SHP9500 page pulls from 95 subreddits, including gaming and deal communities. hook: I'm reading Rand Fishkin 's latest research on internet traffic. Using Similarweb's clickstream data, here's what he fou
text: I'm reading Rand Fishkin 's latest research on internet traffic. Using Similarweb's clickstream data, here's what he found: Rand started with the initial suspicion that the biggest websites are capturing an increasingly disproportionate share of web traffic, leaving fewer visits for the rest of us. Finding #1: That largely didn't happen. Browser traffic across the biggest websites and smaller websites has remained relatively stable over the past 5 years. The top 100 sites gained only about 3 percentage points of traffic share. Finding #2: But traffic to the world's top million websites is shrinking. Similarweb's data shows that visits to the top million websites peaked at 2.24 trillion in Q1 2022 and fell to 1.97 trillion by Q3 2026. Finding #3: The number of people using the internet has increased substantially. Yet traffic to the world's top million websites has declined — a 29.2% decline in visits per internet user over 5 years. We don't know why that web traffic is shrinking. It might be that more and more people are accessing the internet through apps (not so much browsers). Maybe it's some kind of new post-pandemic behavior. Or something else. So now I'm wondering... If website visits per internet user are declining, does that mean marketers who rely mainly on traffic and conversions are increasingly underestimating their impact? I have a hunch that app usage plays a significant role here. Meltwater's Digital 2025 report found that social and entertainment apps accounted for nearly 68% of time spent on Android smartphones in 2024, while browsers and search engines accounted for just 5.8%. (Unfortunately, for their 2026 report, they don't dive into that specific category-level breakdown, so I can't compare them outright.) That doesn't prove a shift from browsers to apps over time. But it does make me wonder how much of our audiences' attention, discovery, and engagement is happening in places our website analytics can't see. If that's the case, then I think we've been trying to keep measuring our slices of the browser-based pie without acknowledging that pie is shrinking. Maybe there's a lot more, different pie we're not accounting for. Check out the research on the SparkToro blog, and then come back here to talk about pie: https://lnkd.in/geUY4RJi

text: Does blocking AI training bots affect your AI visibility? Yes! Jason Saltzman from AirOps was so kind to provide me data for ChatGPT. Turns out you get ~85% more citations when you DON'T block ChatGPT's training bot (broad average). Interestingly, sites using Cloudflare's default training blocker get more citations than sites that block training bots in their robots.txt . The reason? Publishers are more likely to block all training bots (or all AI bots period) and are overrepresented when it comes to citations. The death stroke: blocking ChatGPT's search bot (OAI-Searchbot). That's when you lose almost all your citations. What this means to me: there seem to be real benefits of letting AI training bots crawl your site when it comes to citations and AI Visibility broadly. But there is a real trade-off in giving all your data away. Being cited more is not per se better when it means you lose all the benefits of creating the content. We still need to measure against trade-offs, but at least we now have both sides of the coin. Next, we need to look into how this affects AI mentions as well.

hook: Your AI agent took 40 seconds to answer a simple question. Where did those seconds actually go? The final answer won't t
text: Your AI agent took 40 seconds to answer a simple question. Where did those seconds actually go? The final answer won't tell you. I shared the AI Factory Stack last month. This adds the next piece: the control room. 1. LLM = The Machine Generates text, writes code, reasons over whatever context it receives. What you feed it matters more than which model you pick. 2. RAG = Raw Material Room Finds relevant information and hands it to the model before it answers. 3. Vector DB = Storage Warehouse Stores embeddings, numerical representations of information, so related content can be found by similarity. 4. AI Agent = Floor Manager Chooses the next step, calls tools, works toward a goal. Look up an order, check a policy, draft a response. 5. MCP = Power Outlet Standard A common way for AI applications to reach external tools and data. The outlet doesn't grant permission on its own, the connection still needs the right access. 6. Guardrails = Safety System Checks inputs, outputs, and actions against rules and limits, such as requiring approval before a refund goes out. 7. Evals = Quality Check Tests whether the system completes the task correctly, safely, and usefully. Fluent isn't the same as correct. 8. Observability = The Control Room Shows you what happened while the system was running, across the whole factory floor. Three signals do most of the work here. Traces follow a request through model calls, retrieval, and tools. Metrics track patterns: latency, errors, token usage over time. Logs record the events that explain a specific failure. Say that 40 second request made six attempts to reach a service that was down. A faster model saves you a little time. Seeing six failed attempts tells you exactly where to look. Change the retry behavior. Rerun it. Check whether it actually got faster. You need to know what the factory produced, how it got there, and where it broke down. If a request takes twice as long tomorrow, could your team explain why?

hook: 6 delegation frameworks you need to know. Most CEOs get delegation wrong. I was one of them. These are the frameworks th
text: 6 delegation frameworks you need to know. Most CEOs get delegation wrong. I was one of them. These are the frameworks that finally got me out of the middle: 1. AED: Automate, Eliminate, Delegate Run every task through it, in that order. Automate what repeats. Cut what doesn't matter. Then hand off what's left. Delegate a task you should have cut, and you've just moved the waste to someone else. 2. The Hourly Rate Test Give yourself an hourly rate and check every task against it. Mine started at $5,000, and it's $20,000 now. Yours can start anywhere. Anything below the line goes to a system or a person. 3. Decision Rights Draw a clear line, like "under $1,000, you decide." A lot of the approvals on your plate don't need you. Once the line is written down, your team stops waiting on you. 4. Problems Come With Solutions Every problem that reaches me comes with: • What happened • The options • Their recommendation • What's best for the company long term Your team gets better at deciding. You get fewer questions. And a lot of the time, they realize they already knew the answer. 5. Answer Once, Document Forever If you explain something twice, record a 5-minute Loom. Then turn it into an SOP. Next time, your team checks the guide before they check with you. 6. One Owner Per Task If a task doesn't have an owner, don't expect it to get done. Shared ownership usually means nobody owns it. Put one name next to every task, even the small ones.
