text: Your likes are lying to you. After 1,700 posts, I know which two numbers decide your reach. And you probably never check them. They're private, nobody else can see them, and they sit one click deeper than your likes. For years likes were a fair way to judge a post, back when the feed ran on your network. That time is over, and still most creators refresh that little thumbs-up counter like it's a stock ticker. Guilty? Most of us are. What they believe: Likes + Comments = Reach Reality: it impacts around 15% of reach What the data shows: Saves + Sends = Reach it impacts almost 30% of reach I've posted 5 to 6 times a week since 2021 and researched nearly 10 million posts for the Algorithm Insights Report. My own stats and the research point the same way. Two quiet signals now do the heavy lifting: 1. The Save Someone found your post useful enough to come back to later. A bookmark is a vote of trust, and it happens more often than you'd think. The reach lift shows up on most accounts, not just the big ones. 2. The Send Someone pasted your post into a private chat with one specific person. Nobody forwards a post to their boss because it was "nice." And the algorithm pays even more for a send than for a save. How much more? That's on the carousel. Every creator is measured against their own posts, so the "easy for you with 275K followers" excuse won't work this time. So what do you do with it? Start counting what you've been ignoring. Your advanced statistics already show saves and sends, they're just one click deeper than your likes. Then make it easier for people to keep your work. The carousel has the two steps, and the second one feels almost too simple. One warning. Please don't end every post with "save this for later." That's the new "comment YES below," and people see right through it. Only useful posts earn saves. Likes tell you who was polite. Saves and sends tell you who you actually helped. Which of your posts got the most saves, and did that one surprise you? P.S. Which post types and formats get kept the most? text: Marketing does not have an evidence problem. We have an action problem. James Hurman recently shared a breakdown pulling together 12 core marketing effectiveness principles and the research behind them across markets, including B2B. It is worth reading with your coffee or tea today. When you look across the evidence, four fundamentals stand out: 1. Reach more buyers. Growth requires expanding your footprint across the category, not just trying to squeeze more revenue out of existing accounts. 2. Build mental availability. Most buyers are out of the market on any given day. Marketing ensures your brand comes to mind when that buying window finally opens. 3. Balance the engine. Brand building and sales activation reinforce each other. Emotion, memory, product proof, and reach all have distinct jobs to do. 4. Protect the compounding curve. Consistency and sustained investment produce commercial returns that quarterly dashboards easily miss. None of this is new science. So why do so many organizations still make decisions that run in the opposite direction? We reward immediate pipeline. We abandon creative platforms before memory structures even have time to form. We default to whatever is easiest to measure. The friction is rarely about the quality of the research. It is about how organizations make decisions. Incentives, career risk, internal politics, and the pressure to show fast numbers all dictate which evidence gets funded and which gets ignored. Which brings me to the question: What makes evidence compelling enough to shift human behavior inside a business? Because understanding the research and creating the organizational safety to act on it are two very different things. Have you seen solid evidence hit a wall inside your own organization? Credit to the brilliant James Hurman for bringing such thoughtful work together in one place.

text: Journaling is one of the greatest daily habits ever. But most don't know there are actually 2 ways to journal: • Short form • Long form For short form, I recommend a physical journal. Handwriting is labor-intensive and forces you to choose your words more carefully. Long form, just use Notion, an Apple Note, or a Google/Word Doc. Whatever you prefer. Typing is easier than handwriting, so you can cover more ground. With short form, only write down what is necessary: • Most top of mind • Anything *currently aggravating* • Questions that need answering • Etc. Do this enough, and your brain will automatically start writing what’s highest priority. This is the biggest benefit of journaling. But with long form, it’s sort of the opposite. Your goal is to write down anything and everything. Get it ALL out: • What’s new in your life • What big decisions have you made • What’s getting in your way • What relationships are most dominant right now & why • Etc. The idea with long form is to capture as many data points as possible. That way, at the end of the year, when you re-read everything you’ve written, you can spot Macro Trends in your life. • How many times did you set the same goal? • Which relationships gave/took most? • Etc The purpose of journaling is to vocalize what’s happening in your life. Just say it. Don’t edit it. Don’t think about it. Just say what’s happening & how you feel about it. Because HOW you speak about your life usually says everything you need to know. If you really want to know how your subconscious feels about something, say what’s happening in your life unfiltered in your journal. Then look at how you said it. If you subscribe to this entire POV on journaling, then your goal should be 10-30 min per day. 10 is the minimum. 30 is the goal. 60 minutes is what you get when you are clearly processing through something and need to talk things out with yourself. Those days happen. If you don’t have 30+ min to journal one day, then at least get down 5-10 min of quick thoughts. Again, it’ll seem insignificant in the moment, but at the end of the year you’ll notice what came out on those days. These are important data points. text: Why you never get what you want... You don’t ask. You don’t make it a win-win. You don’t know when to walk away. Here's how to avoid these negotiation mistakes (& get the deal you deserve): If you want to fail in negotiating and alway overpay... don’t read this. Buyers with experience only negotiate on three variables that determine the value of a business. Most sellers don't even understand these concepts, which gives you a massive advantage if you can educate them on how deals really work: EBITDA/SDE Contrary to popular belief, this isn't about the number on their P&L, it's about the cash flow you’ll actually get when you take over. For example: If a seller says "we made $500k last year" but half of that came from a one-time contract that won't renew, that’s a BAD deal. It’d be like buying a house and paying for the furniture they're taking with them. Most buyers get destroyed here because they don't adjust for: - Salary to replace owner - Revenue concentration risks - One-time events that won't repeat - Expenses that will increase under new ownership Think of this as a direct reflection of risk. Everything that increases risk lowers the multiple, and everything that decreases risk raises it. That’s why some businesses trade at 15x while others struggle to get 2x. Lower multiples come from: - Revenue trending downward - Business depends entirely on the seller - Messy financials - High employee turnover These are red flags screaming "this could fall apart tomorrow." Conversely, higher multiples come from the opposite: - Documented systems and processes - Diversified revenue streams - Strong management team - Clean books - Consistent YOY growth You can’t negotiate the multiple arbitrarily, but you CAN influence it by identifying and addressing the risks contractually rather than just pushing for a lower price. You're buying the future but paying for the past, and the multiple reflects how confident you are in that future. Terms Price is WHAT you pay, terms are HOW you pay. You can give a seller their price IF you get your terms. Or you can give them their terms if you get your price. But you CAN’T give them both. Terms are how you hedge against every risk you identified in the deal. For example: If there’s key employee risk → Add retention bonuses to the deal Seller wants higher valuation? → Use seller financing Documentation not in place? → Long transition and training period The idea is to use the contract to protect against your biggest fears, because at the end of the day, negotiation isn’t about winning. text: Stop saying AI doesn’t show judgment. Of course it shows judgment. And actually, you already trust some of its judgment. When you ask it to find you an apartment and it goes on Zillow and not thisapartmentsucks.com , that is judgment. When you ask it to make you a slideshow for a quick presentation to your boss on an extremely dense topic, it will only provide a few slides. That is judgment. When you’re replying to a question from a 7-year-old and their email is filled with emojis, and the AI writes like you but adds 1-2 emojis to better match the inbound email, that is judgment. Probabilistic models reasoning through infinite options toward a goal is “judgment”, though I’m not saying whether AI is literally judging - just that it is showing it. Researchers can weigh in on that nuance. Your personal judgment might be BETTER or WIDER, particularly if it’s in a field you are deeply familiar with, but let’s not pretend we don’t already partially rely on AI’s displayed judgment to get work done.

hook: When another team's agent becomes part of your application, MCP and A2A give you different ways to talk to it. Copilot S
text: When another team's agent becomes part of your application, MCP and A2A give you different ways to talk to it. Copilot Studio's new preview channels expose the same agent through either, so let's look at what actually crosses the boundary! Imagine a support assistant investigating an invoice. - Call the specialist as a named operation. With Model Context Protocol (MCP), the client discovers tool names, descriptions, and input schemas, then sends a tool name plus arguments. An investigate_invoice tool could take an invoice ID and a question, run the investigation internally, and return findings as a tool result. Compatible hosts can use that same advertised interface. - Send a request to a remote specialist and exchange messages about the work. With Agent2Agent (A2A), an Agent Card advertises the specialist's skills and supported interactions. The caller can send "Investigate invoice 42" with supporting files. The remote agent chooses its internal steps. It can return a direct message or create a tracked task, ask which charge is disputed, and later return a report as an artifact: an output document or data object. Task IDs let the caller follow that work across exchanges. An MCP tool can therefore run an entire agent! With the optional Tasks extension, it can return a task ID for the client to poll until the result is ready, provided both sides support it. Duration alone doesn't distinguish the protocols. If your host already calls MCP tools, you can expose the specialist through that same interface. A2A is useful when the caller needs a shared model for agent conversations, task states, and artifacts, and can handle those follow-up exchanges. The specialist can still use MCP internally to fetch invoices. Copilot Studio channels (preview, early-release environments): https://lnkd.in/giDdCmfj

text: An agent can remember yesterday's conversation perfectly and still answer today's question wrong. A customer asks: "Has my order shipped?" At 9 a.m., it hasn't. At 2 p.m., the carrier picks it up. At 3 p.m., the customer asks again in almost the same words. If the agent pulls its 9 a.m. reply because the two questions look semantically similar, the customer hears that nothing has shipped, an hour after the carrier collected the package. 𝗧𝗵𝗿𝗲𝗲 𝗾𝘂𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 𝗜 𝗮𝘀𝗸 𝗮𝗯𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝗮𝗻𝘆 𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗱𝗲𝘀𝗶𝗴𝗻 • What should it remember? • What can it reuse? • What does it have to look up again? In the order example, the customer's communication preferences can live in memory. The approved procedure for checking an order can be reused. The shipment status needs a fresh lookup every time. 𝗛𝗼𝘄 𝗥𝗲𝗱𝗶𝘀 𝗜𝗿𝗶𝘀 𝘀𝗽𝗹𝗶𝘁𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝘂𝗽 Agent Playbooks keep approved answers apart from reusable procedures. An FAQ provides a maintained answer. A skill provides instructions for completing a task. Context Gateway gives the agent an MCP entry point to connected tools and Redis data. Agent Memory handles session and longer term context, with configurable retention. For the order question, I would reuse the tracking procedure and pull the current status through a connected tool. Your application still has to enforce access and decide how fresh a result needs to be. Connecting a source won't make yesterday's result current. With this split, the model stops rebuilding the same procedure on every turn, and the facts that change still get checked. 𝗛𝗼𝘄 𝗜 𝘄𝗼𝘂𝗹𝗱 𝗲𝘃𝗮𝗹𝘂𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝗶𝘁 I would score three things separately: • Did the agent choose the right procedure? • Did it use current data it was authorized to see? • Did it retain only the context it should? An agent can pass one of these and fail the other two, so I would not roll them into one accuracy score. The Redis Iris technical documentation covers Agent Playbooks, Agent Memory, Intent Router, and Context Gateway. For the order example, start with how Agent Playbooks separate approved answers from reusable procedures: https://brij.media/nov Where would you draw the line between context an agent should remember and data it should always fetch fresh? Okay. 3 practical things to know about Businesses for ChatGPT, their new offering that is confusingly named with some of their plans because no one in Silicon Valley can name a product worth a damn. First, read the Terms of Service. You are forfeiting your right to sue OpenAI if their agents and platform screw you over. Second, you need to provide and validate your business via DNS records. Get IT to help you, and while you're at it, if you're not using a CDN, you should be. Then you need to identify with a person's biometric data that's authorized to administer the profile. Have your government documents handy and accept that they'll probably be leaked/hacked, so choose the lowest risk government document that their service will accept. Data security isn't one of their strong points. ChatGPT relays its data primarily on your domain name, so if your business is unlucky enough to have lots of domain names, pick the one that's most important. You may want to set up additional accounts for other domain names later on - you CAN have one person administer multiple accounts. Third, when it comes to setting up your business agent, it's basically a chatbot inside ChatGPT that relies HEAVILY on your current website for its data. You can and should modify it to make sure it's aligned. I recommend strongly taking your existing Google Search Console data and tuning your agent based on the things you're already found for that are relevant, plus things like your ideal customer profiles and current service offerings. When I ran the agent builder setup for Trust Insights, its first rendition was (as expected) bland AI slop that didn't really focus on who our customers are and what they need. After just a few adjustments with our internal data using Codex, I got to a place where I'm confident the agent will respond more intelligently and precisely. AS for the measurement you get... it's lackluster at best and there's no export. I built an Agent Skill for ChatGPT/Claude/etc to do the extraction (with help from Chrome) and make an analysis that's useful, here: https://lnkd.in/dH9d7v89 But these are the bare basics you need to know about the new Business for ChatGPT portal for now. #AI #GenerativeAI #GenAI #ChatGPT #ArtificialIntelligence #LargeLanguageModels #MachineLearning #IntelligenceRevolution

hook: You revoked a user's access. Can their AI agent still query the data? I'd want to verify that before trusting an agent w
text: You revoked a user's access. Can their AI agent still query the data? I'd want to verify that before trusting an agent with production data. I'd look at whose identity the agent uses, where permissions are enforced, and whether another connection can bypass them. If the agent runs under its own service identity, check that identity's permissions as well. Revoking the operator's access doesn't tell you what the agent can still reach on its own. Retool's Governing the Agentic Workplace report found that 20% of organizations had an unsanctioned tool connected to production data this year, and 13% saw an agent take an unintended action in a production system. Give each agent its own identity, and make the authorization decision in one place: access rules defined on the resource and checked before any query runs. A new agent should go through that same check. Retool's Data Access Enforcement applies table, column and row policies to a supported PostgreSQL resource and checks each query before it executes. Enforcement has to be enabled, and connections from outside Retool still need their own controls. Permissions also won't validate business logic. An agent allowed to update a record can still propose a bad update, so the team that owns the workflow has to define what a valid change looks like. As more teams build agents, I'd check whether one permission change applies to all of them, and whether the audit log shows who owns and changed each policy. Read the report: https://brij.media/re When you revoke access, where would you look to verify that the agent can no longer reach the data? Sponsored by Retool .

text: Become the easiest founder to work with. (It's how you protect your team long term) At Bitmaker, I was the decision layer for everything. Every question and every approval waited on me, and I was working 15-hour days trying to keep up. My team was talented. I was the bottleneck. Here's what being easy to work with looks like now: 1. Be Clear About What You Want Vague asks create rework, and rework quietly eats your team's week. Every request I send now has the outcome I'm after and the deadline. If my team has to guess what I meant, I made their job harder. 2. Answer at Predictable Times My mornings from 6am to 10am go to deep work, so my team knows I check messages at 11am and 4pm. Nobody has to wonder when they'll hear back, and nobody has to chase me. They can plan their day around it, which is half of what being easy to work with means. 3. Hand Over Decision Rights Set a clear line, like "under $1,000, you decide," and then actually let them decide. Write the recurring decisions down with the reasoning behind them, so nobody has to guess what you'd do. Every call you keep for yourself is one your team has to wait on. 4. Give Every Meeting an Agenda If a meeting doesn't have a clear agenda and a desired outcome, it doesn't happen. hook: Okay, this Stanford study is sneakily one of the BEST of the year on AI adoption. Not just “be more human!” but actually
text: Okay, this Stanford study is sneakily one of the BEST of the year on AI adoption. Not just “be more human!” but actually how. Check out what they just did, it’s brilliant: Researchers with the Stanford Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence (HAI) followed two near-identical divisions at a law firm. Both got the same AI tool, and the only difference was how their manager introduced it. The researchers watched this play out at a law firm. Two near-identical divisions got the same AI tool, and the only difference was how their manager introduced it. The first manager told the paralegals the tool would help them draft faster. Now, think about it, that's what we say to our people all the time, right?? The result of that, though, was this: Those paralegals said they felt like “just another cog in the machine,” and they only used it on work they were already doing. Now, here's the other approach: The second manager asked which tasks bored them and what they had always wanted time for. Then the paralegals got time every week to experiment. That group used the tool 58% more and experimented with it 70% more. They started doing legal research, and they asked to sit in on strategy meetings. THE MUNDANE CEILING We see this all the time. We call it the Mundane Ceiling. When people think AI is there to speed up what they already do, that is all they ever use it for. Say it with me: And there is nothing less inspiring than “this will speed up your work.” AI is a life thing. It changes how you do everything. The people who use it well are the ones who keep asking what’s next, and that habit usually starts somewhere that has nothing to do with their job. YOU CAN’T FORCE IT The same researchers interviewed 184 employees at companies where AI use was required. Those employees said their work had lost meaning, and they were less motivated to learn new skills. That matches what we see. Hand someone a new AI process and tell them to follow it, and it just feels like more work. BUT. There's another way. HOW WE THINK ABOUT IT We treat AI adoption as a change in behavior. So when we work with organizations, EACH PERSON rebuilds their own workflows and processes. They know their work better than we do, and better than their leadership does. The message is: “This is what you’re trying to do, and we trust you to figure this out better than we ever could.” Autonomy plus a real challenge - that’s the gold. Managers still have to hold it to account, and they have to give people the time. The researchers say that without that follow-through, employees hear it all as “cheap talk.” They also found the firm was still judging paralegals on case volume, which punished the deeper work the second group had started doing. So trust people with the problem, give them room, and measure the new work. The only way to change how people work is to charge them with the charge.

hook: One unexpected infrastructure bill can cancel the next round of AI experiments on your roadmap. Cebr tried to measure ho
text: One unexpected infrastructure bill can cancel the next round of AI experiments on your roadmap. Cebr tried to measure how much these surprises cost. In "The Economic Cost of Unpredictable Technology Infrastructure," research commissioned by Wasabi Technologies, Cebr surveyed 690 senior business and IT decision makers across eight markets. It estimates $63.4 billion in annual infrastructure overspend tied to unexpected provider charges. AI and machine learning infrastructure accounts for $23.4 billion of that total. Of the organizations surveyed, 84% made at least one tradeoff over the past year because of cost. For architecture reviews, budget for the full experiment cycle. Take a new retrieval strategy. Evaluating it can mean reading the source documents again, rebuilding the index, running the evaluation set, keeping the results, then repeating all of it after a configuration change. Each step reads, writes or moves data, and each can carry a charge. Before approving the design, I'd want answers to four questions: 1. What does a complete experiment cost, including data preparation, storage, movement, inference and evaluation? 2. What happens to that cost when we rerun the experiment or expand the dataset? 3. Which charges can we forecast from workload volume, and which depend on pricing rules we haven't modeled? 4. What would it cost to move the data and workload to another provider? Storage is one part of the bill. Licensing, compute, integration and operations need their own cost models. For the storage piece, Wasabi offers storage without egress or API request fees under its usage policies. I'd still check the workload against those policies, minimum storage commitments and storage duration terms. Next to model quality, I'd track how many useful experiments the architecture supports within budget. When a surprise bill lands, those experiments are often the first thing cut. Should cost per experiment be part of the design review for AI systems, alongside accuracy and latency? Read the study: https://lnkd.in/dArF_SRm Sponsored by Wasabi Technologies.

hook: A bulk evaluation and a live agent can compete for the same LLM rate limits. MLflow's new quota-management guide explain
text: A bulk evaluation and a live agent can compete for the same LLM rate limits. MLflow's new quota-management guide explains why request rate, token rate, and concurrency need separate counters. - Count how often calls start. A request-rate limit, often expressed as requests per minute (RPM), counts each call once. A short question and a long document each use one request. Finishing a call does not return that allowance; time replenishes it. Bursts can hit a limit even when the minute's average looks fine. - Count how much text the calls process. A token-rate limit meters tokens over time, often as tokens per minute (TPM). In one minute, ten prompts of 100 counted input tokens consume 1,000 tokens; ten prompts of 10,000 consume 100,000. Same request count, very different demand! Providers can separate input and output limits, and differ in how they count cached tokens and estimate usage. - Count calls that are still running. A concurrency cap gives each active request a slot and frees it when the response completes. Long responses keep slots occupied longer. You can exhaust those slots while staying below both per-minute limits. These controls can apply together. A gateway can hold work in a queue until every applicable allowance has room, pacing starts while bounding active calls. That adds waiting time, but starting more workers cannot create upstream capacity. The gateway can reserve estimated token usage before dispatch, then adjust its counter using the provider's reported usage. Check the scope too: DeepSeek counts concurrency across an account, regardless of API key. Creating another key in that account does not create another pool. https://lnkd.in/eUbagZHa MLflow's quota-management guide: https://lnkd.in/eXsq_yhV

hook: I have one rule before I’m allowed to automate anything with AI. It's one of my most unpopular takes: I have to do it ma
text: I have one rule before I’m allowed to automate anything with AI. It's one of my most unpopular takes: I have to do it manually at least 3 times first. Every automation I’ve shared across socials has followed this rule. I ran my Friday “factory inspections” by hand for months before handing them to an agent. When you do a task yourself a few times, you learn what good looks like, which steps actually matter, and where things tend to go wrong. That’s also what lets you check an agent’s work later instead of blindly trusting it. It also fixes the most common mistake I see when people start building with AI: going into the tools looking for problems to solve. The people succeeding with AI do the opposite. They find the real problems in life and work first, do them manually 3 times, then (and only then) automate them. The time they free up surfaces the next problem. That loop is how real AI productivity happens. It’s never one tool automating everything at once. It’s an iterative process that stacks, and 6 months in, you’re a different operator. So before you build the agent, do the task yourself on Monday, again on Wednesday, and again on Friday. Then automate the version you actually understand.

hook: If a blockchain does not depend on a central computer, how does it work? Computers called nodes exchange data and follow
text: If a blockchain does not depend on a central computer, how does it work? Computers called nodes exchange data and follow common rules. For example: sending a payment on a blockchain. Instead of one central server updating the record, the transaction is passed between computers running blockchain software. Not every node has the same job. Some verify transactions and blocks against the network rules, while others use less data and request what they need from other nodes. But how does the network decide which new blocks become part of the shared record? Through a process called consensus. Different blockchains use different methods, and not every node participates directly in deciding which blocks are added. Now suppose one of those computers goes offline. The others can often continue communicating and checking information, provided enough nodes remain connected. A blockchain still needs computers to operate. The difference is that the work is distributed rather than depending on one central machine. That is the basic idea behind decentralization. #Blockchain #Decentralization

The bigger opportunity is making robot development more accessible, repeatable, and scalable. As physical AI advances, the ability to connect AI agents, simulation, and robotics could become an important competitive advantage. text: You chose a cheaper AI model. Good. But are you sure you saved money? Capgemini warns that errors and human review can change the final bill. Consider a marketing team preparing descriptions for a product catalog. One AI model costs less per request. Another costs more, but its drafts may need fewer revisions before publication. The team needs to compare what it spends for each approved description, including the work required to check the product information. The model with the higher price per request could turn out to be the less expensive choice. Capgemini calls this measure Cost Per Verified Outcome. It shifts the comparison from token consumption to the cost of a verified business result. text: I used to sleep 8 hours and still wake up tired. Then Dr. Christian Poensgen and I wrote Ultraproductive, and I learned there’s a name for it: junk sleep. Junk sleep looks fine on paper. You get your 8 hours in bed, but you miss the deep sleep your body and brain need to recover. So you wake up feeling drained. Junk sleep is like junk food. It fills you up without giving you what you need. 6 ways to spot it and fix it: 1. Judge sleep by how you feel ↳ How you feel in the morning is the better test ↳ Falling asleep fast doesn’t mean you slept well 2. Score your energy when you wake up ↳ 1 is completely drained, 10 is fully charged ↳ A 7 or lower means there’s room to improve 3. Get enough deep sleep and REM sleep ↳ Aim for about 90 minutes of each ↳ Deep sleep helps your body recover, and REM helps your emotions recover 4. Take a hot shower before bed ↳ Your core temperature has to drop 1 to 2 degrees for deep sleep ↳ The hot water makes your body cool down faster afterward 5. Keep your wake-up time after a bad night ↳ Sleeping in makes the next night harder ↳ A steady rhythm works better than trying to catch up 6. Aim for 5 to 6 good nights a week ↳ Seven out of seven isn’t realistic ↳ One rough night won’t undo a good week Aiming for 7 - 8 hours in bed is a good start. text: A lesson I wish I'd learned sooner in my early 20s: Make decisions from a place of abundance, not scarcity. Here's how to cultivate an abundance mindset: I feel least creative when I am "competing" with others and I do my worst work when I am trying to "beat" someone else. A mentor of mine once asked me: "Do you love to win? Or hate to lose?" How you answer this question reveals how you see the world. An abundance mindset is about running your own race. If you "love to win," that means others can too. But if you "hate to lose," that means life is a zero-sum game. There can only be 1 winner. This is a scarcity mindset. In a scarcity mindset, the world is fixed. There is a limited number of: • Opportunities • Relationships • Resources • Money • Etc. You "compete" over them. Your entire mindset is rooted in being "better" than the next person. But in an abundance mindset, there is no "lack." • You can share friendships • You can invent more resources • You can generate more money together • You can create net-new opportunities Your "competition" becomes your collaborators. Life is not a 1-player game. Some rewards require multiple players. So, here's how to cultivate an abundance mindset: • When you are jealous, consider what you can learn • When you compare, consider how you can collaborate • When you want to fight, consider how you can be friends • When you are let down or betrayed, consider the lesson you can share with others • When you are succeeding, consider how you can throw down a rope to the next person Those who measure their success in impact and how many people they've helped achieve their own personal transformation, tend to live life through an abundance mindset. They love they won—but they love that others won even more. This is one of many lessons I learned while building my audience of 352,000 readers on all platforms. text: For years I mistook being busy for being successful. Ten alerts before I'd had coffee. Fires until midnight. I was excellent at the work. The work was endless. I was running my company. I wasn't designing my life. That's the whole difference between an operator and an architect. Operators run the company. Architects design a life the company quietly supports, instead of one it slowly drains. The shift isn't about working less. It's about working one layer up. Here's the psychology of an architect vs an operator, and how to make the shift: 1. Design The Life First Operators run their company. Architects design their life and let the company support it. Most founders build a business and squeeze their life into whatever's left. Architects flip it. They decide what their days should feel like first, then build a company that protects that. 2. Build Leverage, Not Effort Operators wake up to ten alerts and put out fires until midnight. They're excellent at the work. But the work never ends. Architects design the system so the fires don't start. Effort gets spent once. Leverage keeps paying you back. 3. Stack Assets That Compound Leverage compounds when you build the right assets: • clear quarterly targets • a simple business scorecard • an email list you actually own • content that works long after you publish it • a personal brand that opens doors while you sleep Each one keeps working without you touching it. That's the point. 4. Work One Layer Up The shift isn't about doing less. It's about designing on the layer above. Operators ask, how do I get through today? Architects ask, how do I build a system so today runs itself? Same hours. Higher altitude. 5. Kill Problems Permanently Stop solving today's problem. Start designing the conditions that stop it from happening twice. Operators fix the same issue over and over and call it work. Architects fix it once, at the root, so it never comes back. 6. If it falls apart the moment you leave, it isn't a company yet. The real test of what you've built is what happens when you're not in the room. Until then, you don't own a company. He couldn't understand the English, but he remembers feeling the power in his voice and how everything else around him in that moment just faded into the background. “He wants you to know he means it,” Jasmin told me. He learnt English through Tupac, Eminem and 50 Cent. He described taking in so many words and ideas that he needed to start putting his own thoughts into words. That became writing lyrics, and eventually making his own music. But knowing lots of words doesn't explain why someone is so good at making things simple. I said that having the knowledge is one thing, but explaining it in a way so that another person understands it AND can actually do something with it takes a whole different skill. “You're describing what rap music does,” he said. He told me that writing rap lyrics meant taking an idea and finding a way to make someone else understand it. When he became a teacher, he was using that same skill. That’s one part of our conversation. We also talked about: • Why he walked away from his music career and removed his music videos from public view. • How he started earning from writing when he’d never even heard the word “copywriting”. • What he wanted to say when I asked him to finish a sentence beginning “Dear son”. The episode about his personal story is out now on RAW with UMA . Links to watch and listen in the first comment. And be sure to stay till the end. I had to make sure I didn’t burst out in tears!

text: Before I got married, I asked my parents what actually makes a marriage last. And the more pregnant I get, the more I realize just how critical the man you marry really is. My parents have been married 50+ years. Here's what they told me… 1. Make your own money. Marry someone funny. My dad always said this. Life is really hard. My parents still make each other laugh 50+ years later. Find someone who can make you smile even when life isn’t giving you much to smile about. 2. But is he kind? I’d tell my mom all the accolades of my potential gents. Successful, handsome, smart, ambitious. She would respond, “But is he kind to you?” Good reminder. 3. Find a man, not a boy. My dad can hunt, cook, fix anything, ride horses, motorcycles, redo an engine and play dang near any sport. He always told me to look for a man, not a boy. Men do manly things. 4. Protectors before providers. Success is great. Money is great. But when someone breaks into your house, does he stand in front of you or behind you? 5. Look at his circle. His friends are a reflection of him. Maybe that’s why my husband’s friends would be some of my first calls in a moment of crisis. 6. Porching it. My parents had this idea. Imagine the two of you decades from now, sitting on a porch. No phones. No entertainment but each other’s conversation. Are you happy? Because eventually that’s what marriage looks like. Better like the person sitting next to you. 7. You’re his first. He’s yours too. Above your parents, friends. Even your kids. Choose your husband first. My parents always made it clear that they were a team before anything else. Kids grow up. The marriage stays. 8. Watch the little things. Does he open doors? Shake hands with your parents? Look them in the eye? Pick you up on time? Keep his word? Small respects compound. How someone does the little things is often how they’ll do the big ones. 9. Be best friends. My parents are. They tell each other everything. They genuinely like spending time together. Somewhere along the way people started acting like your spouse shouldn’t be your best friend. Why the hell not? 10. Secrets are cancer. Don’t keep them. Little lies become big ones. And as my dad always says, “The truth is always easier to remember anyway.” 11. Respect him. My parents always believed men want respect more than women often realize. Don’t belittle him. Don’t nag him. Being strong yourself doesn’t mean you have to compete with your husband. And ultimately, do you. I don’t know if these rules are universal. I just know what I’ve seen. My mom and dad. Both sets of grandparents. My aunts and uncles. No divorces. Just decades of choosing each other, over and over again. I guess I didn’t realize growing up how rare that was. And now, as I’m about to become a mom myself, I realize something else. The person you marry isn’t just the person you build a life with. They’re the person you build your family with. And I can’t think of many decisions that matter more.

text: Even AI engineers get this wrong, but I still ask it in AI product management and strategist interviews. What are the two main types of multi-agent system architectures? The simple answer is fleets and swarms, or centralized and decentralized. Then comes the trick question. When do you use each one? The answer's depth gives away the depth of experience. Those who memorized discuss trade-offs for predictability, efficiency, and the single point of failure vs. emergent behaviors. Those who have built one or both explain that no one wants to use a swarm. The management overhead and verification effort are massive. You use them if you don’t have a good definition of how to solve a problem or generate an artifact. The swarm learns the definition while it does the work, so it can't be production or customer-facing. In reality, fleets also learn iteratively ‘better’ definitions while they work, but it's controlled and reliable enough for the real world. In every multi-agent system, learning must be a structured process, and agentic architecture must support it. The part that even AI engineers fumble is that every agent improves over time, and multi-agent system learning benefits from a scaling axis. Which one? AI product managers and strategists are a new type of builder. Businesses have other builders who deliver features and products. The new builder engineers competitive advantages (strategist), like scaling axes and their monetization mechanisms (PM), into the platform. Understanding the scaling axis enables both to build their parts.

text: The story of Fractile is wild! Walter Goodwin was doing a PhD in robotics at Oxford when he had a radical new idea for chip design. Walter’s idea was simple; what if you stacked the memory directly on top of the chip doing the maths? In 2022, he founded Fractile to turn this into reality. Just four years later, Thrive, Founders Fund and Lightspeed backed a $720 million round that valued the company at $7 billion. I sat down with Walter and have condensed my notes from the discussion below -- 1. Who Will the Winners and Losers in the Neo Cloud Space Be? One competent neo cloud is much like another, which makes cloud compute a commoditizing layer. What makes the space exciting today is that nobody yet knows which neo clouds are competent, leaving room for huge winners and possibly huge losers. 2. Why Every Model Provider Is Moving Into Building Their Own Chips Anyone serving frontier models is fighting to keep margins expanded and cannot afford to be squeezed by the very high margins of incumbent chip players. A first-party chip effort gives them a counterpoint to that pricing power. 3. Why We Should Not Be Worried About Capex Levels, and This Is Only Just the Beginning The build-out is entirely justified and a collapse is not coming. Unlike the fiber build-out of 2000 and 2001, the GPUs powered on in data centers are fully utilized, with no dark GPU fleets. Many orders of magnitude more inference-time thinking could go into the hardest problems if the compute existed. 4. What Single Company Would Walter Invest in More Than Any Other? Walter picks TSMC, which underpins the world's chip production and builds the majority of frontier chips. He calls it cheap at the price and would buy the stock every day of the week, citing an extraordinary business and team. 5. The Board Member Fractile Do Not Have but Most Want Walter names Demis Hassabis as the board member he would most like to add. He describes Demis as both an academic hero of his and a bit of a British hero. 6. Frontier Intelligence Is Not Yet Commoditizing Some tasks have reached intelligence saturation, where an open model is good enough, but the frontier still carries large margins and big deltas over everyone else. Even serving open models is not yet a race to the bottom. DeepSeek's own inference stack beat everyone else who had built a DeepSeek inference server on throughput and speed, earning it healthy margins. 7. Will Nvidia Be a $10 Trillion Business in Five Years? Walter says yes, and believes Nvidia trades at a lower forward multiple than Cisco did after the dot-com crash because the market priced in exuberance from the outset. With finite megawatts, data centers must replace their chips with better ones every few years, which creates a large opportunity for the market leader and for a new chip vendor serving the frontier.

text: Thinking Machines' new recipe for training the Inkling 2 Small LLM uses 4-bit forward matrix math alongside 8-bit backward matrix math in its expert layers. Mixed-precision training lets us accelerate expensive operations while keeping extra precision where learning needs it! Let's follow a common FP16 training step: - Compute predictions with lower-precision working weights and activations. Matrix multiplications can run faster on compatible hardware and move fewer bytes. Their products can accumulate in FP32, and sensitive operations such as the loss can also use FP32. - Multiply the loss by a scale S before backpropagation. This multiplies the gradients by S too, helping small FP16 gradients survive instead of rounding to zero. Divide the gradients by S before clipping or updating weights. If the gradients contain infinities or NaNs, a dynamic gradient scaler skips that update and reduces the scale. - Apply the update to an FP32 master copy of the weights, then cast fresh working weights for the next pass. A small update can disappear even when the gradient itself is representable! For example, 1 - 0.0001 rounds back to 1 in FP16. The working copy may initially still round to 1, but the FP32 master retains the change so successive updates can accumulate. BF16 changes the trade-off. It uses the same 16 bits as FP16, but assigns more to the exponent and fewer to the fraction. That gives it FP32's exponent range, with coarser spacing between nearby values. BF16 usually avoids loss scaling; keeping accurate weight updates still matters. At 8 or 4 bits, tensors or blocks also carry scale factors to bring values into the format's limited range. Those scales cannot recover detail already lost to rounding. Inkling 2 Small uses NVFP4 for its expert-layer forward passes, then rounds saved values up or down probabilistically when re-quantizing them for MXFP8 backward matrix multiplications. This helps limit systematic rounding bias. Inkling's numerical recipe: https://lnkd.in/gNAjywVZ

hook: You type one question. The model writes SQL back, one token at a time. I drew the whole path on a single page. The examp
text: You type one question. The model writes SQL back, one token at a time. I drew the whole path on a single page. The example request: “Find the top 3 customers by total spend” against an orders table. 𝟭. 𝗥𝗲𝗾𝘂𝗲𝘀𝘁 Your message and the schema get wrapped in a chat template. 𝟮. 𝗧𝗼𝗸𝗲𝗻𝘀 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗲𝗺𝗯𝗲𝗱𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴𝘀 The tokenizer turns text into token IDs. Those IDs depend on the tokenizer, so the same prompt costs a different number of tokens on different models. Each ID pulls one row from a vocab × d embedding table. 𝟯. 𝗧𝗿𝗮𝗻𝘀𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗺𝗲𝗿 𝗱𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗿 N layers of the same block. In a Llama style block that means RMSNorm, causal attention with RoPE applied to queries and keys, then RMSNorm again and a gated SwiGLU feed forward network. The causal mask is lower triangular, so every position only sees what came before it. Grouped query attention lets several query heads share key and value heads, which keeps the KV cache smaller. 𝟰. 𝗖𝗵𝗼𝗼𝘀𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗻𝗲𝘅𝘁 𝘁𝗼𝗸𝗲𝗻 The LM head produces logits over the vocabulary. Greedy takes the highest one. Sampling applies temperature, filters with top k and top p, then draws. 𝟱. 𝗦𝘁𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗺𝗲𝗱 𝗼𝘂𝘁𝗽𝘂𝘁 The selected token is detokenized, streamed to you, and fed back in. This repeats until EOS or the output limit. 𝗧𝘄𝗼 𝗽𝗵𝗮𝘀𝗲𝘀, 𝘁𝘄𝗼 𝗯𝗼𝘁𝘁𝗹𝗲𝗻𝗲𝗰𝗸𝘀 Prefill processes every prompt position in parallel and builds the KV cache. It is often compute bound and it sets your time to first token (TTFT). Decode produces one token per step, reusing and appending to the cache. It is often memory bandwidth bound and it sets your inter token latency (ITL). Speculative decoding is optional. A draft model proposes several tokens, the target model verifies them in one pass, accepts the matching prefix, and corrects at the first rejection. 𝗪𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝗶𝗻𝗳𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲 𝗳𝗲𝗲𝗹𝘀 𝘀𝗹𝗼𝘄 Long wait to start: check the queue and prefill. Slow token stream: check decode latency. High memory use: check context length, KV cache size, and concurrency. One last note from the bottom of the page: the generated SQL still needs validation and execution before anyone trusts the result. As agents chain dozens of model calls behind a single user request, which number do you think should define “fast”: time to first token, inter token latency, or total time to a finished task?

text: I used to think one big exit would finally make me happy. It nearly broke me instead, and here are 5 hard truths it taught me about chasing outcomes: 1. The Big Win Is Anticlimactic I sold my first company at 24. I'd dreamed about that moment for years, and I figured once it happened, I'd finally get to relax. I've had plenty of those moments since: • Closing the big deal • Raising millions • Making the dream hire • Hitting the goal I chased for years And every single time, I woke up the next morning with a new goal already waiting for me. The high lasts about a day, maybe a weekend if you're lucky. Then the treadmill starts right back up. 2. Outcome Thinking Breeds Anxiety In my early companies, I'd lie awake at night running the math. If I can't sell this thing for $50M, what am I even doing? Was all of this for nothing? That kind of thinking ties your whole sense of worth to a number you don't control. For me, it led straight to depression and anxiety, and in 2015, a panic attack that stopped me in my tracks. On paper, the business was working. Inside, I was a mess. That was my wake-up call. 3. Set Goals You Control These days I try to set goals that are fully in my hands. My YouTube goal is 100 videos I'm proud of. My newsletter goal was 100 issues I'm proud of. I can't control views or subscribers, so I don't build my goals around them. I can control whether I show up and make something I'd be proud to put my name on. And here's the funny part. The growth showed up anyway, probably faster than if I'd been staring at the dashboard every morning. 4. Fall in Love With the Craft Have you seen Jiro Dreams of Sushi? Jiro has been making sushi for decades, and he still shows up every day trying to make it a little better than yesterday. There's no finish line for him. The craft itself is the reward. That's the energy I want in my business. I want to fall in love with making the next video and the next newsletter, and let the outcomes be a side effect. 5. Fun Is a Performance Strategy This one took me the longest to believe. When I'm having fun, time flies, and when time flies, I'm doing my best work by a mile. One of my best-performing videos came from a day in the Dolomites. I was feeling inspired on a hike, set up a tripod and just riffed for 30 minutes. So if your work feels like a grind right now, pay attention to that. Find the version of it you'd actually enjoy, and the score tends to take care of itself. Chop wood, carry water, then do it again tomorrow. — Enjoy this? ♻️ Repost it to your network and follow Matt Gray for more. text: When I started networking, I failed miserably. Everything felt awkward and transactional. Until I changed one thing: The types of people I engaged with. text: I suspect Microsoft and the FAA learned the same hard lesson about agents this week. Both experienced prolonged outages due to network capacity issues. Microsoft ran an update that revealed an issue with a prior network update. The FAA was upgrading hardware, and network traffic overwhelmed the system. Both also made recent updates to how their AI runs. From experience, when you switch from centralized AI running at a hub to a hybrid centralized-decentralized model, network traffic increases significantly. Agents are chatty, and surges happen if hub-and-spoke agent communications aren't optimized. That can easily overwhelm load balancers that aren't reconfigured for the new traffic patterns. I don't know if that's what happened, but I have seen nearly identical failures in test environments. I would bet that it was a major contributing factor, even if it wasn't the only one. The surges are extremely difficult to track down and troubleshoot, which would explain why Microsoft's outage went on for as long as it did and why the FAA's explanation is so convoluted.

hook: Every RAG stack I audit has a vector database in it. Maybe a third of them need one. That's not a knock on RAG. It's an
text: Every RAG stack I audit has a vector database in it. Maybe a third of them need one. That's not a knock on RAG. It's an observation about how the conversation got shaped. Retrieval had an ecosystem behind it: vector databases, embedding providers, reranker models, chunking libraries, evaluation tooling. All of it fundable, all of it demoable, all of it conference friendly. Cache Augmented Generation had none of that, because there's nothing to sell. You load the knowledge into context, you cache it, you're done. So the default became "add a retrieval layer," and a lot of teams built one for a corpus that would have fit in the window with room to spare. 𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗖𝗔𝗚 𝗾𝘂𝗶𝗲𝘁𝗹𝘆 𝗲𝗹𝗶𝗺𝗶𝗻𝗮𝘁𝗲𝘀 No chunking strategy, which means no clause getting split across a boundary and half of it never surfacing. No embedding drift, which means no silent recall degradation six months after launch when nobody is watching retrieval metrics anymore. No top k tuning, no reranker to maintain, no retrieval latency in the critical path. The model sees the full document, in order, with structure intact. For a policy manual or a coding standard, that ordering carries meaning that chunking destroys. 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗮𝗰𝗰𝘂𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘆 𝗮𝗿𝗴𝘂𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗽𝗲𝗼𝗽𝗹𝗲 𝘀𝗸𝗶𝗽 RAG has a ceiling that generation quality can't lift: if retrieval misses the passage, the answer is wrong no matter how good the model is. Recall becomes your real accuracy number, and most teams measure it once during evaluation and never again. CAG has no retrieval step, so it has no retrieval miss. On a bounded corpus, that's not a minor convenience. That's a whole class of production failure that simply doesn't exist. 𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗶𝘁 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝘆𝗲𝗱 𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗿𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗱 Context windows were small when the RAG playbook got written. Retrieval wasn't a design choice back then, it was the only option, and the reasoning behind it hardened into architecture diagrams that outlived the constraint. Windows are an order of magnitude larger now and prompt caching made repeated context economically boring. The constraint moved. The default didn't. 𝗪𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝗜'𝗱 𝗮𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝘂𝘀𝗲 𝗶𝘁 Bounded corpus, slow moving content, high accuracy requirement. Benefits handbooks. Product documentation. Regulatory guidance. Internal engineering standards. Content that changes quarterly and where missing a clause is expensive. RAG still owns everything that's large, volatile, or per user. That doesn't change. The point is that the two should be a per source decision, and right now one side gets evaluated seriously and the other doesn't get evaluated at all. Has cheap prompt caching and a million token window changed your default architecture, or is retrieval still the right first move regardless of corpus size? Image Credit - @Rahul Agarwal

hook: Microduck's open training stack lets you train a walking controller in the MuJoCo physics simulator, then export it to t
text: Microduck's open training stack lets you train a walking controller in the MuJoCo physics simulator, then export it to the robot. Sim-to-real robot learning asks how to make that controller useful when real sensors, motors, and ground contact differ from their simulated versions. Let's say we want a small biped to follow a commanded walking speed. In simulation, a policy network reads joint positions, joint velocities, body orientation, and the command. Its outputs become target joint angles. Simulated motors act on those targets, the physics engine advances the robot, and new measurements become the next input. We reward tracking the commanded speed and penalize undesirable behavior such as falling or abrupt movements. Many simulated robots collect attempts in parallel. A reinforcement-learning algorithm uses their trajectories and rewards to update a shared policy toward higher rewards over time. Getting that policy onto hardware requires more than exporting its weights: - Measure how the real robot responds. System identification uses those measurements to estimate motor response, friction, or delay, improving the simulator. If a simulated motor has no delay or power limit, the controller can depend on responses a small servo under load cannot deliver. - Vary the conditions during training. Domain randomization samples plausible friction, motor strength, delays, or sensor noise. The policy gets practice across different versions of the robot and environment, reducing dependence on one exact simulated setup. Wider ranges can also make learning harder. - Preserve the interface at deployment. Use inputs the robot can measure or estimate. Joint order, units, normalization, action scaling, and control timing must match training. Randomizing friction cannot fix a left-knee command sent to the right knee! On hardware, the exported network repeatedly turns fresh sensor readings into motor targets, usually with fixed weights. Physical trials reveal which failures remain; those measurements can guide another round of calibration and training. Success in simulation alone cannot establish successful transfer. Microduck's training and deployment recipe: https://lnkd.in/gVgun_tG

creator: Brij Kishore Pandey
hook: Six processors come up in every AI infrastructure discussion, and each one is built around a different way of moving dat
text: Six processors come up in every AI infrastructure discussion, and each one is built around a different way of moving data. I drew out how each one works. 𝗖𝗣𝗨: 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗚𝗲𝗻𝗲𝗿𝗮𝗹𝗶𝘀𝘁 A few powerful cores handle varied, branch heavy tasks in sequence. It runs the OS, orchestration, data prep, and application logic. It slows down badly on large parallel matrix math. 𝗚𝗣𝗨: 𝗠𝗮𝘀𝘀𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝗣𝗮𝗿𝗮𝗹𝗹𝗲𝗹𝗶𝘀𝗺 Thousands of small cores apply one instruction across many data points at the same time, fed by high bandwidth memory. This is the default for training and high throughput inference. You pay for it in power draw and cost. 𝗧𝗣𝗨: 𝗦𝘆𝘀𝘁𝗼𝗹𝗶𝗰 𝗧𝗲𝗻𝘀𝗼𝗿 𝗘𝗻𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗲 Weights are preloaded and data pulses through a grid of multiply and accumulate cells. Pods link many chips over a fast interconnect. Strong for large tensor workloads at Google scale, and mostly available through Google Cloud. 𝗡𝗣𝗨: 𝗔𝗜 𝗶𝗻 𝗬𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗣𝗼𝗰𝗸𝗲𝘁 Low power inference on quantized INT8 and INT4 models, running on the phone or laptop itself. Face unlock, voice, and private AI features use it because the data stays on the device. It handles small models and is mostly limited to inference. 𝗟𝗣𝗨: 𝗟𝗼𝘄 𝗟𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗻𝗰𝘆 𝗟𝗟𝗠 𝗜𝗻𝗳𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲 Weights sit in SRAM on the chip, right next to compute, and a compiler schedules every step ahead of time. The timing is the same on every run, which is how Groq gets its token speeds. It is inference only, and big models have to span many chips. 𝗗𝗣𝗨: 𝗜𝗻𝗳𝗿𝗮𝘀𝘁𝗿𝘂𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲 𝗢𝗳𝗳𝗹𝗼𝗮𝗱 A SmartNIC that takes over firewalling, encryption, routing, and storage I/O so CPU and GPU cycles stay free for AI work. The model itself runs elsewhere. 𝗛𝗼𝘄 𝗜 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗸 𝗮𝗯𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝗰𝗵𝗼𝗼𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗴 Start with the workload and rank five things: latency, parallelism, power, cost, and scale. A real system usually runs several of these together. A CPU orchestrates, GPUs train and serve, DPUs keep the network out of the way, and an NPU takes whatever can run at the edge. In regulated industries, where the data is allowed to travel often settles the hardware choice before performance enters the conversation. Inference volume is growing faster than training. Five years from now, how much of that serving load do you think will still run on general purpose GPUs?

hook: Two qubits can share a quantum state even when they are far apart. Is that teleportation? No. Entanglement does not move
text: Two qubits can share a quantum state even when they are far apart. Is that teleportation? No. Entanglement does not move matter or send messages. When two qubits are entangled, their quantum state must be described jointly, even when they are physically separated. Measure them individually, and the results may appear random. Compare many measurements, however, and patterns emerge. What makes these correlations so unusual? With appropriate measurement settings, they can be stronger than anything we could explain by assuming the qubits carried prearranged answers from the beginning. But this does not mean one qubit is secretly sending information to the other. The measurement results still need to be compared through ordinary communication. Quantum teleportation is one application of entanglement. Combined with classical communication, it allows a quantum state to be transferred to another qubit without creating a copy of the original. No person disappears and reappears elsewhere. And no information travels faster than light. #QuantumComputing #QuantumPhysics

Everyone’s in a rush to automate things and do the thing as fast as possible with as little effort as you can today... But the way to do great marketing is to actually give a shit. Because of martech and AI and all this stuff, we’ve become so disassociated from the actual marketing that we stopped caring. Now let's talk about the empathy part. When was the last time you actually signed + went to a webinar, watched it, stayed the whole time, took notes, and told a friend about it? text: At 45, I'm more interested in creating free time than I am in making money. I spent 16 years working with people who had big salaries, big titles, expensive homes, and jammed-up calendars. Not surprisingly, many of them were completely miserable. They were stressed all the time, had expensive lives to pay for, and couldn't imagine slowing down. How could they? But over the years, I've also met incredible people running small businesses that most of the world has never heard of. They make awesome money, work very reasonable hours, and have plenty of free time for the things they enjoy the most. That showed me something pretty important: The decisions you make about how you run your business can have more impact on your happiness than how much money you earn. Every new employee you hire, client you accept, product you launch, or obligation you say "yes" to changes what your week looks like. And a lot of those decisions are really tough to undo. That's a huge part of why my wife and I have intentionally kept our business small. We don't want employees. I take very few meetings. I have a small handful of products. The result is plenty of time left over to enjoy life. I still love making money! And I still love doing great work. I just don't want to spend every minute doing it. There's nothing wrong with wanting to build a big business, hire a bunch of people, and make a fortune. If that's the life you want, get after it! But far too many people end up building businesses they don't like running, simply because they never stopped to consider what life should look like. If you're thinking about starting one, I'd encourage you to make those decisions early. I put together a free 30-page guide that covers how I turned the skills I'd developed during my career into a one-person business. text: SEO has seemingly "died" more times than I can count. Yet (baffingly), Google search has grown every single time. I’ve been hearing that since I was 21, building websites from my uni bedroom. Penguin was going to kill it in 2012. Then RankBrain in 2015. Then TikTok, then ChatGPT, then AI Overviews... I built and sold one of the UK’s top SEO agencies through most of those “deaths”. So forgive me if I don’t panic every time someone writes the obituary. See, the numbers tell a completely different story. → Google now handles over 5 trillion searches a year → AI Mode passed 1 billion monthly users in about 12 months → Sundar Pichai says people who use AI in Search end up searching more People have not stopped searching but they are getting their answers from different places. And this is the bit I’ve been harping on about for the better part of a year: AI search runs on SEO. AI Overviews and AI Mode are built on Google’s index. Most of the other models still read the pages Google ranks. I’d say around 80% of winning in AI search is SEO done properly. These are some of the things that carry across both: → If Google can’t crawl your page, its AI can’t quote it → The question-and-answer structure that won featured snippets is what AI lifts from now → The links and mentions Google trusts are the same ones AI leans on when it picks who to cite → Stale pages lose their rankings and their citations at the same time Yes, AEO adds a layer on top. Tracking prompts, showing up on Reddit, YouTube and review sites, earning press... But I see so many businesses jump straight to that layer with a site Google can barely crawl. It doesn't work like that - the foundations need to come first. So the next time someone tells you SEO is dead, have a look at this chart. It’s been “dead” for nearly 30 years, and it’s never been bigger !

hook: Are we building a future where humans become “passengers, pets and parasites”? Stripe’s Patrick Collison asked the quest
text: Are we building a future where humans become “passengers, pets and parasites”? Stripe’s Patrick Collison asked the question most of us ignore. Last week he shared his thoughts on AI in a long post on X. We can easily picture what could go wrong with AI, he wrote, but the good version is strangely blurry. Cured diseases and more stuff for everyone sound great, but he calls them “just ingredients”. What he wants is the recipe; how it all fits together. And he asks some rather thought-provoking questions which nobody has yet answered: → Work: Do people still work? If they do, why, and what do they add? → Scarcity: If they don’t, how do we share things out, and what is still scarce? → Control: How many AIs will there be for each human, and are humans still in charge? → Speed: Nobody in 1700 could picture 1900 either, but that change came slowly enough to fix mistakes along the way. This one may not. The phrase “passengers, pets and parasites” actually comes from the novelist Iain Banks. In his Culture novels, super-intelligent AIs called "Minds" run everything, and humans are free to do as they please. The Culture is sometimes held up as the "good" AI future, but perhaps this isn't the most desirable outcome after all. In 1968, the scientist John Calhoun built a “mouse utopia” with unlimited food and water, no predators and lots of room. The population climbed to 2,200, then the mice stopped mating, stopped caring for their young, and slowly died out. Calhoun saw it as a death of the spirit that came long before the death of the body. Now, sure, mice aren't people, and scientists still argue about the experiment. But it’s a useful warning that having every need met does not equal a good life. I think last week gave us a perfect example of ingredients without a recipe. Anthropic’s roadshow said cancer could be a relic of the past within a decade, which is a wonderful ingredient. But it said nothing about what a nurse, a lawyer or a product manager does on a Tuesday in 2035. My guess is that the answer has to be built from the bottom up, job by job, by people who actually do the work. My suggestion: write one paragraph describing a good day in your job ten years from now, with AI doing most of today’s tasks. If you can’t picture it, list everything you did last week and cross out what AI could already do. What ends up being left is the work to hone in on and prioritise getting better at. Bonus points if it’s stuff you actually enjoy. I wrote about this idea first in my newsletter: https://lnkd.in/gGqQM72g And follow me Alex Banks for daily AI highlights and insights.

text: This is the first fiction novel I've ever written. I always get asked how to write a story readers can't put down. Here's how: Use the ABDCE framework. It's in countless classics—from Romeo and Juliet to The Great Gatsby. Here's how it works (every writer should know this): Action: "It was a pleasure to burn." This is the first sentence of Fahrenheit 451 by Ray Bradbury. It immediately drops you into a moment of action. There is no buildup, no need to "set the scene." Boom. You're there. And you're hooked (whether you like it or not). Background: Only once you have the reader's undivided attention should you even consider giving them the background story. Remember: it's hard to care about characters or ideas before you see them in action. So start with a moment of surprise, then explain why it matters. Development: Now it's time to build the story back up. Where is this all going? Why does it matter? What happens if things don't go according to plan? What's at risk? The development portion of the story is the Action and the Background, compounded over time. Climax: There are 4 types of story climaxes: Oh no!, Haha, YES!, Sigh. Finally., Oops., and SURPRISE! The climax is the tipping point. The thing you knew might happen all along. Ending: When the climax does finally happen, now is the time to explain why it matters. What was it all for? In the end, who wins and who loses and what does everyone learn about themselves and each other? And it's your choice how much you want to explain vs leave open-ended. Now, you just need a vehicle to practice this framework. I recommend writing & publishing 1 Atomic Essay per day. Nothing will teach you more about storytelling than spending 30 minutes on a piece of content and getting immediate signal that it resonates with readers (the feedback loop is instant!). text: We made a mini-quiz on our homepage to help visitors self-diagnose if they need our services. These are the five most common positioning-related challenges: 1) People read your website, but they don't understand what you do This is by far the largest complaint we hear from venture-funded B2B software companies. This could be because you've over-indexed on outcomes (and de-emphasized the "what" and the "how"). It could also be because you are speaking to a wide variety of audiences at once who have different use cases for your product. Whatever the specific cause, the common thread is weak positioning. Getting positioning right makes it so your top-fit customers will immediately understand your value with no confusion. 2) People get what you do, but not why they should pick you over the competition This is a problem with differentiation. We see this most commonly in two scenarios: a) products existing in mature markets b) products existing where there is no market The first category is truly a positioning problem. There is nothing wrong with being in a competitive category... IF you can find a meaningful point of differentiation. However, if you're in the SECOND bucket, it is likely more of a product strategy problem. This is a much more likely scenario for earlier stage companies that haven't found product market fit yet. 3) You're going after multiple segments and don't know who to prioritize This is where the "choice" aspect of positioning comes into play. The act of positioning requires CHOOSING who you are for. My co-founder Rob Kaminski says the act of positioning IS pigeonholing... but in order to dominate a specific market. Companies that refuse to prioritize will always struggle to position themselves effectively. Their resulting message will always feel watered down, vague, and uncompelling. 4) Different stakeholders explain your product in different ways This speaks to the failure to position INTERNALLY. Positioning is not only important for external marketing. It's extremely powerful for keeping your teams all chugging in the same direction. If you haven't done the work to position yourself internally, your different teams will start pulling in opposing directions, which leads to huge inefficiencies. 5) You have multiple products and struggle to explain the suite in a simple way This usually follows a large funding round, where a founder's eyes become bigger than their stomach. Revenue potential surrounds them, and the urge to spend VC money on engineering becomes overwhelming. But if you aren't careful to think how you can position multiple products together, you can end up with a jumbled, Frankenstein of a product that is impossible to explain.

hook: So I've gotten a LOT of questions about getting rid of titles at beehiiv ... my answers: 1/ Why are you really doing thi
text: So I've gotten a LOT of questions about getting rid of titles at beehiiv ... my answers: 1/ Why are you really doing this? Two reasons: costs and opportunity. Re costs — our managers and leadership team probably spend more than 100 hours a year dealing with the operational overheard of leveling and titles. That's time we could spend much more productively on advancing the business. Re opportunity — work as we know it is rapidly changing. We have designers who are shipping code, engineers who are creating designs, and every one else taking on more tasks and responsibilities as roles are evolving with AI. Titles no longer reflect the fluid reality of how we do work at beehiiv. 2/ Who makes the decisions now? The same people who made them before. Titles were never a proxy for decision making before. 3/ Isn't "team lead" a title? Fair. Everyone, including the founders, is now described by job family + "Lead" if you manage people (e.g. Engineering, Lead). "Lead" just means you have direct reports. It's the same whether you lead two people or twenty. It describes what you do, not your rank. 4/ How will I know who does what? When was the last time you opened the org chart, studied everyone's titles, and then decided who to contact? Probably never. It's not like engineers are suddenly going to show up to work confused and start cold calling people. 5/ What do I put on my resume? Whatever (reasonable) title you'd like. You still own how you present yourself externally. Speaking as a hiring manager, the company on your resume opens doors, not the title. A Staff Engineer at a Fortune 500 and a Staff Engineer at a five-person startup have wildly different experience and scope. 6/ Does this kill career progression? We're not taking away anyone's ability to grow, advance, or be recognized. Your growth shows up when you lead larger projects, take on more responsibility and run external meetings... none of which shows up in a title anyway. 7/ Will this scale? We're a small, lean company and plan to stay that way. I have a lot of confidence in this new model and don't have any concerns about its ability to scale. 8/ Is the new system perfect? No. But I sure as hell don't think the old one was either. And when I'm stuck choosing between two imperfect systems, I'll choose the simpler one every time.

hook: Starting another vLLM replica means preparing an inference engine before it can serve a token. NVIDIA's new Snapshot com
text: Starting another vLLM replica means preparing an inference engine before it can serve a token. NVIDIA's new Snapshot component tackles LLM cold starts by restoring initialized CPU and GPU state, so let's compare what caches, snapshots, and warm replicas actually preserve! Imagine an endpoint that scales to zero overnight. Its first morning request may wait for image downloads, Python and CUDA initialization, weight loading, memory allocation, compilation, and CUDA graph capture. Those graphs record GPU operations for replay with fewer launch calls. We can preserve different parts of that preparation: - Save reusable files. Artifact caches keep model weights and compiled code available to later starts. Local weights avoid another download; matching compiled artifacts save compilation work. A model, configuration, or hardware change can invalidate the compiled cache. The new process still has to load weights into memory and complete runtime setup. - Save the initialized process. CPU/GPU snapshots capture memory after loading and warmup. A new replica restores those bytes and resumes past completed initialization. It still needs compatible hardware and software, storage reads, and transfers into GPU memory. This helps when restoring the state costs less than rebuilding it. - Keep initialized replicas running. A warm pool provides capacity already ready to serve. Requests that fit within that capacity avoid startup, but the reserved resources cost money while idle. A burst beyond the pool can still require new replicas. These approaches can coexist. A small warm pool can cover immediate demand while snapshots accelerate expansion. NVIDIA's reported restore times exclude infrastructure provisioning and container image loading, which can still delay the first request. NVIDIA's checkpoint/restore design: https://lnkd.in/gdem3F-K

text: One thing that has become apparent in recent days is that a lot of folks don't realize how much of our computer infrastructure is an improvised system prone to cascading failures. You didn't need offensive AI cyberattacks to have big outages like Microsoft/FAA. Of course, now we DO have to deal with offensive AI (but also defensive AIs and patching). But I have noticed a lot more anxious people as every outage of the last five days gets picked up by accounts on social media who did not pay attention to cybersecurity before, usually with the implication that "this is the big one," which, in turn, leads people on both social media and real life to panic and spread further rumors. To be clear, thanks to AI there really is a nightmare cyber environment right now, with new kinds of risks and dangers. But also people are paying a lot more attention to cyber incidents & making dramatic statements on social media about the kind of outages we see happen all the time because everything is improvised and messy. Things could still go very badly, and I would still expect to see some very dangerous and large incidents, but some of the worst near-term cases appear to have been somewhat mitigated. The Mythos security freakout from Anthropic, much derided at the time, got a lot of organizations patching early, as did the focus on first deploying cyber versions of models with limited access from the Labs. They seem to have been an effective step in reducing some of the downside cyber risk that would have otherwise happened from AI.
